I bought this to power two small (~3"x3") 12 volt heating pads to help keep me warm while working outside at night during a Colorado winter, and for that it performs admirably. While my use case is rather atypical, it should highlight just how flexible this rechargeable power supply is--anything that needs 12 volts and less than 3 amps is good to go.

The build quality is better than I was expecting, in all honesty, and for once I applaud the use of plastic over something like aluminum because the battery pack is already a bit on the heavy side and for something portable like this, every ounce counts.

I marked it down a star for a couple reasons:
1) The documentation that accompanied it was minimal and suffered from some translation issues (though I've come to expect that for products such as this). If not for reviews/questions here on Amazon, I wouldn't have known that the Red/Green LED indicator for charging is on the charger and not the battery pack. The battery pack LED is always Blue.
2) The Li Ion Charging/Protection Circuit is contained in the "wall wart" charger that comes with it. While I understand that this saves space in the battery pack itself (and I did just make the comment about every ounce counting), it also means that if I should lose the charger, I have to get another one to continue using the battery pack (the 18650 batteries used here are unprotected, I believe). For convenience, it would be nice to be able to plug the pack into any 12 volt power supply of sufficient amperage and have it charge without exploding.

These are truly minor gripes, though, and I am overall quite happy with this battery pack and its performance. I imagine I'll find another use for it when I no longer need it to provide life-saving warmth.

The built in camera and apps on the iPhone allow for so much more creative work than most of us lovers of photography ever dreamed possible - there is no reason not to enjoy that technology. Years ago I never would have dreamed of shooting photos with my phone rather than my DSLR but that is, in fact, often the case.

This has led me to testing, evaluating and reviewing many accessories that make creative shooting with the phone even more versatile than it is natively.

I’ve reviewed a few similar lens kits. This one comes with macro, wide angle and zoom lenses, a mini tripod for the zoom lens, the adapters needed to attach the lenses to the phone and a case for it all.

The wide angle and macro lenses are both decent quality - not professional quality but adequate for hobby enthusiasts. Of the three lenses the macro is the best. The wide angle causes photos focus to get soft towards the edges.

Unfortunately the zoom lens is sub par. While I can get it to work images are consistently below average. Zoom lenses work by utilizing a series of lenses that must be perfectly aligned to capture an accurate, crisp image. While I use excellent photography apps on my iPhone X and worked adjusting the zoom lens I never could get photos near as crisp as with other sets.

This is a mediocre set - I’ve reviewed much worse and a few better, although they were at higher price points. At this price point this is not a bad deal but I certainly wouldn’t rave about this set.

Thanks for reading my review. I enjoy writing them as I value reading other’s reviews when I’m making a buying decision. I regularly update my reviews to reflect any changes I may discover and to include helpful tips you may need if you purchase the product. I received these as a free review sample six months ago and use them mainly on my laptop. I have also tested them on Samsung Note 3 and 4 phones, Tab 10.1 and Tab Pro 12.2 tablets, and an iPad Air 2. It works flawlessly with all of them, although some of the features like forwarding and skipping songs using the multi-function button only work with Apple IOS devices.

The main reason why I rated them so highly is sound quality. These phones are balanced across the high, mid and low frequency bands, although there seems to be some emphasis on the mid range, with slight compression on the high end. They are perfect for critical listening and even transcribing if you are a musician. Given the slight bias, though, these are not ideal for listening to monitor or raw tracks. Of course they were not designed for those tasks.

Another set of features I like are the flat, tangle-free cable and the comfort of the in-ear pieces. This ships with silicone ear adapters, but the default ones work well for me. Still, if you have smaller or larger ear canals the chances of this fitting well is good.

Ear adapters provide decent noise isolation, but not totally (not necessarily a bad thing if you are using this for walking and need to be aware of your surroundings.)

Overall, these are well constructed and have excellent sound quality - at least on the devices on which I tested them. Just know that all of the features are not available on anything but Apple IOS devices.

Out of the box, you must charge it for at least 4 hours (the light will turn green on the back of the device when it is ready). Once it was charged I was able to pair it with my Google Nexus 7 with little difficulty.

The build quality is pretty good. It feels reasonably solid in hand, and the plastic shell is nicely made.

I found the manual to be easy to follow. You have to switch the button on the back to "on", then hold down the power button for 8 seconds to get it into "pairing" mode (not the usual 3 seconds to simply turn the device on). Then initiate pairing on your device (in this case, my Nexus 7) and it's ready to go.

Sound quality is good, and pressing the - and + buttons adjusts volume. The peak volume is impressive, which I like because my primary use for these speakers will be to hear over exercise machines. It also works well in the shower, and it's more than loud enough to hear over the shower spray.

The manual says the battery can provide about 25 hours of use when fully charged. I haven't timed it, but it does seem to last a good while. It lacks a battery gas gauge, so there's no way to determine how much battery life is left.

There is one issue I've been having with the speaker - stutters and skips. I determined streaming quality was not the issue and the speaker was correctly recognized by and paired with my tablet. I was able to fix it once by unpairing the speaker from my tablet, and then pairing it again. On another occasion I went into the Nexus 7 settings to disconnect and then reconnect the speaker (as opposed to fully unpairing/pairing it) to get the audio to play smoothly. It's a little annoying to have this extra step, which makes this a 4 star experience, but ultimately not a deal-breaker for me.

It's a capable speaker that provides the portability and audio volume I was looking for.

I have a growing interest in photography and I have been learning as I go. One of the things I have discovered is that a good camera bag – sufficiently large to hold the camera, lenses you need and any accessories – is absolutely essential. I have a messenger-style camera bag that works well enough but I have run out of room in it and it does not have the capacity to hold all of my extra lenses and filters. I looked to this camera bag as a solution. It definitely holds more than my old bag, it seems to be made well and there are some nice features to this bag.

This is a backpack style bag and it is about the same size as a small travel backpack, though it is an order of magnitude thicker. There are zippers and pockets everywhere. There's a lot of padding to protect the camera and multiple movable partitions.

The main compartment is large enough to hold a small laptop if all of the partitions are pulled out. There are three small partitions and two large ones and these can be arranged in any configuration to accommodate a wide array of accessories. As shipped, the partitions are arranged to allow for the camera lens and camera to sit through the middle of the pack which maximizes the padding and protection for the most valuable parts of your setup, and the smaller partitions are about right for 2-3 lens kits. I have a smaller camera – a Samsung NX300 with the 18-55mm lens – so I need less room for my camera and rearranged the configuration to permit room for several filter kits, a telephoto lens, a fisheye lens and a few smaller accessories, all in the main compartment. I have not yet purchased additional lenses but will rearrange when I do.

The main compartment also has a pocket that is suitable for either a thin book or a tablet. So, even with all of my other gear in the main compartment, I still have room for my tablet. I really can't ask for much more than that.

There is a smaller zippered compartment on the front that has room for even more accessories. In this I have loaded up a spare set of macro lenses that would not fit in the main compartment. Inside this compartment there is yet another pocket suitable for holding a tablet as well as a mesh pocket for loose items, my choice being a couple of pens. However, the most interesting item in there, attached by a tether, is a waterproof nylon cover for the whole bag. So, if you need to go out in the rain with this backpack, you can do so without fear of getting your equipment wet.

On the sides there are two small pockets, sufficient for holding a couple of small items like a filter or two or even a very small flashlight.

On the front there is one more zippered pocket that is well suited for thin items, like a map, magazine or papers.

The shoulder straps are adjustable and padded so getting the pack to fit just right is not an issue. However, there is a carrying handle loop on the top of this bag and I prefer carrying this bag using that instead (I have always preferred carrying backpacks this way).

This is a very nice camera bag. A lot of thought went into the design and it can hold a lot of equipment for its size. It has replaced my other camera bag outright.

I’ve wanted a physical keyboard to use with my phone for a long time. I often write when I’m stuck waiting in places, and even after years, I still don’t love touchscreen keyboards. I can actually slip this keyboard into my pocket or keep it in my car for days when I know I’m going to have a lot of extra time. The USB dongle stores inside the keyboard, which makes it almost impossible to lose it.

Connecting it is easy, just plug in the dongle. My phone only has a USB-C port, so I needed the extra step of an adapter. The touchpad section doesn’t work super well on a phone, but does work well on other devices. Out of curiosity, I tried the keyboard with my laptop (Mac Book Pro) and found the keyboard touchpad to work almost as well as the built-in trackpad.

I love GPS units. Ever since first using them when they first came out for the consumer market years ago (and were horribly expensive) I'd no sooner drive a car without a GPS than I would without a spare tire. For me, it's a must have.

Given this, plus my enjoyment of anything that has buttons, I've owned several, and have tried out several more. So far, the Moto is the hands-down winner.

GPS' have matured quite a bit over the past few years, so the days of having one manufacturer being worlds better than another is pretty much over. What I mean by that is that a GPS from any of the major manufacturers (TomTom, Garmin, Magellan, etc.) will do the basics of getting you from point A to point B just fine. It's the fine-tuning that has begun to matter.

This is where it gets difficult to provide a recommendation, since what's important to me may not be important to others. For example, I've always shunned units that didn't "ding" at an upcoming turn, or always display the next turn direction regardless of how far away that turn is. Others may find those features not all that important.

So, what makes the Moto best for me? Basically the form factor. I love, love, LOVE the extra wide screen! You can maintain a good map view but still have a portion of the screen dedicated to all sorts of useful info, such as the complete turn-by-turn list, an aerial view of your trip (both close distance as well as the entire journey), all sorts of stats such as arrival time, elapsed drive time, traffic notifications, upcoming POIs and so on. Absolutely wonderful. Plus it has the upcoming turn ding and the always-visible next turn direction.

The build quality is solid, routing is good, the PC interface (the Moto Toolbox) is far more stable than the TomTom Home software (at least for me - running it on Win 7 64 bit), and I love how they have integrated the POI database into the address database. For example, with other GPS if I wanted to go to the XYZ store and didn't know the street address, I'd have to open up the POI database, then select the store category, then find the store. With the Moto I just type in the name of the store using the same screen as I use to type in an address.

Also like that it has real buttons on each side rather than be forced to use the touchscreen. For me, that makes key features (such as muting it) a lot easier to use. The screen is very clear and easy to see even in bright sun. Excellent refresh rate. In fact, very speedy in every aspect, from searches to plots to route recalc's.

The Moto gives you a lot of value for the money. I must confess, however, that I didn't purchase it at Amazon, but rather at another online store when they had it on sale for under 2 bills. At that price, it's a fantastic value. But, even at the regular price of less than 3 bills, it's a solid value.

Can't comment on the services such as the Bing search or Google connectivity since I have never used them (those are some of the features I don't see much value in). But, the traffic info is solid, and just as good (if not better) than the XM traffic feed I have with my built-in GPS (in an Infiniti EX35).

Downsides are that it runs hot. You can toast a sandwich on it after just a short while in use in the car. Doesn't seem to cause a problem, but don't know if that's a long-term reliability issue. Moto is also relatively unproven in the GPS world. So far so good - they've provided software and map updates at no charge without any problem, and have responded promptly to an email for support info. Lastly, the quality of spoken directions is just OK. You can understand them, but it's not the best out there by any means.

For me, this provides the best mix of features I've seen so far. Granted, in a few months I'll be looking at the next newest and greatest one out there, but for now, I could not be happier with this.

This review is for the Uniden BCD436HP I see reviews here for other radios, so not to be confused.
I used Amazon Prime Now to get the radio to me, in less than 1 hour (about 45 minutes) the delivery person was knocking on my door with my new receiver, wow, I was highly impressed and I will always check to see if Prime Now is available for all my deliveries from now on.....
So, the radio....
This receiver has a 4 gig SD card preloaded with every known frequency with text for the entire US and Canada. They have software called Sentinel you install on your PC and this is your gateway to all updates and firmware and it can control your radios SD card any way you like. Sentinel has an extensive database of all frequencies and let me say this again, all frequencies have text description included which is the most highly advanced scanner database system I have ever seen and I have owned scanner receivers most of my adult life, (long time)..
This is a digital receiver using the latest technology available. It can monitor any analog or digital TX (with some exceptions, like encrypted signals) and gives you extensive control over what you're listening to. There are FCC laws regarding what is legal and not legal to monitor and Uniden has got us right up to the maximum legally allowed to be monitored by civilians. If you are law enforcement persons you will have much more powerful receivers available to you capable of Cell phone conversation monitoring etc., things no civilian should even be interested in.
There is another version of this Uniden radio, the BCD536 which is a tabletop version. If you have large powerful outdoor weatherproof antennas the BCD536 is a good option and it is completely transferable to vehicle dash mount and back from your work desk to your vehicle.
I like this handheld BCD436 best personally for my purposes.
This is basically a plug and play receiver. It comes with 3 2300 milliamp rechargeable batteries, load those, charge them or just leave radio plugged in, enter your zip and you're in. Well theoretically that's how it works, in the real world? No.
When you first receive the radio I would suggest positioning yourself in front of your PC. Have the paper manual, the radio, you and your PC right there in front of you. Get ready to read and learn your radios keyboard layout and what these great, well thought out keys can do for you. You will learn, trust me, you will quickly come to love this radio.
Some cons:
No wall charger adopter included. You can charge from your PC's USB ports but you will need a wall charger with USB port. Most of us have several of these around the house from old cell phones etc. They work fine.
This unit should come with a nice wall charger adopter. That's really the only con, not to bad really.
Antennas:
Your ability to scan and receive signals on any scanner is proportionate to your antennas. The more robust and correct (correct meaning size, materials used etc).. You will need some nice antennas for this nice radio to increase your scanning powers. Amazon has some nice antennas, scannermaster.com has some also. Your local radio shop retailer will have some also. The included rubber ducky antenna is garbage, toss it from across the room to your garbage can, see if you can make a rim shot. Like I said, I have been playing with scanners for many years so I have many antennas to pick from.
Verdict:
This is without a doubt, the most powerful handheld scanning receiver available from any manufacturer. It is the luxury sedan of the scanning receiver world. It is easy and robust. It is backed up by Uniden's Sentinel software which will future proof your radio for many years to come.
I give Uniden 5 stars for this winner.
I give Amazon 5 stars for Prime Now 1 hour shipping, also a winner.

Go to scannermaster.com and look for the Austin Condor All-Band Portable BNC Antenna and the SpectrumForce Desk Mount for One Portable Scanner.
The Condor all band antenna is unsurpassed.
The desktop stand holds your handheld at the perfect viewing angle, you can listen and see all text clearly right beside your computer.

I believe you can configure this with standard Cicso command line, but it has a GUI very similar to other business and consumer products, so you can configure everything at your leisure and with just a search engine to figure out some of the protocols you may not be familiar with. Importantly, though, is that it just works when you hook it up - just like an unmanaged switch - and you can take your time with everything else (you should sign in and it will more or less force you to change the password right off the bat). There are a few "wizards" to help you through some common functions as well.

I'm using this in a small server cabinet, which is outside of my telecomm closet. I have three sets of 2x1Gbps port trunks for the servers, which all have two network ports, and then I'm using ports 8-10 as a 3Gbps link to my Cisco 250 series switch in the closet, which connects to all the end user devices. This is all new functionality for me, but something I've been looking for for a long time.

Here's some random stuff I figured out along the way:

-I knew this, but you should know that you can't use both the two extra RJ45 ports and the SFPs - It's a 10 port switch, not 12, but if you're just using <100m links, this will save you money on SFPs.

-I am using 10Gbps copper DACs between the two devices. They do negotiate down to 1Gbps, they are cheaper than buying multiple SFPs, and I can use them later when I get 10Gbps ports (so the only reason you'd use fiber is if you needed a >100m link.

-Port trunking works between DAC and regular Cat6 (apparently it won't work with fiber SFPs mixed with Cat6.

-Not sure what I was doing wrong before port trunking on another switch, but I couldn't get anything better than high-error best effort to work as far as speed. On these 250/350 Cisco devices I'm using, all four of my trunks are working perfectly and clearly working at full speed without uncorrected errors (if any at all).

-There are "green features" included, but off by default. The one looks at link length and lowers power on those links if less than 50m. You can only use this if you turn off the Energy Efficient Ethernet standardized protocol, which you might do if the device you are using doesn't work, but I haven't found a case where it correctly reads my link length (and my testers do figure out the correct length, so I don't get this). The other green feature is Energy Detect, which I've turned on across the board, but it's hard to tell if that really saves energy or not, because it just is "on" when the link is down.

-I noticed on my other switch - the 24Port 250 series (I'm telling you this because it would probably apply to 24+ port 350 switches) - the ports are counted funny. Port 1 is the top left. Port 2 is bottom left. Port 3 is top second from left, etc. This caused me some brief confusion. The great thing is that you can name all your ports in the GUI so that can make things a lot more clear for you, especially if you keep all ports in your building hot or if you at least keep most of the devices static.

I know you can probably blast through all these settings pretty quickly if you know what you are doing and can use the command line efficiently. I will say that even though the GUI is intuitive, it can be pretty cumbersome if you want to use it to go through and turn on a feature on every single port individually. Part of the problem is that you have to save each port individually and then use the drop-down to do the next port. BUT, at least on this switch, it is quick and responsive. The other switch - a 28 port Cisco 250 series - is a bit slower and gets pretty frustrating. I'm not sure if that one is slow because it has less resources being a "lower class" switch or if because it has more to deal with being a 28-port switch vice this 10 port switch. Oh, and you have to do the "save to running config" thing like you do with the Enterprise stuff. Seems strange, but I guess it more or less makes sense why. But at least in this case you can just click apply...and then go up and click the blinking disk to save (to running config).

All that said, for a guy like me with just two switches, it's not a big deal at all - it's not like I have to go back in there unless I want to make some real changes (and that is a privilege).

But there is just a ton of features here - nothing missing that I've ever heard of, and plenty of stuff I had to look up to even know what it is. Do I need all this stuff for my home network? Well, I guess not really, but I certainly am happy to have a lot of it!

Oh...worth noting is that the 350 series apparently allows many more trunk groups than the 250 series, which only allows 4, so I would not necessarily want a 250 series for my 24 port switch if I didn't have my servers separate on this switch (yet, ironically, it seems unlikely you'd need more than 4 trunk groups on this 10 port switch).

Other real-world applications for a home network would be setting restrictions for kids or renters or whoever from getting to all areas of your network. There is all kinds of port security features here, protected ports, and VLAN features, so you should be able to do just about anything you want to do with these switches. Also QoS, traffic limiting, etc.

If you're deciding between the 250 and 350 series, I suggest you do some serious homework to figure out if you actually need the 350 series. Here are just a few of the things I noticed the 350 series has that the 250 does not (not a comprehensive list):

On the 350, you can set link speeds lower on LAGS, use protected LAGS, more LAGS, UDLD, Ethernet tagging, VLAN mapping/private VLAN, lots of VLAN grouping options and more VLAN settings in general, and ISCSI status for QoS.

Oh, one last thing - unfortunately something I don't like. On some rack mounted equipment, you have one set of "wings/ears", but multiple positions/mounting options. These mounting brackets at least are included, but seem like they'd only work with this switch AND you can only put them on in one position, which means the switch will protrude about an inch forward in your cabinet, and that is really annoying for my small cabinet, so I had to get a recessed mounting kit. ALSO, I know it's pretty normal for a small switch like this to have an external power supply, but since I rack mounted it, I would have really loved to have the power supply be internal, especially because the whole thing would be small anyway.

Despite those two nitpicks, there's really nothing about this switch I don't love. Well, okay, I'd like some 10Gb SFPs, (which are available in this line). But having some real Cisco equipment is actually all it's cracked up to be!

My parents used to have a Polaroid camera and it was everything that we remember those old cameras for – it spat out a white square of plastic that slowly developed into a grainy, faded-looking picture within a few minutes, it was bulky and it had a very distinct sound. It was a great old camera but when Polaroid quit making film for it it became a paperweight. It's nice to see that some of these old cameras are available with film again. That said, there are some oversights with this package.

I will start with the two negatives (no pun intended). First, the way the camera was packaged for shipment was sub-par and the package was partially crushed when I received it. It did not appear to be damaged beyond the packaging, but it was a disappointment to open the package and find the merchandise box partially crushed. Second, the camera comes with no film or batteries at all. So, the camera by itself is still a paperweight. It would have been nice to have at least a lower capacity pack for film to get started.

The camera came out of the box without a mark on it. It looks to be brand new, in spite of being an older unit. Some of the other reviewers have complained that the camera they received either was scratched up or was partially damaged, but mine is pristine. It's a simple, straightforward device too, and it does not require much thought to use.

In use, it works just like it would have when new. It fires the flash, spits out one exposure with that same distinctive sound I remember and the film develops in front of you. The exposure still looks grainy and old when it is all done, but it is a real photograph that does not need a separate printer or software to get a hard copy. This is not the kind of camera a photographer would use, but rather it is for the tourist or enthusiast.

Why would you want a camera like this? For me, it is a trip down memory lane to a time years ago, when candid pictures were a part of daily life and the exposures were lined up on the pinboard for all to see without needing a computer or tablet. It is not going to make pictures that look like they could be in a magazine, but it will produce pictures you can enjoy right away.

I am not super-thrilled with the buttkicker. Set-up was difficult because the instructions are not as clear as they should be and are very different from the instructions given on the buttkicker website. A simple parts list is not included. Setting it up underneath the couch was fairly painless, but getting the amplifier to get a signal from the processor would not occur unless it was hard-wired. The wireless set-up would not work. The red light flashed but would not go out after 10 seconds. It should have worked, the processor was definitely sending a signal.

Wireless problems:

1.) Instructions with unit said there did not need to be a "line of sight" between the transmitter and the receiver, but the instructions on the website said there had to be a direct line of sight between them.

2.) The website instructions talked about adjusting the "potentiometer" on the back of the transmitter, but there is no potentiometer on the back of it to adjust.

3.) The website offered very little in the way of trouble-shooting this problem. I will have to call them directly tomorrow to try and resolve this problem.

As far as the "buttkicking" goes, we (husband and myself) did not find it a particularly wonderful addition to the home-theater experience. We put in "Polar Express" to test it out and found that it was interesting, but not something we could not live without while watching movies. It was literally the same experience we had when watching the movie, "Earthquake" in the 70's. The couch and floor vibrated on varying levels depending upon the intensity of what was happening in the movie, and loud low frequencies were heard, but I guess we might have been expecting too much. When the train in Polar Express was powering up, the shaking and low frequencies were tremendous, but did not necessarily course through our bodies like others have written about.

I think the buttkicking experience would have been much better if we were able to mount it in the center of our couch instead of at one end. Our couch does not have center support leg so we had to place the buttkicker on one far end of it. Much of the vibration was wasted by going away from the couch. Possibly "buttkicker" could have included an inexpensive substitute adapter in order to place it in the center of couches that don't have a center support. That would have been great.

We will continue to work on the wireless problem, and if we are able to fix it, that will increase our happiness with the buttkicker. Otherwise, we will still use the buttkicker, but not as often as we would if it worked wirelessly. Having to manually connect the amplifier to the processor via wiring every time we want to watch a movie is a pain in the.......butt.

I was able to enjoy the Transformers even more than my initial viewing. For a second test I tuned into a show on ScienceHD. Again, the sounds were spot-on and projected from where they should, the front of the TV. Very nice since this was a normal cable HD program.

I'm quite happy with my new speaker bar. I'm kicking myself for not embracing this technology earlier. It also has a 10 year warranty, which is just icing on the cake.

An excellent pci tuner card. You insert the card; install the drivers and WinTV software. I can record two channels at once or record one and watch another at the same time. Next I have a FM radio antenna and, the card with media center acts like a digital DJ for playing and recording FM broadcasts. Windows Media Center finds and sets up the signal for both cards and, with a DSL connection will automatically set up your digital TV guide for your area code which you can configure to automatically update, once a week or whenever. The same applies to cable or satellite. All you do is surf the guide, click what you want to watch or record, recordings are automatically saved to your hard drive. I've recorded hundreds of over the air, free, broadcast shows and movies, most of them I was totally unaware of until I bought these tuner cards and set up media center with TV guide. I received these earphones from Amazon Vine in early January, 2018. I liked the over-the-ears design. It makes the earphones far less likely to fall off when exercising. The sound quality is also excellent. I found its wireless bluetooth function quite handy for listening to music on my smartphone while walking, biking, lifting weights or doing calisthenics.

In short, as long as the battery could be charged, these sport earphones worked quite well. But suddenly, a few weeks ago, after only 7 months of use, the battery simply would no longer take a charge. The manual says that the battery should last through up to 300 charges, and there is absolutely no way that in only seven months I charged this device 300 times. It holds a charge well while the battery is working, much better than the other bluetooth earbuds that I have owned. So I could use it for up to five days without charging the battery. This means that, in seven months, I only charged the battery about 42-50 times, at most. This means the life of the battery was a mere 16% of what the manufacturer promised!

This is not a device in which the battery can be replaced. Therefore, once the battery dies, the earphones are worthless. Since the warranty is only for 90 days, there is no recourse with the manufacturer for replacing this device after that length of time.

The way that this product works is a good idea, but until the design includes the possibility of replacing the battery, the high price is simply not worth it. I will have to stick to cheap earbuds which are not such a hit to my pocketbook when their non-replaceable battery dies.

At the tender age of fourteen, Davie Adams's life is ripped apart. His mother's loose ways leads to a series of events that leave him homeless after his she dies in his arms. Grief-stricken, Davie makes the decision to leave Blackburn and go in search of his father.

Davie could have returned to his grandfather's house but he can't imagine remaining in Blackburn and having to endure the pitying looks and talk about his mother. After his mother's collapse, Davie runs for help and finds Tom Makepeace. They get his mother situated in the back of his wagon and are getting ready to head to the infirmary but she passes away moments later. Immediately afterward Davie jumps from the wagon and runs into the woods. Everyone assumes he'll return. Tom even yells into the woods for Davie to come to his home when he's ready that he's welcome there. Davie has other plans though.

He does go to the Makepeace's home but it's only to spend the night in their barn. He hadn't expected anyone to see him but Judy, Tom's daughter and Davie's longtime friend spots him from her window. She goes out to see him and reassures him that his mother's body is taken care of and his grandfather will be just fine. Judy realizes that Davie has to do what he feels is right for him but she also knows that her feelings for him have gone beyond friendship.

Davie leaves the following morning with nothing more than the desire to leave his memories behind him. Life on his own isn't everything he thought it would be and his search for his father proves fruitless. For years Davie travels and holds many different jobs but through it all Judy and his life in Blackburn remain firmly at the forefront of his mind.

THE LONER is sure to pull at readers' heartstring. Spanning over an eight year time period, you get a lot of insight into the characters' personalities and backgrounds. I love that Josephine Cox doesn't focus solely on Davie and Judy's story, there are many other characters who possess stories of their own which add a feeling of realism to this storyline. Davie's journey of self discovery is the main theme and it's a story you won't want to miss. Josephine Cox is a gifted storyteller who knows how to keep readers engrossed page after page so that the doldrums of winter just disappear.

I have a Fuji X-T3 and I have not shied away from third-party lenses at all. I have been looking for good wide-angle lenses and I have been aware of TTArtisan for a while. I was curious how well this lens would perform and I decided to take a chance on it. So far I am very pleased with it though I am still working with it and learning that it can do.

This lens is a brick! Right out of the box I was startled at the overall weight. It has a lot of glass in it, but it also is all metal - very little (if any) plastic. Even the front lens cap is metal. In spite of the price, this is a solid little lens.

It is probably the tightest fit lens I have used. It requires a little pressure to get it to click into place and to remove it later when mounting on the camera body. I was a little concerned at first, thinking I could potentially damage the camera. However, it does fit and does not harm the camera in spite of how tightly it fits.

Optical quality seems to be good, though that varies a little with the aperture setting. At the widest settings (and f/1.4 in particular) there is a little softness in the corners and a slight vignetting. As the aperture is closed more the image gets sharper at the edges. This is not unusual or unexpected for wide-angle large-aperture lenses, and it is actually slightly better than I was expecting.

I have not yet had a chance to get out and determine the coma with this lens. I am waiting for a clear night so I can get a starry sky shot with the aperture wide open, which will highlight not only the coma but also the chromatic characteristics. If it is particularly bad I will come back and update.

As a portrait or landscape lens this one works very well. Initial exposures have worked out well, but I am still learning what this lens can do.

Are there better wide-angle lenses out there? Sure - and they cost a lot more too. For the price this lens is far better than expected and I am looking forward to working with it more. It is good enough that I am staring to look at other TTArtisan offerings.

This camera is what I call a "subcompact" - the smallest point and shoot cameras that have vertically mounted lenses which allow protection, compactness, and quicker start up times. Normally, you'd expect a small trade off for these features, so I wouldn't compare this directly with a camera endowed by a telescoping lens.

Sony invented the subcompact with the T1 a few years back (at least in my world), and I was able to compare the FinePix Z90 with the one-generation-older 12 MP Sony T90. I'll go the pro/con route...

PROS of the Z90:

-Price is something like half of the latest subcompact Sony.
-Operational costs are cheaper: USB cable is non-proprietary (in case you want a second one or need to replace it) and SD card is cheaper and more universal than Sony's Memory Stick.
-Separate physical buttons to record movies and to take pictures. This is genius to me, because I hate to miss a great video opportunity while fumbling through the menus.
-Does not come with a memory card, BUT cameras that do usually come with one so small that it is worthless. Internal memory is better, because it allows you to copy from one camera card to another, which can be useful.
-Can set it up to take two photos at once, with and without the flash. As an amateur, I often do this manually anyway, but this way you get closer photos (chronologically)to compare in a dynamic scenario, and the subject needs only to pose once.
-The panorama mode works better than in other cameras I've used. They use internal weights alla smart phones (I'm guessing) to help you line up the next picture. Allows you to "pan" a panorama shot in play mode.
-There is a time zone mode that allows you to temporarily change the time (for timestamps).
-The display changes from horizontal to vertical as you move the camera respectively.
-"Touch and track" mode follows a subject.
-Side by side picture compare.
-Search by face, couple, group, favorites, scene, or date, and view a small picture next to thumbnails.
-Charger is smaller with the plug offset to allow it to use only one receptacle on a power strip (as long as it is at the end of said strip).

CONS of the Z90:

-Picture quality was not as good as the Sony 80% of the time (tested in various modes and lighting conditions). That said, a tripod really helps with low light and no flash, where both cameras struggle without it.
-By numbers, it is not much larger than the Sony, but it feels significantly larger.
-Sometimes the "buttons" in the corners of the touch screen need to be pressed more than once.
-Tripod mount has plastic threads, instead of a machined metal insert.
-Cannot take shots as rapidly as on the Sony
-Does not tell you what zoom level you are at. 5x zoom does not appear to make a great difference over 4x.
-"play" and "camera" buttons could be one button used as a toggle.
-Battery can be put in backward, as the slot is not keyed (although the battery is). No big deal, but shows something wasn't thought out thoroughly.

Bottom Line:

The Fuji is trying to deliver everything the market leader has to offer for a much more manageable price tag. It gets an A for effort, delivering a lot of great menu options, and may actually win in that respect, but the picture quality is not as good. If they could pour a little more money into the actual optics and the touch screen and still keep the price reasonable, they might win the battle in the future. For now, it's purely a personal budget vs. quality decision.

The Defender GK300- 7M2 Hands Free 2- wire color video intercom system is a relatively inexpensive intercom system designed to provide peace of mind with minimum hassle. This device is simple enough to install and is instantly ready to use with the flick of a switch.

Besides the simple setup, this monitor has some other interesting features that make it useful. I really like the night vision option because it makes visible what would otherwise be difficult to make out. I like the sound- it is easy to tell exactly what is being said- and I like the loud, easily noticeable chime when someone rings the doorbell. The fifty- foot cable is also nice because it is long enough that I was able to place the viewing monitor in my bedroom with no problem.

As for the cons, I can find a few. The video quality isn't the greatest- it is a little fuzzy, even though I can still tell who is on the screen. Then, there is the duration of the video- it displays for only about thirty to thirty- five seconds. After that, the screen goes blank and you have to keep pressing the video button to get it back. This latter feature is one I wish was different. Often, you will want to watch and listen to the person at the door, but because you have to remember to keep pressing the video button, you could easily miss something important.

This is a basic intercom unit, hence the average quality overall. I know there are more sophisticated products on the market, but they all cost several times more than this, the Defender GK300- 7M2 intercom. I suppose for the price, it is an acceptable option but don't buy this expecting a fancy, high tech intercom unit. All you get with this are the basics, making it good enough for only for those with minimal security needs.

As a freelance camera operator, I'm no stranger to these. This is clearly designed for us low budget video shooters using small DSLR style cameras, which is why it uses a Sony camcorder battery plate and designed with a hood for outdoor viewing. It has some pretty great features for the price point, including crop mark overlays, peaking indicators, and individual color channels. That being said, it can be used for all sorts of things, such as a Raspberry Pi monitor, backup camera screen, or even a second monitor for your laptop (that's a fun one!). It even has included sound, something a lot of these monitors do not, more on that later.
This is really designed for video use, and for that it does a pretty great job for the price. It comes with a hotshoe mount adapter to put on top of your camera, and uses standard batteries (most LED lights and other accessories also use these batteries, so you probably have some already if you work in video). The colors are vivid and sharp, more accurate than my Atmost Ninja 2 recorder screen, and nice and big for focus checking.
The hood is a nice touch as well, but it requires the snap on frame to attach, and the frame has a weird problem in which it partially obstructs the HDMI port. Maybe I'm just doing it wrong, but I found I needed to leave that corner off the frame if I wanted to use the HDMI plug.
Speaking of the HDMI plug, it comes with one included which I thought was pretty rad of them, but it isn't the more modern micro HDMI type, but the slightly older MINI one. That's the outdated kind that older devices use (such as 3rd generation Intel laptops or cameras like the GH2), but pretty much everything made in the last few years has been using the newer micro one. So it seems weird that they included this one. Personally, it will come in handy because I DO have a laptop that still uses that plug, but I don't intend to use it with this monitor. All my cameras that use that plug are long gone at this point.
Another couple of things to note: The focus peaking is pretty much useless. It oversharpens the image and thinks high contrast parts of bokeh are "in focus", which is weird. Thankfully my Sony cameras have peaking built in so that isn't much of an issue. Also, the screen is large enough and is HD enough resolution (not full 1080 but more than 720) that you don't really need peaking to tell what's in focus. You can see it with your eyes. Also, if using with a camera that is outputting a 16:9 image, you have to change the screen size setting from the default, which is to maximize the screen. Everything looked a little stretched because the display is a little taller than the output of my camera until I turned that off.
As far as sound, I mentioned earlier that this monitor has a speaker. That's good for when you want to review footage on the monitor, and even better if using with a Raspberry Pi or monitor for other things where it might be your only source of sound. It is also really useful if shooting with a Sony A6000 or similar smaller camera that doesn't have a headphone jack... this offers a headphone jack so you can monitor off the HDMI feed. That's pretty useful right there! But don't forget, when you turn the live view back on, you are going to get major feedback from the mic to the speaker unless you quickly turn the volume all the way DOWN first! Or just leave headphones in if that's how you roll.

It is important to note however that it will not accept a 4k signal. The actual resolution is 1280x800, and it will accept up to 1080p as an input, but more than that fails. At the time I'm reviewing this, it seems that there are similar monitors that can accept a 4k input for around the same price. I'm guessing they are updated versions of the same design, as there are no monitors that actually have that resolution for this price, rather they just accept the feed and down-sample to 1280x800, just like this one. So at the end of the day, it probably won't matter if it accepts 4k or not. Some cameras don't like outputting a different resolution than they are recording, so if you are recording in 4k and outputting 1080p, that might be an issue. Otherwise, this is a solid value.

This MOTOROLA MDC100 FULL HD (1080p) DASH CAMERA (Black) suits my needs perfectly. It’s mounted on the windshield, behind the rear view mirror, with an extremely strong suction cup. The suction cup is made of something that sticks to the windshield, and a ring tightens the suction cup so that it really, really sticks. The dash camera itself plugs into your car’s repurposed “cigarette lighter” outlet, and video recording turns on automatically when you start your car.

The camera requires a micro SD card (not included) for recording the video of your auto trips. I installed a [[ASIN:B00M55C0NS SanDisk 32GB card]] (the maximum size), and filled about 15-20% of the card with an hour’s driving. So the maximum size should record for 5-6 hours before it starts recording over the oldest recordings. The camera’s internal software allows you to “protect” designated recordings (or still photos) if you don’t want them to be recorded over.

Using an adapter, I inserted the micro SD card into a Windows 10 PC, and the PC was able to play the .avi videos without any problems at all. I also deleted selected videos that I made while learning to use the settings. The camera has a “delete” function, but it’s easier to use a PC for deleting selected files.

The camera has three modes--recording, photo, and replay. In photo mode, you can take still photos; in replay mode, you can look at your recordings and photos. You can replay the videos at various speeds (up to 8x maximum). You can also fast forward and fast rewind your videos as you replay them.

The camera takes excellent high-definition footage when it’s set to the highest (default) setting. The camera’s on/off functions for both power and recording are a bit confusing at first, so I strongly recommend that you sit down with the camera and familiarize yourself with all the settings and features before you install it in your vehicle. Of course, the camera is easy to uninstall/reinstall if you want to leave that step for later.

One very important thing to know is that if you turn recording off manually (by hitting the OK button) for any reason, you must turn recording on again manually when you’re done with Settings or whatever made you turn recording off. Otherwise the camera won’t start recording automatically when you start your car.

The camera has a built in battery for holding the settings and powering the camera while the vehicle is parked. I didn't test the Park function, which is disabled by default, because I don't like to leave an electronic device in plain sight when I'm going to be away from my car for a while. The battery can be used to replay videos or to look at photos, but it doesn't last long when used this way.

In my opinion, this unit makes the GH4 into a professional video camera. However, it's certainly not perfect. I begged the Nikon guy at NAB 2013 to build something like this for the D800, but nothing yet. Panasonic is listening. I'm commenting here because as of June 4, 2014, you cannot download the YAGH manual from Panasonic's website for details you may need.

1. Cost

It's more than the camera body, which is to say, really expensive. I can only hope the YAGH will fit future GH5 and GH6 camera bodies. Please, Panasonic: don't obsolete this thing.

2. Power

There is no internal battery. It has to have external power, supplied via the industry-standard 4-pin XLR. This is good and bad. Stated power requirement on the bottom plate is 12VDC at 1.4 amps.

Power is applied to Pin 4, Ground to Pin 1. (Pins 2 and 3 are not used.) The manual says voltage can vary from 11VDC to 17VDC. This means any professional AC camera supply or brick battery like an Anton Bauer 14.4VDC. (I'm using a 12VDC battery pack built from ten NiMH D-cells and supplies 10,000 mAhs.) You'll need a 4-pin extension power cord and drag the power supply with you. Hello battery belt? Sort of going backward. It would be great to have the ability to add lith-ion batteries somehow but perhaps it draws too much power for smaller cells.

The external power powers both YAGH and the GH4 body.

Once the YAGH is attached to the camera, an "Interface Unit" menu appears on the "Motion Picture" tab. There are many options. One setting allows you to set low battery warnings at 11, 12.5, 13.5 and 15 volts. This is very professional.

UPDATE Sept 26,2014: I built a 12VDC power supply from a computer monitor power supply and a 4-pin female XLR jack. I also have a 14.4 volt battery power supply. I found that if I leave the battery warning set to 13.5 for the one power supply the 12VDC power supply won't work. The battery warning settings actually stop the camera from working. Be sure to set the battery warning levels to match the batteries you are using.

3. Fan

Yes, it has a fan. You can barely hear it (can't hear it six inches away), but hot air blows out the left side when it's plugged in. I assume there's a lot of electronics inside to supply all the outputs. Have not demonstrated the fan can be heard by the camera-body's built in stereo mics.

4. Inputs:

a. the 4-pin XLR power plug

b. two, 3-pin XLR audio inputs, switchable between Line (0dB), Mic (-50dB) and 48VDC phantom power. A stereo/mono switch sends the signal from a single mic to both left and right channels. You can select which mics to use: the built-in stereo camera mics or the XLR inputs.

c. time code-in on one of the BNC connectors

d. the micro-HDMI plug that transfers the HDMI camera output signal to a full-sized HDMI on the YAGH unit. This HDMI interface is implemented clumsily; I hope there is a better reason than engineering laziness. It's basically a short Micro-to-Full HDMI extension cord. The dovetailed arm that sticks up on the unit holds the micro-HDMI cord with a plug. You mount the camera to the unit, open the rubber door on the camera's left side so that it sticks straight out of the camera, then slide the YAGH's dovetailed micro-HDMI plug into the camera, then tighten the tiny thumbscrew. The rubber door disappears into the dovetail arm and is not removed or abused by being bent back too far. This sturdy plastic arm with its metal dovetailed very definitely protects the extremely fragile Micro-HDMI socket on the camera body. (I personally would not directly connect a cable into the camera. One yank and your camera is broken. I thought the Mini-HDMI plugs on Canon 5D's and Nikon D800's were bad. This Micro-HDMI is even smaller and weaker. The YAGH solves the problem.) It would have been better if Panasonic had routed the signal through the bottom of the camera, but that would mean another 15 pins down there, and it's already crowded.

e. One drawback of this HDMI interface method: if you screw the dovetail in, it takes up the whole left side of the camera and you cannot pivot the flip-out viewfinder down at all and upwards only about 5 degrees. The whole point of the pivoting viewfinder is the ability to frame low- or high-angle shots. If you don't need to remote the HDMI to the YAGH (say you're using the audio interface and DC in and not monitoring via the HDMI) you can let the dovetail hang there, flopping in the wind, and allow the viewfinder to rotate.

5. Outputs

a. full-sized HDMI socket under a rubber door on the left side outputs 4:2:2 8bit or 4:2:2 10bit. You can't record both internally and externally if in 10bit. You access this setting while in "Creative Video Mode." The 8bit is good for sending to an external monitor while recording to the card.

b. 4, SDI BNC connectors under a rubber door on the right side, marked 1, 2, 3 and 4. They output different signals based on the resolution of the recorded signal.
- any of the four BNCs can output a 1.5G HDSDI signal if resolution is set up to 1080-29.97p.
- 3G-SDI is output on BNCs 1 and 2 if you record in 1080-59.94p or 1080-50p
- 1.5G-SDI Square Division (whatever that is) is output on all four BNCs as a group if you want to output the Cinema C4K (4096x2160-24.00p) or Broadcast 4K (3840x2160-24.00p/23.98p/29.97p). Apparently you will need all four BNCs to get enough bandwidth to send the 4K signals to an external monitor or recorder.

UPDATE: the four BNC SDI outs supply "QuadHD" -- that is, each delivers one fourth of a 3840x2160 picture or, four 1920x1080 streams. If you have a device that can accept QuadHD, you're in business.

6. Plug and socket covers

Minor point, but of some concern. The camera is not waterproof but is touted as "splash proof." To achieve this, rubber doors seal the camera all over. The bottom of the camera has two rubber seals that cover two sets of contacts -- one with five, one with 18 contacts. The YAGH unit has quite exposed corresponding spring-loaded pins sticking up. When you attach the camera to the YAGH, you obviously need to remove the four covers. There's no place to store them. You will want them if you split the units apart, especially the camera seals.

7. Audio Controls

a. two 8-segment LEDs indicating level: 4 green, 3 yellow, 1 red.

b. two approx. 1/2" diameter knobs to adjust level, shielded by a clear cover so they won't get hit accidentally yet are easy enough to adjust during a take without shaking the camera or making noise

c. brightness is adjustable to either "Hi" or "Low" via the Interface Unit menu item under the Motion Picture tab

8. Mechanical

a. two locating pins register to the camera body and are held tightly via the 1/4-20 tripod socket. It really becomes a single unit

b. Both 3/8-16 and 1/4-20 threaded tripod mounts on the bottom. There's also a hole for the tripod plates that have an anti-rotation pin. Having both 3/8-16 and 1/4-20 allows you to use two screws to mount the YAGH to your tripod plate so it cannot rotate.

c. two 1/4-20 threaded holes are supplied on the lower front of the YAGH to allow mounting a set of matte box rods, once some third party supplier starts making the rod/rail adapter. The two holes are exactly 32mm apart and centered 85mm below the optical center of the lens, conforming to the 15mm Light Weight Support (LWS) standard.

d. It's still not too giant for hand holding, but it's getting there. It's really designed to be tripod mounted.

e. Because the YAGH extends forward of the camera and slopes downward, if you use one, the Metabones Speed Booster tripod foot must be removed for the adapter to fit the camera while attached to the YAGH. Fortunately, Metabones allows this and supplies necessary Allen wrenches and caps.

Overall, the YAGH is useful -- allows (well, requires) external power for long runtimes, protects the camera from HDMI socket damage, outputs all kinds of signals up to true 4K via SDI, allows timecode input and allows professional audio inputs.

However, if you don't need external power, SDI-out or HDMI-out, a simple audio interface like the JuicedLink Riggy [[ASIN:B009YLRZFE JuicedLink RM222 Riggy-Micro Dual-XLR Preamplifier with Phantom Power]] or a Beachtek [[ASIN:B009R89SNQ BeachTek DXA-SLR MINI PRO HDSLR Audio Adapter]] might suffice to get pro audio in.

I have been using Wacom Intuos and Bamboo tablets for years, not really for graphic arts but more for digital handwriting and for use as an alternative to traditional mice and trackballs. My present solution is an Intuos 5 medium which seems to be about the right fit for my hands and my work space. The one drawback has been that it’s a wired solution. This new Intuos is a Bluetooth solution and it is definitely a step forward. For me the challenge is downgrading to the small from the medium, but it’s a good fit for me when traveling and when working in cluttered spaces.

To approximate the size, it is roughly equivalent to 7” tablet in size. It’s small enough to tuck away in a corner of a desk when not in use, and when it is being used it does not take up large amounts of real estate. The design itself makes it suitable for use just about anywhere it can be set down and kept stable - one of the reasons I like drawing tablets more than traditional mice.

The Bluetooth connectivity is new to me, and I was pleasantly surprised to find that this unit can connect via USB as well. So, if your system is like one of mine and the Bluetooth doesn’t work, this drawing tablet still will work.

I have it connected to my Windows 10 system. I have not yet made the effort to get it working with my Linux system, though I expect there will be some labor involved to make that work. I’ll revisit that later.

In operation, this is a straightforward drawing tablet though it is an improvement over my Intuos 5 in some ways. Of course the Bluetooth is a step up, but I was surprised by the increased number of pressure levels which is effectively doubled over my old tablet - 4096 vs 2048. For someone like me, this is not a huge difference and I don’t take advantage, but for someone who is very serious about fine digital artwork this can be a huge benefit. For use in handwriting, it is not especially important as even 512 pressure levels (like my original Bamboo small) is more than sufficient.

When you register, you get a choice between three Corel titles, of which you can select two (for the medium you get all three). Some may find the choice difficult - Painter Essentials 6, AfterShot 6 and Clip Studio Paint Pro (2 years) - but for me, having AfterShot is more than enough.

There is a downside to this little tablet, though - the pen is mediocre. There is no comfort grip, changing the nib is a pain, and there’s a very limited number of replacement nibs for it. It’s the one weak spot in an otherwise nice product, and even then it’s not all that bad.

The hardest part for me with this specific tablet is the move from a medium to a small, but this this counterbalanced by the Bluetooth connectivity and the inclusion of the Corel titles, specifically AfterShot. This is a very nice drawing solution and is it priced nicely. I’d recommend the small for anyone either just getting started or experimenting; the medium is a better fit for those more experienced or needing more real estate. I would choose a different pen if available, though.

I'll admit, I'm a fan of Sony. I've owned all sorts of things from the brand, from the aftermarket stereo in my car to my professional camera equipment I use at work. They just make reliably good products. However I've mostly owned Samsung television sets just because it's what I had access to on a more regular basis.
I was therefore excited to try out this TV and see how it compared. To be honest, I really REALLY like Sony's color science. It's part of why I prefer their camera equipment, and it shows on this display. The contrast ratio and dynamic range are everything I wanted it to be and more. The skin tones as well, however the average consumer probably wouldn't notice or care about these things. Where the big differences lie in major TV brands these days is going to be features. The latest crop of Smart TVs have so many bells and whistles, you practically don't need anything other than an internet connection anymore. Unlike Samsung's UI which has embraces Amazon's Fire Stick style UI, Sony has gone the Google TV route. There are pros and cons to both approaches, although I think perhaps arguably there isn't as much free included content as Samsung (Samsung actually includes free live TV channels via "Samsung TV", which Sony does not have). But for all the content I actually WANT to see, Netflix, Prime, Disney+ etc, it works perfectly!

So why only 4 stars? This isn't the fault of Sony's TV, but I really wish they'd make it easier to spot and turn off... I really REALLY hate the default motion smoothing (aka "soap opera effect") that all the big brands use these days. As a content creator, I shoot videos in a particular frame rate on purpose. The motion blur or lack thereof helps tell the story in some kinds of scenes. But most TVs want to show off their high refresh rate and therefore use realtime smoothing algorithms to create fake overly-dramatic effects to pump out extra in between frames. The motion looks too smooth to the point it seems CGI (because it sort of is). It just looks off once you notice it, and Sony is no exception. You have to dig around and figure out what they call it on every TV just to make it look normal again, on this set it is called Motionflow and it can be confusing to turn it off. I wish manufacturers would make it a simple and easy to understand toggle switch... maybe even present it as an option to the viewer upon setting it up so they can understand what they are enabling and decide if they want it or not (I strongly recommend not!).
But again, that's true of all modern Television sets, on its own right this is a solid TV and I would recommend it.

I bought this router in December, 2010 to replace my Linksys WRT54GS wireless router. I was a bit surprised to find that there are no external antennae and no place to install one on the E3000, but I haven't encountered any problems with signal. This router hasn't bottlenecked once, whereas my WRT54GS would bottleneck if the wind blew wrong. The only time I have unplugged this router was because I had to reconfigure it from scratch when I discovered I couldn't configure any of the settings using the built-in software once I'd changed the router configuration in the browser config pages. I read some work-arounds in the Amazon.com reviews and had to reset to factory defaults. I had to fully uninstall and reinstall the Cisco Connect software as well. As long as you go through that software first and THEN make adjustments in your advanced configuration settings via your web browser, you can still access things like parental control and guest wifi security. If you change your router's address, however, from 192.168.1.1 to anything different, expect to never be able to get into Cisco Connect again. The only reason I can envision needing the Cisco Connect software is to access the guest wifi and the parental controls, so if you don't need those things, don't worry about making changes you normally would via the browser interface.

The wifi button on the router is handy for setting up wireless devices such as cell phones and internet tablets, it hooks right up to your wireless network and you don't have to rely on the guest access to connect. You will also have the ability to set up a physical key using a USB thumb drive (you must provide your own) for setting up other computers on your wifi network, which works like a charm. It is especially compatible with the Cisco-Linksys WUSB600N Dual-Band Wireless-N USB Network Adapter, which I also highly recommend. I haven't tried the networked storage option yet due to the location of my router in relation to my external drives, but it is definitely an option that I will look into setting up some day.

I would say this router is worth the $150 I paid for it (locally), with the biggest reason being that so far I haven't been able to bottleneck it, even with my 60MB cable service, wireless-connected computers, Wii, and other various wireless devices. Cisco/Linksys really did a good thing with this model and I'm quite pleased with it; it is definitely worth the price.

I bought these primarily to use as studio monitors. I have or have had a number of high end cans over the years, Grado, Beyerdynamic, Sennheiser, Etymotic Research, etc.. however for recording purposes I have always preferred my AudioTechnica ATH-M40 due to their sealed design and extremely neutral response compared to most of the aforementioned cans which 'color' the sound in one way or another.

I've had the M40 monitors since they first came out in the early 90's and they were really starting to fall apart so I decided to look for a replacement. I was somewhat surprised by all of the praise for these Denon cans considering that last time I paid attention to the headphone scene Denon wasn't even making headphones. However, after looking at the response curves and reading all the glowing reviews from knowledgeable users on these and the D5000 series I decided to give these a shot as my new studio monitors.

Overall, I would say they live up to the hype. These are definitely the best sealed cans I have heard, the highs are very accurate with an airy presence which feels like you are listening to an open headphone. They do not sound quite as neutral as the M40 to me, primarily due to the punchy low frequency response which can be a bit excessive with certain sources but that may soften up once they are properly broken in. Like any good headphone these will greatly benefit from quality amplification, but I must say they sound quite good unamped compared to some of my other high end cans like the Beyer DT990 which I consider useless without proper amplification.

These are also very comfortable although they could have made them a bit smaller, my head is somewhat small and they just barely fit me on the smallest setting.. all of my other headphones are too tight on the smallest setting so I am not sure what denon was thinking when they came up with the sizing for these.

For the most part I have had good fortune with Logitech peripherals. As I write this I am using an MX Ergo trackball which is the best mouse/trackball I have ever used. I looked to the MK470 mouse/keyboard combination with the idea of using it with a laptop running Linux. I had high expectations for the keyboard but lower expectations for the mouse due to the size and shape. Both failed me, but in completely different ways.

I will start with this: this combo does not use a unifying receiver so if you want to use another peripheral with this combo you’ll need either another USB port or connect via Bluetooth. That’s all right as long as you recognize that up front. It’s a mild disappointment, but it was clear up front so this was not a surprise.

The mouse and the keyboard both have the batteries installed already. The keyboard takes 2 AAA batteries and the mouse takes one AA battery. I question the logic behind using different battery sizes.

I plugged the receiver into my laptop running Linux with the latest kernel, and both peripherals were immediately usable. That’s a plus.

The first problem I have is with the mouse. The mouse works just fine but is such a low-profile device that it is uncomfortable for me to use. I have a travel mouse that actually fits my hand a little better and that says a lot. For someone with very small hands this one will serve acceptably as a basic two-button travel mouse. To be fair, I knew this ahead of time so I cannot complain too much. It does work correctly and in a pinch I can work with it.

The keyboard is a completely different matter entirely. It works just fine – except for the “P” key. For that specific key, I have to bear down very hard to get it to register at all. I tried leaning the keyboard on its side and tapping it gently in case something was caught in the switch and I have tried my best to clean it without disassembly. No matter what I have tried, the “P” key continues to be insensitive to the point of rendering the keyboard unusable.

I really wanted to like this keyboard, and I knew the mouse would be small. Unfortunately, because the keyboard I received doesn’t work properly I can’t use it and can’t rate it favorably. It’s a shame – I imagine I got a bad unit (it happens), but I cannot recommend a product based on an assumption.

UPDATE 10/31/2019:

I popped off the "P" key and looked at the mechanism underneath, since the keyboard was not otherwise useful. It does not appear to be broken, damaged or obstructed in any way. For this particular key, the plastic key cover needs a small bead in the center underneath to push down the silicone membrane to make contact. Using a very small piece of tape and a tiny ball (about the size of a pin head) I was able to add such to the key cover to get it working without damaging any parts, without changing the feel while typing, and without spending any money. However, this should not have been necessary as this should have been tested properly before pack-and-ship; my review and rating stand.

I have to say, I was excited to get this thanks to the zoom for the video, but I was sorely disappointed in its quality. The indoor video I took of my son's music concert, in admittedly relatively low-light (but nowhere near dark) was nearly unwatchable. The focus was terrible and the output was super grainy. My wife, sitting right next to me and thus experiencing the exact same environment, taped the show using our Kodak playsport and it came out absolutely wonderful, well worth sending out to family members. There was simply no comparison between the two. While the sound quality was a closer match, I'd still give the nod to the Kodak over the Phillips. The still photos in the same situation came out just as bad, also grainy, also often blurry, and often washed-out as well. I tried both video and stills at various levels of zoom--without a zoom the quality of both was noticeably better, but still poor quality. I then took stills out in a well-lit hallway and again was disappointed in the quality and again, the Kodak completely outmatched the Phillips.

I've used it in outdoor conditions and better lit conditions and there's no doubt the picture quality is better in those conditions, but in all of them it comes in quite below the Kodak in quality.

Other issues:

The zoom was very slow to auto-focus and took several long seconds before settling in.

the choice of a micro-SD. Not only is it annoyingly different, which I could live with, but it really took some force to get it into the slot. In fact, the first time I used it I left it sticking partway out assuming it was a clever design that shutting the cover would put the card into the slot as it needed to go. This did work--the card obviously slipped in and had no issues--but then, when I needed to connect it to the computer to download, which necessitates leaving the cover open for the cable, I realized what I had thought was a clever design wasn't purposeful, as I needed to get the card all the way in. I eventually used a pen cap to push it in, wincing at the pressure needed to do so. (I won't discuss the times it popped out and I had to search on the floor/desk for it).

it has its pluses, but to be honest, since its primary purpose is taking good pictures and video, and so far it hasn't, I don't see the point in outlining the good points which are so secondary to its primary objective.

I'll use it a few more times to ensure this review is a fair one, but there is no way I will do so at special events or without using the Kodak as backup (or one of my point-and-shoots which also shoot far better video based on the samples so far--two Canon elphs and our larger Canon IS). Purchased this 4 year plan in November 2016 on a Dell Laser Printer. Thus the printer was a little over 2 years when it started doing weird things and I made a claim.

Basically ... the printer stopped printing black ... it just got lighter and lighter. I attempted to clean the heads and change the cartridges to no avail. The printer would also keep running and not stop after done doing a printer job.

I printed my receipt / invoice off Amazon to PDF. I then went to SquareTrade's website attached the receipt. I then made a claim. The claim process was pretty easy and they actually approved me for a full refund. I just needed to fill out an affidavit. I did this but a week later I still had no refund. Somehow my affidavit didn't get logged even though I got a confirmation email. I called them on the telephone and they fixed everything and were kind about it. Within 24 hours they emailed me an Amazon gift certificate (my choice) which gave me an additional 5% back. I this received a $121 refund on an $118 printer that died in its 3rd year.

I have no complaints and would purchase a square trade warranty again.

Bits of interest as I read other people's low reviews:

1) You purchase a 4 year warranty, but really, for example, it is just 3 extra years beyond the purchase's original 1 year warranty (or however long applies). If your item dies in a year, you have to go to the manufacturer for help.

2) You need to have your receipt. No biggie. Amazon is super amazing that way. I can see all my order back to when Amazon just sold books. Print the invoice / receipt to PDF and there you go. Receipt. Proof of purchase.

3) There is no paper copy of this plan. This is great. It saves trees. You would probably lose it anyway. But Amazon also kept a copy of the fact that I purchased this along with the printer. It was in my order history. There is your proof and all the telephone numbers are there. It is so easy. You don't need a stack of papers.

4) If you file a claim and get 100% of your purchase price back, you cannot file a claim for the same item again. No brainer.

5) This isn't accident insurance. If you do a dumb thing like leave your camera on top of your husband's big rig fender and it ends up in a million pieces 1/2 mile from your house ... it is NOT covered. If you think it should be ... well then ... Take out an insurance policy ... not a warranty. Those are two different things.

6) If you got a deal and paid $65 for your item, but the item now sells for $400 ... you still only paid $65 and $65 is all you are getting back. You don't make money off warranties.

Wow, these inexpensive fitness tracker watches have really come a long way! I've used WearOS, Fitbit, Galaxy and Amazfit brand watches, and usually find the cheap ones are cute for my kids but not very accurate or full of mostly gimmicky features.
This one actually looks and acts a lot like a cheaper version of my current Amazfit GTS3 watch. The way the menu works, the way the app works... it's all very familiar. Granted, this watch does not have the high resolution OLED display that my Amazfit does, but the display is capable of vivid colors and looks great!

The accuracy is surprisingly spot on, I even tested my heart rate with this and other smartwatches I own since usually there's a lot of discrepancy, and it often lined up exactly. Steps were interesting- most smartwatches don't count steps unless you move for more than a few steps at a time (disregarding a step here or there as an error). This one goes a step further and actually refused to count steps I made unless I was WEARING THE WATCH! I'm not sure if this is a attempt to prevent cheaters from shaking their watch or something, but I noticed it would not count any of my steps when I held it in my fingers, but when I put it on my wrist, it counted! Perhaps there is a proximity sensor on the back of the watch, I'm not sure. This might be a problem for those who occasionally put the watch in a pocket or something to get steps if, for example, pushing a shopping cart (since your wrist doesn't move, pushing strollers and carts tend to not count anyway- one workaround is to put the watch in a pocket but that might not work now).

Another thing I wish it had is a better notification system. Certain apps which aren't in their list of known notifications won't work correctly (Google Voice, for example). But that's true of all cheap tracker watches. It also can't install apps or extend functionality like the more expensive ones. There is definitely a reason my regular watch costs 5-6x as much as this one, but for what it is on a budget, honestly, it's pretty amazing!
