This is the first Logitech keyboard I've gotten, and now I see why Logitech is considered to be a proficient manufacturer in keyboards and other computer-related paraphernalia.

Without installing any such programs or software, either from the website or from the included disc, I plugged in the USB receiver right out of the box, followed the easy-to-setup instructions engraved on the back of the keyboard, and away I went. I was able to type flawlessly at the office, and the keys are very smooth and quiet. Even though it's just a keyboard, I kept opening up different programs to test out the typing. Pure joy! (For a nerd like me, at least.)

I guess the only gripes I have, and I noticed it almost immediately, is that there are no lights to indicate locks for the numbers, caps, or scroll. It's a minor gripe, but a gripe nonetheless since I have to utilize the Caps Lock every so often at work.

When I used the extra buttons for various computer software, I found that the respected programs opened up right away. There was some stall, but that was the result of my slow, crunching computer.
The mouse worked just as it should.

Now, I have to admit, what I really wanted to get this keyboard for was my Wii at home. I know, it sounds nerdy.
But the keyboard I was using before was an old office wired one that was given to me. That one worked fine, but I wanted a wireless one. So, I took home this MK300 keyboard and USB receiver, plugged in the latter into the back of my Wii console, opened up the Internet Channel and found, to my delight, that the keyboard worked flawlessly.
There was some range betwixt the keyboard and receiver--about ten feet or so--but it made no matter: my sitting spot isn't too far from the console, so it's not like I'm going to be typing in a completely different room.

Since this keyboard works so well, I was hoping to use it on a Mac. I've yet to buy the MacBook Pro--which is why I'm stuck with the Wii's Internet Channel for now--and since the specifications for this certain keyboard doesn't include Apple's OS, I'm assuming that there is simply no way around hardware setups (ever tried?) and will have to resort to something else, when the time comes.

All in all, though, if you're looking for an excellent wireless (not Bluetooth) keyboard at a relatively inexpensive price tag for any PC machine or Wii, look no further. The MK300 works like a charm.

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

Personally I really like the flood light security cameras. Flood lights are a natural deterrent for criminal activity - when the light comes on it startles the person trying to sneak around and having the light almost guarantees that you will receive a clear image.

I have tested and reviewed several similar floodlight camera systems. As with all security systems my advice is never use cloud based recording - this opens your entire network to not only the company who you are giving blanket access too but also to hackers. The same is true for WiFi. Obviously WiFi is more convenient but if your privacy is a concern this really needs to be taken into account. Hackers have become quite adept at hacking into WiFi cameras and being able to not only watch your feed but control your cameras and access your entire network. If you choose to utilize WiFi cameras take the time to understand your router and employ proper VPN protocols.

In terms of this particular floodlight WiFi camera by FREECAM it comes with a 16GB SD card but while the manufacturer claims the camera can accept up to 64GB, I’ve been unable to get mine to accept anything but the included 16GB.

The app, while certainly not the worst I’ve used, is far from the best. It is not particularly user friendly and support is non existent. I was able to achieve a reasonable reliability in terms of video capture although the alert system is not reliable.

The bulbs are bright - 1400 Lumen and while they are not replaceable being LED, they should last a long time.

Installation was as straightforward as installing any floodlight and required around 15 minutes.

In terms of WiFi flood light cameras, I’m disappointed with not being able to get anything but the included 16GB SD card to work - this tends to point to the company trying to force buyers into their cloud services. I have carefully monitored all traffic and if the camera was attempting to access the internet independently - my internet blocks will prevent this but I have not detected anything in my testing thus far.

The app is not dependable nor is it user friendly.

All around this is a product I would avoid.

I pre-ordered this product 6 months before it was released. Three different release dates came and went until finally it arrived at my door without notice. When I opened the Amazon box, I saw the first problem. Although I ordered it in black, I received a white one. I was replacing a white one so I figured, what the heck, let’s go with it. I opened it up, looked at the very sparse instructions, plugged it in and within a few minutes it was up and running. However I wanted to use this as an access point and not any of the other three options offered on the setup wizard. More on that later.

Prior to this arriving I would comb through the dozens of questions people posted on the pre order page. One of my favorites was repeated by several people, “Do I still need internet service if I get this”? OF COURSE YOU DO! That’s like asking if you still need food if you get a new refrigerator. If you are asking this question, I highly recommend you enlist a qualified professional to help you assess your needs and get you set up. With that out of the way, let’s get into what this little guy can do.

As Wireless Range Extender (Repeater):

Think of this as a relay race where one runner reaches a mark, hands off the baton to the next runner, who then takes it to the next mark. This assumes you already have the first runner and of course the baton. So to use this as a wireless repeater you need an existing internet connection and wireless router. You will put the Almond 3 somewhere in your house where you get a good wireless signal using any other device such as a smart phone, laptop or tablet. Check to see you have most of your bars on your device, find a wall plug and fire up the almond 3 and follow the on screen directions to set up a “Range Extender”. (The device is just for checking the signal, not for setting up the Almond 3) If you put the Almond 3 too far from your existing wireless router, you will have the same crappy wireless speed you do now. Only you will be confused because you will see you have all the bars on the device which will be coming from the Almond 3. Remember, the Almond is only handing off the same signal it gets. If the signal is bad, that’s what you will get. So keep the Almond 3 as close to the existing wireless router to the point where you just start losing bars on your devices. However don't put it too close to the existing wireless router, or the signals may compete with each other.

As A Wireless Router:

This assumes a few things. First, that you have an existing internet connection. Second, that you are comfortable replacing the main router in your house. This means you will be taking the internet connection from your provider, disconnecting and turning off the the main router and plugging this in its place. In the case of cable internet, you will have to at least have a cable modem from your provider. (NOTE: Only qualified network engineers would ever have two routers in one home). If you set up the Almond as a router and you already have a router, you will start experiencing all kinds of network issues up to and including completely crashing your network and internet connection. Once you have put this in place of your existing router, simply fire it up and follow the on screen wizard.

As A Mesh Network:

If you don’t know what a mesh network is, then do not attempt to try this. Just use one of the above choices. If you know what a mesh network it, simply fire up the Almond 3 and follow the on screen prompts.

As An Access Point:

Again, unless you know the difference between a router and an access point, you are better off choosing one of the first two configurations. To start with, an access point assumes you have an actual Ethernet cable coming from an existing router somewhere in the house. This could be next to the router, or anywhere in the house using a switch or a switched port on the main router. If you are already lost, stop here and choose one of the first two options. If you know what you are doing, then follow these steps. Connect the Almond as a router with your network cable in the WAN port. Configure the setup wizard as a router (its ok to do that for now). When you complete the setup, go to the home screen, select the MORE icon followed by the Access Point icon. Once that’s done you can set up the SSIDs the way you want. It’s unfortunate that Access Point is not an option at startup. It seems an obvious deficiency.

Once You Are Set UP:

Once you get through the first setup screens you get the option to configure the Almond trough an App on your phone. I would download the Almond App before you get started on any of the above options. That will make the final steps of the wizard go much easier. Follow all the prompts to configure the App. (NOTE: this does not connect your phone to your new wireless connection; it only connects the App for future use). Once you get your phone connected to the new wireless connection and get the App set up, you can configure some of the more frequently used options right from your phone. Also don’t forget to update the firmware by going into the setup icon from the device. Finally, make sure you password protect the Almond 3 display so no one can change you configuration.

The App:

The app is a great tool for many reasons. With the optional smart home dongle you can connect all sorts of devices to automate your home. But right out of the box, you can track your family coming and going using their smart phones as sensors. You can be alerted every time someone connects to your network. You can turn on a “guest” network when you have company. The guest network is segregated from your home network so you don’t have to worry about prying eyes on your other network devices. . I am not sure how much I trust this, but a quick test did in fact block traffic from the guest network to the rest of the house. Just make sure you remember to turn it off or your neighbors will be stealing your internet. Finally you can rename your wireless connection from the App for both the 2.4 and 5.7 MHz connections. I suggest using the same wireless name (SSID) and password for both. (NOTE: never name your wireless connection your real name).

The Range & Conclusion:

Most of the headphones with which I have worked have been active noise canceling (ANC) phones which have their strengths and weaknesses. I have a few pairs of nice non-ANC phones, some of which are excellent for studio work, but this is my first pair of true studio phones. After working with them, I am very pleased with them. They are comfortable to wear for long periods of time and they sound great with a very balanced sound profile.

These are over-the-ear phones, not on-ear, and I prefer that. They do not pinch or press my ears and I can wear them for several hours without them getting uncomfortable. The pads are soft and do not irritate as some phone pads sometimes can. The pads do not breathe, though, so after some time they do eventually get a bit warm.

If using these as Bluetooth phones, operation is simple – turn them on. They’re immediately ready to pair and my system discovered them and paired without incident. The Bluetooth range is good and I was able to get between 30’ and 50’ with walls in between before the sound began to stutter a little.

If you prefer to use them corded, that works too and these come with several audio cords with which to connect. Speaking of the cords: these do not use a standard audio cable with a standard connector on the phone side, so you can’t simply use any audio cable with them (though they will work with extension cables). Bear this in mind.

Volume can be controlled by touching the connector on the left side – flick up to increase volume, flick down to decrease.

The most important aspect of any headphones is the sound quality and these definitely deliver. The highs are sharp and crisp without being piercing. The midlevels are full and warm, and the base is strong without being overdriven. Most headphones anymore are tuned to overdrive the bass at the expense of the midrange making music sound hollow while pounding the listener to a headache. It is refreshing to listen to music that is properly balanced without needing an equalizer to get the sound right. I would not call these audiophile phones, but they’re better than many headphones I have used that cost much more.

If I could change one thing… I prefer a headphone set that clamps down on my head and fits snugly. These are not as snug as I’d like, but they are better than some I have used. When I turn my head and look down, they remain in place without slipping which is an issue with loose-fitting phones. Since these don’t slip, I’m satisfied.

I’m happy with these phones and based on my experience with them I am pleased to recommend them. They sound great and they are comfortable enough for extended use.

Pixels per inch is where it's at!

I bought the 24" 1440 model for one reason: Pixel density.

I'm not a gamer. For me it's all about legible screen fonts for easy reading. And pixels per inch is where it's at. The higher the pixel density, the clearer the type looks. Fonts on a larger monitor with a lower density won't look as clear as a smaller one with a higher number of pixels per inch.

The density on the 24" model (2560 x 1440 resolution) is a little over 120 pixels per inch (ppi). A Kindle Paperwhite pixel density is 300 ppi. So if this monitor is a bit over twice the distance from you as a Kindle Paperwhite, the density and clarity will look about the same.

There is one thing I do want to mention: brightness. Wow this thing is bright. In the early days of LCD and LED monitors, brightness and color accuracy were issues. The brightness issue has certainly been solved, and maybe too well. I have mine set on just "5" on the on-board brightness setting. Occasionally I have dialed it down to "0" and it's still readable.

The major issue I have with this is that I fear it's not going to last. The mechanism by which the tablet cradle turns isn't too sophisticated, and it's difficult to turn. I'm not entirely sure it won't come apart before it loosens up.

However, that aside, this is pretty much everything I could want for the Fire. It supports the tablet both horizontally and vertically at three different angles, so it pretty much has you covered for hands-free use. It also has a hand strap for ease and security of holding if you're not using the easel. The cover is nicely padded and there is an elastic band that will help keep the covers closed either during use or while not in use. It's pretty well designed in those respects.

I can't swear that the cradle will hold the tablet securely, but that's a worry with a lot of different covers. It's something you take on faith, I guess. In all, it's pretty darn close to the cover I wanted, and that's a good thing.

I prefer a good messenger bag to a backpack most of the time. I prefer the way a messenger bag looks, how it is organized and how it provides protection to the contents of the bag most of the time, the trade-off being reduced space when compared to a regular-sized backpack. This is a nice bag and I am pleased with it. It recently came in very handy when we were traveling.

This is a large, canvas messenger bag. The canvas used is not the heaviest grade canvas I have seen but it is not the lightest or softest either. It seems to be the right balance of durability and softness as the bag is durable and holds up to abuse but is still soft and pliable enough to be workable in most spaces (like crammed behind a car seat).

Most messenger bags I have seen of late have used magnets as the closing mechanism and this one does so too. There are two leather straps on the flap that have buckles, but these buckles are strictly decorative. Attached to the main body of the bag and to the buckles are magnets and plates that work to close the back with little effort. They hold as well as metal snaps in most cases, the exception being if you overstuff the bag. There is a zipper to supplement the flap, so if you can zip the bag then you can snap it shut too.

The bag has a large main compartment that has a padded divider in the middle. This compartment is large enough to handle a smaller laptop (and I have a 10” tablet and keyboard that fits it very well) and it also is large enough to handle a couple of books. It also has a zippered pocket in the main compartment that is a good size for a phone, a calculator or a small note pad. On the front of the bag on the outside there are two small pockets that are also good for small items. This bag is about the right side for a school bag or a “go bag” with essential tools in it.

This is a good bag and I like it. It is well-made, roomy and has a good layout for the space and pockets. It’s a good choice if you need a durable and useful daily bag or even an emergency tool bag.

Note: the 4K term is marketing, just about all consumer devices are UHD (2160p). So I'm going to use the UHD term, feel free to translate to "format commonly referred to as 4K" if you prefer.

I tested this cable on my newest UHD tv, with streaming UHD video from multiple sources, and then with a UHD nature documentary on a bluray player. I'd been using a very good 18Gb ("4K") cable before, so possibly a side-by-side test wouldn't show any difference. But I did immediately notice how sharp and bright the picture was in both cases, so I can at least say that this makes a very good video cable for UHD.

The cable is well made and feels sturdy, with a nice grab handle at each end, and inserts just the way it should into HDMI ports, with neither wiggle nor overmuch tightness. I didn't notice any minor flaws that might make me concerned about build quality, and I would expect it to last, at least until it becomes obsolete.

What should you buy if you don't have any so-called 8K media or devices, like most of us, and don't see them in your immediate future? In that case I'd just go with very good "4K" or "8K" cables, but without paying premium prices. The product description might say "Premium High Speed HDMI Cable" (18Gbps) or "Ultra High Speed HDMI Cable" (48Gbps). The first corresponds to the HDMI 2.0b standard, the second to HDMI 2.1.

I don't know how it happens but I somehow ended up buying over 20 pairs of bluetooth headphones over the course of my life. I'm also finding that I can't pass up a good pair of bluetooth headphones.

So of the over-head style bluetooth headphones, I've run across problems with short battery life (had one pair that lasts only 3 hours), too tight against the head, presses on the ear (supra-aural) and gets sweaty, active noise cancelling that can't turn on independently of the bluetooth function, and no carrying case.

This pair of RCA Active noise cancelling headphones don't have any of those problems. I sit at my desk all day with an air outlet behind me that is constantly blowing. I'm able to use them the entire day with music playing without the batteries running down. I don't keep the noise cancelling on the entire time but when I do, the fan noise is completely blocked out. Being circumaural headphones, the ear cups completely surround my ears and do not press on them. In addition, the spring isn't too tight to make me feel like my head is being squeezed in a vice.

As far as sound quality, because the speakers are not pressing against the ear, the sound seems to have a wider-room feel, making me feel even more like I don't have headphones on.

Overall, I'm quite satisfied with this purchase and don't feel the need to splurge and buy the much more expensive Sony and Bose products.

The prices on big-screen smart tvs are in free-fall these days; projectors are always a bit of a project. But you're sure you want a projector, right? If so this is a great choice. Easy set up, great image, amazing keystoning (more on THAT in a moment), powerful internal speakers, and a decent price point (under $900 currently.)

Setup could scarcely be easier - provided you have your screen and the (not included) input cables/stick - or a wireless dongle. As I already had a projection screen and an HDMI cable for my laptop, all I had to do was switch on the projector, adjust the lens, run the start utility to keystone for the projector being offset from the center of the screen, connect the cable from laptop to projector, then allow the device to find the video source - the device finds the input in a few seconds and is soon streaming video and audio.

The projector's own audio is surprisingly good - and loud. Response to the remote is... a little slow, depending how close you are to the projector. The projector's own audio is great, and as we have it closer to the screen than we sit, I haven't felt the need to connect speakers. Persons with more demanding tastes in audio will of course differ, but the device's own speakers do a solid job.

Video quality is OUTSTANDING. Colors are vibrant and although a light source placed near the screen washes them out, the image is still clearly visible. With a light source more than 10 feet away and even with natural light through windows (at the opposite end of a 25-foot room) the image is perfectly clear; even though as I'm using a white screen the blacks are clear and dark. There was one strange exception to this with a streaming video (Extant) where the darks were warmer in the projection than on the laptop, but we have run other video and also had a DVR player (hooked up via the triple cables), and run DVRS with perfect light levels. I recently got an Amazon Fire Stick, and actually set it up on the projector - setup was easy and there have been no adjustments needed for the streaming video.

The keystoning is an amazing, but somewhat tedious, feature; you can offset the device and still get an excellent image. Using the keystoning feature on the remote, some tweaking gives you a near-perfect image. I say near perfect because when we had the projector placed eight feet back and some feet down to the left of the screen, the upper right-hand corner of the image frame bent inwards - although the cast image itself was clear and undistorted. This was apparently because the projector was not on a perfectly horizontal surface. The real issue was that when the projector was moved back in front of the screen, I had to redo the keystoning manually; holding down the OK key was supposed to reset it, but this didn't work for me.

The projector is relatively light and easy to move around. The feet are easy to unscrew to manipulate the image, but for the afore-mentioned keystoning issue, it was necessary to adjust the surface the projector was resting on; this would obviously be a whole different matter if ceiling-mounted.

I think it's a great projector. So really it all boils down to whether you WANT a projector - the VERY big picture and/or the portability, eh? You don't care about having to control light levels, positioning the device itself (and the associated transmitting device,) maintaining a screen, dealing with multiple interfaces... You're not the complete couch potato, surfing the channels via remote... Not to go on and on - this is a projector, not a tv. You can hook it up to a tv, or a laptop, streaming stick, etc, but - a projector is always going to be more complicated. This, however, is an amazingly uncomplicated projector!

I have had 2 Tom Tom-Go GPS units and have been reasonably happy with this brand. My first Tom Tom Go lasted less than a year at which point it lost its "mind" in the LL Bean parking lot, uttering, "Turn, turn, turn." The 2nd Tom Tom lasted 2 years when it suffered screen damage. When both units worked, they were reliable and paid for themselves many times over in gas savings.
I decided to invest in the 1350 Nuvi refurbished Garmin to try out a new brand, to be reassured of having up-dated maps and to receive a 1-year warranty on this refurbished product whereas Tom Tom provides only a 6-month warranty on its refurbished GPS. I also liked the prospect of using the GPS for walking tours of NYC, Philadelphia, Boston, etc.
My Garmin 1350 arrived quickly and in perfect condition. It could be used right out of the box.I was impressed by the sturdiness of the case and by how well the suction gripped the windshield. The unit seemed to turn on a bit more slowly than my Tom Toms but the route planning may be somewhat faster. I liked having the points of interest scroll down the screen. There appear to be many more POI choices on the Garmin than the Tom Tom. The categories are intuitive and it is helpful to quickly see both map location and contact information. Since my cell phone is paired with my car, I did not use to Blue Tooth feature to call up the store via the GPS unit, but this would be very helpful.
I don't think that the default setting gives as much screen detail; e.g., providing names for all the streets. I have found the greater visual detail of the Tom Tom helpful when driving at night, but it is probably a needless distraction most of the time. It is very helpful to have the streets spoken at turns. The volume was perhaps even better than that of the Tom Tom. This surprised me, having read numerous complaints about Garmin being inaudible. I even had to turn down the volume to 80%. The pronunciations were reliably clear with only a few oddities; e.g., the town of St. Davids was spoken as "Street Davids."
Route corrections were made more quickly than I experienced with Tom Tom and it is helpful to know which side of the street the destination is on.
In making comparisons with the Tom Tom Go, there is a feature which I miss: the IQ routing. My Tom Toms had an uncanny knowledge of different routes and respective drive times at various times of the day. Quite fequently, the return route would differ from the original Also-- and more importantly-- the drive time was extremely accurate.
In contrast Garmin seems clumsy and mechanical. Perhaps, this is because I am stil getting used to the Garmin? So far, I am extremely frustrated by Garmin's under-estimation of drive times. Even when I go 4 miles above the posted speed limits, I am seldom able to catch up with the predicted drive time.There seems to be no allowance for stopping at lights. The greater the distance, the more this discrepancy.This is surprising given the Garmin's close attention to changing speed limits.
Also, I do not think that Garmin provides a warning about toll roads and the option to avoid them. I found this a very helpful Tom Tom feature.
The option of adding a memory card to the Garmin provides increased flexibility. I am yet to download additional points of interest to the card from the various on-line web-sites which provide such information free. I also look forward to trying out pedestrian information for NYC, including (I hope) public transportation details. Had I known that Garmins with MP3 players are needed for auditory tours, I might have chosen such a model.
A convenient feature is that the Garmin turns off automatically less than a minute after the car engine is stopped.The unit comes off the windshield readily for toting.
While a manual is available at the Garmin web-site, the curious user will find various hints and tips on-line.
I e-mailed 2 questions to Customer Service and received a helpful response within a couple of days-- even on a weekend!
I am still exploring so have not firmed up my opinion as to which brand is the better choice. I am tilting toward Tom Tom because of the IQ routing, but then I would not want to give up the more detailed points of interest given on the Garmin.

I stopped reading as much when my eyes got old and tired. I finally broke down and bought a Kindle, and it's been a game-changer. I'm blowing through books again! Overall, it's been very helpful.

Pros and cons are:

Pros:
- can enlarge fonts as needed so it's easier on my eyes
- Paperwhite backlighting is also really easy on the eyes; I don't get fatigued and can read anywhere, night or day
- can download a crap ton of books and only carry the one small device
- great battery life

Cons:
- miss the tactile aspect of turning pages, skipping back and forth, feeling in your hands how much book you have left
- can't remember as well where a passage is in the book because I don't have mental image of where it was on the page, and about how many pages in it was
- touchscreen is kind of spazzy and sometimes will change font size on me or if I accidentally brush against the screen while reading -- this has been the most annoying bit
- touchscreen is also kind of slow: I touch something, it takes a moment to react; by this time I think it hasn't registered so I touch it again, only to have it do something twice and take me somewhere else, and I end up lost

Generally speaking though, the pros outweigh the cons, so I will keep loading books on this little guy!

o Ethernet via Netgear Powerline AV500 to switch/router, media server on same switch (no wireless bandwidth/routing complications).

The Fire HD 10 tablet is pretty much an unbeatable deal for a tablet these days. You get a really good display and decent processor and memory for a great price---especially when it's on sale. And the Fire OS (a rebranded and modified version of Android) works smoothly.

A trade-off is a not-so-good camera resolution.

And there are some limitations on what you can do. If you already own some Android apps, you might not find them in the Amazon app store, and those you do will not credited as paid for. You'll have to buy them again (if you choose to buy).

One option is to follow online instructions for installing the Google Play Store on your Fire. But that's kind of iffy. You don't know when the next Fire OS update might break that installation. And Play Store might download updates to some of the core Fire OS apps that might conflict with proprietary Fire OS modifications.

Another consideration is that this device serves as an advertising and sales platform for Amazon. It's tailored for that. Something to keep in mind.

The thing to consider is if you can be happy with what Amazon gives you. If you're going to be trying to root and work around the OS and app store limitations soon after you get it, maybe it's worth just getting an Android tablet and foregoing the Fire.

If you can be happy with all that, overall it's a great deal for a capable tablet.

I own a DJI Ronin S which I use with my Sony A7 series cameras (an A7S and A7Rii). It worked well enough, but after trying this Crane 3 Lab, I'm blown away and ready to sell my Ronin for this.
For starters, I love the ergonomics of the extra handle. Being able to hold onto it with 2 hands and shift from the handle to the pistol grip makes using this thing far more stable than trying holding just the pistol with both hands. It also makes it easy to pass and shift to a low angle mode, as well as seamlessly pass it to another person easily for those really impossible looking tracking shots (thought a window, down a staircase, etc). I'm also really impressed with the buttons and controls- if you've got a USB cable controlling your camera, there's a lot more you can easily access right from the gimbal without touching the camera than you can with the DJI Ronin S. With the Sony cameras, unfortunately, you can't control the focus motor of an automatic lens with the follow focus wheel... that's a limitation of the camera since Sony doesn't have that protocol in their USB remote interface. Other features work perfectly, however, and I've been told that other cameras like Canon and Nikon work with the focus control as well (this is something I'm hoping Sony changes in the future, but for now I'll just rely on auto-focus during gimbal shots).
Another HUGE improvement over other stabilizers is the ability to LOCK the axis motors in place. This is a fantastic tool to help when balancing (you can lock the other 2 axis and work on balancing them one by one, rather than holding the other positions in place as you work backwards like on the Ronin), and its also great to lock it in place when you are powered down and carrying it around- I've found that when taking a break with my Ronin, it is always awkward to walk around with it since the camera can flop and swing around as I walk. The Crane 3 doesn't have that problem if you just lock the motors in place with a little red switch.
Honestly, I wish I would have waited just a little bit longer before buying my Ronin S so that I could see how much better this is. The app is honestly just OK, I've heard people say they like the DJI app better and I would probably have to agree with that, but this just does everything else so much better that it I'd still say it is worth it in the end. The crane 2 is easier to balance in my experience, more forgiving (less crazy vibrating when the gimbals shifts out of balance), has better features and ergonomics and overall just seems to do a better job.
I STRONGLY recommend it if you are shopping around between those two options.

I have been interested in a device that can find hidden cameras for a while as we do tend to travel periodically. This device seemed like a good one and I wanted to try it out before I travel again. It seems like a pretty neat device that works fairly well, but it is hamstrung by very poor documentation.

This does more than just find hidden cameras. It is able to pick up Wi-fi signals, wireless phone signals and more. The sensitivity is very much like working with a metal detector - turn it up too high and it becomes nothing more than a sight and sound show; turned too low and it hardly sees anything.

With the unit turned on and set to a reasonable initial detection level I set about looking for devices in my home office. I have several Wi-fi connected devices and I usually have my smartphone there too, and I messed with this detector until I found the level where it was able to find everything. I did not try going near the router which is in another room but I imagine that one would require another sensitivity adjustment.

Most of the functions are self-explanatory, but some took a little trial and error to figure out. This is where good documentation would come in handy, and unfortunately the documentation with this device is poor. It's sufficient to identify the different functions of the device and where to find different components, but the actual descriptions and explanations of the functions are written in very poorly translated English.

Aside from the documentation, it would have been nice to have a carrying case for this device for storage and travel. That's a minor gripe, though.

I am happy with this device, though better documentation would make it much easier to use right away. It has some useful functions that will appeal to wary travelers, and it seems to work well once you figure out the right adjustments.

As for the functionality of the GPS, it has some problems, thereby preventing me from giving this a 5 star review. I'll simply list the Pros and Cons.
Pros:
Start up time is quick and option to start from last destination can save time if the satellite connection is delayed.
Menu options are easily learned even if at first they seem to include extra steps.
Responds quickly to need for alternate route when a turn is missed.
Ease in moving through functions on screen.
POIs are expansive and easy to discover
Map identifies a location I frequent which is not identified by any other GPS I've used.
Identifies traffic light cameras adequately. Have yet to receive speed camera warning.
Voice commands are intuitive and a little printed card is included if you're in need of prompting.
Connectivity to my Mac is easy and the option to automatically check for updates can save time.

Cons:
Speed is not always accurate. Often has my car going at 10 mph less than actual speed.
When setting a new destination, I've been unable to change the state unless I do it using the voice command. This may be possible, but I haven't had the time to investigate. Since I'm in a metropolitan area and may venture through 2 states and the District of Columbia in less than an hour, it's important for me to access the individual states.
When using phone through the GPS, although I can hear the conversation with no problem, the person on the other end of my call can't hear me clearly. Every time I've used it with a phone, the call has been dropped. I've never had a call dropped otherwise with my phone or other Bluetooth capable device.
Does not recognize voice commands at times.
Voice prompts are very frequent and I'd love to be able to reduce them but not turn it off.
Seldom comes up with the routes I usually take, even with a second try after selecting the Change Route option.

I only purchased a smartphone about a year ago, previously being in the flip-phone-for-life crowd, due to the requirements of a job I was on. Since then I have slowly been picking up the various accouterments of such devices, the latest being this magnetic mount. I bought it mostly so I can use Google Maps for navigation.

It is remarkably effective. I have a Motorola Moto X4, in a slim silicon case, and an 05 Subaru Outback. The kit comes with the magnetic mount, two metal plates with adhesive (a rectangular one and a little circular one), a clear adhesive interposer, and, as a nice surprise, an alternate, black bezel.

What you do is attach the metal plate to the outside of your case, the inside of your case, or your phone. If you choose the lattermost option, then you don't attach it directly to the phone, but to the clear adhesive interposer (just a clear plastic sheet with adhesive on both sides), likely to prevent surface damage and dampen shock/reduce possible strain. If you have one of those pop-socket devices, you attach the little metal circle to the center of that instead. Then, you fit the magnetic mount to one of the grilles of your car's vent system, wherever it is most convenient. Now you can mount your phone to it, the magnet clinging to the metal plate.

I attached the metal plate to the inside of my case. It is very thin - I would say 1mm or less - and even on my slim silicon case it leaves only a very slight rise, hardly visible from the outside. I also attached it about 2/5ths of the way up from the bottom of the phone, as recommended (the Moto X4 does not have wireless charging). The magnet adheres quite well to the phone - the silicon case actually slightly pulls away when detaching the phone from the mount - not nearly enough to dislodge the case, but enough to let you know that the magnet is really sticking. As the mount has a rubber pad, and my case has a rubber texture, the phone does not slide at all in any lateral direction, the shear resistance is quite high. I am not concerned about the phone just falling off during normal operation of the car.

The tines of the mount grip the vents quite well - I have only had the mount pull off the vents once when detaching the phone after parking. There are two sizes of gaps - narrow and wide - and the narrow gap seems to fit pretty well on the Subaru. I like how you can pivot the mount a little to the left or right, and use the vent's own hinge to pivot it up and down.

There are some basic shortcomings of design. Obviously you can only attach this to the vents of the car, which limits your choice of positioning. I tried putting it on the left vent, but that caught too many outside reflections. I tried the right vent, but my hand was mostly blocking the screen. I tried the left passenger-side vent, but found that this took my eyes too far off the road while checking the navigation. In the end, I went with the driver's side right vent, since it required the lease eye-movement to check navigation and it was actually helpful to have my had block the screen, so as to avoid distraction. The tines hold, but they are not as secure as a hard mount would be. Likewise, the magnet could, in theory, be bumped out of position by kids/pets/carelessness and fall down into the foot well.

However, I would generally recommend this, at least as someone's first mount, to get a feel for what they are looking for if nothing else.

I recently purchased a new zoom lens for my camera after I broke the old one when I took a tumble. I had filters like these for my old lens but the thread size was different so my old filters were no longer useful. I selected this filter for my new lens, somewhat apprehensively because of the relatively low asking price. It has proven to be a decent filter but it is not useful in all situations.

The idea behind this filter is light diffusion which will give an image a very slight haze or softness, depending on the lighting and subject. This is an effect that can be emulated in software during post-processing but in doing this type of enhancement I have found it is sometimes unnatural. It certainly is less fun than making it happen while shooting, which is why these types of filters are available.

In use it works, though I have had mixed results. When using it with certain light sources, the filter seems to have no real effect at all, while with others it creates a subtle, soft glow around the subject. I am still working out the situations where it is most effective. I have had similar issues with filters like these with other lenses, and as such I assume the problem is in my lack of practice with them. It will take some time and practice to make my results more consistent, and for now I lay the fault on myself.

The build quality seems to be good. I have received filters in the past where the glass rattles in the frame which is unsettling. This one is tight and there is no play between the glass and the frame. It screws on to the lens securely and is easy to clean.

The asking price is quite reasonable. I have seen these filters priced much higher, and I have also seen much cheaper ones that do not work well. The pricing seems in line with the product, if not slightly low.

I have no complaints with this filter. The issues I have with it are probably my inexperience, and I will keep working with it to improve my results. I will return here and update my review if my impression changes. For now, though, I am satisfied.

I've been shooting with my DSLR for a while now, and I never really had a use for film cameras until I got intrigued by the toy camera phenomenon that's been sweeping the nation. I thought about getting the Holga 120, but after doing extensive research on the cost of developing 120 film in my area (about $12 per roll, which has 12-16 exposures), I decided to go with the 35mm camera, where if I'm using Snapfish, i can get the whole roll developed for $3-5 for 36 exposures.

I must say, the Holga 135BC is a fun little camera! I took it on a trip to the mountains and got some great shots of the fall foliage. The vignetting (black corners) came out on about half the pictures; some of them came out without much vignetting at all, which was surprising. There haven't been any light leaks, which may disappoint some users, but I know there are some mods out there (involving drilling holes into the side of the body) to create that effect if you wish. Double exposures are quite easy to do. I recommend using ISO400 speed film for best effects, especially when you're just beginning. The aperture is pretty much set at something like f8 and the shutter speed is around 1/100 (though this can vary), so most indoor pictures and even outdoor pictures in overcast lighting came out dark and dismal. I kind of wish I had bought the one that comes with a flash unit (holga 15b) but I'm gonna purchase that separately. The ones I took in sunlight are great though, so i recommend taking your Holga outside on a pretty day for your first roll. As for loading and unloading the film, it's quite easy to do. Just remember to press the film release button on the bottom of the camera before you rewind your film to avoid stretching or ripping apart your exposed film.

Overall, i think that the Holga 135BC is a wonderful little camera, great for those of us trying out a plastic camera for the first time, and a great attention-getter in public. I would definitely recommend it!

I live in a rural area and find myself in areas with no cell service frequently.  Radios like these can be a lifesaver if you get separated from your group and can't make a cell phone call.  I plan to leave one radio home for my spouse while I go hiking away from the cabin.  This radio has a few functions that are important to have.  First you can set your channel number and be sure to make it the same on each radio.  You can find a channel that sounds the best or just pick a number where you don't hear any other radio traffic (people talking).  In addition to the main channel numbers there are 0-121 tone codes you can select.  This code in addition to the channel number provides more confidentiality to your calls.  The channel and tone code it is set at out of the box is 01 and 01.  You can set the volume.  If you don't want to have to press the PTT (push to talk) button you can set it to Vox and you can talk without pushing a button.  You can still only have one person talking at once but lets say you were doing something where your hands weren't available, like rock climbing or kayaking, you could still respond to someone calling you are start talking and others will hear you.  You should also be aware that each channel may or may not be capable of transmitting under hi power.  For maximum power, use channels 1-7 or 15-22.  To get the most range, be sure that you are using high power mode on the channels that allow it.  If you are unclear what channel someone else is using you can put it into scan mode and it will cycle through the 22 channels until it finds a signal. Lastly you can get weather channels on this so if you are uncertain about incoming weather you can go to an active weather channel and hear the latest forecast for the area.  You can also setup weather alerts so an alarm will sound should a weather emergency be forecasted.  In summary, for the money, you get a lot out of these 4 radios and they will make any trip safer if you use them.

Basically these phones have a distinct bias towards the higher frequencies, with a crossover to bass in my right ear and flat mid range response. In other words, if you are a critical listener you may want to consider other phones on the market.

I was able to get decent bass response in my right ear using my phone's EQ app, but could not get any decent mid range. The net result is music sounds one dimensional (even with the bass response in one ear.) I am guessing that the crossover threshold is such that you get high frequencies in one ear and low in the other, with the mid somehow cut out or deemphasized. First, let me preface that I in NO way count myself a photog. I am just a shutter bug who has been firing frames almost non-stop since the age of 18. I learned on my dad's 'old' Nikon SLR with an f/1.2 lens. The Nikon SLRs/DSLRs I have owned are: N50, N60, N55, N80 and D50. My N50 ad N80 had the best lenses. The N60 and N55 were not as great and the D50 was a fabulous entry-level digital. The only medium format camera I own is my Holga. But hey, unlike the photographer at Portrait Innovations, at least I know 'medium format' does not refer to the number of megapixels at which I am shooting. As for my working knowledge, I had three semesters of photography in college. I can process/print both B&W and color film. (Not that that does me any good these days LOL) I can shoot completely 'manual' and I have stood among many pro photographers on the bridge at sunset, waiting for the color to be just right on Half Dome. (My Bogen tripod was way too heavy to be practical for an amateur but it gave me street credit.) So, in a nut shell, I shoot by the 'Sunny 16' rule. I know that opening my f-stop should increase my shutter speed give me a shorter depth of field; and, per the great Ansel Adams, f/8 is a proper exposure for all pictures.

That said, I hate my D3100.

I have had metering issues since I opened the box. I bought the camera so I could take 'even better' pictures of my infant son than I was getting from my D50. Ha. Joke was on me.

The contrast was BLINDING on the factory settings and every shot was over exposed. I have tried every metering option in the menu but the only changes I can achieve are under-exposure, blurred focus and missed shots. It's go high or go without.

I always lower my ISO to 100 when I'm outside because I crave rich color but it's just not there. I have tried Aperture Priority, Shutter Priority and Manual. Nothing. f/16 over my film speed on a sunny day. That's supposed to work! I have used it on many a 'less complicated' camera and achieved photos that make jaws drop. Well, there's no jaw dropping with this camera.

The metering overrides my manual choices every time. It's like I'm having a battle of wits with my camera. :( It reminds me of the days when Kodak was marketing 800-speed film as a universal, never-miss-a-shot solution to all your photo woes. Bleh. Just because there's always an image doesn't mean it's the RIGHT exposure.

I get that being an entry-level/made-for-the-masses DSLR really does mean it's a glorified point-and-shoot but it should preform at least as well as it's predecessors. Honestly, I got far more reliable results from my Canon SureShot and a roll of Kodak 100.

My expectation for a camera is that the image should be very close to perfect when the shutter closes. I know there's always room for improvement before printing but that's the art of photography. The hours I spend working on my photos after the shot should be to make them pop. Instead, my time is spent trying to rescue precious memories.

If you are considering this camera as your first DSLR because you think it will improve your skills, skip it. Invest in an equally expensive point-and-shoot that will give you all the same manual controls and preform much better in low-light situations. The D3100 does not live up to the standards of a Nikon SLR.

Our antenna rotor broke and for 3 years we have been waiting for new chips to come through so we could get another one. It has taken WAY too long. I got this to help with the problem in the meanwhile. What I got was MORE problems.

HOW THIS COMES
This comes in a blister pack. It has a long cord and a double tail plug on it. The idea is that you put the plug into the antenna spot on the TV and the other is a USB port that you put into your TV. There is a sticker to put this on the wall and instructions.

HOW THIS WORKS
I have had no end of frustration with this thing. We do not have an OLD TV but we do not have any USB ports in this that work with the antenna. The outlets are such that I can not fit ANY adapters into the plug to use an adapter for the USB. The cord from the USB to the intersection where the antenna cord is is very short- only 13 inches. Put that together with the other cord for the antenna which is also about 13 inches and you can not spread them tightly so you only have about 22 to 24 inches tops to get from the TV on the wall down to a USB outlet if you don't have USB on your TV.

I TRIED TO MAKE THIS WORK
I have tried many different USB adapters to get this to work and none of them will work with this unit. I am frustrated and have spent so much time on this, I am giving up. I really wanted this to work, but despite this being an HDTV, it just isn't working out with this unit. I guess we will have to go without antenna TV on that TV longer.

THE BOTTOM LINE
If you have USB available on your TV and an antenna hook up, this might work for you. If you don't have a USB port that will work with this unit, you will have to have an available plug that has USB conversion in it, or USB on a power strip that is not more than 24 inches away from the antenna jack on the TV to make it work. You can also use an extension cord and adapter, but honestly, it is a lot of expense for a unit that might or might not work as you like.

MY RATING
THREE STARS. I can not give this a terrible rating like I want to in my frustration. To be fair, three stars is about right. I do not like that it does not come with adapters or alternatives for TVs. Most people who watch antenna TV do not always have the newest equipment. We happen to have this TV that needs the hookup. We have another TV which is newer but the picture is not that great and we already have it set up with another antenna hookup.

I would like this a LOT better if it came with a streamlined USB plug adapter for the power outlets.

UPDATES
If by some miracle, I can find a USB adapter that will fit in this situation and actually WORK, I will update this review and reconsider the rating. For now, it stays as it is. I have put enough time and resources into trying to make this work.

I also have an Alienware 17 with GTX 880M GPU. Comparisons are somewhat unfair considering the nearly $1000 price difference, but I believe they may be helpful to a prospective buyer:

You can look at specs and framerate comparisons of the GPUs all over the web, but my experience is that both deliver seamless perfection in the newest games. If I'm dropping some frames with either, I don't notice, but I often like to play on my TV, and I know I lose something there. I am also not obsessed with gaming like some, so I'll concentrate on some of the other factors.

The displays themselves are both fantastic, and I cannot distinguish a huge difference there.

The GTX970M included with this machine does make a noticeable difference in terms of power consumption, as this machine is much thinner and lighter than the AW. At the same time, it feels slightly less robust because the entire chassis is not metal.

I don't like the CD drive placement on this machine, as I keep popping the slot open from time to time.

USB 3.0 is on only one side of the machine (2.0 port and card reader on the other side). AW has two ports on each side.

What I really like about the AW is that it has a second full size HDD slot for added versatility. It's the only laptop I've ever seen with that.

There are no obvious annoyances with the touchpad or keyboard as far as accidental hitting a key or something not working correctly, which I've seen with other laptops. I am not thrilled with the placement of the delete key on this laptop, and I don't really like the fact that the arrow keys are scrunched up with the numbers and other keys, either. By contrast, I believe AW got their layout perfect, including their four programmable keys.

Lights. The keyboard by itself may actually look cooler on the Apache because the lights are in the height of the keys. BUT, there are only three zones, compared to AW's four, plus multiple chassis zones. I really love the light-up touchpad on the AW. What really annoys me about the lights on this keyboard is that despite the controller software that allows lots of per-key and per-game customization, there is no setting that allows the keyboard to turn off at the same time that the screen goes blank (or any time for that matter; you have to wait until the computer goes to sleep). I have it rigged to change from one profile to a dark profile when I press the special command button, but that's not seamless.

Windows 10. Actually, I love that I got the AW at the time when they were still loading Win7 (Win 8.1 was out, but nobody wanted it). I'm still not thrilled with Win10 due to their moving some settings out of control panel and into settings, getting rid of other settings altogether, still having a ridiculous start menu, and wanting to control your life as if you're some dumb tablet/phone user. I installed Classic Shell to get my start menu back, messed with the control panel and settings for a long time, turned off everything they were "offering" me, and I have this working just about as good as a Win7 machine. Oh yeah, and I ditched MS Edge; God, what was wrong with Explorer? Anyway, if we're stuck with it, may as well make the best of it.

Very little crapware on this machine. On most computers, I disable even the proprietary controls since most of them do nothing. This machine has a System Control Manager that doesn't do anything that Windows Power settings cannot do, but it confuses things and messes up my settings, so it will be turned off. The other stuff seems harmless so far.

I was telling someone that computers like this are a status symbol to some people (like cars are to some people). And it came with a key fob, like a car... Oh yeah, this and the AW both come in fancy packaging, including a suitcase-style box that you'll be tempted to keep, but practicality keeps me from doing so. However, you may want it if you frequently transport your machine. Also comes with the largest - but not softest - microfiber cloth I've ever seen (the size of the screen).

In conclusion, you can see that there are a few minor things I prefer about the AW. Are they worth an extra thousand bucks? No. This is an impressive machine that can handle anything I throw at it. It should definitely be on your consideration list.

This is a nice little set of radios, improved from my last three-pack of similarly priced Motorolas, but has some room for improvement.

Goods:

+ Good size - small enough, but big enough to fit in your hand comfortably like a radio should. Yes, it could be smaller, but at some point you don't really want smaller.

+ Some basic options to customize, mostly the noises the radios make. LCD screen shows you what you need to know.

+ Batteries can be charged while in the radios via standard Micro USB adapters - two are included. One charges one radio while the other charges two simultaneously.

+ Belt clip included. Head sets can be added.

Bad:

- While it's great that the battery packs can be charged via USB and the chargers are accepted worldwide (whereas my previous set for work had barrel connections to the charger and I burnt one out the first night I tried to charge due to being in Europe, the battery/charger setup is still imperfect for two reasons:

1) Battery packs are not three separate batteries that could be charged with other chargers and switched with other batteries (think Eneloop). My Garmin topo GPS came with actual rechargeable batteries that could be used elsewhere. This makes sense when you want to be able to carry standard alkaline batteries for emergencies/backup. These battery packs are great that they can be replaced with AA when necessary, but not as good as standard, replaceable rechargeable batteries (but you can use rechargeable batteries as your backup batteries).

2) N-MH doesn't make sense for this application because these are the type of batteries that develop a "memory". If you use these every day for work, then you want to recharge them every night. Actually, you would be inclined to recharge every time you want to use them, period, to be sure you get the most from the batteries. But because of the memory, you really want to discharge them fully. The appropriate type of battery would be Li-ion, because they would be chargeable every night AND would last longer. This is the biggest negative to this rig. If the battery packs were Li-ion, I would not care that they are packs versus separate batteries.

- Belt clip should be taken off to remove battery cover without beating the two up. This is apparently an obvious issue to the manufacturer because they have a protective piece of plastic between the two for shipment.

Neutral (strange):

Two standard USB chargers included, at 500mA output each (1A would be minimum standard and expected these days, but whatever; they may have done this to avoid overcharging overnight). Both have the same rated input, but the output is the same (samex2 on the 2 output charger). That actually doesn't make sense, unless the single charger is half as efficient (or they are just too lazy to change the nameplate). Not really sure what's up with that, but I sort of like the 2-output charger. I expect most people have so many USB chargers laying around that they'll use whatever is at hand anyway vice these.

These are a good way for me to extend my wifi to areas in my house that needed a signal boost.
Setup required a bit more effort due to vagueness or incomplete instructions. I had to reset these several times and start setup once I figured out what the units were doing. One key is to decide if you want to use these as a WIFI extender or a wired router system and setup the units with this understanding.

Once setup on the main router was complete adding the satellite units was as simple as pushing two buttons, and now you have a new MESH wifi network where your devices automatically transfer connectivity to the unit with the most powerful signal.

For speed the primary unit is pretty good. if my main router wifi speed is around 450mbs, the primary wifi is around 300mbs which is pretty good. Now the satellite units speeds drop down to around 45mbs which is good for an extender setup, and is somewhat dependent on how far from the primary unit they are, but the speed is never above 50 mbs. That gets us to range. if this was a wide open building with no interior walls I could see where two units would cover 2000 sq feet, but in reality 2 units are good for a around 1400 sq ft. This still isn't bad considering the install footprint.

What I do like these for is the network is always up no matter the main WIFI router condition. In other words if my main cable modem WIFI goes down, but I have my PC and Printer on this mesh system I can still print while the primary cable modem is down. Also devices connected to the mesh WIFI stay connected to the mesh WIFI, so those WIFI cameras outside are still able to record to my NAS drive even though my cable modem is offline.

Without repeating what everyone has said here, I will speak for Roku's support of the Plex media streaming software which is a free Roku channel. If you have never heard of it, it is a fantastic solution that allows you to use Roku (as well as all your portable devices and remote computers, including ones on the internet-at-large) to stream all of the movies on your computer, regardless of the format. On Roku, you can browse the movie collection on your computer using a slick interface and watch it in full resolution. (This is only if you have a fast connection like a home wireless network, and you need to configure it to do this- an easy settings change.) If your computer can play it, so can your Roku. The key to this is because all the transcoding of the video file happens on your computer so all Roku has to do is play the video stream. The result is that you can easily fast-forward and rewind, as well and have the jump-back feature like the TiVo has. This was the primary reason that I bought the Roku as it is a lot easier to use than trying to connect your computer directly to your TV and muddling about with computer controls to watch movies. The Plex interface on Roku is easy to use and very slick. It does nice things like look up movie data so you have the cover art, theme music, and movie info for you to peruse as you are browsing your library. Finally, there is the "Plex it!" feature which you can use with your computer's browser, so that when you find a video on the internet on your computer, you want to queue it up for later to watch on your TV, and it will appear in your movie queue in Plex on Roku, regardless of the video format! This also gets around the one annoying thing about Roku and that it doesn't have a native YouTube channel for some reason.

Most of the USB cables I have are either 3' cables or are really short ones that come with electronic devices. Sometimes a longer cable is really handy, especially when the immediate area surrounding a work space is cramped. I looked to these 10' cables to help alleviate one such issue and I learned a few things. One of those things is that a cable can be too long in some cases, though this is a failure in organization, not in the cable.

These are flat USB cables. Flat cables are less likely to tangle than their round counterparts, but I will confess to preferring round cables anyway (it’s a personal preference, not a technical preference). These are shielded in woven nylon which is great; the nylon is stronger than soft plastic shielding and gives the cable a little more stiffness but does not make the cable so stiff that it’s awkward to run. The connectors are interesting - two-tone plastic that is different than anything else on my desk which makes it a lot easier to determine where both ends of the cable are plugged in. I tried stressing the cable ends at the connectors by trying to pull out the shielding from the plugs and they held firm.

I tried one of these with my phone and it worked just fine, I was able to charge the phone and move data between it and my laptop. I did not attempt a speed test.

There is a big difference between 3' cables, 6' cables and 10' cables. If you need a 6' cable, a 10' cable will leave you trying to figure out what to do with the extra 4' of cable. In my case this meant having to use a twist tie to bunch the cable up in the middle. This is not a criticism but rather a suggestion - get a cable that’s the right length for the job. If you need a 10' cable, these have worked great for me.

These are nice USB cables. They seem to be made well and they work as expected. If you need a really long cable, this is a good choice.

I got a new 50 inch 7 series samsung tv that has a curved back, so the screws that came with the stand does not fit. The required screws were M8 x 45mm, but the longest screws were m8 x 35mm. I'm ok with that as this screen is newer and has a different curve on teh back than most flatscreen tvs out there.

After a run to Fastenal to obtain the right length screws, everything installed fine. In order to level horizontal axis properly, I left the screws on the horizontal bar slightly loose. After putting on the screen, adjust for horizontal level, and then tighten the screws on the horizontal bar.

Only issue that i came into after that was the whole tv would lean backwards ever so slightly, like 4-5 degrees. Very noticeable since my tv is next to a door and bookcase. I noticed the problem was in the design of the vertical bars that are installed onto the tv itself.

The upper hook part that clips onto the top part of the horizontal bar is not the same thickness as the bottom hook part that sits on the lower part of the horizontal bar. Thin vertical top, thicker vertical bottom, you get a screen that is angled looking slightly up. Maybe its a design flaw or maybe its designed to accommodate heavier TV's that may cause the screen to lean forward (my tv was kinda light).

A fix for my TV leaning back was shoving a few shims under the back of the base plate to get it to lean more forward (i used a stack of like 8 business cards on both rear corners of the base plate; seems to work fine).

Overall, i'm happy with my product. The ability to swivel was the sole reason i bought this.

--I dont have small hands, but they aren't exactly big either. Size can be in length and width. I have quite small fingers, but wide palms (3.75"). So typically a size "large" in gloves, but the ends of the fingers always dangle quite a bit. Hope that gives impression going forward with my review:

-- Not a loud click, but I can feel the click. I personally find that satisfying. Gentle yet makes me feel my action.

--Scrolling is smooth.
--No stuttering or jerkiness
--Instant connect when I first got this, and no problems since

Somewhere there is an ancient marketing survey that identifies teen-age boys as a prime segment of the gaming market and that says they really like bright, flashing lights. So manufacturers who want to sell to the gaming market still think they have to add flashy lighting to all their products. Well, the gaming universe is much larger than teen boys these days and bright, flashing lights have nothing to do with playing a game. With that pet peeve off my chest let me add a couple of things to give this review some context. First, I do spend a lot of time online playing an MMO but I'm very much a casual player, not a hardcore competitive one. Second, I am not an audiophile. High end stereo gear is wasted on me as the music coming from most any clock radio is good enough for me.

To my non-audiophile ears, the sound from this speaker is fine. It provides a nice range without being too heavy on the bass end or too shrill on the high end. Whether gaming, streaming videos, or listening to music and audiobooks, this speaker holds its own nicely. Though, like the flashy lighting, the sound quality really doesn't make any significant difference while I'm playing in my MMO world. The ambient noise, NPC chatter, battle music and such, all come through nicely but that's a perk, not something that particularly improves my game play.

The under the monitor design of this speaker really doesn't save me any desk space. The mini speakers I was using before were much smaller and were out of the way on the side of the monitor. This space bar basically sits in front of my monitor and takes up more room than other speakers. One strong plus to me for this speaker is the fact that it really is plug and play. I had it up and running in just a few minutes. Other "gaming" gear I've tried with flashy lighting systems require software to control the lighting and sometimes getting that software to install and run properly can be a major, frustrating effort. So I really, really like that this product lives up to its "plug and play" claim.

There is one last negative point to mention. a minor one. The volume and other controls are flat buttons on the side of the soundbar. So to adjust the volume, change the lighting, etc, you need to move the soundbar to look at the side of it so you can see what you are doing. I call that a minor issue because my keyboard has mute and volume control buttons on it and I can just use those to adjust the sound as needed.

The bottom line of all this for me is that I wouldn't buy this speaker as a "gaming speaker" but simply as a nice mid-range speaker who's sound quality I like, one that is easy to set up and use. Oh, and lest I sound too much like a Grinch, the lights really are pretty, the way Christmas lights are. It's just that they have nothing to do with gaming. :)

I still hook it up to external speakers (I'm partial to the Bose Companion 20) for movies and music when I'm at my desk, but it puts out more than adequate sound all on its own.

Response time is more snappy than the original Fire, and the carousel is easier to navigate (smoother scrolling). Picking up a WiFi signal seems to be better with the new fire - I'm getting all signal strength bars displayed in areas of the house where I could only get 2 or 3 bars with the original Fire.

The form factor is great for video watching. The extra screen size makes a big difference. The other huge advantage to the size is typing. It's MUCH easier to see and use the onscreen keyboard than on the original Fire. I had no problems typing without a stylus; on the original Fire a stylus is a must.

So far I don't see many misses other than a hard-to-find power button. The casing and build quality is not at the same level as an iPad, but neither is the price. I'm very pleased with the price-performance level of the HD Fire.

This is not replacing my original Fire - I'll continue to use that for most of my book reading and when I need portability. For everything else, the larger screen is well worth the additional cost.

I have a Nexus 7, the iPad 2 and an HP Touchpad and the Fire is my favorite by far. Not because either the original or this new Fire are the best in terms of build quality or speed or tech specs, but for one simple reason: the Fire makes it so incredibly easy to avail myself of entertainment and content. The tight link to the Amazon ecosystem is, for me, a huge plus - it keeps my entertainment pipeline full of things I want to read, listen to or watch with little or no effort on my part. And, best of all, a lot of that content is free through Prime.

Love it, and highly recommend.

First thing's first, it is important to understand what you are getting. This isn't a VR headset - you aren't going to be bringing these on a trip to play some beat saber. These are simply a screen that you can strap to your head.

Now that we have that out of the way, lets go into the things I love about these. Plugging these into a device is (usually) a breeze and you can get to consuming your content on a virtual screen in no time. The included blackout shade is a great addition, giving you the choice between maintaining situational awareness of your surroundings, or closing yourself off to the world and immersing yourself in the content.

I particularly like using these on a plane. It is great to be able to shut out everything that is going on around you and just watching content without your seatmates peeking over to see what you are watching. I do recommend using in-ear headphones since on or over ear types of headphones can get uncomfortable when combined with the glasses.

If you wear glasses, I suggest purchasing prescription lens inserts - it will really make your experience just that much better.

I think it is really smart that these are powered by whatever device they are plugged into. This allows the device to be less bulky and lighter; hence more comfortable for long term wear. The downside being, your device will consume power quicker. This can be mitigated with a wireless charger (since your glasses are plugged into your device).

I am not a huge fan of the iphone adapter solution, but it does work, and I find the experience better on iphone than other devices I have tried (samsung phone, iPad pro, and laptop).

Finally some affordable earbuds that sound great, and both sides actually work. For this reason I highly recommend!

Whether or not you'll like this case depends to a large extent on two things: 1) how much of a klutz you are, and 2) how you use your iPad.

Here's where I fit into that picture: I'm not generally klutzy -- I can count on one hand the number of times I've dropped any of my portable electronics in the past 10 years. I use my iPad mostly when I travel and don't want to bring my laptop, and it stays in my bag unless I'm using it. Otherwise, I bring it out now and again for games or to read (I have the Kindle app installed, and it works great for that). For me, this Otterbox case is probably a case of "overkill": perhaps a little more case than I really need.

The basics:
This is a multi-part case: the two-piece inner plastic "shell" with a clear window over the screen, the outer silicone "slipcover" that hugs the back and sides of the plastic shell, and another hard plastic snap-on outer "cover" that includes a pop-up stand, that snaps onto the back of the silicone cover.

The good:
This will definitely protect your iPad Pro 9.7. The thing is built like body armor -- solid, form-fitting, not too difficult to install. The colors "damson purple" and "hibiscus pink" aren't too garish, either, and match the photos on the page here.

The concern(s): The only screen protection is the thin plastic "screen protector" -- that's all. I'm a little concerned about how protective it would be in an accident. It would have been really nice if they had designed the outer cover/stand to snap onto the FRONT of the case. I've tried it a few times, and it doesn't work. The corner "clips" get caught in the silicone slipcover so that it can't snap securely. It only fits securely onto the BACK of the case. Pity.

Also, it's VERY heavy. I realize that you don't get this level of protection without adding weight, so that's a trade-off that you either choose to live with or not.

Soooo ... bottom line: if you have klutzy tendencies, if you're looking for 5-star protection for your iPad Pro and you're willing to live with added weight, this might be a super option. If you're more like me -- light user, not of the klutzy persuasion -- this might a little more protection than you really need. For me, it rates 3 stars: "It's OK."

I received this as a free review sample. This is not a zoom type telescope. You can adjust focus for your objective (the 52mm end) as well as the eye lens (the 16mm end), but you will not be able to zoom in. Think of this as a mono scope that can bring a far object into sharp focus.

Another thing to note is the field of vision is less than the 18 degrees marked on the body. It's about half that, and the night and day marking does not imply that this is a night vision scope. You will still need an external light source in low level lighting conditions. For example, moonlight will work, but in total darkness you will not be able to see a thing.

For me this is very useful for a hobby of mine, which is reptile spotting. Where I live there is an abundance of species, especially turtles and snakes, but we also have alligators and many interesting lizards. I prefer observing gators from a distance, and when walking down trails in parks (and there are many in my area) it's nice to be able to sit in a stationary point and scan for gators on banks as well as swimming. Same for various snakes, both land and water.

What I love about this scope is it's rugged. There are no lens caps, but the nylon case that comes with it makes it ideal for outdoors activities in harsh environments. It's outer material appears to be rubber, and I have dropped mine a few times without damaging it.

When you do bring an object into focus it's sharp and crystal clear. The field of vision may seem narrow, but you can actually take in a lot of details by slow scanning. It may take a little time to get accustomed to viewing wide fields of vision with it, but once you do, it's easy to use.
