Trying to decide if we were ready to cut the cord, we installed this antenna to see if we could get all the local channels. We got 40 digital channels about 20 miles west of Washington DC and the major networks are crystal clear.

The network towers we use are clustered together about 20 miles away. We have 2 or more topographical obstructions between our house and the towers (no line of sight). The Noise Margin on the networks is 35-40 dB. TVFool.com listed my location as "yellow" (which means use an attic antenna or higher). The cable drop is about 25 feet and I did not use an amplifier.

This antenna is supposed to be omni-directional but we did experience occasional signal drop on the networks with the initial "eyeball" installation (which was off about 15 degrees). Standing directly under the antenna and looking through a compass I had my son walk through the yard until he stepped into the path to the towers. Then I had him stand still, facing the antenna, and rotated it until he told me it was pointed straight over his head. That seemed to fix the signal drops. Given all the factors of our situation, I am probably maxing out the performance of this antenna. If I have any issues I'll just buy the add-on the reflector shield to increase directional performance...but for right now I don't need it.

Installation was easy (I just mounted it to the Direct TV mast). This antenna is small and light which was a big plus when climbing up a 25 foot ladder.

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential. Unfortunately while the hardware has improved dramatically the software often has not - which is the case with this set.

The set I got did not come with a hard drive which wasn’t a big deal as I always have a few around. A suitable SATA Hard Drive can be purchased for $25-$400 depending on size and quality.

In terms of this system it should be clear based on the price - this is a budget system. That doesn’t mean it won’t work but these cameras are not going to pan, tilt or zoom (the lens is fixed).

If these are installed with this in mind they can still be very effective they just need to be positioned correctly.

For instance if these cameras were placed up high on a second floor overhang you would see an overview of the surrounding area but would not be able to zoom in to see facial characteristics. On the other hand, if placed on a porch a bit above head height you will have no issue making out the same. Placement is key.

In terms of wiring any POE (Power Over Ethernet) camera is excellent. The cameras are powered and transmit data over the same Ethernet cable. There are several advantages to these systems the most important is security as the cameras are not broadcasting wirelessly making them more difficult to hack.

The camera operation is excellent for the price. The images are clear and crisp and night vision operates without issue.

Where this set falls apart is on the software side - unfortunately this is often the case. The software is so non user friendly that it is almost unusable. I have used countless similar systems and this has to be among the all time worst software operating systems I have ever encountered.

There are countless glitches and bizarre, nonsensical methods for how it has to be initiated that it became comical as I worked through them all. I’ve actually used it as an example with colleagues as why a system must be actually set up prior to recommending it as on its face this appears to be an excellent value but the software unfortunately ruins what otherwise would be an excellent budget system. Unfortunately one depends on the other.

Due to the horrid software this set depends upon I would not recommend it. I can only hope the manufacturer would scrap the current software completely and rebuild with modern usability standards being their primary concern.

These devices are supposed to emit a 90-decibel beep when you point the hand-held radio transmitter at them. Well, if that's 90 decibels, then 90 decibels isn't very loud. According to Purdue University, 90 db is as loud as a "Boeing 737 or DC-9 aircraft at one nautical mile (6080 ft) before landing (97 dB); power mower (96 dB); motorcycle at 25 ft (90 dB). Then I was able to format it with Windows from the existing SSD (hidden partition). Finally I removed the laptop cover, took the old SSD out and put the new SSD in. The old SSD went into the SSD external enclosure. It was easy to copy all the files from the external hdd to the new 1 TB drive, and I've been up and running with no issues. I have worn these for thirty minutes and up to three hours consecutively in vary increments, every day for five days now and never had cauliflower ear. Nor do my ears get hot. I'm using these with my Fire Tablet, my LG V10 phone and Sceptre 55" television playing music through our cable provider's music stations. The connection plug is tight and the cord has proven to be long enough for use in bed at night while reading, on the sofa reading & it rolls up to put in my pocket while wandering around cleaning house and doing barn chores.

Simple acoustic vocal pieces from James Taylor, Tracy Chapman and Paul Simon are beautifully rendered and you can appreciate the realism of a live performance. I have several of the Logitech M510, and think this is the best general purpose mouse you can buy. It's comfortable in the hand -- I have a large hand, some in the family have larger hands, some have smaller hands, but everyone finds the mouse comfortable to use. It's precise, easy to configure, and I'm very fond of the tiny usb adapter.

I particularly like the fact that you only need use one usb adapter for multiple devices (the "unifying receiver"). In fact you can switch between different Logitech mice if you need to do so (e.g., for a portable).

As for the keyboard, I was a little wary of the "wave" shape, not having used one before, and having some mild carpal tunnel issues. But to my relief, the keyboard is really comfortable to use, the wrist rest is well placed, provides support just where I need it. The keys have a nice touch, not too light, not too heavy, so perfect for me. There are a number of programmable buttons on the keyboard, most of which I tend to use only occasionally, mostly because I forget I have them. But the volume control is very useful, as is the button to bring up the calculator.

Do make sure you install the Logitech SetPoint software (you can download from their website) to properly configure the devices. You'll need that to make good use of the unifying receiver, among other things.

So if you're looking for a good mouse keyboard combo, I can happily recommend this set. If you just want one or the other, I still recommend the M510 mouse, and one of the many Logitech wireless keyboards that you can buy separately. (For instance, I also have the K270 keyboard, and find it to be quite good.)

USB hubs are one of those computer extras that don't get a lot of attention or thought until one runs out of ports. When needed, though, a hub can greatly expand the USB capabilities of a system. This particular hub is one that comes with its own power supply, which is in my opinion better for most uses.

This is an unassuming little device, about the size of a small harmonica and about as solid. Its small size allows it to take up a small amount of desk space, tucking easily behind a monitor or case (or, if being used with a laptop, behind the whole system). In my specific situation I have it plugged into a laptop with an external monitor attached to it so I have the hub just at the base of the external monitor where it is out of thew way but still easily accessible.

In use, it works as it should. My one real test for the hub was to connect up an external USB hard drive, which does not work well with my other USB hub (coincidentally, also a Belkin product). When I attached the hard drive, the system immediately saw it and assigned a drive letter to it, just as if I connected it directly. This is how a hub should handle such a drive and I was pleased when there was no issue.

The one complaint I have with this hub is that the power cord is not snug. When the hub is moved while attached it is very easy to disconnect it from the power supply. My workaround was to use a twist tie to attach the power cord to the USB cable that attaches the hub to the system, after which I can move the hub without any difficulty.

This is a decent USB hub that works as it is supposed to work. Other than the less-than-secure plug for power I have no complaints.

At first glance the Asus VivoBook V551LA-DS17T appears to be a nice touch-screen UltraBook-class computer, but it is a few steps beyond a typical UltraBook. Combining features of UltraBook systems and multimedia/entertainment workstations, this computer is what new systems ought to be. There are a couple of design decisions I would change and it's by no means a high-end gaming rig, but Asus got the important things right.

There are two things that set this system apart from a normal UltraBook. First is the inclusion of a slimline CD/DVD R/W drive. I have seen no other UltraBooks out there that include one, so finding one in this system was a very pleasant surprise. Carrying an external CD/DVD drive around can be inconvenient (especially when traveling) so having a built-in drive is a huge plus. Asus managed to include this drive in the system while still keeping the system to roughly an inch thick. The other differentiating factor that makes this system different than other UltraBooks I have seen (and not in a positive way) is the weight. This is a particularly heavy system and will make toting it around a chore.

I booted up the system and configured it for use and immediately went about looking for the utility for making recovery/restore DVD media. After searching the file system and the installed program list with no success I finally resorted to calling technical support. I spoke to a charming young lady who was exceptionally helpful and got me on my way to creating a recovery USB drive. So, from that experience I can say that technical support is courteous and helpful. However, I never did figure out how to make DVD media, but at least I can restore the system now should I have a need to do so.

After power-on for the first time it performed a bunch of hands-off updates and when it finished and finally allowed interaction with the OS it was loaded with Windows 8.1; it wasn't obvious if the initial OS install was 8 or 8.1 but that is irrelevant - 8.1 is what is there when the user can finally begin exploring the system. I spent a little time digging through the list of installed applications and was pleased to see that Asus did not load this system up with excessive bloatware. There are several applications I do not need and I intend to remove them - MS Office and McAfee protection services being among them - but at least what is there is not unreasonable. Interestingly, most new systems I have used have come with 1-2 years of internet security protection, but this system comes with just 30 days.

One design decision that really surprised me is that this system does not include a solid-state drive (SSD). I understand the reason - it drives up cost - but to me having an SSD in this system would make it even faster and make the battery last longer. This is by no means a deal-breaker but bootup times are slower as a result.

Asus makes a big deal about the touch screen on this system and touts it as more sensitive than most other touch screens. Asus' claims appear to be well-founded as the other touch screen systems available to me are nowhere near as responsive. After spending a couple of hours working with this system I unplugged my trackball and I don't think I will need it again for this particular system. If you are buying this system for the ability to use the touch screen, you will be pleased.

Battery life so far is excellent. I charged the system up completely and spent a good three hours using it for web surfing and typing up documents and the battery still maintains more than half of its charge. I plan to load up my development environment and see how the battery holds up under load, and I expect that to make the battery drain faster, but for typical use (surfing the web, writing document and watching online videos) the battery seems to be very much in the game.

The graphics system is provided by the Intel chipset and it is acceptable for most uses. It's not high end graphics but it's not terrible either. Serious gamers will not appreciate this system whereas most casual gamers and people using the system for more business-types of functions will be more than satisfied. As an experiment I had my teenage son load up Minecraft (an online game that uses 1st-person perspective) and test the graphics. He noticed that while the game played well enough it is not quite as smooth as a system that has a dedicated graphics card.

Wi-Fi connection speed seems to be about average with other wireless-n devices on the network.

One thing that really startled me is the quality of the sound system. Asus says that this is the best configuration for embedded sound available and I found the sound quality coming from the embedded speakers to be more than acceptable. The speakers are on the bottom of the unit and are visible via two inch-long slits in the case. In spite of the small aperture, the output is very good, better than one would expect.

With the slimline DVD and the decent sound quality, paired with the i7 processor and 8GB RAM this system is well-suited for multimedia tasks such as video production and music creation. It has the horsepower to handle the renders and so far has performed well while working on either audio or video composition. As I mentioned above I expect these types of activities to take more battery than less strenuous tasks but I have not spent enough time with these types of applications on this system yet to determine just how much they will impact battery life.

The touch pad is a bit better than average and is placed well. One issue I have with most laptops is that I tend to tap the touch pad while typing and on occasion I can highlight and delete a whole section of text unintentionally. So far this has not been a problem with this system and I think it has a lot to do with the way the touch pad is positioned relative to the open space on the keyboard. Asus includes a very nice utility (accessible by a special key on the keyboard) that makes turning the touch pad on and off very simple, so it's easy to eliminate any issue with it if it's "in the way" while typing.

The power adapter is odd and I am not sure I like it. The shape requires a little planning as it is a square block pressed against the wall when it is plugged in. Most adapters typically have the brick in the middle. So, plugging this adapter in when working in a cramped space could potentially pose a challenge. Another observation - the adapter gets rather warm.

I do not like the way the hard drive is partitioned right out of the box. It appears that the drive was simply chopped into two roughly equal partitions, the D: drive labeled as "data". I decided to toss in a Linux LiveCD and boot it up to see how well supported the touch screen is with a current distribution. I have waited a while to review this because I got it for my daughter who was very interested to have it, but after a while, she lost interest so it was back to me. Let's take a look.

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?
This comes in a box with a cord for recharging. It has a type C connector. There are also earbuds in the box. Insturctions? Well, not so much.

TOUCHSCREEN
That is kind of deceptive. This has a touch screen on bottom, but the top is not - where you see the photo of the album playing, the play button or other information.

MUSIC QUALITY
The music quality of this is fabulous. It is better using bluetooth headphones than the speaker or the cheap buds that come with this.

EAR BUD JACK
The problem with this player is that the jack is very touchy. If you move just right it will disconnect either ear and that is totally annoying when using this.

MUSIC SEQUENCE
That is another odd feature of this player. This will play in order when I have albums in it and so far they play in alphabetical order which is rather strange. I can not get it to play any other way than this way, so if you are using this and want to hear what YOU want to hear in a certain order, plan to play around with this a lot.

RECORDING BUTTON
This has some storage on it, so you can record with the little red recording button. That can come in handy if you need it, but I don't use it much. It works.

SPEAKER
This has its own little speaker on it which is handy for using the auto alarm function if you are camping or something and don't want to use your phone for that.

AUTO ALARM FUNCTION
This will wake you up if you want it to.

FM RADIO
This works pretty good, but again, the jack is toast, which is part of the antenna grounding the signal, so in my case, it is good but not WOW.

INSTRUCTIONS
This really is frustrating. This should have extensive instructions in it. This thing is really frustrating despite it being almost user friendly in some ways. In others it is downright frustrating.

BATTERY LIFE
The battery life on this is great. If not in use for a long period, it will keep the charge nicely, a feature I appreciate.

TOUCHY TOUCH SCREEN
This bottom half with the touch screen is very touchy. If I have it in my pocket and it hits my body just right, it will change to another song. Sometimes it will go to another direction if I put my hand in my pocket which is frustrating. That part is also difficult.

BLUETOOTH
This is a great feature. I had no problems hooking this up to my bluetooth headphones at all. It was easy and stayed connected, but I am at home when I use this and not around other wireless items, so I am not sure how well this would work when around other devices.

WHO MIGHT LIKE THIS?
If you are in need of some music and don't want your phone handy and feel like it does not matter what songs you hear in what order, then this might be a good mindless device for running, or working around cleaning, etc. It also might be nice for a young person who is not supposed to be using their phone and you want to give them something else to play music with.

THE BOTTOM LINE
For the price, the music quality is fantastic, the bluetooth connection is also very easy and one of the best I have used. As for other things like the music order, lack of instructions, and super touchy controls, this takes the fun out of using it.

MY RATING
I am between 3 and 4 stars for this. I am going with FOUR STARS. It is BARELY four stars though. The bluetooth and music quality are excellent. The screen is also decent too. The price is right. However, the other frustrations and lack of instructions frustrate me a bit. I am sure there are ways to put the music on there, but I just don't have the time to mess with it. Kids would probably have a lot of fun messing with this and making it do all sorts of amazing things.

It's hard to find ear buds that aren't specifically made for iPhones so this is a great find. I use it successfully on my Samsung Focus smartphone.

The sound quality is crisp and well-defined. Every pitch from the really low to the really high is clear. The 'extreme' port isn't as boom-y as you would think and I use it for all types of music, though music with really heavy bass like Deadmau5 or rap can be a little intense (but I'm too lazy to change the port to a less boom-y level.) The cord is better than other ear buds because it has less 'micro-phonics', meaning when it rubs against your clothes you get less loud, irritating noise coming into your ears.

The remote control/mic is very nice to have and is an important reason why I bought these. You can switch to talking on the phone and you can use it to skip forward or backward between tracks. However, I have 2 complaints about it. First, it is very difficult to find the actual button that you need to push to operate it. It is flush with the body of the remote so you can't feel it. I have to reach for the remote and actually look for the markings on it to find the button. Also, I wish it had volume control.

It is also great because it has an angled jack which, in my experience, lasts much longer than the straight ones that tend to short out quickly because of the way they get pulled back and forth within the phone/mp3 player you are using.

I use the flanged ear tips that it is packaged with and they don't fall out. The little case that is included is hard-sided and provides a lot more protection than fabric pouches. It could be a little larger, though, so that the cord could be coiled more loosely.

Overall, after lots of research and testing, these are the best I've found. The complaints I have are minor compared to the brilliance of the sound quality. I highly recommend them.

***** UPDATE TO REVIEW:

After 4 months, the earphones still sound great. There is one complaint that I didn't mention in the original review: the cord tangles and can be a little irritating to untangle. But I imagine that is a problem with all earbuds. I still like them overall.

I hate to change the battery for the Ring Doorbell. It's one of the reasons that I didn't purchase those "stick up" cameras to put up around the house. I am not interested in having to change batteries every month. With that in mind, I set out to find a solar panel that works with my Ring Doorbell 2.

Looking at other listings, I saw that the ones that claim to work with Ring generate 5v, 3amps. I confirmed that this board also generates 5v, 3a (check my pictures) and took the chance to cut off the microusb connector that it came with.

What was exposed were two wires; red and black so there was no guess work necessary to figure out which wires would be positive and ground (usb usually has 4 wires). After stripping the wires, I screwed the wires to the back of the doorbell and crossed my fingers.

From my pictures, you'll see that the Ring app recognized the solar panel and also charged from 46% to 55% after one day in the sun.

Note: The wire is a little bit short so it may not reach your roof. I was able to get around this by soldering a longer wire from an old cell phone car charger.

This review covers two different models of the Arctic fan:

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>Model with USB hub:
I have been using the original ARCTIC Breeze for a while and have been very pleased with its performance, and especially pleased with how quiet it runs. The Pro model builds on that and adds a few more useful features.

Unlike the original model which had a bendable stem with a USB plug on the end, the Pro has a base so the fan can be positioned away from the USB port on the PC. The attached power cord is a little over 5 feet long, making it possible to put the fan on my desk and plug it into the PC on the floor.

The base also has 4 USB input ports, so it works as a USB hub. It has a 5V power input jack if you want to turn this into an active hub. The power adapter to do so is NOT included.

Unlike the single-speed original version, this has a knob so you can vary the speed. It's not precise, but there is a somewhat noticeable difference between low and high. It's a continually variable speed - you can turn the dial to whatever speed you like.

Best of all, it's just as quiet, if not quieter, than the original model. That's the biggest plus for me by far, since the cheap USB fans make a racket. This just makes a low-pitched hum. The build quality is solid - the base is sturdy, and the bendable arm holds its position well.

One negative: the packaging. It's in a clam shell package that is a major, major pain to open!

While it's more expensive than the original, the added benefits of being able to position it on a desk and use it as a hub makes the upgrade worth considering. Highly recommend.

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>USA EDITION:
I've have (and use) a couple other Arctic USB fans and have been 100% satisfied with them. This new version (their "USA Edition") has a couple of improvements over past designs.

The base is a metal plate which increases the fan's stability when you're bending the stem to point the fan. The on/off/speed dial switch no longer has a lit LED ring around it. I never found the lit LED ring to be bothersome on the other Arctic fans, so having or not having it is not a big deal to me.

The base also does away with the USB hub connections that other models have. That's keeps the base more streamlined and allows it to have a lower profile. It also does away with the clam shell packaging, instead using a very easy to open box.

The build quality of this, like the other Arctic fans I have, is excellent. The stem is bendy by stays put where you want it; the operating sound is pretty hushed; the on/off/speed control works well. The overall design is attractive, with a red/white/blue color scheme and graphics.

It moves a surprising amount of air. No, it won't blow your hair back as a Vornado fan will, but this makes a noticeable difference in circulating air. The size makes it very easy to find a spot on your desk to position it.

While I can't speak to the long-term reliability of this as of yet, I expect it will last for some time. I have an Arctic fan similar to this that I've been using almost daily for the past 1+ years, and it still works as good as it did when new.

This is the no-BS line from Cisco. Enterprise features, but nothing proprietary, no forced contracts, no stupid power port that requires special power cords...

You can hook this up and it will work right out of the box, just like an unmanaged switch, which will make network setup and augmentation very easy. Once I signed into the box, I pretty much had to change my password, but then I had a world of options at my fingertips that I could change at my leisure. There were a few things I wanted to configure right away, and plenty of others I realized I wanted after doing some research. I still have plenty to learn and play with when I have time I want to spend on this.

I do believe you can use Cisco command line to configure these, but it also has a very familiar (to other consumer/business equipment) GUI that is intuitive to use. I will say, though, that the GUI it can be pretty cumbersome if you want to use it to go through and turn on a feature on every single port individually. Part of the problem is that you have to save each port individually and then use the drop-down to do the next port. This switch can be a little slow to respond and therefore frustrating when changing multiple features in a row. I also have a 350 series 10 port switch that does NOT have that problem. I am not sure if it has more resources available or just has less to keep track of because of having fewer ports., but that might be a consideration if choosing between the 250 and 350 series. And if you use command line, you might not care at all...

Oh, and you have to do the "save to running config" thing like you do with the Enterprise stuff. Seems strange, but I guess it more or less makes sense why. But at least in this case you can just click apply...and then go up and click the blinking disk to save (to running config).

I am using this in my telecomm closet, which manages to keep nearly all the ports in my house hot. I'm using ports 25-27 as a 3Gbps link to my Cisco 350 series switch in my external cabinet, which connects my servers with multi-Gb links. This is all new functionality for me, but something I've been looking for for a long time.

Here's some random stuff I figured out along the way:

-I am using 10Gbps copper DACs between the two devices. They do negotiate down to 1Gbps, they are cheaper than buying multiple SFPs, and I can use them later when I get 10Gbps ports (so the only reason you'd use fiber is if you needed a >100m link.

-Port trunking works between DAC and regular Cat6 (apparently it won't work with fiber SFPs mixed with Cat6.

-Not sure what I was doing wrong before port trunking on another switch, but I couldn't get anything better than high-error best effort to work as far as speed. On these 250/350 Cisco devices I'm using, all four of my trunks are working perfectly and clearly working at full speed without uncorrected errors (if any at all).

-There are "green features" included, but off by default. The one looks at link length and lowers power on those links if less than 50m. You can only use this if you turn off the Energy Efficient Ethernet standardized protocol, which you might do if the device you are using doesn't work, but I haven't found a case where it correctly reads my link length (and my testers do figure out the correct length, so I don't get this). The other green feature is Energy Detect, which I've turned on across the board, but it's hard to tell if that really saves energy or not, because it just is "on" when the link is down.

-The ports are counted strangely. Port 1 is the top left. Port 2 is bottom left. Port 3 is top second from left, etc. This caused me some brief confusion. The great thing is that you can name all your ports in the GUI so that can make things a lot more clear for you, especially if you keep all ports in your building hot or if you at least keep most of the devices static.

There are a ton of features here, and even more on the 350 series. If you're deciding between the 250 and 350 series, I suggest you do some serious homework to figure out if you actually need the 350 series. Here are just a few of the things I noticed the 350 series has that the 250 does not (not a comprehensive list):

On the 350, you can set link speeds lower on LAGS, use protected LAGS, more LAGS, UDLD, Ethernet tagging, VLAN mapping/private VLAN, lots of VLAN grouping options and more VLAN settings in general, and ISCSI status for QoS.

Oh...worth noting is that the 350 series apparently allows many more trunk groups than the 250 series, which only allows 4, so I would not necessarily want a 250 series for my 24 port switch if I didn't have my servers separate on the 350 (yet it seems unlikely you'd need more than 4 trunk groups on a 10 port 350).

One thing I don't like is that on some rack mounted equipment, you have one set of "wings/ears", but multiple positions/mounting options. These mounting brackets at least are included, but seem like they'd only work with this switch AND you can only put them on in one position, which means the switch will protrude about an inch forward in your cabinet (Well, you can also mount the switch backwards, if you consider that helpful). It would be better to have the option of recessing the switch an inch if you needed to. I also wish they could recess the power supply port on these things since - even with the heatsink on the back of this - the power cord is still the thing making this a tight fit in my closet.

Despite those two nitpicks, there's really nothing about this switch I don't love. Yes, I can absolutely imagine this to be a great line for a company to use, and I think I could even get a robust network up and running without too much stress or trouble. But there are plenty of other real-world applications for a home network as well: setting restrictions for kids or renters or whoever from getting to all areas of your network. There is all kinds of port security features here, protected ports, and VLAN features, so you should be able to do just about anything you want to do with these switches. Also QoS, traffic limiting, etc. I love having these features at my disposal, even at home!

As befits its price tag, the Sony has the look of a budget receiver with its old-school silver chassis. Build quality is decent enough: the fascia has a mixture of polished buttons and knobs including an input selector and volume control. The unit's remote control will be familiar to some - it features styling similar to the remotes that come with Sony's W Series of LCD TVs.

Before we get stuck into how the SRT-DG820 sounds, it's worth noting that Sony went back to the drawing board for its whole 2008 receiver range. And the Japanese giant has introduced various new features that, it claims, help improve performance.

For starters, the chassis of the STR-DG820 has been strengthened and embossed in certain places to help control any nuisance vibrations and minimize their effect on the key video/audio components found at the rear of the receiver.

High-definition audio decoding

Sony has even used custom-made brackets to secure the front panel and chassis and improve rigidity. The key video circuitry has been positioned as close as possible to the receiver's HDMI inputs for a shorter signal path and minimal interference.

The STR-DG820 offers 7.1 channels of surround sound (100w per channel) and can decode all major high-definition audio formats, including Dolby Digital TrueHD and DTS-HD Master Audio.

An inquisitive look around the rear of the receiver reveals a good selection of sockets. These include four HDMI inputs, (including a dedicated Blu-ray input), one HDMI output and three sets of component video inputs. The receiver also includes one coaxial and three optical digital inputs.

However, there is one notable omission: multichannel analogue inputs. So, your player has to be able to stream the HD data through HDMI for everything to work properly. In addition - not that you'd really expect them at this price - there are no pre-outs.

At this point it's also worth pointing out that the STR-DG820 can't upscale (Sony's step-up 'ES' range can upscale to 1080p), nor can it upconvert (again, the 'ES' range can). These features aren't vital, but upconversion would have been a welcome addition.

Sky HD usability issues

It also has to be noted that early versions of this receiver have had compatibility issues with Sky HD, which does not carry surround sound via its HDMI connection.

When you hook the Sky HD box's HDMI feed into the Sony and the Sky HD surround sound in via an optical input, the receiver over-rides the optical so you only hear the stereo feed supplied via HDMI.

Sony is working on a fix that will be applied to all existing and future STR-DG820 models. In the meantime, you can get round the issue by connecting your Sky HD via HDMI directly to your TV or projector, and via optical through the receiver - in this way you'll get both HD pictures and full surround sound.

Silky sound, dynamic dialogue

But back to the receiver in action. Set-up is done through Sony's Digital Cinema Auto Calibration system. It's ridiculously quick, easy to use and accurate - the receiver takes just a few seconds to set up.

And, hooked up to a Blu-ray player such as the Panasonic DMP-BD30, the Sony sounds sensational. Fed the Dolby TrueHD soundtrack from Batman Begins, the STR-DG820 impresses with its solid, controlled sound.

When Batman's Tumbler causes havoc on the streets of Gotham City, the Sony delivers explosions with a fine sense of immediacy and impact. Bass notes don't wallow or linger. In fact, you soon forget you're listening to a `budget' receiver.

The Sony is a dab hand at dialogue, too. Voices sound full-bodied and boast exceptional clarity, even during the most boisterous action scenes. There's no trace of brashness or harshness in the sound that could prove tiresome over prolonged listening.

Sure, more expensive receivers can give you a greater spread of sound and greater scale but, for this sort of money, the STR-DG820 is an absolute star.

It's equally adept at music

Dare we say it, the Sony also sounds adept when it comes to CD playback. Press the Analog Direct button to turn off all unnecessary internal processing and the receiver's clear, composed sound once again comes to the fore.

It exhibits a fine sense of rhythm for an AV receiver and dishes out decent bass weight during Eminem's Without Me.

When it comes to hands free devices, I am pretty particular about what I need to have handy. I like to have ear pieces like this handy when I am shopping or out doing errands should I need to receive important business calls. I also have to be available due to health issues of family members. Let's see how this one measures up.

WHAT IS THIS EARPIECE LIKE?
This hands-free earpiece is black. That does make it harder to find in a pocket of a purse or carry case. The outside of the entire unit is black.

LIGHTS
There is a green battery light on the outside and a blue bluetooth light on the outside when you turn it on. When you turn it off, the battery light turns to red so you know that is what you are doing with it. I LOVE this feature.

EAR BUD
The ear bud is only one size. There are three ear covers in this set. Two of them have an ear circle in them which allows you to wear it with or without the ear loop that hooks over the entire ear. One of them has no ear circle (the kind that fits into your hear cartilage).

EAR HOOK
There is one ear hook connected to this ear piece and then there is an extra in case you break that one. This fits around the outside of the ear hooking it into place for added security.

Mini USB
The charging plug on the outside is pretty uniform.

CORD
It comes with a 12 inch cord that goes from USB to mini USB for charging. You will need to have a receptacle to plug that into.

INSTRUCTION BOOKLET
Instruction book is minimal. This is a basic set which I LOVE. It is pretty straight forward. You turn on the phone, turn on the ear piece and they pair. Then to turn up volume, you press one side of the bar, down is the other side and muting is both at once. To hang up press outiside of earpiece.

BATTERY TIME
This thing stays charged a LONG time. I rarely have to recharge it, although I do not use it daily. It also holds a charge when not used for a long time as long as it it not left on endlessly.

RECEPTION/MICROPHONE
Here is where my review gets difficult. The first few times I used this, the caller at the other end complained because the sound was so bad. I was even told that the old handsfree speaker in my car was better and that was like a tin echo chamber.

I was all set to write my review, after all, it was pretty cut and dried. Then for some reason I could not write my review, and I had to use the earpiece to call someone again. WOW, the comments:

"I am so glad you are not using your ear piece, that thing was awful. Your voice has never sounded so clear."

"WOW, your phone is so CLEAR. I can not hear anything around you. Where ARE you?"

That second comment, I was shopping in a loud area. Now I had a dilemma. It was like I had two different earpieces! People were commenting on how wonderful it was now, but previously, these SAME PEOPLE could not stand it before. Nothing had changed. Same phone, same earpiece, same people.

So, I tested this quite a bit and the more positive feedback outweighed the negative, so I will say that this is a fantastic OMG marvelous earpiece sometimes and other times it is not as good.

STREAMING MUSIC
This is a decent earpiece for streaming music or programming on the phone, but I tend to use it more for temporary phone answering when I am not in my car.

COMFORT
This is not as comfortable as other earpieces I have had. I still prefer my older plantronics ear piece as it is so comfortable I don't notice it is in my ear after a while. This one is a bit too large. I actually prefer to wear it without the rubber cushion on it if I have to use it for any length of time. The ear hook helps it stay on pretty well. Once in a while I will use the rubber cushion and it is not too bad.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is a solid performer as a hands free earpiece. It has potential to deliver fantastic phone calls much of the time, and once in a while not as nice, but it still works. For comfort, I have had better, but this is not too bad. It has extra pieces which I love, and the colored lights on it are fantastic.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. This is a nice solid hands free ear piece. Despite a period of time when I was not so sure, longer term testing brought out its good points and solid performance. I would get this again.

Unboxing: Wouldn't usually make a section of this, but every once in a while a product makes it a pleasure. Especially a weird one like this. It's like unboxing a little UFO. It starts out in something like a hat box with a couple sticky tabs of tape to remove. Wish they could have found a better closure method, but the box is nice. Inside that you're immediately presented with the odd looking earbuds and a starter guide (also round) that has you immediately trying them on and fitting the best sleeve size for in your ear. There are no extra sleeves obviously apparent, so time to dig deeper. Next up is the UFO. A large earbud like this needs a large charging case. This one is round and unzips like some of the nicer headphone cases, but it's also a hard case with lights and buttons. Nothing inside but a charging dock. Under it is a secret compartment (made less secret by the thumb holes for easy removal). At the bottom of the hat box we have our missing sleeves and a charging cord.

Even with a diagram, putting these on was confusing and took four tries. Once they're on though, they are quite comfortable, and I think I'll learn to put them on after a few more tries.

Back to the book, and ugh! now they're telling me to put them in the charging case to pair. But I just finally got them on! &*^@#!

Ok, after getting things paired and back on, I'm able to put them through some testing. I'm not really an audiophile, but I've tried a lot of earbuds. Comfort is good. They don't rely on being stuck in your ear to hold themselves up, so there isn't a high stress point that's going to get sore first. They sound good. Better than most, but not the best I've heard. The control button is on the back of your ear, and I find it awkward and unreliable. Noise cancellation is solid, but like every other one I've tried, it is hard to tell sometimes because it scales with volume. Turning them on in a noisy room doesn't result in a quiet room, but turning up what you are listening to will result in noise other than what you are listening to disappearing quite a lot. There is a passthrough mode if you need to hear what's going on around you, but it doesn't sound very nice.

I like that it's USB-C. No more having to turn the cord over three times to figure out which end is up, and much faster charging. The case has three lights to show you charge progress for the case Each one represents enough charge for one full use of the earbuds. There's also a light on the top to tell you whether the earbuds are charged yet.

It's a solid product. Not my top favorite, but definitely innovative and a competitive offering.

I really like the "ZeroTouch" voice-command app that comes with this ZEROTOUCH DASHBOARD CELL PHONE HOLDER (With Voice-Command App for Android Phones). It was easy to set up on my Galaxy S7 Edge, and it seems to work very well "on the road".

I haven't tested it a whole lot (because of physical installation issues, more on that later), but it seems to have an excellent, up-to-date GPS Navigator, and a terrific Text Message Handler. To send or reply to a text, you wave a hand to wake the app, tell it to "Send a message to (name a contact)", dictate the message, listen to the readback, and answer "yes" to the query "Should I send it". If you have the Samsung "S Voice", it's quite similar, except that "ZeroTouch" notifies you of incoming text messages, and lets you reply to them strictly with voice commands.

The "ZeroTouch" app only works when your cellphone is docked with the cellphone car mount base. Docking and mounting are where I ran into problems. First, there aren't many places in a Honda Civic that are suitable for a suction-cup-base cellphone holder--at least not if you worry about the suction cup losing its grip and dumping your expensive smartphone on the car floor.

Second, the cellphone docks with the car mount base via a thin, adhesive-backed magnetic plate that you're supposed to attach directly to your cellphone or cellphone case. (Tip: If you're having trouble pairing during setup, place the thin metal plate that attaches to your phone directly atop the round part of the base until the magnet grips.) Attaching the plate was an issue, because I didn't want to apply it directly to my new phone (and maybe mar the finish). Applying the plate to my cellphone case worked for a short time, but the adhesive wasn't strong enough to hold the cellphone case through repeated dockings and undockings. Now the adhesive is worn out and won't adhere to anything.

However, there is a workaround. If only the magnetic plate is docked on the base, the "Zero Touch" app will work whenever your cellphone is NEAR the base--within Bluetooth range, I guess. So my hands-free calling/messaging arrangement uses the Honda Civic's two cupholders. The base with the docking strip goes in one cupholder, and the cellphone with the "Zero Touch" app goes in the other.

With this setup, I can use all of the "Zero Touch" features. Of course, if I want to use the handy "parking location finder" feature, I need to undock the magnetic strip from the base when I leave the car, just as I would if the strip were still attached to my cellphone.

The magnetic plate did NOT interfere with my S7 Edge's wireless charging feature, when I had the plate attached to the lower quarter of the cellphone case. (The "ZeroTouch" app setup has a diagram showing you where to attach the plate, if you use wireless charging.)

Because I love the easy-to-use "ZeroTouch" app, but am dissatisfied with the holder mounting arrangement (suction cup and adhesive may not adequately secure the cellphone), I rate this product at 4 stars ("I like it" on the official Amazon scale).

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

If you are new to home security camera systems, I recommend going with wired (non-WiFi), NVR or computer based recorders run with systems such as Blue Iris. This type of system is infinitely more secure and stable. While initial setup costs are a bit more the security it affords is worth every penny. It always pays to research the products, discuss them with those in the field, understand vulnerabilities and PLAN YOUR SYSTEM PRIOR TO PURCHASING ANYTHING. If you are at all tech savvy at all you can do it. While there is a bit of a learning curve it is not awful and in the end you will be thankful for the time you spent in the beginning as it will save you time, money and endless frustration.

I have set up, tested and reviewed more security systems and individual products than I can possibly remember. Without question my go to solution for home security solutions is a computer based, Blue Iris system with POE cameras run off of quality POE switches. This type of system is not only easy to operate but is highly secure.

As with any component there are a host of factors to consider. In terms of cameras more megapixels is not always better. For instance 2MP cameras often perform better in low light while 5MP will allow for more detail when lighting is good. One disadvantage of higher megapixel cameras is the recordings will take up more hard drive space. Depending on the number of cameras, this can become a larger concern.

When I saw this camera at this price point I knew it was something I needed to check out. I appreciated the fact it was 2MP because with this lens you are not going to want to be eating up the hard drive space required for a 5MP.

I was able to get it set up within my Blue Iris system after playing with it for a while. Typically this takes me no more than a couple of minutes - this camera required much more extensive programming in order to have it functional.

Once I did have it up and working image quality is substandard even compared to other cameras with similar specs.

I figured it still could be utilized as a tertiary filler camera but it kept going offline for absolutely no reason. When a camera is connected via PoE to Blue Iris this simply should not be an issue unless there are issues with the camera itself.

While the price point is excellent on this camera, unfortunately this is an example of getting what you pay for. In my four months of testing this camera has proven to be unreliable, difficult to connect and keep connected and the images captured are far lower quality than expected from cameras with similar specs.

This is a product to pass on.

Bell & Howell's Wireless Video Door Intercom System is a simple system that can be used to communicate directly with someone outside your front door. The device is not just an intercom system- it also presents a video image of the person at the door, for better security.

This device pretty much works as it promises to work and it is basically a walkie- talkie with a video screen. One has to press the button to talk and, likewise, the person at the front door has to press the button to respond. The two- way communication has to be initiated on both ends for the device to work the way it should. You can still view the person at the door regardless, but for them to respond to your questions, they have to press the button. Don't be surprised if you have to instruct the person at the door to press the button before they speak. Most will not know this and will start to answer questions that cannot be heard on the other end until the button is pressed.

Besides the manual operation mentioned above, another issue I have with this system is the video quality. Now, I realize that the product is a simple one, but for the price, I expect a little clearer and more accurate image. It appears I am not alone with this complaint- many other consumers have said the same thing. You can easily tell who is at the door, but the video quality does not display the colors very well.

Security is nice and this Bell & Howell intercom system does provide some security and ability to tell who is standing at the front door before you turn the knob. It is overpriced for what you get, but it is easy enough to use and it does offer wireless operation, making it a decent choice for some consumers.

I picked this router up at another online retailer as soon as I spotted it was on sale. I had my eye on the Tenda 1800/1801 routers for a while before that though, as these seem to be the only decent Gigabit / AC routers that are directly compatible with Tomato right out of the box, that don't break the bank!

My router is essentially the same thing as the much more expensive ASUS RT-AC66U, but with less memory. Having less memory on a router is not really the same thing as less memory on a computer. In other words, most people (including myself) will not notice the difference.

Hardware Look and Feel:
This Tenda sports the basic router design, and includes wall mounting screw holes that are 6” apart, and 3 movable antennas that are easy to install. There is lots of good ventilation on the sides and bottom, and a glossy white top. Altogether, the router seems will made, and doesn't feel cheap at all. Glad to say that it doesn't have a gimmicky cylindrical shape, or a stupid upright design, with an even more stupid non-adjustable plastic stand. I don’t mind at all that I can't take selfies next to my neat looking stylish black router to post on Facebook; Boring routers are just plain under-rated!

Stock Firmware:
I spent about 5-minutes poking around in the stock firmware before flashing to Tomato. To me the stock firmware seemed like an unpolished version of Asus firmware. This is not necessarily a bad thing, but why settle for stock when there is a specific version of the very stable, configurable, and admired Tomato USB written just for routers just like this! Enter Shibby K26RT-AC...

Tomato Flashing Process:
No feverish searching the internet for firmware “that will work” with your router, simply go to the Shibby download page, find the latest version for your router, download the compressed file, and unzip it.
Then unplug your WAN cable, open your routers firmware page, go to tools, upgrade, navigate to the folder your just unzipped, select the .TRX file, click upgrade, and wait about 10 minutes. Once it is done, you might want to do a factory reset in Tomato to clear the RAM.

That’s it people, no messing around with cumbersome flash utilities, no 30/30/30 resets in restore mode while holding your nose and saying the alphabet backwards in Pig Latin while crossing your fingers that you won’t brick your router. This one is as simple as it gets!

As I am sure is the case with many, I purchased this after seeing it listed by the New York Times in their portable BT transmitter review list. It was bought specifically to allow me to transmit BT audio from my computer to my Sony WF-1000XM3 earbuds. As the Sony earbuds only support SBC with these, I wasn't expecting stellar audio quality - I usually use them for lectures or podcast-like content, or for fairly low-bitrate music anyway. I wanted to see if the advantages of true-wireless earbuds were worth the sacrifice in quality before I invested in a more expensive BT transmitter and BT receiver+high-end IEMs. As such, I do not use the receive function, and I do not use the battery on the unit - it is always plugged in via USB. I did briefly test the battery though and can confirm it lasts at least 30m.

Note: I went with this type unit, instead of USB, because I wanted to have the ability to test it in multiple environments, including while running and in the car for single-ear usage. Normally, I'd go with a USB solution for computer use in order to avoid the conversion of the audio from to and back from analog.

Initial Setup

Dead simple - I connected the Line Out on my computer to the input on the transmitter, and alternately, the HP out on my stereo receiver to the input on the transmitter. I also tried it with a Sansa Clip+ MP3 player. It worked in all cases, though with the WF-1000XM3 I had to keep the input volume on the BT transmitter under 30% and allow the headphones to do the real amplification, as otherwise the audio would distort.

BT Setup

Fairly simple. I put my earbuds into pairing mode, the transmitter into pairing mode, and they connected within 10s. Afterward, they maintained their connection for the most part, I've had to re-pair a couple times over the last three weeks, but that is mostly a learning curve. Re-pairing is easy - just hold the pairing button down for two seconds and place the receiving device in pairing mode.

Range

Unpredictable, and sensitive. If the transmitter is located on a desk, at least twelve inches away from other electronics, then the range is remarkable. I can leave the room, pass through the adjacent room, and enter into the next room - a total of maybe thirty feet, through two or three walls - and start to lose audio at the end. This is despite being only five feet from a wireless router. However, if I move the transmitter six inches over so it is next to my monitor, or a couple feet so that it is within three feet of the router, the earbuds will begin to drop out even at ten feet. So it is very sensitive to environment.

Audio Quality

Decent. Better than I expected, but I haven't used bluetooth audio in ten years. It can be hard to really gauge it, because the Sony WF-1000XM3 are true wireless earbuds and I can't A/B test them to compare BT quality to a cable. I would say that the BT audio quality is equivalent to that produced when my Sony earbuds are connected to my smartphone. While it is decent, it can't compare to wired earbuds of even fairly middling quality. You lose highs and lows. For dialogue content, lectures and the like, no issue.

Summary

Seems to be a great entry-level transmitter for the average consumer. I'm glad I bought it, because it is reliable and easy to use, and has shown me that the freedom of using wireless earbuds is definitely worth the hit to quality - I can always use my full circumaural headphones if I want to watch a movie or listen critically. Would recommend.

Enthusiast of World of Tanks BEWARE! I am not the only one out there to report serious problem with the game vs. this card (and more nVidia cards in general).
I have had World of Tanks crashes on EVGA GeForce 9800 GT and they, unfortunately, continue to happen on this very card - my newest MSI N650Ti-1GD5/OC GeForce 650Ti. They happen regardless the driver version (usually at the beginning of a battle), and they do still occur with the newest 314.07 drivers, though less frequently and at a different moment.
Worked with World of Tanks support and we went through several iterations, including clean re-installations (incl. registry cleanups) of the game/drivers in different combinations, underclocking, etc., but that did not help at all.
To be fair - the card never gave me problems with Portal 2, Order of War, Medal of Honor and a few other games needing solid 3D rendering - it appears to be issue with World of Tanks game in particular.
Not sure whose fault it is: 1) may be game developers, with whom nVidia claims to have business partnership), but, equally valid, 2) it may also be nVidia drivers that crash the program (the issue seems to be reported more often with newer nVidia drivers by multiple players).
Anyway - if you're into World of Tanks a lot - I recommend picking up some decent Radeon card - the one I have on the other PC (HD 6870) never gave me any issues with my favorite game.

EDIT as of 08 March 2013:
I added one more star and here's why:
1. The crash of World of Tanks occurs due to client (program) issue, which was admitted couple days ago by the developer's support folks (they're still working to resolve this, with me). So, as this is not the card's fault I am adding one star, especially that graphics is really stunning (especially for such a price point!).
2. Why not 5 stars? Well, I would, but then one thing stands out - if you want to keep that (factory overclocked) card stable, you need to speed up the fan a bit and that makes the card pretty noisy (louder than a fully spinning DVD drive, in my instance)! So if you do not mind it (or you have a well noise insulated computer case) then go ahead with it.

As a general rule, I hate hands-free handsets.

I hate it when I begin speaking with someone, and I think they're agreeing with everything I say, and then it turns out they're actually talking to someone else using their dratted ear extension with the flashing blue light.

I hate the fact that my ears are the wrong size and shape for the majority of headsets.

I hate it when my untrained (clumsy) fingers hit the wrong part of the headset when I'm simply trying to stop it from falling to its death from a height of just over 5 feet, and I either redial the last number or hang up on the one person who hates being hung up on.

Plus, they're UGLY, and don't accessorise well with any wardrobe!!

HOWEVER,

I hate it even more when I have to pull over and park to take or make a call.

And I especially hate it if I DON'T pull over, and then get busted by the only policeman on the entire empty highway who has insomnia and a full book of blank tickets waiting to be filled in.

SO,

Hands free it shall be -
But ONLY when I'm driving.

That said, this device fits most of my basic needs, and throws in some convenient extras. The EASYGO Headset was indeed very easy to set up and even easier to use. Sound quality was good and the spoken connection status and audio volume adjuster are useful features.

The headset is also relatively small and stylish (as hands-free headsets go) without any flashing lights or buttons that attract unwanted attention (or cause an attack of photosensitive epilepsy, or signal the letters N-E-R-D in morse code.)

The most impressive feature of this headset has to be the long battery life, which is great because the miserly charger cord is so awkward to use that you don't want to have to use it more often than necessary. Besides, as I only use it in the car, it lasts me several trips, depending on how often and how long I prattle.

Admittedly it is more comfortable to use than I expected. The extra ear hook prevents suicidal leaps from ear to earth, and it doesn't weigh my head down on one side.

In summary, for a simple headset, it delivers.

Reviewed by my husband, a photography enthusiast.

Over the last 20 years, my husband has purchased several LowePro camera bags/backpacks (i.e., Mini Trekker & Micro-Trekker 100). He has found that they have been some of the best he has ever owned. He prefers backpacks because they are easy to carry and keep up with, especially if you are on the go. Backpacks also allow for easy storage and are super convenient. They give you freedom of movement and your hands are free to capture those special moments that you may not otherwise get if you were holding a bag in your hand. The Viewpoint (LowePro) BP 250 is the perfect addition to his bag collection especially since it is specially designed for small video equipment.

Here’s what he liked:

• This bag is attractive. The design is smart, functional and full of surprises. The Viewpoint BP250 is well-made with plenty of room for your Go Pro and accompanying equipment. There is a ton of storage (inside and out). There are several compartments where you can store your accessories, cords, lenses and other equipment. On the outside of the main bag, there is a zipper pocket (which allows for small items like a memory stick/card or thumbdrive). There is a pocket on the other side of the bag which will fit a small tripod or other item (like an umbrella). The entire bag can be zippered so you won’t lose any of your accessories.

• It is ideal for those who use (small) video and other digital equipment. There is a space dedicated to a small computer. While this backpack will not allow you to carry one of the larger sized laptops (our 17” didn’t fit), it has adequate space for the smaller ones (about 15”), a SurfacePro, iPad or other small notebook or tablet. He finds that the option of carrying a computer is great because it will allow you to quickly upload and edit your videos wherever you are. There is no reason to wait….just review, edit (if needed), and upload!

• The straps are unlike the traditional ones that come straight down the shoulders. The BP250 LowePro’s straps are curved which he found to be less stress on his shoulders. After some adjustments (he’s 6’1, average sized with average shoulders), it was a good fit. The straps are slightly padded and comfortable. There are small snaps that lock the straps in place to ensure that they don’t fall down when walking or hiking.

• There is a small (lunch box sized bag) that can be removed and can hold your GoPro camera and equipment. Once closed, it fits directly into your main LowePro Bag. It is padded and once inside, will protect your camera and smaller lenses. Or if you want, this smaller bag can be used instead of taking the large one.

• This bag comes with a rain cover. Not sure how much you will use this feature, but if you are ever caught in a drizzle or rain storm, there is a plastic cover that can be removed (unzipped) from the bottom and cover your bag. This is perfect for keeping your bag and equipment dry.

• The price. While this bag may seem a little pricey (about $130) it’s worth it. The craftsmanship and functionality will prove invaluable for the amateur or professional photographer. It’s a small investment with some heavy returns. You’ve got protection and functionality.

Overall, my husband gives this bag 5 stars. He finds that it is not only good to use for a GoPro, but other small video and photography equipment. Backpacks are useful for photographers because they allow your hands to be free to capture those moments or events as they unfold. In the past he has purchased Lowepro equipment and found them to be sturdy and durable, and the Viewpoint BP250 is not different. It looks good and he won’t leave home without it.
Value for the money..

OK, here are the facts: my other (similar) camera developed a glitch -- it will not allow me to delete photos without loooooong delays. So I went in search of an inexpensive replacement camera. I settled on this Canon.

I did so with trepidation because some of the reviews were lukewarm at best. Yet other reviewers loved it. (This, by the way, is what makes horse races!) So I thought I would take a chance.

Here is why I am happy with my choice: (1) the viewer seems larger than its dimensions suggest; (2) the camera fits in my shirt pocket; (3) the pics are crisp indoors and out; (4) the on-off button is clearly marked and the shot button is nice and robust. For me, these features are all I need. To be sure, the camera has a few video bells and whistles -- I'll try those one of these days. No rush.

A Con: the shot button takes a little getting used to, since it appears to have two stages to it. If you just press and disengage, nothing will happen. It requires a little patience and then it will take the picture. I can live with that idiosyncrasy.

Another Con: no internal memory. You must purchase an SD card before you can use the camera. This too I have accepted, because having pics on cards does make it easy to load them into PCs and laptops.

I’m a big fan of the Panasonic Lumix line of point and shoot cameras. I’ve been using one for years and, while it has limited features by today’s standards, it has yet to let me down. This latest one in the Lumix line offers a huge range of capabilities, provides outstanding image quality, but continues to suffer from a less than ideal user interface.

The camera comes with just the basics: the camera, a single battery, lanyard and a charger (plus manuals and software). I was a little disappointed right off the bat when I saw the charger. Unlike the older Lumix chargers that had a wall plug built into the charger than flipped out, this has a separate power cord. While that does make it easier to plug into the wall, it also means I have to remember to carry the cord with me to charge it.

Initial setup is straightforward, with the usual time/date setting. Since this has a GPS there’s also the need to go through initializing that option as well. All of these steps can be skipped, but you’ll be reminded to do so every time you power on the camera. It also displays a warning on screen about the waterproof limitations of the camera (and provides ample documentation as to what it can/can’t do re: underwater use).

The view screen is wonderful. Sharp, clear, and easy to read in all lightning conditions. The menu system will be familiar if you’ve ever used a Lumix camera but, if not, it’s still pretty straightforward. I still think Canon has the lead when it comes to having an intuitive point and shoot menu system, but Panasonic does a decent job. I like that with most options there’s a scrolling line of text that comes up to explain what the option is/does. That’s very helpful for options you don’t often use and need help with, but it does not interfere or slow down operation should you know exactly what you want to select.

I won’t list all the camera specs in this review since those are easily available in the listing and the Panasonic web site. Suffice it to say this offers a huge range of options and capabilities that cover pretty much any shooting situation. The Intelligent mode shooting scenario options (of which there are many) are helpful when you just want to point the camera and have it do everything else for you, including compensation for specialized lighting/scene situations. I especially like the macro option, which produced some impressive close-up shots that were sharply focused and clear even though I didn’t use a table-top tripod for stability but relied on the image stabilization features of the camera.

The video recording image quality is excellent good for a point and shoot cam. The performance of the built in mic is decent as well. This won’t compete with a dedicated HD cam, but for casual video shooting it’s a small, simple and easy to use setup that gets the job done pretty well.

The WiFi setup was surprisingly easy. I was dreading that since it often can be a bear, but this was quick and easy, and the included instructions were easy to follow. I use the WiFi option a lot since the USB port to connect to a PC is inside the camera (located under the battery compartment door). It’s done that way to maintain a water-tight shell, but is also means it can be hard to get to easily.

What has not been improved, and actually has slipped a bit, is the overall user interface (e.g., the buttons on the back). They continue to be small, hard to read, and don’t provide solid feedback that they have been pressed. Given that the camera is designed to be used in “rugged” conditions, larger buttons would have been a big plus, especially for zoom and the main menu keypad since those are used so often. Using the menu buttons is hard enough with bare hands; it’s impossible if you have gloves on.

I would certainly recommend this camera if you’re looking for a rugged point and shoot for outdoor use, but also if you’re looking for a high feature camera that never leaves the house. The performance and feature set are both excellent. The user interface brings my rating to four stars but performance and option-wise, this camera offers a lot for the price point.

The barrel connector comes with an adapter to a larger size barrel connector to cover Sabrent hubs. I have checked every source I could find to get the barrel connector specs, but none are to be found. This is frustrating to say the least because this is truly a multi-purpose power supply that can be used on non-Sabrent products. Since it is not claimed to be universal I am giving it five stars because it works perfectly with the hub with which I tested it.

One feature that I particularly like is the fact that the cable is heavy duty with good strain reliefs on both ends. This is not your typical, flimsy power supply cable. Another thing I like is this runs cool even with constant use. I am using it to power a hub with a disk drive and both the hub and this power supply are running cool even after a twenty-four hour period.

This is capable of providing up to four Amps, but will only 'push' what the device requires. What that means is if you are powering four devices that draw .6 Amps each this supply will only push 2.4 Amps, so there is no worry about overloading. On the other hand if you are attempting to power a hum that requires over 4 Amps this is not the proper power supply and will not work.

If you own a Sabrent powered hub this is a safe choice, Do make sure you know the total current draw of the devices into the hub and make sure that the total does not exceed four Amps.

Senior citizens who are uncomfortable with technology (although I would not be above putting the app on a big bright tablet for a parent or grandparent who is open to the idea, especially since many tablets can be made to play a sound that will let you find where you set them down). People who are fine with having/using a few different remotes or who really don't use more than one or two remotes. I've had several pairs of Sennheisers before the momentums namely a pair of HD580's from back in 1999 & much more recently a pair of HD650's. I bought a pair of in ear headphones from Sennhesier of course & these sounded good, better than than the Apple buds. Then I ran into the Momentums! Bottom line: While there are design differences between these two brands that affect how they are used, the performance of both is excellent. There is no “winner,” with the best one being the one that offers the design that works for your specific baking needs.

Full review: I’ve been a Chicago Metallic fan for many, many years. I have yet to have one of their pans or sheets fail on me even after 20+ years of use for some. So, I was very interested to see if the Island Ware sheet would stack up.

The build quality of the Island Ware (IW) is very good. It feels sturdy with zero racking/twisting of the pan when cold no matter how much force is applied. The finish looks attractive. There are some machining marks here and there, especially on the edges, but nothing objectionable. I’d rate the build quality the same as Chicago Metallic (CM) sheets. While I can't speak to the longevity of the IW as of yet, based on the way it looks and feels, I'd hazard a guess that it will last just as long as a CM sheet.

The IW pan is lighter. It weighs 1 pound 15 ounces versus 2 pounds 7 ounces for the CM. Despite the lighter weight, the IW feels just as sturdy. (Note: I weighed both on the same scale. While the actual weight listed may not be 100% accurate, the variation between the two is accurate.)

The corners and edges are where the IW takes a different approach than CM. The CM has the traditional rolled edge, has fairly perpendicular walls, and has rounded inside corners. The IW has no rolled edges, eased walls, and more of a squared off inside corner. There are pluses and minuses to both designs. The IW fits square silicon sheets or parchment paper better, and there is zero risk of having gunk get caught inside the rolled edge. On the other hand, the rolled edge is more comfortable to hold and grab without it cutting into your hand, and the perpendicular walls work better when baking a pan cookie or dough where you use the full sheet.

Baking performance for both was very similar. The IW seemed to heat a little faster, but the difference with the CM was minimal. Both heated evenly and didn’t have any hot spots. The IW did rack a small amount when hot but nothing that was objectionable or problematic.

So, there really is no winner – both are great pans and are 5-star performers. The choice is mainly on what you plan to do with the pans. If you mainly bake cookies, I’d go with the IW. The eased rim and square corners make it easier to line with square silicon sheets or parchment paper, and make it easier to lift cookies out using a spatula. But, if you’re looking to bake pan cookies, flat breads, pizza, etc. where you press the dough throughout the full pan, the rounded corners and more vertical walls of the CM will work a little better.

Again, these differences are not deal-breakers – you could certainly bake a pan cookie in the IW and have it come out just as good as the CM. You’ll want to take a look at pricing and see which one is the better deal in terms of cost. Neither will disappoint when it comes to performance.

My mom ordered 2 of these thinking she'd be able to play music out of both of them at the same time from her iPhone. They come in the mail and we cannot figure out how to do this at all, and the instructions that came with them were unclear, as well as what we found online.
After a few hours of trial and error, this is what we figured out:
Pair both of the speakers to the iPhone

Having tried several Garmin models, Apple Maps, and Google Maps, I was excited to try TomTom. And I was disappointed.

Problems:
•Screen is VERY dim in the sunlight, and living in Florida, this is most of the time. It is NOT easy to see the map, which even in my ancient Garmin is much more visible and automatically switches from day mode to night mode. Likewise, my iPhone screen automatically changes brightness for the amount of sun coming in. And this? It looks horribly dim and takes a lot of effort to see.
•Routes don’t always make sense. I’m used to some amount of this in the other systems I’ve tried, but they’re really wacky on this thing, taking a REALLY scenic route that sometimes involves making a full circle for something that was literally as easy as just turning left in the correct place.
•Point of interest search is slow and ineffective. Even with my ancient Garmin (and obviously with my phone), it would never find most places, even ones that have been there many years. This after waiting an interminable amount of time for the list to compile. Did I get the long update on my computer and add it to the GPS? Yep. I thought that was the problem, did the update, and then discovered it was Not the problem.
•Doesn’t appear to take traffic into account. Neither does my old Garmin, but it should do better than a piece of tech that’s 10 years old and at least be comparable to a current smartphone’s GPS; otherwise, what’s the point?
•Hard to stop. You want to sometimes say, “OK SHUT UP. I know the rest of the way!”, and in all other GPS systems I’ve tried, getting to the “end route/stop” place is usually two steps, max. It is long and complicated, and I don’t want to die in a car accident, so I end up having to suffer through unnecessary and often over-complicated routes that make no sense.
•Doesn’t default to turn-by-turn. Sometimes it shows an aerial view, which is zero helpful, has no detail, and requires me to think a lot about “is this to MY right or left if my car is facing this way and the map is oriented North Up and I *think* I am moving East maybe, but I can’t tell because this stupid thing is both dim and also has an unbelievably zoomed out map view where I’m not sure Where my little dot is going?!?!”

So yes. Unless I sit in the parking lot and fiddle with it for a good while, nothing is quite right, and everything takes a long time to find or set up. I tried it for a month now, and my opinion has not changed. This is frustrating.

This is my second SSD, my first being a Kingston (with the Taiwan firmware thank God) so I thought install was going to be fairly easy; it was not. My system (Win7) did not recognize the drive, but the included software, Samsung Magician, said the drive was there, operating properly, but was "frozen". I googled the malfunction and found out that the drive had no partitions.

So first step was to get in Disk Management, find the drive, click on the 113+gb unallocated space and create a partition.

Step two, reboot and change my boot sequence because Samsung Magician felt it was necessary to change it for me and made this new SSD my boot drive, even though it had no OS on it to boot.

Step three, change my power management plan back to what I had before because Samsung Magician felt it was better to change it to hibernate instead of what I wanted. I hate Hibernate.

After that it worked great. I use this SSD for games only because it's so damn fast, but I wish the included software and instructions were better, hence the 4 stars and not 5.
