Standards have changed.

I was surprised to find that Osiris STILL makes the controller in this MX-350 variant. It was a 30-minute transition.

If you have a complicated AV system, programming one of these master controllers with your decided wiring scheme is NOT a snap. It does take mental discipline and iterative attempts to bring it all together. The MX-350 is up to the demands of a Smart TV/DVD system. The programming was straight forward ... the device itself has no discernible external changes from the legacy product.

Given my experience with the MX-350's predecessor, the continuous use, dozens of accidents, and the robust software behind the controller ... if there was ever a bulletproof AV component, this it.

Additionally there are the standard water bottle mesh pockets n the outside and interior pockets and loops for pens, a phone etc, as well as plenty of room for notebooks and a text or two. There is a good sized zippered pocket in the front, and a slightly smaller sized one in the back that would be completely concealed and secure when the pack is being worn. There is a bonus small zippered pocket large enough to hold an id or keys in one of the padded straps that would be easily accessible when the pack was being worn. All of these features make this an excellent bag for school or for a work commute.

This bag is also listed as a travel bag, which is why I wanted it and here we have some problems. First the pluses - even packed it is small enough to fit under an airplane seat, and would protect a laptop or other electronics while doing so. There is even a strap in the back to secure the bag to the handle of a roll on case. Inside there is plenty of room to hold electronics, travel documents etc. The inside is divided into two main compartments so some clothing, and items that shouldn't be checked (jewelry, medications etc) could be carried as well. There are some drawbacks for using this bag for travel, particularly air travel. The bag does not open flat so electronics would need to be removed to go through TSA screening. Also, since it doesn't open flat or have interior ties clothing would probably need to be stuffed inside or packed into packing cubes to carried in this.

Original review:
I received the Amcrest ProHD 1080p IP PT "WiFi" camera yesterday, 10/30/15.

I downloaded the Amcrest Lite iPhone app. Followed instructions. It would not connect via Wi-Fi using my router's password. Tried again and again. I have a TP-Link C9 dual band wireless router with both 5gHz and 2.4gHz transmission. The Amcrest website says in an obscure forum post that the camera operates only in the 2.4gHz band. I changed my iPhone6 (iOS 9.0.2) from 5G to 2.4G. Still could connect via Wi-Fi.

So I plugged the camera directly into the router via ethernet, completely defeating the purpose for the initial purchase. It finally connected. I saw the picture for about 30 seconds, trying to get the camera to full screen, I clicked around on the mysterious icons. Nothing seemed to work. I clicked on the "X" box. The camera disappeared. I tried to reconnect. It came back with "USER LOCKED." I went to their website to search for an answer. They said (at least for their DVR line -- virtually nothing was about this camera) "users are locked out after two failed logon attempts and that I must wait 30 minutes for the reset." I waited. Still USER LOCKED. No camera. I don't even recall trying to log in. I was in the app, trying to reconnect the camera.

I created my Amcrest user account and received their confirming email. I created a user and password for Amcrest.com. The account is actually for something called amcrest.Zendesk and Accumed.zendesk and Foscamhelp.zendesk. I then tried to log in at Amcrest.com. It won't take my log-on credentials. "Invalid Logon or Password." How many user names and passwords does it take to plug in a camera?

Trying to start over, I deleted the app and rebooted the camera. Still USER LOCKED.

Finally, I found that if you push and hold in the little LED network-activity-indicator button on the back of the camera for 10 seconds, the camera will reset to factory. Deleted the app again, set my phone to operate in the 2.4gHz band. Still won't connect via WiFi. Plugged in via ethernet, then used my router's password and it connected. Per the prompt, I then created a new secure password, replacing the default "admin/admin". Finally, I can see and control the camera. So, I have a WiFi camera that won't WiFi. The camera needs to connect to the router at 2.4gHz band (and in my case, via an ethernet cable) but after getting it set, the phone can go back to the 5G if desired.

They claim their products are "Simple, Reliable, Secure." Not quite. They fail to hook to Wi-Fi and then lock me out. Their website won't let me log on even with a user and password.

I downloaded the camera's big PDF user manual to find what the icons mean. The document looks nothing like the camera's icons. They went into great detail...about a previous firmware version, then changed the firmware to look very differently.

The camera works, eventually, and only via ethernet in some cases, but getting there is a real test of patience.

I received one of these as a review sample and for what it does it deserves a full five stars.However, I am docking a star because there is a learning curve, due in part to sketchy documentation. I''ll get the challenges out of the way first.

Even with the included documentation it's difficult to figure out some aspects of this case. Some examples: there is a pull strap on the hard, snap-in holder for the iPad that is held in place by two labels that say 'do not tear'. That strap is intended to remain as is and the friction and pressure of the iPad will hold it in place. The instructions do not mention this and I removed it anyway because it looked like a temporary shipping solution.

Secondly, there are adjustable straps on the right and left sides of the case that prevent it from fully opening and remaining open. They are probably unnecessary and do create confusion. This case is not designed to fully open like a conventional case - it's designed to slide the iPad in and out using the T-shaped track. If you do want to use this as a conventional case you need only unfasten the two side straps and it will operate as such.

On the plus side, this case if one of the best I have come across with respect to protection. You can literally drop it from shoulder height and it will protect your iPad. The shoulder strap is designed to function as a set of pockets as well as a comfortable way to carry your iPad. And the material from which this case is constructed is built to take a lot of abuse and last much longer than your iPad.

Bottom line: this is a little over complicated and under documented in my opinion. However it's also ideal for folks who need a fairly rugged case. While the video on this page implies the target customer is a business user I think it's more ideally suited to first responders and folks who work in harsh environments.

I was confused by the product photo saying you need a MEB1100. Basically, if you're a current Frontier customer, and you don't have and don't know anything about the MEB1100, and everything has been working fine in your house with just the Arris, then don't worry about the MEB1100. However, if Frontier set you up with both the Arris and the MEB1100, then I recommend buying both. You want the set-up to stay the same.

I do use moca adapters to bring internet to rooms with coax cable. These are the ones I use: https://www.amazon.com/Motorola-Adapter-Ethernet-2-Pack-MM1002/dp/B078HMDDVS/ref=sr_1_2?dchild=1&keywords=Motorola+moca&qid=1617140900&sr=8-2 With the Arris router, you do not need to put an adapter next to it. My connection is like this:

* Ethernet from ONT in my garage goes to WAN port of the Arris router in living room.
* Coaxial from ONT goes to a 4 way splitter, one line goes to the living room, I connect this line to the coaxial on the Arris.
* Coaxial line in my bedroom goes to the network coaxial port of my moca adapter. I then hook up an ethernet hub to the ethernet port of the moca adapter. Voila! That's how I bring ethernet to my bedroom.
* I do the same to the other coaxial lines in my home to bring ethernet hubs to those rooms as well.

This has been how my home has functioned. All connections were left untouched. I simply swapped out the Frontier Arris for this identical Arris. I then made sure to go into the new Arris admin and create the same wifi SSID with the same password as before. All your wifi and network devices will function as normal, no need to re-enter any passwords. This Honeywell smart home security starter kit has a great video and is easily expandable.

When opening the box I was pleased to see that it was packaged very well. The box even has a magnetic closure. Maybe a little over the top but a nice feature to make it feel like more of a luxury product. I also have the Honeywell thermostat and that box wasn’t as nice.
Each item in the security kit was simple and clear to find since they were labeled in their own little box. There is an instruction sheet that is quite large for the info that it holds. The instructions have nice graphics and it is spaced out well so it is very easy to read. The instructions are simple for initial set up. Though I would appreciate another manual to help with the “extra” things it can do. I relied on the Honeywell videos and reviews (video and written) by other people to get it functioning with all the bells and whistles. I could see the need for a manual for those less tech savvy.

The base station could be a little smaller but it looks very nice in my kitchen and blends in very well. It’s a nice design with only one button, for the speaker. You can touch the top to check how it is working and run your finger around the top to change the volume. The camera is small and has a privacy ring that can be twisted to block the camera. It would be a nice feature if I could twist the camera from the app in case we forgot to open it when we left.
The middle mesh part is the speaker and it has a good range of volume and the sound is good.
The bottom has a light inside and it changes colors when you choose the different settings. It also lights up to help when you set up new devices.
The base has a backup battery. You will get an alert when it doesn’t have power. This has been handy when there is a storm so I know when the power goes out and when it is restored.

To start the set up I downloaded the Honeywell app. It was easy to use and is a nice looking app. The main page is very simple. When you go to the settings that’s where all the extras are.
My husband also has the app on his phone so he can use it just as I can.
Set up was very easy besides having troubles with it connecting it to my WiFi. I decided to wait till the next day and it worked after a couple tries. I don’t have a fast internet so that might be why. I haven’t had any issues with the connection since set up. Besides the WiFi wait it was about 15 minutes to set up the app and base.
The key fob was very easy to pair up and only took me a couple minutes to have it ready to use. Nice to have when a babysitter comes over.
The access sensors were very easy to install and set up. I didn’t need the extra piece. It only took me a few minutes to stick them on and pair them. I did use painters tape to attach them to my doors and frames. I am worried about the tape they have ruining my stained trim. I haven’t seen any comments about it. I also wanted to try it on other doors and windows first.
When you open a door or window in home mode it chimes and sends you an alert. When you open in away mode it will sound the alarm. I wish the door sensors were a little smaller or gray. They stand out too much on my wood trim and door. If my trim was white they wouldn’t be very noticeable.

The camera is very clear and has a wide angle so if you position it right you can see a lot. You can switch the video to full screen and the picture is still good. You are also able to zoom in on the video in the app and it has options to take a snap of the video, talk through the base or have an alarm go off. Sometimes it takes a while for the video to load or it will just turn off. I am assuming this is from my slower internet. Usually after a few tries I can get it to work. Also there is a delay in the video and the movement is jumpy, this could be due to the slower internet also. You still get a good picture of who is there. I was impressed with the night vision.

The motion detection is a nice feature when you are away. I have been trying to figure out the best setting while we are at home. It will send me alerts all the time when we are home. Most of the alerts are during the people detection time. Maybe because our camera covers so much of our main area. I do like that how the people detection can let me know who is in the house and I don’t have to look at the video. When it detects motion it will take a short video clip and save them below the live video. You can scroll down to look at the older ones. It looks like the clips are saved for a day. The people detection is limited to 2 hours. But I did notice that you could set it for the morning then when that time was over you could change it for later in the day. You would have to remember to change it but good to know if you wanted it on for longer or multiple times in the day. Not sure why they don’t have an option for more time.

The geofencing didn’t work well for me. It would switch to away mode even when the phone was close to it. We’ve decided to turn that feature off. It’s easy enough to turn it to away with the app, key fob, or talk to it. We are at home a lot so it makes more sense to do it manually. But I could see it being a great feature for people gone more during the day.

The kids like the Alexa feature that it comes with. They can ask the weather, time, kids jokes. I use it for the timer and to ask it questions. We had problems with playing songs. It wanted us to subscribe to amazon music. We have found other ways of playing music but it’s not very easy. Alexa seems limited but still useful. This is my first Alexa enable device so hard to compare.

I like that the security base links to my Honeywell thermostat (it was very easy to pair it) and I can tell Alexa to turn it off or change the temperature or use the same app. I would like to get other devices that link to it. This is a great starter kit and I like that it is expandable for your needs.

You are able to do two way taking with the app. It’s not always easy to understand and you have to talk slower.

The box says you get free 24-hour cloud storage. I’m not sure if that’s for the video clips or what you are actually storing. I haven’t found where the cloud is accessed.

Overall it is easy to use and looks nice. It’s nice that you can have a security system that is easy to use and it doesn’t have a monthly fee. I don’t usually need all the security features that this security system offers but it’s nice to have it set up and ready for when I do.

I ordered the 'Nomodo U Wireless Wearable Bluetooth Speaker, Rechargeable and Portable' for review and would like to share some of my thoughts and experiences.
First off, out of the box this Bluetooth Wireless Speaker not only looks interesting but it is beautiful. I say interesting because I have never had a Wireless Speaker like this, and I wonder where would I use it and would it be practical. Well after some time with this device I must first report that it really does sound amazing. The sound is clean and immersive. It is hard to describe the incredible sound sensation while wearing it. It is almost as if you have speakers floating on either side of your head (pointing directly to your ears) and it is nothing like I have experienced before but it is pretty cool. I have been trying to think of how this Speaker would actually fit into my life. It's not like you are wearing headphones that only you can hear. While wearing this speaker, everyone else around you can hear it too but it's just not as immersive as it is to you. It's hard to describe, but what I will say is that it really is an incredible experience. If the volume is down low you can still hear your surroundings yet when you crank it up, surprisingly your surrounding sounds seem to disappear. Personally I have decided that this would be best worn while alone in your home while doing simple household chores. Like doing dishes or folding laundry. The Nomodo U speaker stays put pretty well for the most part due to the rubber neck pad, yet if you are constantly bending over or doing anything where you are moving around a lot and twisting your head and body, it tends to need re adjusted. Sitting in bed listening to Music or listening to an audio book works really well with this device as long as you wont be disturbing your partner. As for watching movies, for me this really doesn't work. I can't find anywhere where it says what version of Bluetooth this is using but I don't think it is Bluetooth 5.0 unfortunately. There are noticeable sync issues and this just gets annoying. Speaking of the Bluetooth, it connects/pairs effortlessly to all of my devices and that is a bonus. I am disappointed however that it uses Micro USB (the cable is included btw) for charging. With this being a new device it should have USB Type C. I always have to mention this with any new devices. Call quality is acceptable. Those on the other end can hear you just fine, as long as you are not in a loud environment. This is pretty typical with most wireless headphones. Overall I do love this device and think it is a great value for what it is.

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?

THE DONGLE
The little USB dongle has to be put into the device you plan to use the keyboard with. That stores in the back of the keyboard so you don't use it if you plan to use this keyboard with multiple devices.

SLEEP
This keyboard will go into sleep mode when not in use for a while to save power. There is a power button to turn it right back on again.

MOUSE
There are multiple ways to use this as a mouse control (pointer). You can use the touchpad or the right and left mouse button have buttons on the keyboard too. They are separated so it is easy to keep them straight when using it.

THE BOTTOM LINE
As long as you make sure to have the adapter cord for anything with mini USB port that you plan to use this with, it will work great even for tablets and phones, at least it does for mine.

MY RATING

Yes, this is a good hard drive that works just fine. No, I didn't waste my time with the preinstalled bloatware.

Just want to give you some details about the interface (something I would have wanted to know):

Although USB 3.0 is meant to be fully backward compatible, there are still some reported issues with some devices such as the Wii. I haven't heard about any with standard PCs, though.

The saving grace is the ability to change the connecting device to an old USB 2.0 cable. The problem is, it costs $20 for the privilege. That's pretty steep for going backward.

The fact is, these hard drives have a standard SATA connector on back just like any other hard drive, except that they manage to make themselves semi-proprietary by having the connector both recessed and more to the middle. I suspect that it is more to the middle only because the hard drive is a little larger than a 2.5" hard drive stuck in an external case. This keeps you from using a hard drive dock. The fact that it is recessed keeps you from using a hard drive bridge. Of course I understand the reason for the company trying to make this proprietary, but I don't have to be happy about it. I'd respect them more if they gave me more options that didn't involve going to them for replacement parts every time I need them.

Even so, the highest capacity external hard drives are almost always cheaper than an internal hard drive of the same size (especially after you buy a case as well), so this is not a bad pick if you are fully aware of your current needs and have considered future needs.

I was forced to waste time and energy going to the website just to put some crapware on my computer that I didn't want to waste resources on just so I could set that sleeping bit to "never". Then I wasted more time to uninstall the unwanted software. I guess this is standard business with these "external" hard drives; makes me want to go back to buying OEM internal hard drives with an external case; that usually allows the most freedom and flexibility anyway.

What about clusters, galaxies and nebulae? YEP! Over all, it's fairly easy to set up, and you only need to set it up once (with minor adjustments later.) I don't think I've ever seen a more detailed image of the moon outside of a planetarium. I highly recommend this scope for anyone looking to start out!

I really only have a couple complaints, and in the grand scheme of things, they're pretty minor. It's big, so transporting it in a small car is a challenge! If you plan to take this guy anywhere, I recommend buying the padded bag for it (Orion sells it, and you can order through Amazon.com.) I also didn't like the finder scope. Trying to locate objects higher than say, 45 degrees is a pain in the neck (literally!) Picking up a finder scope with a 90 degree bend in it will be very helpful! The stock scope sits parallel to the body of the telescope, and the telescope sits low to the ground (I'm 5'10") and can be rather uncomfortable to get into position in order to look through the finder scope.

Another note I'll put here is that it flips the image, since you're only looking off of 1 mirror. Tracking objects can be awkward at first, both because of the flipped image and the size/bulk of the scope.

I'm a mildly dyslexic, hands-on learner; reading books or trying to visualize how things work doesn't cut it for me. I am still bewildered by volts and watts and amps, as well as the different types of plug types, but the more things like this I can get my hands on, and the more I can actually physically plug them into this or that, the more I can learn about how to put together a modest system that takes some advantage of solar. If something I'm using requires more juice than I have power for, it's helpful to me to actually see an error message when I try to run it underpowered. My next purchase will be a strip of LED lights that takes the add-on adapter type this power supply comes with.

I have a Samsung NX300 camera and so far the main problem I have had has been the battery life. I can get approximately 250-300 pictures between charges (assuming auto settings with average exposure times) which is very low and it has stranded me without battery power more than once. I was looking for extra batteries and an external charger when I found this one here on Amazon. I decided to take a chance on it and I purchased it, and that has paid off for me.

First things first: the batteries in this pack work just fine in my camera. The size and footprint are the same as the manufacturer’s battery, but the capacity is actually higher. The original battery is 1130mA, but these are 1500mA which means more exposures per charge - in theory quite a bit more. I have not yet drained one of these so I do not know exactly how long they last but initial indicators are strong that I will get more than 300 exposures per charge. So, since there are two batteries in the package and I still have the original battery, I should be able to get 1,000 or more exposures per outing if I have all of them charged up when I start.

The external charger is a big plus for me - no more plugging in the camera itself to charge the battery. It plugs into a standard outlet, but it also has an adapter so it can be plugged into the 12V outlet in the car. That’s handy for road trips. So far I have not used the adapter but I am pleased to have it and will use it at some point. The charger does a good job and I was able to charge up one of the batteries in 3-4 hours (I wasn’t paying attention so I am not sure of the exact time it took).

If there’s anything at all I would add or improve: it would have been nice to have a USB cable to plug into the barrel adapter port, so it could be charged over USB too, even if it took a lot longer. That would be very convenient, but the package does not suffer from not having this.

This is exactly what I was looking for and is exactly what I needed to eliminate my camera’s power issue. I have more than triple the battery power now, I don’t have to plug the camera in to charge the battery and I can even charge it in the car. The fact that the charger and both batteries together cost significantly less than a manufacturer’s replacement battery is just the cherry on top.

This is one of the more compact 10-port USB hubs I've come across. It is 7.5 inches long and 2.25 inches wide, but still offers a total of 10 USB ports on the top. To get that many ports into that small of a space means that the ports are pretty close together - there's only about 1/4 inch space between the back edge of one port and the front edge of the adjacent one. I didn't have any problems plugging in cords into adjacent ports, but did have a problem with large thumb drives fitting side-by-side. But, since there are 10 ports, there's room to configure things so that the thick drives don't get placed adjacent to each other.

I have the "basic" model (model P10-UR-BK). The build quality is decent. The case is plastic, and I don't expect that it would stand up to a lot of abuse, but for normal use I think it's more than sturdy enough. All of the ports are well-anchored.

It has a master power switch, plus there are individual lights for each USB port. Both are nice features to have on a hub.

It is a powered hub, and it comes with a power supply. The transformer is in-line, so there is no wall wart at the plug end. Wonderful to see that since wall warts are a true pain to deal with. The power cords and the included USB cable feel well-made and stout.

Straightforward plug-and-play installation on both Win 7 and XP. Zero problems with functionality.

No complaints at all. This is a great way to add a lot of USB 3.0 ports without spending a lot or taking up a lot of desk space.

I walk to school everyday, it's about a 30minute walk. That combined with all the time walking to different buildings once I'm at school, is a lot of time to get cozy with this backpack.

A little back story, I previously owned a unisex North face backpack, I got rid of it because it was too big and hurt my back. I downsized to a women's North face. It was better but it still didn't seem very comfortable and never felt very light even with few items in it.

Cut to this backpack, it's a women's backpack so it's made smaller. (Also I'm 5'7" 120lbs so I'm not terribly small bit still). I typically have 2 binders and two medium sized textbooks in my backpack, occasionally I'll bring my laptop. With everything in it, It doesn't irritate my lower back or shoulders after hours of wear.

The backpack also comes with 2 straps on the side that allows you to compress it in even further. When your stuff is closer to your back, and not hanging far out, it's a lot more comfortable. There are several pockets, a large padded pocket for your laptop, another for your books and such and 2 smaller but still very spacious pockets, as well as an interior pocket and nonzippered outer pocket.

The pockets do zip all the way around, but the straps will need to be unbuckled to do this. I'm not gonna lie, I'm very lazy and have not unbuckled the straps since getting this item, (it's been a month), and I've been able to get my books/laptop in and out without a problem.

The pockets for waterbottles are nice and deep so your water bottle won't fall out, and there's also a strap on either side to secure it even further.

The chest strap on this is awesome too. It doesn't compress your chest in an awkward or uncomfortable way which is something I always look for.

The shoulder straps and back are vented so it's been really great for me, a very sweaty person walking in the summer time. Haha

Overall I think this backpack is awesome! I've already recommended it to my school friends, looks like Osprey is my new go to backpack brand!:D

Full review:
I'm familiar with the higher-end earbuds from RHA (such as their model MA-350, which I use almost daily), so I was very interested to see what they could produce for at the lower end of the price scale.

The overall build quality is quite good. They are just as comfortable as the MA-350 in my ear, which is to say they are nearly perfect. They have the right amount of cushion so they don't get tiring but still fit securely so I don't have any problems with them falling out while exercising. The MA150 comes with three sets of ear cushions so you can adjust them to fit what's best for your ear.

The cord is less stout than the MA-350 (it's a conventional rather than woven cord) but still seems durable enough for typical use. I very much like the plug connector - nicely made, and is angled to alleviate stress points (the connection is where many of my buds end up failing).

The sound quality is good. I used them on my Kindle Fire and a SanDisk MP3 player. No, it won't knock your socks off, but it's a lot better than I expected for the price. The bass is clear and more than plentiful for my taste. Where I noticed the most difference between these and the MA-350's is in the mid-range and treble. Definitely less crisp, which I would imagine is due to the fact that these are made of plastic rather than the aluminum construction of the MA-350s. But it didn't cause any significant problems when I used them when movie watching - the dialogue was quite clear.

Noise isolation is excellent. Very little ambient noise leaks in when wearing them.

The biggest miss is the same complaint I have with other RHA `phones - the R/L markings are on the stem in raised black letters on a black background. VERY hard to see. So, the first thing I do is to color in the RHA logo on the right bud with a Sharpie so I can spot L & R easily.

But that quibble aside, these are excellent and a great value. Very good sound, comfortable to wear for extended periods, good noise isolation and nicely made. I also like the packaging - rather than a blister pack with lots of plastic, these come packed in what RHA calls an "eco pack" - minimal thickness and packaging that is mostly thin cardboard. Much easier to recycle and open.

Definitely worth a look if you want a low-cost set that provides a very good music listening experience, and an excellent movie sound experience.

I love that this surge protector and plug strip has two USB ports for charging my Kindle and cell phone, but the placement of the USB ports, which is a major selling point for this unit, is hindered by the position of the cord wrap feature as well as the areas to plug in your larger electronics that have the big boxy plug. The USB ports are tucked right in between the cord wrap spot and the place to plug in larger plugs, so if one isn't blocking your USB ports, the other is.

In addition, I kind of wish that the majority of the plugs were spaced farther apart. I have a few electronics that have very small boxy plugs, and those don't fit right next to one another on the main area of the plug strip. The only thing that will fit on those plugs without overlapping are the traditional small plugs that are on lamps and other uncomplicated items. I don't have too many of those, and I'm guessing that most people buy plug strips because they have a bunch of electronics, almost all of which would have those bigger boxy plugs.

That said, the surge protector feature is absolutely effective, and I know this because we had PG&E replacing some poles in our neighborhood recently and we had many incidences of brownouts, surges, and spotty power, and this unit kept any harm from coming to any of my electronics that were plugged into it.

Disclaimer - I've only had these for about a week so far and these are the very first Truly Wireless Earbuds that I have ever owned.

I purchased these earbuds on a great sale while waiting for another more expensive brand to get restocked, and honestly didn't expect to much from these. Even though these are my very first Truly Wireless Earbuds, I feel that after tons of research and watching reviews, I know what to look for in sound and quality. There are so many budget wireless earbuds on the market right now with so many more on Indigogo (which from comments and reviews I've seen and read, I will NEVER buy from). This makes it quite hard to know what to buy. For me, I have been waiting for that perfect very small and discreet Truly Wireless Earbud with amazing sound. The Iyesku YK-T02 TWS Sport Earbuds didn't hit that mark for me but at the price I paid, I honestly can't complain.
Pros:
1. Bluetooth 5.0 - This was one of my main requirements when searching and the YK-T02 has it.
2. Easy to pair (I am using the Samsung Note 8) and pairing was very easy. Once the buds are initially paired, they connect super fast once you pull them out of the charging case.
3. No loss of connectivity to either earbud. I've seen a bunch of reviews where this is an issue with MANY other wireless earbuds on the market. Even some of the more spendy ones.
4. Fit is very comfortable and seem to be very secure though I have not put them through the test of running nor exercise. However I don't think this would be an issue at all.
5. Sound quality is decent. More about this in the Cons.
6. Tons of ear tip options. Most earbuds come with a few extra sizes but these come with a plethora, for that perfect custom fit.
7. Quite small and discreet.
8. Small pocketable charging case.

Cons:
1. Sound. As I stated in the Pros these sound "good" (for the money) but the Highs are quite loud (Mids and Bass are not) and almost hurt when the volume is turned all the way up. Mids are not to bad but the bass is nearly non existent which was a huge let down. HOWEVER let me say, once I played with the ear tips and found the right fit, Highs, Mids, and Bass are much better, but still not what I would have hoped for but again these aren't "High end" earbuds right?
2. Because the volume of these buds are quite low, Audio books are hard to hear when in a loud environment.
3. No satisfying magnet to hold the buds in the charging case like many others on the market. (The case does click shut to ensure the buds wont be falling out.)
4. Speaking of the case, my first impression was that the case felt very nice and lightweight, but it does feel cheap.

Final thoughts:
Like I said earlier in this review, if you can get these from Amazon on a lightning deal or with a coupon, I would say grab you a pair, but just don't expect these to compete with higher end buds. These would be great for the kids and anyone that just wants a good pair of Truly Wireless Earbuds that wont break the bank.

I've been a Magellan user for several years - have owned four of their GPS systems, and always appreciate how they have improved their products. This unit is my 5th, and replaces a Magellan 4040. After using it for a while I've confident in saying this is the best one yet!

The most visible change is the actual size of the unit. The screen size has been increased, but the unit is thinner and lighter. Very sleek appearance, and the screen is a real joy -- sharp, clear graphics even in the sun, and bigger on-screen buttons for easy use. The mounting system has also been streamlined, and looks and works well. It mounts very easily on a NavMat holder (basically a bean-bag system that I got on Amazon. I'm a huge Navmat fan - makes it a snap to hide the GPS with narry a trace. Best accessory by far for any GPS).

The power connector was not well thought out, however. You have to connect it to the GPS unit AFTER you mount it in the holder. They should have moved the connector it a wee bit to the side to avoid that.

The only button is a slide-type power button on the top. Boot-up time is OK -- not speedy, but not a huge delay either. It does not have a "sleep" mode, so you have to do a cold boot every time. Not a problem in real world use - by the time you get situated in your car, the unit is ready to go.

Voice is clear and easy to understand. Not as natural sounding as a TomTom, but understandable.

Pretty much any recent GPS unit will get you where you want to go. I've found the routing on the Magellans to be very similar to Garmins - could be because they both use the same mapping set (Navteq). The Magellan shines, however, in features that I find helpful. The direction of the next turn is always visible regardless of how far away the next turn will be. Up until recently, Garmin did not offer this (they do now on some of their units). Sounds like a small issue, but I find it very helpful. The Magellan also allows you to very easily exclude a route (or portion). That's a fairly standard feature nowadays, but Magellan allows you to do it in a snap.

In terms of routing, Magellan offers four options (fastest, shortest, most use of freeways and least use). You can see all four options on the map (as a summary) at the same time so you can pick the best one for your needs. Perfect!!

Love the AAA Guidebook, which is a unique Magellan feature. Lets you get details about restaurants and other points of interest just like the paper version from AAA. I used it a lot in my 4040, especially when traveling out of town.

Other unique Magellan features I appreciate is the "ding dong" sound right before a turn (incredibly accurate!) and the fact that the software reminds you to "stay on the current road" when you encounter major exits. Some find that to be nagging, but it has saved me from inadvertently exiting on more than one occasion.

A new feature for Magellan is the lane guidance. Very nicely done. I've used this feature on Navigon units, and found it rather unhelpful. Magellan's implementation is far more useful, with better, clearer graphics. However, lane guidance is not available for every road.

The software is also nicely done - very logical to use. If you're a past Magellan user you can pick this up and use it in a second. If not, there's a short printed user's guide in the box (plus a CD-ROM with more in-depth info) that gets you up to speed quickly. The box also includes the mount, power connector for the car, and a USB cable. It does not include an AC adapter.

OK, now for the bad news. When it comes to customer service, Magellan has been horrid. We're talking so bad it's almost funny. I'm hoping this situation will change - the company was bought by Mitac late last year, and perhaps this will signal a change for the better in terms of customer support. Lord knows, they couldn't get any worse.

The leader, in my opinion, for customer support is Garmin. They are nice to deal with on the phone, answer emails promptly, and offer regular firmware updates. Whenever I buy a GPS as a gift I always buy Garmin since I don't want to saddle the recipient with the miserable service that Magellan offers. It's a shame, since Magellan offers some real benefits over Garmin, and more value for the money. Tom Tom is also decent when it comes to support, but they use TeleAtlas maps which are less complete than NavTeq (sp?).

Bottom line -- if you're looking for a straightforward GPS at a good price, this should be on your short list. It lacks features such as Bluetooth and an MP3 player, but for me, I want a GPS to offer guidance and not entertainment. This has a very robust feature set, great screen, and well-designed software. It also has traffic capabilities -- did not test that feature out, so I can't comment on it.

The "safe" bet continues to be Garmin. You'll pay a bit more, and get less features, but you can be assured of solid support. OK I admit it, I am leery of Linksys wireless routers. I have had four routers in my life (the E4200 being the fifth) and only the Linksys router gave me headaches. I vowed to never get another Linksys in my life, but I like Cisco so this was a dilemna and so far I am have been happy with it.

Design

This is a very slick device. I love the low profile that lets it hide on top of the cabinet it is on. A nice looking piece of hardware.

Setup

I have never had an easier set up on any wireless router. I installed the software onto my MacBook (mac friendly) and it self-discovered and prompted for the rest of the set up. Very nice setup, although a little long from beginning to end (7 minutes or so.) I loved that it prompted to personalize the SSID and password right up front. Software was slick and straight forward. Once set up I had all 7 wireless devices in the house on-line in about 20 minutes. Even my wireless printer worked instantly. - Five stars on Set-up

Functionality

I have only had the device installed for a weekend now, but I spent that time backing up my hard drive to a wireless SAN, watching streaming netflix and uploading a new website. No hiccups at all. About the only thing I did have an issue with is trying to set it up with my Ooma. I needed to rebooted the router and modem after removing the Ooma. No blame here, the Ooma doesn't seem to want to play nicely with any router or cable modem.

I really like the ability to have a guest network. It is easily turned off and on so I can easily provide a connection to visitors, but turn it off and totally deny the Brazilian students next door (actually it is password protected so it is not wide open, but less secure.)

Speed

I may not be the best to judge speed. I am not the type to watch the throughput numbers, but I can say that netflix streamed Mars Attacks wirelessly to my Wii without any issues. I have no issues with the speed at all.

Conclusion

I am very happy with the router. Who knows, two years down the line, I may be able to let my prejudice against Linksys go. If things continue to go well, or if they take a turn for the worse, I will update this review.

Summary:
I bought this kit because I needed to recover the data on an 80GB Hitachi 1.8" Drive from a dead Vaio notebook. No setup was required after I finished installing the drive in the enclosure, and it was recognized and read on my XP machine without a fuss. The enclosure is a thin aluminum extrusion with channels on the inside. The end caps appear to be pot metal castings. One end cap contains the interface board with LED activity light and the USB connector. A USB cable is provided. The kit is cheaply made but did what I needed.

Installation:
Installation consisted of mating a flex cable and connector, sliding the drive and active end cap into the enclosure, and screwing in the end cap(s).

It takes a bit of care and patience to insert the flex cable into the connector on the drive, but I was able to get it done in a few minutes.
The cable needs to be made to assume an S-bend after attaching it to the drive so that the entire assembly will fit into the box. That is best accomplished by gently pushing the end cap and HDD together and guiding the cable into an S. I suggest you place the assembly next to the enclosure first so you can see how much length the bend will need to take up. It's not much. Then, slide the drive into the enclosure followed by the cable and end cap, gently guiding the cable bend as needed. Make sure the end cap fits properly in place before and while you install the screws.

Here's the part I deducted a star for: The screws go into unthreaded channels in the enclosure and their alignment is less than perfect. It took quite a while and a better screwdriver than is provided to get the screws fully seated. YMMV.

If the drive rattles around more than you like front to back, you may wish to install one or two of the stick-on rubber bumpers that are provided onto the far end of the HDD or the inside of the blank end cap. Be aware you'll have to deal with two more screws if you put them inside the end cap.

I am using this strictly to boost the sound on our smart tv- a secondary but often used tv. I had purchased a similarly looking sound bar for my smart tv several months ago that works well. When this item came up as an option for review I figured it would an interesting item to try out since it has the addition of a subwoofer. Maybe it would be louder? Maybe it would sound more dynamic? We would see.. er, hear. So I tasked my husband with replacing our other sound bar with this set. It took him very little time to get it set up (less than 10 minutes, and it only took that long because our cat was helping. "helping").

The sound is definitely better and clearer than just using the speakers the tv comes with (which is usually the case). The sound is on par with the sound bar we had been using, except with the added dimension that the subwoofer provides. Without the subwoofer, it sounds just louder. With the subwoofer, it adds some depth and a nicer overall sound. We really just needed our tv to be louder. Cable is typically loud, but some programs on the various streaming services we have all have different levels of audio, with many being much too quiet. So better speakers have helped a lot.

The subwoofer connects to the soundbar via bluetooth. Both plug in, so plan to have 2 open spots in your power bar or wall receptacle. We have this system set up so the volume can be adjusted using the smart tv remote, rather than having to use the remote it came with. No issues there at all. Easy!

While I have the soundbar directly under the tv, I have the subwoofer set up in a corner a few feet away

The soundbar has spots in the rear in case you want to mount it to a wall. Subwoofer, does not.

Both are basic and minimalist looking. Subwoofer is black on black, soundbar is black with dark gray. No obnoxious branding or colors.

The instruction booklet is thorough, including information about the remote, battery info, placement and mounting, general operation, bluetooth operation, AUX in operation, Line-in operation, Optical-in operation (which is what I am using for use with my tv).

Overall sound is decent. Not home theater experience, but it definitely provides a sound and volume boost to internal tv speakers. I haven't yet tried it as a speaker for music. I really only purchased my original soundbar for use with tv (and replaced it with this for same purpose). I may give it a try anyway sometime soon. If I do, I will report back on how it does.

I like the added dimension that the subwoofer provides. I like the overall aesthetic. And because the combination of the two allows me to hear shows better than just using the tv speakers (on low audio streaming, as cable is always loud), I am pleased to use this.

I don't know hat this product costs, so I can't compare it. But, in short, it is about the same as just about any other low to mid priced soundbar. This is better sounding with addition of subwoofer. Not amazing, but definitely adds to my listening experience. 4 stars so far.

Notebook computers can overheat. It isn't a worry when you use your computer sparingly, but it can become a problem with extended usage. This cooling pad was designed to solve the problem by circulating air via two small fans with the power supplied by your notebook's USB. The movement of air is, supposedly, enough to keep your notebook from overheating or at least lessen the chances.

A product like this certainly sounds like a good idea and a practical solution to a problem, but does it really work as promised? Well, it does cause some extra flow of air, as expected, but the cooling effects are minimal. The main reason is because the flow of air is so light. Turn on the fans and place your hand next to them. You will barely feel anything and this is reason enough to suspect that it makes little difference.

Another thing to keep in mind with this cooling pad is that it will not work if you do not set it up properly. It has to be standing on a flat surface so that the air can flow underneath. If you're the type who holds your notebook on your lap, then a product like this will not work for you. There has to be space underneath so that the fans can operate and get the air moving.

The Mac Cooling Pad does fit securely on Mac's of different sizes and can be used for non- Mac pc's as well. I suppose it could make some difference in temperature, but it seems like a novelty product to me. Unless you are already experiencing an overheated notebook, a product like this is a waste of money.

UPDATE (2/21/19): So far, my clock is working well. I did buy a second clock, and succeeded in pairing it with my 1st Gen Echo Show. If you make a pairing mistake, you can press the clock's pairing button 5 times to unpair the clock and start over. Oddly, when the Show was correctly paired, the light turned solid orange. The Echo Show is hard to pair because it isn't completely integrated with the Alexa app when it comes to setting up a wall clock. However, for me, having two clocks, with visual timer displays paired to different Echo devices, was worth all the Setup hassles.

This ECHO WALL CLOCK does two things that I really want. First, it keeps accurate time by using an Internet connection (through an Echo device) instead of a radio signal (which can malfunction in bad weather or at Daylight Savings Time changes). Second, it gives a bright visual display of the time remaining on all the timers currently set with my first-generation Echo. (Yes, it simultaneously displays the time left on multiple timers.)

If my clock continues to work without requiring frequent Bluetooth re-pairing (as other reviewers have reported), I will order a second clock to pair with my Echo Show. The visual time-left display is very useful when I’m timing exercises or post-exercise ice treatments.

The instructions warn you NOT to try to move the clock hands. (Other reviewers warn that touching the hands will break the clock, or cause it to tell slightly inaccurate time forever if you succeed in replacing the hands.) It’s too bad that the clock does NOT have a plastic cover over the face--dusting it is going to be a problem. I put mine on a wall, to protect it as much as possible from dust, and from accidentally being knocked over.

SETUP PROBLEMS: Out of the box, the clock paired effortlessly with my Echo Show (using the option of asking the Show to set up the clock). However, I ran into a lot of difficulty when I tried to pair it with a second device (a first-generation Echo). The instructions do NOT make it clear that the clock PAIRS WITH ONLY ONE ECHO DEVICE.

Probably because I failed to start the second Setup attempt by using the Alexa app to un-pair the clock from the Show, the second attempt failed. It ended with a green light that has no defined meaning in the paper or online setup instructions. Worse, the clock no longer worked with the Show. Still worse, the clock did NOT appear as a device in the Alexa app; and the app did NOT display the clock as a Connected or Bluetooth device under the Show settings.

Eventually I found the clock under the settings for the Echo (subject of my second, failed Setup attempt). I was able to unpair it, delete it, and start Setup again. At long last, the clock paired with the Echo, and began working again (with the first-generation Echo).

However, I failed in all attempts to use the Show to set up the clock again. Those attempts always concluded with a red error light or with that mysterious green light. At some point, I had to remove the batteries and replace them so that the pairing button on the clock would work. Naturally I now dread having to pair the clock again with any Echo device, should the Bluetooth connection malfunction.

SUMMARY: The concept of the Wall Clock is great. I love my clock now, and really do intend to buy a second one, if the clock that I now have continues to work normally. However, I hope that later generations of the Echo Wall Clock will have a covered clock face, and that later versions of the Setup software will have much better integration with the Alexa app.

Ok, to be fair I work with cameras for a living. I wasn't expecting this to compete with my cinema cameras or even popular DSLRs for video, but I was expecting it to at least hold up to the standards people are expecting from cell phone cameras these days. It doesn't. Aside from filling a 4K frame, there aren't a lot of positives to say about the video quality.
To be fair, this has a LOT of advantages over using a cell phone. Recording for long lengths of time onto an SD card is a big plus, not the mention the ability to mount it to a standard tripod and have accessories like a mic and light attached to the body (which are all included!). It comes with a wide angle lens (that is oddly called "macro", but no- it's not for macro shots, its for going wider) which screws on to the front, as well as a handle mounting bracket, an LED light and a microphone. It even comes with a 64GB card, a spare battery, and not one but TWO useful carrying cases (a large one for everything, and a smaller one for just the camera solo). But that's about all the positives I can say about it. If you are outside with a lot of light, you can get decent shots, but this isn't a zoom lens, the zoom is digital only. You can go wide with the external lens or just stay at a fixed medium without it. So no closeup shots for soccer moms. The dynamic range when using it indoors was pretty bad, worse than your average mid-range cell phone. Forget about low light. But that's ok, because the ergonomics of a camera make it better than a cell phone, right?
Well, sorta. Holding it with the strap and the flip out screen is nice. But the UI is confusing, it's hard to go back and watch clips you took because everything is kind of sluggish and not intuitive- once we went past the first page of recorded clips, it was really difficult to move to the next page without accidentally clicking and opening a clip for playback. It just feels really laggy to navigate. Then there's the mic input... it's actually a proprietary plug that goes into the charging/USB plug, and gives you a pigtail for USB on one side and a mic input jack on the other. Odd, considering it COMES with a mic, you'd think it would have an input directly on the body. But no, just this weird mess of wires. Everything about this feels like jumping through a hoop to make it do what you want, and at the end of the day you have to wonder if you couldn't just be better off getting a mic adapter for the cellphone you already own and putting it in one of those holster cages.
Speaking of cell phones, this does have an app which supposedly lets you remotely control and perhaps even copy files from it, but I didn't get that far. I tried to install the app but then gave up when I decided I didn't want to grant this all the permissions it wanted from my personal phone. And I didn't think the video quality was worth it either.
Oddly enough, I kind of like the accessories it comes with. The LED light is pretty nice, the mic isn't terrible either. But for the money, I feel like I would have rather skipped those accessories and just gotten a better camera for a little bit more. It feels almost like they realized this camera was a hard sell so they beefed it up with lots of a accessories for the price.
In conclusion, you DO get a lot of accessories for the money. It's not the worst camera I've ever used, and you can't really get a set with everything you need for any less so I'd say it's worth at least 3 stars for being a functional kit. But I can't really imagine a scenario that I would recommend it.

I am an audiophile who is determined to get great sound without spending large amounts of money.  It is esy to get world class sound if you are willing to spend over $5,000.  I will never do that, however.  In the 1970's, I worked part time in two high end audio stores -- hence I know what good sound is and is not.  I was interested in the Motion 4's because they are Martin Logan speakers and Martin Logan has been a leader in producing remarkable speakers for decades.  And I was interested because of the technology employed in the Motion 4's. I got a pair of the Motion 4 speakers about one week ago after auditioning them three times at my local Best Buy. In the store, they sounded far superior to any other speaker even close to their price range.  Once I got them home, they sounded even better as I hooked them up to a Denon 3805 receiver.  I got the 3805 used for $200 after doing much research on receiver performance vis a vis 4 ohm speakers -- which the Motion 4's are.  This is a big deal -- matching you amp to your speakers -- since there are many amps that simply fall apart sonically under 4 ohm speaker loads.  Many receivers won't even rate their output into 4 ohm loads because of their embarassing performance. This particular Denon receiver, however is a throwback in terms of build quality and handles 4 ohm loads exceedingly well. The Motion 4's are not big speakers but they will fill an average sized listening room quite nicely. There is not much low end but that did not surprise me and it wasn't needed since I have a subwoofer. The midrange and the high end, however, are nothing short of glorious.  They are spacious and very open and incredibly detailed. I absolutely was hearing more and better sounds than I have heard in years. The folded tweeter -- a smaller version of the incredible Heil Air Motion transformer of 30 years ago -- clearly is amazing. Any high frequency -- cymbals, pianos, acoustic and electric guitars, etc -- simply come to life with a sense of immediacy and aural acceleration lacking in any other speaker near its price range and size.  The only possible reason anyone would find these speakers lacking is if you installed them in a very large room that they couldn't possibly fill OR if you hooked them up to an amp that could not handle 4 ohm loads -- and beware, there are a lot of amps out there that have this problem.  Otherwise, buy the Motion 4's with confidence.

I do a lot with photography and I always keep my eyes open for good lighting solutions that will help me get the lighting effects I want or need for given situations. I saw this one at a reasonable price and decided to take a chance on it. So far I am very pleased with it. It meets the biggest requirement I have for lighting - it does not strobe.

So many LED lights have an issue with strobing, especially when they’re low-cost. This light is not expensive when compared to a lot of others, so even though it is marketed as a video light I was only cautiously optimistic. To determine this for sure, I set my camera to use the electronic shutter only, sped up the shutter speed as high as I could and pointed directly at the light when it was powered on. Strobing lights always show banding in pictures with higher shutter speeds when using the electronic shutter; this one did not (though the display on the camera sure did but that’s a different problem). This test proved to me that this LED light does not strobe, at least not slow enough for my camera sensor to see it at high shutter speeds.

This is a fairly large LED panel, designed for video use of course but I also can work just fine for photography or even general lighting in the right setting. It comes with a clamp mount and a pole so it can be attached to a desk or shelf, then the mounting head allows for angling the light as needed so it can light a surface at just the right angle desired. The mount is sturdy and there should be no issues with stability when it is set up properly.

The light is super-easy to adjust. There are two dials on the back for tweaking the brightness and the temperature range, and there is a remote included that does the same. The temperature can be adjusted from a warm 2800K to a blistering white 8000K and everywhere in between so you can get the lighting just right.

Power is via an AC adapter and there is no battery. So, this is not a travel light by any means, If you need a light to use in the field, unless you have a power generator with you then this light isn’t it. For a static setting in a studio or room, this light is very good.

One design decision that would have been nice would have been a detachable mount so it could be used with a standard tripod instead of a clamp mount. That’s not a big deal, especially at the price point, but it would have made this light so much more versatile. I have other lights that I can mount on a tripod, so I am not too concerned.

This is a very good video light, especially when considering the price point. It has excellent temperature range, it has a solid mount for stability, and it does not strobe. If you’re looking for a solid video LED light that won’t cost a fortune, this one is better than could be reasonably expected at the asking price. It’s an easy one to recommend.

I have some cognitive impairment and mobility challenges from lupus, and I was able to set up Fire TV really easily. The batteries go in the remote; the hdmi cable goes where it goes, and the power plugs in where it plugs in. The interface is simple and intuitive, and you can get everywhere with the home button, the directionals, back, and select. The only painful part for me/my hands was logging into my wireless network via the onscreen qwerty keyboard.

The screens are responsive with virtually no latency, thanks to the quad core processor and 2 gb ram. And video streaming is also very smooth. I have only been using this a day, but I haven't had it pause to buffer yet. I have a Chromecast in my son's room, a recent model Mac Mini in the living room, an older C2D Mac Mini in my room with Boxee on it, and a Raspberry Pi, and they all buffer at some point during just about every movie. I stayed in a vacation home with a Roku 2 last summer, and it was great, but it also had to buffer a lot. We also have three game consoles that have streaming video apps, and they buffer, too. I think the Fire's secret may be its wifi card. I am sure that, at some point, my ISP will find a way to slow it down.

So, yeah, I am giving the Fire TV four stars for doing exactly what I need it to do. The reason it doesn't get five stars is that there aren't yet enough content apps. There is a manga channel, a documentary channel, an art house channel, along with Crackle and Flixter and Plex (Plex is a for pay service that lets you stream your home content). There is plenty to watch if you are a Prime member (I am - and I appreciated having that already set up on my Fire TV - Thank you, Amazon!) I am also a Dish subscriber, with HBO and a Hopper. I have apps for those directly on some of my devices. I can get them on the internet on the tbs I have hooked up to computers. I can even blast them over to my Chromecast from my tablets. But they aren't on Fire TV, and none of my tablets will screencast to Fire TV. Soon as they are, this is a five star device for me.

I read in Entertainment Weekly that HBO and Amazon Prime have come to an understanding that will make lots and lots of HBO shows available through prime, which will also make them available through Fire TV. For the ones that are not, HBOGO will have an app for this. Between that news and my son's enjoyment of an eight dollar (as opposed to 40 to 60 dollars) platformed on this thing, I am adding a star.

We've been using an older first generation Portal and like it very much. I was not expecting to be so impressed with this one, but wow have they managed to improve almost everything about the original! It still has the very cool zoom-and-pan style camera feature that follows the subject, as well as all the fun filters and of course my kids' favorite, story time... but the polish and style of this unit is really premium. The speaker is fantastic and LOUD if you want it to be. The clarity and bass rivals my bookshelf speakers so well, sometimes the kids play music off it and I could have sworn they were using the speakers in the living room. But the biggest improvement over the previous generation is the ability to run off battery power and move around. The "portable portal" honestly makes so much sense, I wonder why the original stationary style ones came out first!
Make no mistake, it is NOT a tablet, it is not thin and won't fit in an attaché case nicely. It is wedge-shaped making it stand easily at an ideal angle, and even has a cut-out handle to pick it up and carry it to a better location for video chat. This is great for bringing it to wherever my kids happen to be congregating currently, and it can be put back up on the shelf when done to charge. Like the original Portals, it has Alexa built in and can act as an Echo for most things, however it is very tied into Facebook's ecosystem. That means that although it seems to run something akin to Android behind the scenes, this is NOT going to offer a standard App store, and even things like Youtube are not available for it (licensing issues with Google I'd suppose). However there is a browser, and you can navigate to YouTube and play it from the website just fine, although a proper app would be much easier to navigate. It does have Plex support, which I found interesting since I have a Plex server. I never thought I'd find Plex available where Youtube is not! Meanwhile, between Youtube in the browser, Amazon Music through Alexa and content on Plex, there are plenty of ways to make it a music streamer on that glorious better-than-it-should-sound speaker. And the camera works just as well if not better than the OG Portal!
Calls over FB Messenger or Whatsapp work well, and of course the camera / mic not only have a switch to toggle, but the camera has a physical cover that can slide over the lens in case you don't trust Facebook not to snoop. But that's another story.
All things considered, this is a solid product.

I believe you can get this to show up on an app all by itself if you don't use an NVR, which is an awesome feature if you only have one camera or a few by the same brand. I'm also sure I can get this set up with my QNAP NAS if I wanted to, but when I played around with that on my last camera, I wasn't super-impressed (plus, I'm not about to pay for additional licenses on this stystem that is going to be augmented many times). Since I knew I was going to use the NVR, I just went right to it with this camera.

The NVR way sort of automatically makes a VLAN on your network so your cameras aren't taking up IP addresses and getting in your way. You can also set it up so it takes a regular IP address on your regular network and your NVR sees it and records over the network. There's less traffic eating up your other connections if you go straight to the NVR, though. Personally, I don't need a lot of IoT IP addresses obfuscating my network when I'm trying to track down a new device or other computer. But the variety and versatility of these setups is unmatched compared to DVR systems (although those are perhaps unmatched in their simplicity...but you can make the NVR thing as simple as you want to as well).

Anyway, I love the camera. Love the security. Love being able to see if I have a package. Love being able to see what cars are in my driveway. Love having great newage features on an old house.

I use active noise canceling (ANC) headphones all the time and prefer them to normal headphones as I tend to work in noisy environments and I’ve found that with ANC engaged I can play music at lower volumes. I like Sony headphones so I was excited to try these ANC ear buds. They’re a bit unusual in a few ways but they work well and are worth their asking price.

These are truly wireless and have no physical connection between them. Power them both on and they find one another. They pair via Bluetooth to a phone, tablet or PC, and the connection is stable up to about 40’ around corners. This is a good start.

There are several modes to these when it comes to the ANC function and each has its uses. I usually just use full ANC without any of the ambient sound modes turned on as it gives the best music experience. One of the two ambient modes is optimized for speech and voice, the other for more generalized noise. Neither completely cut off noise canceling, but rather they allow different bands of outside noise to come through. In full ANC mode, these are good noise cancellers, though not as aggressive as some others like Bose.

These have proven to be comfortable, and they have the little wings on each bud for keeping them in place in your ear. I used them while working in the yard and never once did I have a problem with slipping or falling out, even though I have the wrong size silicone insert on one of them.

The sound is very good but I would stop short of calling it outstanding. The bass is heavier than I like though not so bad that it gives me a headache unless I pump the volume up too much. The midrange is warm and full, and the highs are bright and crisp without being piercing. The sound can be adjusted a bit in the app that you can download, as it has an equalizer of sorts that lets you tweak the levels or choose a preset.

Ah, the app… This is the primary downside of these. The method to adjust these is either an Android or iOS app, not a physical piece of hardware and there is no Windows equivalent (for those who want to use these with a PC). The app is a little clunky though fairly self-explanatory and it does do what it’s supposed to do. Given a choice between an app or an additional piece of hardware, I would choose the hardware.

These charge up in the carrying case, which has leads that connect to each bud. Pay attention when you put these in the case – it is possible to reverse them, and while it hurts nothing the charging doesn’t work well… The case has some sort of battery in it and it charges the buds without being plugged in itself, though it does require occasional charging. Charging is fast – I charged them from empty to full in about an hour. One thing that could be improved, though: the buds can be popped in the charger while still powered on, and the act of charging them does not make them cut off. So, you can end up with dead buds and a dead charger too.

These are decent wireless sport buds that have good sound and good ANC functions. They’re comfortable and not overpriced. There are a couple of areas for improvement, particularly in charging but also in the app control, that would make these even better.

This is a 3-piece accessory kit for a camera with a threaded lens (in my case, a 58mm thread). I use this kit with a Samsung NX-300 with the 18-55mm zoom lens and it fits that lens well. My experience with this kit has been mostly positive.

Included in the kit are two lens hoods and one lens cap. I will discuss each separately.

The lens cap is, to me, the best component in the kit. It does not look like a particularly exciting item, but in this case this lens cap actually fits my lens better than the original cap from the manufacturer. It is tight and is seated evenly on the lens assembly. As an added bonus is has a lanyard that allows it to hang on the lens barrel so it does not need to be specifically tracked when it is not in place covering the lens.

The second item in the kit is a tulip hood for the lens and it is neither better nor worse than the one that came with the camera. It does an acceptable job of keeping the lens in the shade instead of allowing sunlight to hit it directly. Note that when the tulip cover is in place the lens cap will not fit.

The last item in this kit is a rubber hood that works similarly to the tulip hood and it helps prevents direct light from angling in to hit the lens. This one component is the only one in the kit about which I have anything critical to say, and it’s this: when the lens is zoomed all the way in the edges of the hood can be seen in the picture. It does not take much to zoom out past it but it still merits some mention.

I am satisfied with this kit. It includes two hoods and a lens cap that in my case is better than the original that came with my lens. This is a decent kit at a good price.

I'm on my second old house; this one (1924) is the keeper. The first one I had spent years of random free time painstakingly installing a robust wired network through plaster walls - the result was every bit as rewarding as you can imagine. WiFi is great for the exception, not as the rule. Now I'm on my second old house. I intend to do the same, but - after roughing in the new telecom closet and getting the primary TV/stereo/gaming area roughly wired in, the rest of my cabling dreams take a backseat to some other stuff I want to do (besides, it's supposed to be fun, but it won't be if I put myself under the gun). The point is, this Ethernet extender is really a fantastic device to keep some of the A/V devices (like one for the TV, smart speaker, and computer setup in my office) from junking up the airwaves (i.e., using WiFi throughput, which is already limited due to the fact that everything likes to connect via 2.4GHz, even when I use band steering, and that my AP is downstairs (and I really only wish to have one for the actual house, even when I have the wiring to support multiple).

As other reviewers have mentioned, I am also not getting Gb speeds through this thing, but I guess I really didn't expect to. What matters to me is that I am actually have a good connection even when my WiFi shuts off for the evening (by design) and that I don't have all these random issues that I've always attributed to wireless. I probably need to get another of these for the other office that houses the printer - for the longest time, I wanted an Ethernet-capable printer, and when I finally get one, I now only have WiFi for it, and it suffers as a result.

One thing about this that isn't perfect for me is the typical plug-in design that takes up half an outlet. My outlets are all in the baseboards, which I sort of like because it seems like a fancy style from back in the day, but then of course if I don't use an extension cord with this, it just keeps me from being able to push the furniture back as far as I might otherwise. When I do use an extension cord, it's even more difficult to hide, and then I have an extra link, which is never desirable.

The nice thing about this is that I can re-purpose it multiple times as I finish work on my house. Of course I'll probably wire that office next, but then I can move this to the next office, then to the bedroom, etc. These days, I have plenty of Ethernet-capable devices around the house (and I avoid anything that is WiFi only).

I'm also very curious to see if this would work out in the garage, even if after a sub-panel. That would also be a great backup use (I have one garage connected by a low voltage contactor, so I'm not sure that will work, am soon building another garage, but will have conduits for telecom immediately upon putting that building into service.

Even so, I could see using this for IP cameras as well...Oh my God, I literally just thought of this. I may re-purpose this early and then buy another if it works flawlessly, but I could get three IP cameras on this to work in my attic (hanging down from my eaves, discreetly) since the big problem right now is getting cabling from my telecom cabinet area in the basement to the attic for distribution to the upper rooms. And of course now I realize I could also feed multiple rooms from the attic a while...

Well, clearly the options are endless. It won't ever be as nice as having homeruns from every work area back to the switch, but it's certainly better than WiFi in most cases (and especially in the case of cameras, etc.). Great device to have for network flexibility, especially in an old house with limited pathways.

These are longer than average skewers, too, so it is possible to string more food onto them. It is easy to optimize use of space too, by snaking the skewers on the grilling surface.

Finally, the tips stay cool when you hang them over the end of the grilling surface. The lid of the grill will even close with the ends hanging over the sides.

These are excellent skewers and make grilling with them instead of with traditional skewers eaiser and more pleasant.
