This MP3 player, which I was given at a discount in exchange for my honest review, is sleek and lightweight yet potentially—via a firmware upgrade that I hope Lonve will consider—very powerful. (See my photo of the player lying on top of my MacBook Pro trackpad to get an idea of its size.) It can be listened to without hooking it up to anything else, either with wired headphones or through the surprisingly good-sounding on-board speakers. The view screen when the player is powered on is quite readable, and I love how the surface of the screen becomes a classy grey-bronze mirrored surface that is so clear you can use it to check your appearance. The ability to add up to a 32GB SDHC card you've preloaded with music or video is a great feature.

The included wired headphones are better than some I've listened to, although I prefer another pair that fits my tiny ears better; unfortunately, those are Bluetooth, so they won't work with this player. I will likely listen to the player my itself, with no headphones, through its speakers.

I can't five-star love this player because I can't set the time to a 12-hour clock and it doesn't allow for adding playlists, which I was thinking it did. Maybe I'm missing something, but I can't even start an album folder playing by tediously navigating to it in the Explorer; it appears you have to navigate all the way into the files in the folder and then start it playing, although I haven't even been able to get this to work. It takes too many steps and is so very aggravating that I usually just quit trying to play either music or video.

What really shines on this player is the radio. I'm sure reception will vary depending on where you are, but in Lexington, KY, I can pull in NPR very clearly and easily. It would be nice to be able to store favorite radio stations—if there's a way, I haven't figured it out after days of fiddling with the player—but I'm happy that I can leave it sets to my main station and it always comes back there even after I've powered off and then back on. If you're a person who likes to listen to the radio at night with the lights off, going to sleep, but don't like fooling with headphones, this will be a great little player for you.

The Game feature has a neat little Tetris-style game that's amusing while stuck waiting somewhere. The Photo feature is nothing to write home about, but it can be used to show off a few photos of your pets or kids or maybe a logo or graphically produced emergency contact info. There is an Autoplay Time setting you can set in the Settings/Photo. The text feature allows for reading text files, so you can take along a grocery list or study notes. I started to knock off an extra star (down to three) because of something I really dislike about this player, and that is the dedicated left-side button (one of only three) that seems to serve no purpose but to turn on the voice recorder. When I press it by mistake or forget that the On/Off button is the button on the right, not the left, the Recorder comes on. Then I get a file format error when I try to get out of it. It would have been better, I think, had they used that button for something more likely to be used constantly (Explorer with the ability to set either the internal C: card or the external D: card as the default for the button maybe) or, better, allow the user to define the function of that button via a Settings selection. I want to be able to disable the Recorder completely, although I know some people will want to have a recorder. But I hate it.

You do have the option of upgrading the firmware, but the instructions are very poor. When I select Upgrade in Settings/System (which you reach by scrolling down to the end, near the Language setting), I am warned to connect to USB. When I connect the USB cable to my computer, however, I get the Connect screen on the player and there does not seem to be any way then to access the System/Upgrade selection. The instructions, such as they are, are clear in how to navigate through the features and which of the two non-Recorder buttons (middle, right) to push in connection with the up/down, left/right arrows. But, needless to say, there are bugs in the player I am reviewing. Lonve has been good about getting back quickly with answers to questions, though, so I'm hopeful they'll work hard to get this one right.

I’ve spent the last month using and playing games on the Lenovo IdeaPad Gaming 3. It’s a decent entry-level laptop. I wouldn’t consider it a dedicated gaming machine, but more aimed at daily use plus some gaming.

The laptop includes 3 free months of Xbox Game Pass, so I’ve played games available through that library. Games like Moonlighter, Moonglow Bay, Tunic, Sims 4, and Hades. The laptop handled all of those just fine, but many are older games and/or not very hardware intensive.

However, I don’t think 8GB of RAM and a 256GB SSD are enough. In my very first day of downloading games, I filled more than half the hard drive (and only ~236GB is available to start). As for the RAM, my 5-year-old laptop has 8GB of RAM and I’m feeling it. A laptop from 2022 should start with at least 16GB.

The Quad Vent fans vent in the back and on both sides of the laptop. I wish there wasn’t a vent on the right, because it’s right where the mouse sits. After maybe twenty to thirty minutes, my hand gets sweaty, which isn’t great when playing a competitive game.

There are 2 USB-A ports, one on each side. The back has an HDMI port, Ethernet, USB-C, and the power input. I actually really like the power input being on the back, as that way the cable isn’t in the way when using the mouse. But I’d like another USB-A port in the back, because I can see using a hub with this laptop.

The keyboard is not my favorite. On the plus side, it’s a full keyboard. I can’t remember the last time I saw a laptop with a numpad. The keyboard has backlighting, but only one color option: white. The keys are flat on top and somewhat slippery. The keyboard itself feels cramped, especially when gaming with WASD.

The laptop is heavy, about 7 or 8 pounds. It’s not something you’ll want to tote from class to class. The battery lasts about an hour if playing games, and about 3 hours for normal use.
Fit and versatility is good

I've been using a Keurig machine for several years -- I currently own 2 of them. But I've always had an ethical issue with all the little plastic cups that get tossed into the environment. To that end, I've tried and used several different varieties of reusable K-cups, and had finally settled on the Ekobrew cups.

I was offered an opportunity to try this set, and decided to do a side-by-side comparison. The results were interesting. These Brewooze cups perform just as good as the more expensive Ekobrew cups.

I tried several different coffees and several different grinds. As with all reusable cups, you have to be careful how fine/coarse the grind is. Too coarse, and you get weaker coffee; too fine, and you get either overflow and/or sludge. I found that a medium-fine grind worked best for both cup brands. This way, I get the right strength and almost no powdery sludge in the bottom of the cup. One advantage of the Brewooze over the Ekobrew: I was able to use LESS coffee in the cup to get the right brew strength. With the Ekobrew, I needed to fill the cup; with the Brewooze, I filled it about 2/3 full to get the same flavor/strength.

As with all reusable K-cups, you need to take care when you seal them prior to use. These are no trouble to seal correctly -- you can easily see if there are gaps and do an extra "squeeze." Inserting them into the machine takes a bit of attention, too -- otherwise, you can pierce the cup. There are arrows on the lid that show which direction, so that shouldn't be a problem.

This set comes with 20 paper filters plus a replacement charcoal filter for the Keurig filter wand. I didn't see much advantage to the paper filters except possibly ease of cleaning. The coffee was weaker, and using a finer grind didn't seem to help. And it still resulted in some grinds getting "around" the paper filter and onto the mesh, so I still had to clean the cup. It's not a big deal, really -- the cups are easy to rinse clean after use. So I won't be using the paper filters, but you may find them useful.

I'm a little surprised at how nicely these performed, given the price. You get 3 cups (brown, medium tan, and light tan color -- the photo makes them look orange, but they're more of a tan/brown), so if you want to assign a color to different family members, there you go. Since I usually brew 2 cups into a large mug, I just fill 2 of them with the same coffee and run them one after the other in the morning.

kI have to say I was impressed. I didn't expect these to perform as well as they did. Definitely comparable to the Ek​​​​obrew so far -- the only question I have is durability, and only time will tell. I've been using these for about 4 days, and after the initial side-by-side test (when I brewed about 12 cups total), I've been brewing 2-3 cups every morning, rotating them, cleaning after each use, and so far, no signs of any wear problems. If I notice a serious issue, I'll update this review.

This is one of the better sounding shower radios I’ve used. Although it’s pretty compact (roughly 3.5 inches square and 1.5 inch thick) the sound quality is pretty impressive given the constraints of a single rear-facing speaker. The big negative is tuning. It uses a rotary dial to set the station. It’s not very precise – it’s very easy to overshoot or undershoot the desired station. Once you tune it to the station you want it stays put, but getting there can be a challenge.

This is a decent choice if you’re looking for a low-cost shower radio and tend to listen to the same station all the time. However, if you like to change stations frequently, the tuning can be a bit frustrating.

I've been obsessed with fully wireless earbuds for years and have tried out at least a dozen different ones throughout.

I fully support some in the $30 range, I had a pair of old soundcores that worked great. I've also tried the more expensive Samsung Galaxy Buds (2018 version), which worked well enough. I've also tried some mid-range ear buds in the $70 range. Earbuds have gone through some growing pains with drop off issues between the left and right buds and battery life. In my experience, I believe the $30 buds are great value and >$100 buds are worth it only if they have good sound and good app support. For me every one of the $70 buds that I have purchased have broken down in less than three months, so I'd say stay away from those.

Now on to the review:
The Cleer Audio, Ally Plus II True Wireless Noise Cancelling Earbuds are in the >$100 range (although just barely) but in the last few weeks that I've used them, I truly believe they are worth their asking price. I will of course update this review if they break down in a few months.

There are so many wireless earbuds being produced these days, which most imitating the airbuds with their ugly stalks in one form or another, Cleer has gone with a tear-drop shape and capacitive controls that I appreciate. I purchased the tan-colored buds and they don't stand out like a pair of white or black buds would. There is only a single dim light on the earbuds to indicate charging status and they are the in-ear-canal style of earbuds.

Features:
- Light-weight.
- Charging/carrying case supports type-c connection as well as wireless charging. Interoperable with products designed for airbuds wireless charging.
- Long battery life. I listen to audiobooks and they have lasted for hours while I worked on chores around the house.
- Passthrough with good app support (more on it later)
- Active Noise cancellation
- Can be used as a single earbud without having to pair each separately
- Touch controls: Only tap, double tap, and triple tap are supported. Configurable through the app.

The App:
When I first received the Cleer earbuds, the app was unimpressive. There was a single slide bar that changed the balance between noise cancellation and passthrough, a equalizer with no presets (and no reset for that matter), and there was limited control over what the tap functions did.

Since then, the app has been updated and the earbuds had a firmware upgrade. While the app still has room for more improvement, they did separate the passthrough, normal, and noise cancellation modes into separate controls. Passthrough now has a slider to control the strength of the surrounding noise and the noise cancelling has a "smart noise cancel" mode. In addition, a new personalized audio feature was added. The app takes you through a hearing test and adjusts the sound to your hearing levels. Quite cool.

The limited controls over the touch function is still there and the barely passable equalizer is still there but I'm hoping that they will be improved in future updates.

I use this to connect my MP3 player to a 3.5mm jack I installed in my car's center console. The low-profile 3.5mm connector was very important to me because I wanted to make the connection as slim as possible to avoid accidentally torquing it, catching things on it, or applying pressure to the jack when moving things in and out of the console.

It works quite well for this purpose. the connector is slim - about as slim as they come, such that it basically clamps right up against the side of the player and the wall of the console. The plug itself feels solid and has a small snap when connecting to things. The cable is soft and almost as flexible as a woven cord, even if it does prefer some orientations to others. Sound quality is typical - which is to say, as good as every other cable I've owned.

The only thing I didn't like about the cable was the colors - it really doesn't go with the car interior and stuck out as a result, a bit distracting. So I used a Sharpie Pro - the big chisel-tip type - to turn it black. It is cotton sheathing, so this is quite viable. I was careful - after inking the entire cable and letting it dry, I washed it in warm water, then dried it and ran a soft, clean rag over it about a hundred times, until it came away basically clean. After the fact, while you could tell the original black bits from the inked threads, it's just different shades of black, rather than looking blotchy. I imagine using something like RIT black dye would be about equally effective, if you heated it and let it soak for a good long while.

So I would recommend it. The braided cable looks premium and is much easier to work with than its equally-thick rubber counterparts. This makes it easy to handle the MP3 player while it is still plugged in.

Great Addition to Home Security System

First I should say there is no 100% perfect home security system. That is why I have a home security “solution” that incorporates several different, but tied together systems. I have a full Lorex Camera System, Smart Things Hub and a wired alarm system. But even with all that there was something missing. If I wasn’t home, all of the other items were only good after the fact. Meaning I could see who was at my door, or in my house after I got back home. Sure I could set alerts on those other devices, but when your phone chirps 10 alerts per hour, it just becomes white noise. These other systems had so many false positives I ultimately turned them off.

Pros: But the Ring Bell filled several voids in these other systems. One, the false positives are almost nonexistent due to the ability to mask the alert area of the camera. My existing security system may alert me, but then I had to log into the camera system to see what was going on. The time it takes to do that could make a real difference. The ability to answer and interact with someone who rings your bell from your couch or from at work is invaluable! The person ringing the bell has no idea where you are answering from. But the best part is being able to ignore solicitors and screen people before you answer. It’s as easy as answering a phone call and the live image is instantaneous. The fact that it integrates with my SmartThings hub is just icing on the cake.

I was able to install the Ring Bell Pro in about 15 minutes following the simple instructions. It is extremely well thought out. The video quality of the Ring Pro is excellent! It does not have a very wide angle and there is a slight fisheye distortion, but it should be more than sufficient for most applications. The mobile app is also very intuitive. As I mentioned, when you get an alert, you can immediately see who is at the door and you can choose to answer and speak, or just watch.

Cons: I was confused by the wall plate not having the mounting holes line up with the existing wall plate holes. This required drilling holes above and below the existing holes to mount the plate. I could see no reason for this.

The unit can easily be ripped off the wall with one hand. Because the main unit mounts onto a plastic wall cover, it would take about 2 seconds to remove and disable the unit. But at least you will get an alert and when you went to log in you would know something was wrong. However, the Ring Pro has a unique purchase protection that sates “If your Ring™ Video Doorbell is stolen at any time after your purchase, Bot Home Automation, Inc. will replace your Ring™ Video Doorbell at no charge to you”. That’s pretty impressive!

If you want to keep your Ring History, you have to sign up for their paid service. Otherwise you only see live views. Prices vary by plan, but they do offer one free month for new customers.

Overall: There is no perfect security system. Each one has its plusses and minuses. But the Ring Pro should be part of every home security solution. Also, if I had to choose only one component for a complete home security solution, this would be high up on my list.

Update: I really love this machine. You give a lot of things five stars if they're really good products, but this one deserves bonus. Also, I give a lot of things controlled by apps low ratings because I tend to hate screwing around with my phone, but in this case, the Yamaha AV controller app only adds to the value, with the best part being you don't NEED it to take advantage of all the receiver's functionality, but it's a joy to have sometimes to make fine adjustments without having to turn on the TV. Original review:

Before this, I had two Sony receivers in my living room. My secondary is a much older model - about 12 or so years old - that does not have HDMI and I use it for my whole house audio system. My primary is (was - it just got replaced) a 3-5 year old Sony model that is admittedly in a lower class than this Yamaha receiver (the secondary was in a higher class in its time, I think).

While I usually have all Sony stuff, I was completely willing to try another well-known Japanese brand who specializes in receivers and amps. And - it's just awesome. Totally. Not a single regret about the switch. The RX-A880 gave me back everything I lost going from my older, higher-end Sony to my newer one, AND it gave me so many nice surprises on the way! As anyone can tell you that it sounds good and looks good, I'll concentrate on this little details that I discovered during setup:

1) Besides the seven HDMI inputs, it also has a composite video, a component video, two optical audio, one extra (second belongs to component) coax audio, and two composite audio inputs, not to mention phono.

The great thing is that you can assign different audio inputs to any of the video inputs. So, for example, I decided to keep my Wii around since I now have a component input (and it takes up almost no space), but the cable is component video with composite audio, but the component video input on this has coax for the audio. Bummer. But no, you can change it. Example number two is I have a computer in my telecom closet hooked up to this with both HDMI and line-out audio. For circumstances too complicated to define here, audio does not output via the HDMI. But because of this feature, I can make the audio appear when I select the HDMI input OR when I just want to listen to the audio directly (with no HDMI output). Perfect.

2) 9 Speaker outputs. First, I'm so happy to have the 2-zone thing back (my secondary receiver has it, but my other, newer Sony did not - it only had A/B speakers that shared an amp). But this one you can actually have 7.1 AND a second zone (although you can't play them at the same time. This is really cool if you want the best of both worlds. I don't know if I can find a place for two more speakers in my setup, but ...it's nice to have the option. Supposedly, this all works automatically. I imagine it could work fine, but I am unable to try it at the moment.

3) 2-zone done better. My older Sony had 2-zone, but the controls were - frankly - atrocious. It was always confusing, even for someone like me who can be a super A/V nerd and memorize anything. The way I use it now is just to keep the remote on Zone-2, and do Zone-1 on the unit itself.

This Yamaha, however, has a simple switch on the remote, and you're either controlling one zone or the other depending on that switch. Simple and effective. You can also control it from the unit, unlike the older Sony.

4) 8 custom presets, all controlled directly from the remote. Another 8 for Zone 2?!

The one complaint I read by a reviewer was that you have to scroll through all the inputs from the remote to get to what you want. But that doesn't matter for two reasons: first, you can change the settings to skip anything you don't want. But, second, with 8 custom presets - and each with their own remote button - you probably don't even ever need to scroll through the inputs anyway.

And the custom presets are great. You can turn on and off a bunch of features like whether or not it changes your HDMI out settings, if it uses your YPAO settings, extra bass, which speakers it uses, etc. And it even can link the second zone!

Two great examples:

I can't stand to watch regular background TV with the surround sound on because it makes the commercials that much more obnoxious. But of course I like big booming bass and surround for movies. And it's also annoying to switch the unit off and on all the time, especially if you want to use control for HDMI. So I have one preset for very flat TV sound using just the front speakers that is clearer than-, but no more annoying than-, my regular TV speakers. Then I have another preset for surround sound and big bass for movie watching.

I have one preset for straight music just in zone 1. Then I have another preset for straight music in both zones one and two. It turns on zone 2 automatically. I could not figure out how to make a preset just for zone 2, but it seems that when I am controlling zone 2 on the remote, I can make 8 more presets just for zone 2. You can not adjust these presets via menu, from what I can tell, though.

5) 14 character names on the front of the unit in dot matrix. My other receivers were all limited to 8 characters. You can see all 14 at once, which is great.

6) Much more robust networking. I haven't played with this too awful much yet, but it seems that if you start listening to a playlist or an album on your NAS, then the next time you go back to "server", it will start playing where you left off (well, the song you left off at will start over again, instead of at the exact moment you left at), but at least this way you don't have to turn the TV on just to play some music. I suppose you could create a playlist of all Death Metal, and then you just have a stream going whenever you want it. It also seems like you can actually sign into Pandora and all the other stations and listen to your own account. And all the Internet/Network stuff is a separate scroll-through than the other inputs. I really like how that is set up.

6) The "program up/down" buttons on the remote can be programmed to do about 10 different things. I picked to have the dialogue increased or decreased for when you can't hear what people are saying even though everything else is loud enough. To be clear, I think this depends on if the dialogue is known to the decoder. I haven't tried all the other options yet.

7) Remote is awesome. Besides what I mentioned above, you can also make some changes to the red/green/yellow/blue buttons, but I wish you could really program those completely to your liking. Everything is laid out nicely, and the second zone even makes sense, as I mentioned above.

8) I realize the second HDMI output would be great if you also have a projector or something like that. With it, you can have access to all your devices without having to rewire anything. Haven't used it yet, but am glad to have the extra functionality.

...

There's plenty more, but I'm forgetting some of the details right now. I've only played with this thing for a few days, but I like it more and more. The one thing that is missing is that you can't change all the options via the webpage. You can change some, but I liked with my newer Sony the fact that I could look at and change all my custom presets without having to turn the TV and go through all that. I'm only comparing this to my two Sony units so you get my frame of reference, but realize this Yamaha model is in a higher class than those. Regardless, I love this thing, and it has a lot of great functionality and no serious drawbacks that I've noticed yet. Recommended (obviously).

This isn't a good first telescope, if the intent is to introduce and encourage someone to pursue the hobby of astronomy further. The images were fuzzy and distorted and varied in focus across the field of view. Any reflector telescope, even this small one, requires the mirrors to be precisely aligned (collimated) to get sharp images. Out of the box, the two mirrors were not aligned well. I did take it apart. I unscrewed the primary mirror holder from the bottom and drilled out larger diameter holes so that I could adjust the positioning of primary mirror I reseated the secondary mirror (below the eyepiece) which was not level. The 3 existing screws in the secondary mirror can be adjusted to adjust the alignment of the secondary mirror. After some manual collimation, the image is now much better. Stars no longer look like fuzzy balls. But this process isn't easily done in this telescope, nor is it described in the included instructions. Reflector telescopes can be quite persnickety because of their need to be precisely adjusted. My advice is to either spend more money on an reflector which has better optics which can be collimated, or choose a refractor telescope which I think is easier to use for a beginner and doesn't require such adjustments such as this one for not much higher cost:
Celestron 21035 70mm Travel Scope https://www.amazon.com/dp/B001TI9Y2M/ref=cm_sw_r_other_taa_QTn5zbPV2FBNX

*Acoustic auto calibration- you sit wherever (like on your couch) and it sends these loud sound blasts that sound like alien gun blasters. The blasts reach the mic in your remote where you are sitting and then the tv records the information and auto calibrates the sound so it reaches you better based on your room and where you're sitting.
*The speakers use vibration to turn the whole display into a loudspeaker- sending sound everywhere. Small subwoofers in the back to give it an extra bump of bass. You absolutely notice this technology working- the sound is amazing and PLENTY loud. You can always add surround sound if you have to have a deep boom of bass like in the movie theater though.
*XR Motion processing- means blur-free scenes. You can really notice this on things like watching sports from football to surfing.
*Upscaling is great. HDR is fantastic too- I really notice the differences in skin tones, they look a lot more natural on this tv. The XR processor really puts noticeable light into the highlights of the picture which really helps the image pop.

CONS:

The 80J doesn't have the heatsink in the back that the 90J does. This might become noticeable for gamers and is a letdown. The speakers are a little less powerful in this tv than the 90J, they sound good but don't have as much power. The 80J doesn't have the backlit Sony remote that the 80J has which is crazy and a replacement remote in case you're wondering costs a whopping $80!!

At $1300 less than the 90J, the decision for me is clear! I definitely say go with this 80J because the small improvements aren't worth paying the $1300 more. BUT if price isn't an issue- go for the 90J. I can tell you for sure, you'll be happy with either that you choose, they're both fantastic devices that are well built and jam packed with the latest tech and features.

For streaming Amazon and Netflix videos, playing Steam games, and general web browsing, the screen is beautiful and the computer has been working flawlessly since I got it four month ago. I have no complaints on those fronts. However, there are some other things to talk about.

One of the minor flaws is that the mouse turns off after several minutes of inactivity. You have to click it to turn it back on again before you can use it. That may sound like a trivial thing but it can become an ongoing irritant, especially if you work on several different computers and have to remember to click this particular mouse before usage.

Another minor flaw, one that became a major irritant for me, was that the screen would turn off after 5 minutes without any keyboard or mouse usage. It would even turn off while I was watching movies. In the Windows 10 Power & Sleep settings I would change the screen turn off time from 15 minutes to Never. That would fix the problem temporarily. However, every time I rebooted the computer, the screen turn off time would reset itself to 15 minutes. So I would have to go back into the settings to change it again.

Fiddling with the Windows power plan and scouring the net for solutions turned up nothing. Yes, the power plan was set the way I wanted it. No, the problem had nothing to do with a screensaver. No, there was nothing in the Bios that would trigger the reset. After four months of constant irritation, I finally stumbled across the solution by accident. It seems that ASUS has it's own power plan that overrides the Windows one. The default setting on the ASUS power plan was to turn the screen off after 15 minutes. Changing the ASUS setting to Never finally solved the problem. Why ASUS felt the need to put it's own power plan on their machine when Windows 10 already had a perfectly good one, I have no idea. I especially don't know why ASUS set their plan to override Window's.

That problem touches on the potentially major flaw with ASUS. In trying to find a solution to a minor problem on another ASUS machine, I found that their customer service sucks. When, after much effort, I finally got to talk with a live person, their accent was so thick that I literally could not understand what they were saying. When I asked for someone who spoke clearer English, the service rep got all huffy and I never did get to talk with anyone else and my questions never got answered.

This happened after I had already bought the ASUS Zen Z240-C1, otherwise I wouldn't have gotten a second ASUS machine. Now I've got my fingers crossed that nothing major happens to this one lest I get tangled up in their customer service mess again. The Philips GoGear Raga is the first exposure I have had to Philips' line of mp3 players and I was unsure of what I should expect of it. The price is comparable to other mp3 players of similar capacity so I expected it to be in the ballpark with them. For the most part I was correct, though there are a few things about which one should be aware when using this particular offering. It's a good product, but it has its quirks.

Setting up the Raga is easy. In the package is a USB cable that allows one to connect to a PC (packaging does not indicate if MacOS supports the Raga), and upon connecting Philips Songbird downloads and installs automatically. The installation is painless and does not take long, and a few clicks of the mouse along the way and the software loads up.

The first thing I tried to do was load music into the Raga, and once I got the music into Songbird the Raga disappeared from the available devices list. I am not sure what happened. I unplugged it and shut down Songbird, plugged the Raga back in and everything was as it should be, so I dragged 67 songs to the Raga for transfer. I saw two problems. First, the user has to know to drag and drop - there is no "transfer to..." option that I could find in any of the menus. The bigger problem, though, is that the transfer speed is abysmal and it took close to 2 minutes to transfer 67 songs that average 5MB in size. With my old iPod and with my ZuneHD, transfer speeds are appreciably faster. This doesn't make the Raga a piece of junk, of course, as the problem may be Songbird itself, but the transfer speed is something of which to be aware, especially if transferring large amounts of music.

Navigating to the newly transferred music is simple. For that matter, navigating the Raga is simple, period. Anyone with even slight familiarity with music players will have no problem finding and playing music on the Raga.

For comparison, I matched the Raga against my ZuneHD for playback. Of course, the Zune HD produced a more natural and clear sound, but only slightly. For the difference in price, I would have expected the ZuneHD to REALLY outperform the Raga, but this was not the case. In fact, when playing with the built in equalizers in both, I was able to get the Raga to get very close to the ZuneHD for sound quality. The difference was more pronounced with higher end ANC headphones, but this is unlikely to matter to the large majority of users.

The Raga has a tiny screen (the package says it's 1" diagonally) so this is not the kind of player one would want if frequently messing with settings and searching through. That said, the Raga is designed as a player to be worn with the included arm band, suitable for using at the gym. The ear buds that come with it have over-the-ear hooks to help keep them in place.

Considering the price and size, Philips has put together a very nice music player that will suit active users very well. It has some idiosyncrasies, in particular the transfer speeds, but it really is a capable player.

Install this on your compatible motherboard and you will think you have installed the heart of Superman in your computer.

I've had this processor running in my new build for about a month now. I was being annoyed by the stock cooler fan buzzing at very high rpm whenever the heat rose to moderate levels like 52C. The fan was really buzzing like a little aircraft prop at full throttle for takeoff. It would crank up to 6600 rpm at the slightest provocation like CPU temp hitting 50C.
I decided to take everything apart down to the motherboard coming out and all components attached to it.
When I pulled the cooler off the CPU and looked at the thermal paste situation, OMG what a mess. The stock thermal paste was not covering the whole area, it was reduced to a gummy, sticky glue. I had to pull very hard to get the cooler off the CPU.
I cleaned the cooler base and the CPU thoroughly and applied a pea sized spot of Arctic Silver 5 then reassembled everything.
Instant cure. Instant quieter fan. Instant low CPU temps andQUIET!AMD needs to stop using whatever they're putting on the coolers and just include a syringe of a high quality thermal paste for customers to apply themselves because whatever they're using is junk.
The stock cooler and fan they include with the fx 8320 are very high quality but the pre applied thermal paste is garbage.
Just apply new first quality thermal paste, you don't need to spend big dollars on third party hardware and I suspect those of you who have installed new coolers and seen great results is because of the new thermal paste used during installation.
The fx 8320 is a very powerful processor don't smoke it because of 10 cents worth of cheap thermal paste, use the best for your investment and this hot CPU will give many years of great performance.

However, the keyboard experience is something of a pain, especially since there's no trackpad and you have to touch the tablet face to do the mouse-like things. And using the mail program is harder on the iPad than it is on a mac laptop or on the transformer book.

The transformer book is noticeably slower than either of the other devices, but I was able to do everything I set out to do on it. The Office apps are good and integrate seamlessly with the other Office installations on my other stuff. The screen is as nice as or nicer than my iPad Air. I had a MeMo for a year, and I loved the screen on that. This is very similar - excellent resolution, nice and bright, a bit wider aspect than what the iPad Air has.

The sound is about as good as one would expect. Which is to say, meh. But that's what headphones are for.

Cortano makes it easy to get set up. I asked it to find the apps I wanted. When I want something from the control panel, I ask for that. Since this is my first time with Windows 10, having the assistant helps a lot.

There do seem to be some battery issues. Charging takes a long time. There was an issue with the MeMos, as well, that I sort of resolved by fully cycling the battery a couple of times.

All things considered, I like this tablet/transformer book quite a bit. My only significant issue with it is weight. For my purposes, the ultralight notebook or the regular tablet will meet my needs on any given day. However, if you like your PC desktop and need, essentially, a shuttle craft, though. this is a pretty good compromise machine. It's a decent enough tablet. You can do business stuff, check email, surf the web, and watch movies. You won't be transcoding video or playing resource intense games, but this ultimately is a nice tablet with a keyboard. Not a desktop substitute. Maybe not even a laptop substitute, depending on your needs. But definitely a nice tablet.

Very nice high quality item, but you're sort of left in the wind to figure things out yourself. Here are some things to note, so you don't encounter the same issues as I did.

-The app to download is called PRINT MASTER. You'll naturally want to download Phomemo app, but you'll soon realize it won't connect with your printer. Then you'll notice there is a specific Phomemo 110 app, so you download that as well. But after installing this app, a pop up says "we are discontinuing this app, please download PRINT MASTER." There, I saved you from the run-around I encountered. LOL!

-You are given a starter roll of labels, but to use the templates in the Print Master app, you'll need to choose the proper dimension. It would be nice if this info was given in the manual, but the manual doesn't even mention the free roll. Everything is in mm, but I happened to have a mm ruler and measured the labels to be 40x30mm.

-Lastly, the most important advice you need to know is you need to turn on AUTOMATIC. You might ask AUTOMATIC what? My reply is.. EXACTLY. LOL! You see, once you go to print your label. There is a setting called AUTOMATIC. There is no explanation as to what this means. The default is WHITE, which is OFF. What it means is where it will stop after it prints your label. If it's OFF, it will NOT stop. It will continue spitting out blank labels. I saw a YT reviewer who had this issue, and I didn't think anything of it, until it happened to me. LOL! You need to turn this to GRAY, which is ON. It will then automatically stop after it prints your label. Why in the world is the default set to continuously print blanks? We all tend to use default settings because we trust the manufacture knows what's best for us. I mean why would you turn something on if you don't know what it does? So I can see why many make this mistake. But now you know. Turn it on! Even if you need multiple copies, for example 5 copies. You still need to turn it on, so that it will stop after 5 labels. I would love for someone experience with these things, or the seller, to comment below what that setting is for, and why is the default off?

I have come to understand the value of a good camera strap. It is more than just a designer item and more than just a simple strap to keep the camera hanging around your neck. It needs to be strong enough to keep the camera secure and it needs to be long enough to allow for grabbing the camera and taking a quick shot instead of having to struggle with getting the camera from around your neck and risk missing the shot by a second or two. The strap that came with my camera is functional but much too short and I expect it to rip eventually. This strap by Orota is a much better strap than that provided with my camera.

This is a well-made strap. One side is a heavy weave not unlike a car’s seat belt but not as smooth and shiny. It is also quite a bit thicker than a seat belt and will have no issue with supporting the camera. Sewn to it is a decorative layer that is also a heavy weave, similar to but not exactly like canvas. These are stitched together with heavy thread and I see little risk of them separating.

Each end is clamped with a leather reinforcement that is held in place with four metal rivets. The leather ends each hold a metal buckle with the thinner nylon straps that actually connect to the camera. Looking closely at each component I found no loose threads, no uneven seams, no flaws in fabric or materials. There is nothing about this strap that suggests it will fail under daily use.

This is a much longer strap than what came with my camera, measuring a little less than 3' long. I like the fact that with this trap attached to my camera I can lift my camera and quickly get the shot I want and I don’t have to take it from my neck in order to focus on it. I can hold it far enough from my face to actually focus on the camera. This is a very big improvement over my old strap which was short enough that I could not get the camera in front of my face at a comfortable distance.

This is a very well-made strap and I am very pleased with it. It is stylish, well constructed and it is long enough to make it much more useful to me than my old strap.

I have tested and reviewed several WiFi extenders and this one works nearly as well as one that cost over six times as much and was far easier to set up.

I set this up simply using the WPS pairing method with the extender being plugged in next to my primary router. It paired perfectly in just over a minute and I was able to unplug it and move it to an outlet farther away where it would then repeat my signal for greater range into my shop in my back yard. This worked perfectly.

Here are a few tips for getting the most out of this or any similar device.

1. Understand this will only extend the coverage you already have. If you are not satisfied with your current speed when located close to your current router this type of device will not help. In this instance you will need to improve your internet service, modem or router.
2. An extender / repeater must be placed close enough to receive an optimal signal that it then repeats - if it is too far away, it can only transmit what it picks up - if this signal is weakened due to distance from your primary router the end result will be a reduced signal. It can only work with the signal it is receiving.
3. When placing any extender / repeater pay attention to what is between it and your primary router - keep in mind interior walls tend to not have insulation and are thus easier to penetrate than exterior walls, metal objects deflect signals more than other materials as do especially dense materials.
4. Optimally a primary router should be placed in a centralized location within a home and where the bulk of the time is spent. Extenders / repeaters can then be utilized between that and where you have found weak signal points.
5. In some instances, such as within Mesh WiFi networks extenders / repeaters can slow down the entire network and are thus not advised. A lot of this depends on advanced settings.

In all of my testing over the last 4 months I have found this to be an outstanding unit at frankly an unbeatable price.

This is definitely a product I recommend.

This is the first mesh system I've used. I had a Linksys router and an Asus router before this, both installed with third-party firmware. After the Asus upgrade, I used the Linksys router as a repeater. The signal was okay; considering I had Xfinity 250Mbps, the Asus worked fantastically, while the Linksys trailed behind. We live in an old apartment building with thick, plaster walls, so signal can be very spotty.

With this mesh system, I saw a huge upgrade the first week. Setup was very easy; quick instructions are provided. As soon as the setup was complete, I delved into the firmware. I recall being a little disappointed as I was used to the Asus custom firmware (Asuswrt-Merlin). The Asus firmware "just werqed." I run a small server, and setup was super easy with the Asus. With the Netgear, it was a lot more involved. Setting up outside ports was a pain; at the time, there was no simple way of forwarding ports. I recall a little workaround I was able to conduct with the server, but it took me days to figure out.

The firmware also lacks time restrictions for devices (at least of this writing). Asuswrt-Merlin allows me to set specific times to shut off internet for devices, which comes in handy with a large family.

As for the actual mesh system, so far so good. I can't tell when I'm using the main router or the satellite. The devices connect automatically without hiccup. THIS REVIEW IS FOR THE ZBOX Bi323-U.

DO NOT BUY FROM THIS MANUFACTURER--REASONS:
The ZOTAC WEBSITE happily shows you the line of products available and that's were things stop being great. WHEN YOU ACCESS THE WEBSITE AND CLICK SUPPORT, DOWNLOADS (updated drivers, and so forth) OR OTHER LINKS YOU MUST CANNOT GET IN UNTIL YOU SIGN UP AND SUPPLY SOME PERSONAL INFORMATION, SUCH AS YOUR NAME AND EMAIL ADDRESS. TROJANS-MALWARE-AND VIRUSES ARE INCLUDED WITH DRIVER DOWNLOADS FROM ZOTAC'S website. Once I got in, and was able to download updated drivers, I unzipped the file. Worst of all, the download could not be done on the ZOTAC unit because the install wasn't complete. I downloaded on another Windows 7 PC and after my virus software got rid of the infection in the zip file, I had to run a full scan of that PC using the virus app, as well as two others to make sure that PC was clean. Who needs this kind of nonsense from a seller/manufacturer's web site.

GOOD STUFF ABOUT THE ZBOX Bi323-U
--It's a decent piece of gear... at least for now. I'll be back if it fouls up later on. The memory and hard drive installation couldn't be easier.
--Once you install an OS, it boots into the software very quickly.
--Windows 7, 8.x and so on install well.
--Debian 8.4.x installs on this unit as well. It takes some tinkering and it finally installs.
--I installed Win 7 Pro, and then removed it and installed Debian. Just wanted to see how easy it is to do that. Notes about Debian are at the end.
--For a very low end item, this isn't a bad choice so long as you're willing to set aside a few hours to set it up and are willing to put up with a poorly designed manufacturer/seller website, and poor customer service.
--For my purposes it was an okay choice. I had a few extra SSDs around as well as memory that were compatible with this unit, so this was a cheap solution to add an extra computer.

NOT SO GREAT STUFF ABOUT THE ZBOX-Bi323-U
--BE SURE TO SCAN EVERYTHING FROM THE ZOTAC SITE AND THE CD/DVD THAT COMES WITH THE UNIT
--The documentation is really thin, almost useless.
--At first boot, the BIOS screen appears and you may (likely will) have to change some settings. It's best if you're familiar with what the settings do and what they effect. TIP: the Legacy Boot seems the most reliable. Complete the settings, save and exit.
--The BIOS (after adjusting settings) looks for an OS on the hard drive or CD/DVD. It does not look at USB thumb drives or SD cards. Have the external CD/DVD attached with install disc inserted.
--How to get back to the BIOS or BOOT SEQUENCE settings DOES NOT appear on any boot screens after the first power on, as it does with most other systems. How to access the BIOS settings IS NOT included in the docs. You have to press F8 for the bios or Delete for boot sequence settings. Found it on the web.
--Zotac site uses a squeeze page to get your info before you can access anything useful.
--The combination SD reader/USB port is just weird. You cannot use this port for both at once.

About Linux (Debian 8.4.x)
--I installed this successfully after several attempts. Zotac's site shows Linux drivers, but they download only the Win 7 drivers. You don't really need them for a Linux install. Set the bios for Legacy Boot or it won't boot into Linux after an install. ISO DVD 1 is the only file you need for the install. Graphical install is the only option that worked out.
--DO NOT TRY AND CONNECT WITH DEBIAN MIRRORS FOR NEWER APPS, it fails on all. Later use terminal to upgrade.
--After a successful install, the Zotac restarts and you end up at the Debian login screen for you user id and password. The password is rejected. --Power off with the power button. Power back on and this time you can login with the credentials supplied at install.
AFTER LOGGING IN, your user ID won't be in SUDOERS. Use terminal, SU into root. After that, use apt-get update followed by apt-get upgrade.

I purchased this Panasonic Soundbar in June of 2013. At the time, my requirements were:
- Good sound (can't afford GREAT sound)
- Wireless Subwoofer
- HDMI input and good HDMI-CEC support
- Bluetooth support

In my search, I tested the [[ASIN:B00811NMMI Toshiba SBX4250]] and the [[ASIN:B00BLX9510 Samsung HW-F450]] from my local Costco. My final choice was the Panasonic.

Sound:
- Acceptable sound -- The front speakers are not a big improvement over the built-ins. With the subwoofer turned off, it is easy to mistake the Panasonic sound bar with the speakers from the Television.
- Good subwoofer -- The sub sounds good even at high volumes and fills out the overall sound from the sound bar.
- The Samsung has clearer mid and high ranges so the Panasonic seems slightly muffled in comparison.
- Overall sound better than the Toshiba.
- Wireless range for the subwoofer is short -- especially if placed behind the sofa (interference from people sitting in front of it). Range is about 15 feet with clear line of sight.

Decoders and Passthrough:
- AC3 and DTS Decoder (Toshiba lacks DTS)
- ARC (Audio Return Channel) -- If you use the Netflix app built in to your TV, audio is generated by your TV. Normally, an "optical out" cable from the TV back to the sound bar is necessary. ARC removes that need.

HDMI-CEC (also Aquos Link, Anynet+, Bravia LinkSync, Regza Link, etc):
This is where the Panasonic beats the Samsung. HDMI-CEC allows Televisions to control a connected device -- no matter the brand; The TV remote should be able to turn on a bluray player and send navigation (up/down/etc) and standard playback buttons without the need for a second remote control.

In the case of a sound bar, through HDMI-CEC:
1. The sound bar should turn on when the TV turns on -- Panasonic does this, Samsung does not.
2. The TV should play all sound through the sound bar and volume buttons on the TV remote should control volume on the sound bar -- Panasonic does this.
3. Turning on a bluray player, the sound bar should turn on and switch to the correct input automatically. The TV should also turn on and switch to the correct input -- Panasonic does this. It's then up to your TV do its part.

In conclusion, I chose the Panasonic because it gave me the ability to eliminate a remote control through HDMI-CEC (which Samsung didn't) and it had both AC3 and DTS decoders (which Toshiba didn't). With the added ability to play music from my phone through bluetooth, I'm still happy with my purchase one year later.

Tip: Unlike the Samsung and Toshiba, the Panasonic has a small "receiver" unit that adds another machine to your entertainment center. For me, I use some velcro strips and attach the "receiver" to the back of my TV. It is only 1 ¾" thick which was thinner than my wall mount.

This crystal-clear screen protector film is very easy to apply. It's pre-cut to exactly fit the Kindle Fire touch screen, and it presses on without any need for additional adhesive. After the film is applied, there is no loss of sensitivity in the touch screen.

The application process is very simple: (1) clean the screen thoroughly, using the included microfiber cloth; (2) use the #1 tab to remove the plastic stiffener/shield from one side of the double-sided film; (3) position the uncovered side of the film on the Kindle Fire screen (holding the film by the #2 tab, starting at one corner, and allowing the film to fall gently onto the screen); (4) use the included smoothing card to get rid of bubbles; (5) use the #2 tab to remove the remaining plastic stiffener/shield; and (6) use the smoothing card again to get rid of any bubbles. The whole process took me less than 10 minutes.

Whenever I apply screen protector film, I usually have to try two or three times to get everything right. With this kit, the first application was successful, because the film adhered properly at the edges, and all but one tiny bubble smoothed out. Now, should I ever need to re-apply the film, I have the second shield in reserve.

It's probably worth noting that the Kindle Fire has a larger screen than an iPhone or iPod Touch or camera viewfinder, so that the risk of getting dust particles under the film during application to the Fire is higher. Also, it may not be necessary to install protective film on the Fire at all, because the touch screen is supposed to be made of particularly tough, scratch-resistant glass.

Wow, before saying anything, the screen on this laptop is stunning; bright and sharp. It is not the first nice thing I noticed about the laptop. Screen

We watched a number of HD nature films on it and felt comfortable. The screen hinges completely around to create a tablet which I far prefer to swivel options. CPU/Performance

My son wanted to put it through the paces with STEAM games but I'm passing - It's mine, but it should handle most reasonable games although it is obviously not optimized for hard core gaming.

Summary

This is a well built, solid laptop. It has the makings for a great Netflix platform with it's screen and flexibility of viewing positions of the screen as well as crisp, bright HD. This is hands down the best laptop I have owned as a complete package.

Pros
+ Super Bright, HD screen

Cons

Ok, so I have to admit at first I was wondering why someone would spend this much on a Bluetooth headset that isn't a feature-rich entertainment one like those from Sony or a major fad brand like Beats, both of which I have some experience with. But this, no... this is actually something different. This is a serious tool for serious use with serious built quality and seriously useful features. Seriously.
For example, the telescoping mouthpiece means you'll get unparalleled mic quality compared to headsets that pick the mic up by your ears (looking at YOU, airpods!), both in clarity and isolation from background noise. You can also physically bend it out of the way, or use the button on the mic itself to mute. Try doing that with airpods. Then there's the button based features. Shortcuts and touch-sensitive buttons are cool on aesthetic devices, but the physical controls on this are an ergonomic user experience DREAM. Everything is easy to access and control, no apps or press-and-hold or counting LED blinks, etc. Sort of makes me miss the old days of phones with physical switches and buttons. When you want your equipment to get serious, this is the sort of user experience you expect. Then there's the charging rack. OMG I love that, I can store it on my desk and it's charging automagically. Pick it up and put it on, ready to go. Never needs to be charged because it's been charging in between uses. Finally, I'm really impressed with the USB dongle option. You see, the one thing I really dislike about wireless headphones is that you usually need to pair it with a device, then unpair it to switch to another device. For example, using my Sony headphones on my phone and tablet, if my wife wants to borrow them for a zoom meeting, I need to pair with her device but then also unpair with mine so that it doesn't keep trying to reconnect to it. Sometimes we just give up and use a wired headset to avoid that mess. Non-bluetooth wireless headsets have a dongle, which makes it easy to swap what you are connected to (no unpairing needed, just move the dongle) but then you can't connect to devices without a USB port like a phone. This is the best of both- you can pair it with your phone, but ALSO use the USB to quickly connect with your desktop or laptop without going through the process of pairing and unpairing. This is the kind of usability and professional quality I would expect from a brand like Plantronics, and all the while it works well as a stereo headset for music/gaming/etc as well. Very comfortable to wear for long hours, I'd highly recommend it for serious users.

After doing some research, I read that these headphones are the best "bang for your buck" earbuds and so far, they aren't wrong. This product does some with six different silicon eartips, an small instruction booklet, and a small but durable pouch to put your eartips and buds in. It took me about five minutes find the perfect removable eartips for my ears. It would have been shorter but I was afraid of tearing the silicon tips (so far none have ripped). Everybody's ears are different but my ears prefer the smallest snowman shape ones for both my right and left ear (Pictures of the tips can be found in the 'Wired' only version of this product).

They are easy to clean and the remote is secure (meaning that the remote button or volume slider won't move or activate if it accidentally hits your clothes or something). I haven't used the microphone yet. These things are very secure once you install them in your ears. You can talk, yawn, chew gum, run, jump and drink water and these tips wouldn't budge (you can take them out easily though). The sound quality and noise blocking are great too for when I run. It also works well for people that wear glasses like me.

However I have two small issues with this product. One is that the wire is a little long for me but it usually doesn't get in your way (only once so far but this was my second time using them). You may experience burning in your ears. I did at first when I was trying to find the best way to wear them. For me (using the smallest snowman ones), You just put them before the ear canal so the silicon tips rest comfortably in your ears. Don't push/force them in your ears because that will cause your ears to burn.

In conclusion, if you're looking for the best sleek 'bang for your buck' earbuds that stay secure during rigorous activity who doesn't mind a little burning in your ear canals at first, then I would recommend this product and I'll probably buy it again when/if this product wears out.

Edit: Just after a month of use the the remote button is a little glitchy. Before it could be resting against by chest while running and it would work fine. I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

I have tested and reviewed many wireless doorbell systems. Typically I always advise to avoid any wireless cameras due to the inherent security vulnerabilities but this is often not possible with doorbell cameras. That being said there are key components I look for in wireless doorbell cameras: clear picture that provides a wide viewing angle, it either be hard wired or have excellent battery life, when chime button is pressed alert is sent and app can be opened and responsive in a quick time, 2 way audio communication is clear on both ends, motion sensitivity is adjustable and accurate.

I have thoroughly tested this product over the last 4 months and in comparison to the others on the market around this price point this product has proven to be clearly the best.

In terms of what is excellent - the internal battery is long lasting and dependable - I have found that it will last nearly 2 months on a single charge. The vast majority of wireless doorbells use proprietary batteries which forces users to purchase secondary batteries typically costing $30-$50. This factor is a huge bonus.

The camera is quite good. Images are clear and the wide angle provides a full view of the area in front of the doorbell. The AI Smart Human detection is without question the best I have found. This is a huge feature that helps prevent constant false alerts.

The base station holds up to a 128GB SD card for video storage. This is awesome for multiple reasons. If the camera was stolen the evidence will be saved on the base station within your home and all of your recordings are stored locally. This is an outstanding system.

Unfortunately, as with many similar products, while the hardware is good the software needs some work. As is typical, I can not find any way to force this doorbell to work with better software. It is obvious this was designed on the Tuya platform though I have not found any way of integrating it. I would much rather use the Tuya app where I have the bulk of my automation set but this will not migrate.

The lag from the time the doorbell button is pressed until you can see who is there is mediocre. The FASTEST I’ve been able to get this to work is 18 seconds - and I’m using an iPhone 13 Pro Max with 512GB on a super fast 1G mesh WiFi with a node located within feet of the doorbell inside the door.

The 2 way audio is spotty. It sounds like ordering through a drive through where every 3rd word is audible. Since I don’t use these to have in depth conversations it isn’t a huge deal but should be noted.

This is definitely among the best wireless doorbells I have tested for a while. It is not perfect, the sound leaves room for improvement as does response times but overall this is a quality unit.

While the vast majority of the doorbells I tested I advised to avoid all together this one is one worth using.

Had a 45 inch Sharp Aquos in the living room for over three years, and always thought it delivered wonderful HD output. On my PC, I own a Nvidia 3D Vision Set for the past two years for my PC gaming. The 3D Vision uses shutter technology, and definitely works beautifully with a 120HZ Monitor. Being a huge fan of all things tech, I've been watching the 3DTV market for the past few years, and finally it happened: Passive 3D! An affordable option which can feed 3D to a group of four+ without making you bankrupt.

I transferred the Sharp to the bedroom, and plugged all peripherals (PS3, 360, HDDVR and Roku) into the LG. Fired it up and immediately noticed how the colors popped. It actually ran rings around my Sharp Aquos! I transferred some 3D tech demos I saved on my PC to a USB drive, then ran them on the LG and was blown away by the 3D quality. Clean, bright and wonderful depth! Next, I popped in a BluRay movie (Monsters vs. Aliens) and again, my jaw dropped. I understood that the passive tech on the LG is suppose to have one drawback: horizontal resolution is decreased in 3D mode, but I'll be damned if I can see any difference. The TV arrived the day after Thanksgiving, so we still had the Thanksgiving Day Parade saved on our DVR. We used this to test the 2D to 3D on the fly conversation and it worked out pretty nicely. It definitely adds depth to any 2D broadcast, but nothing compared to true 3D.

As for gaming, the PS3 recognized I had a 3D TV from the start, and the few games I quickly tried (Wipeout, Uncharted 3 & Super Stardust) were mind-numbinlgy gorgeous. I didn't get a chance to try any 3D gaming on my 360 yet, but that's next!

Overall, I couldn't be happier with my decision to go for this LG!

Some quick notes:
- Unlike my 3D Vision PC shutter set up, the LG Passive does not darken the screen; colors remain bright and vibrant!

- My eyes were able to handle much longer periods of 3D viewing with the passive glasses. The 3D vision shutter would screw me up for the night if I played a long gaming session wearing them.

- The LG uses the same glasses they give out in theaters; go see Hugo and keep the glasses! :-)

- Get access to YouTube on your TV, and search YT3D! The LG Passive supports a number of different 3D formats which work brilliantly with most of YouTube's 3D showings'; there's TONS to see on there!

- The only ghosting I noticed was when you were not watching the TV from a normal viewing angle. For instance, if you stand up and move a bit close, you'll see overlapping images, but who watches TV like that?

- The two negatives: LG supplies a set of two orange and two white glasses. Orange and White? Really? What happened to the black glasses shown on the box and in a zillion ads? No big deal though, glasses are cheap. I found an eBay vendor selling a lot of 10 Movie glasses for $15.00! Try doing that with shutter technology. The USB input does not support DTS sound, so if you have a movie stored on a USB drive, it has to be converted or you will have no sound.

When I saw this I thought it would be a great addition to my camera gear. The description says it's good for DSLRs and up to six pounds. After opening and inspecting this monopod system I reluctantly tried my ultra-compact Sony WX9 camera on this mounting system. My conclusion is I can't and won't trust this rig with my WX9 let alone my much heavier mirrorless Fuji gear.

The padded extendable main monopod shaft consists of three sections that are secured with a twist. It's easy to not torque the sections hard enough for them to unexpectedly collapse while you're trying to take a picture.

The ball-head mounts, this system comes with two, are fairly smooth metal on metal construction. Alarmingly these have no secure locking system. You simply use your thumb to engage a friction locking system. All it takes is a tap to cause the ball-head to be completely free moving. I would never trust a camera I liked on these mounts.

There are two feet that come with this set. A rubber edged magnetic mount and a suction cup -
The magnet is too small for a secure mount. With the monopod vertical and not extended it was reasonably stable. Horizontally it felt unsafe set up in any configuration. Extending the monopod drastically increases the ease with which this tips over. The magnet is just not wide enough to be stable.
The suction cup mount was surprisingly strong but like every other securing point in this rig the slide to release the mount does not lock in place. It's just too easy to hit the release while trying to set things up. I had thought I could mount this low on the car to get some interesting video but after trying this out I'd be worried road vibration would cause this to release and drop the camera.

In conclusion: While the materials are of decent quality this system lacks security. I won't risk my cameras on it.

Having outdoor safe speakers is essential for my household. Not only do I have audiophiles who are addicted to headphones and speakers, I have a husband who insists on taking his speakers to outdoor jobs. that is fine except when the job turns out to have a sudden rainstorm or high dust going on. Before giving it to him, I had our daughter put it through the grind at work (food prep) and in town events. Let's see how this speaker performs..

WHAT IS THIS SPEAKER LIKE?
This speaker is gray in color. The housing is very rubbery in consistency. The right side of the speaker has sealed controls under a rubberized pad over top of the buttons. The speaker stays put and is heavier than expected.

ON/OFF BUTTON/PAIRING
Holding down for over a second powers up the speaker. Next to the power button is the PAIRING button. This is not for pairing the speaker to a device but it is for pairing with another speaker just like it. A coworker with my daughter has this speaker and they tested it out- works GREAT so you now get two synced speakers.

CALLS BUTTON
You can send and receive calls with this button. You can also access your voice commands on your phone with this button.

VOLUME BUTTON
This is plus or minus sound controls. You can also skip by holding down- + is forward, - is backward.

PAUSE/PLAY
You can control pausing and playing with this button.

DOCKING
USB for charging, mini USB port (to use to charge a device if need be), and auxiliary outlet for like an old MP3 player or other device that does not have Bluetooth capability.

CHARGING INDICATOR LIGHT
Red when charging and turns white when fully charged. Will indicate when the power is running low so you will know.

SOUND QUALITY
Sound quality with this is very good. My daughter has a coworker with the same speaker so they both have had a chance to experiment with their speakers. So far it has been a great speaker. The balance of the recording of course affects the speaker, but so far it has not been overly muffled, out of balance, etc. Where you put the speaker affects how it sounds too.

When put on the floor, it really does sound better than on, say top of a box, or couch, etc. A very hard surface seems to really make it sound best.

VOLUME
When using the volume controls on the speaker, the sound is better than when you use the volume controls on the device (tablet, phone, etc).

DURABILITY
This speaker was taken to a huge town chicken and biscuit dinner and was dropped and still is working perfectly.

BATTERY
Two 10 hour shifts at full volume, and this speaker kicked through it all before needing to be recharged.

THE BOTTOM LINE
For a really nice durable speaker that is dustproof, shock proof, and supposedly water proof, this is a good choice. It is solid, has decent sound , and even can be synced with another speaker if you get two of these for coverage around a room.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. This is a decent speaker, and I feel more comfortable having my husband use this on his jobs than the other really nice speaker he was beating up.

I really like that this charger has an ETL electrical safety certification printed on the bottom of the device. ETL is an independent safety testing laboratory. Many US companies will not buy electrical devices that do not have ETL or UL safety certifications.

If you are using all of the features, I think $80 is a reasonable price for what you get. I have a few other Baseus products and I am impressed with the features and build quality of all of them and prices are generally cheaper from other popular brands like Anker, Belkin, and Satechi.

I have a Foscam WiFi security camera in a steel pole barn. Even with a high gain antenna on the camera and a fiberglass door, my connection was pretty bad. Choppy video and lost connections were common. I needed to get the antenna outside.

Although this antenna isn't outdoor rated, it is pretty easy to make watertight. Some tape over the mounting screw holes on the back and a little self vulcanizing rubber electrical tape around the antenna joint and no water is going to get in. You could use something like RTV silicone too. Keep the moisture out and you now made it outdoor capable. It was pretty close the way it comes and I'm sure it would probably be fine for a long time, but sealing it completely is pretty easy. The magnet mount works great on the steel siding. The camera I have, like most, comes with a standard SMA connector vs.the SMA-RP (reversed pin), but you can get an adapter here on Amazon. [[ASIN:B005H488Y4 SMA Male to SMA-RP Female Adapter]]

Added a 20 foot cable with standard SMA male and female connectors and now I have a great outdoor antenna for an indoor camera in a steel building that is great for blocking radio signals. It works very well and the results exceeded my expectations.

I received this as a free review sample. I'll spare you a regurgitation of the product specs or paraphrasing the previous two reviews, but will focus on what sets this one apart from the pack.

The biggest surprise I had was volume. This is a relatively small speaker and most bluetooth speakers in this one's size and price range are designed as personal speakers that are meant to be nearby on a desk, night stand or counter top. I can clearly hear this one two rooms away indoors and even outdoors in areas with high ambient noise this can cut through and project sound.

Sound quality is neutral, and I mean that in a good way. While there is some bias towards the mid range frequencies it does not 'color' the sound of music being streamed to it. To be honest, this is not going to crank out heavy bass, so if you listen to bass-centric music you may be disappointed. On the other hand, the highs and lows are practically seamless, with a slight emphasis towards the mid range, so if you listen to jazz, blues or some forms of rock and Americana this speaker will probably please you.

One review discussed bluetooth range issues so I specifically tested that. Even two rooms away, which normally causes drops in quality, I was able to get crystal clear streaming with no drops in the music quality streamed from a Samsung Note 3. The distance is approximately twenty feet, but definitely not line of sight, so I am happy with that aspect.

While the product specs claim six hours of music, you can realistically expect somewhere between four and four and a half hours if you have the volume cranked. If you drop it to about a quarter - perfect for near listening up to two or three meters - you will get the claimed play time.

I tried the first generation Kindle but didn't really care all that much for it. While I loved the screen, it just didn't feel right, and remember thinking this would be perfect if it had a touchscreen.

When the Touch was announced I ordered this along with a Fire with the thought that the Fire would be for me, and I'd give the Touch as a gift. The Touch got here this morning and I opened it up just to make sure it was OK. It looked so nice that I carefully peeled off the plastic just to try it out for a few minutes. After all, one wouldn't want to give a gift that didn't work, right? Well, it's now been a few hours and several chapters of a few books later. I'm keeping it. A second one will be on order for Christmas giving.

Why keep the Touch when I also have a Fire? If you skip over the obvious answer (I just love electronic gadgets) the e-ink on the Touch is much better in terms of clarity and lack of glare. Not that the Fire is bad. It has a very clear screen, but there is some glare. The Touch is better for reading under all lighting situations, and remains highly readable in direct sun. I can't imagine getting better screen clarity than this for black and white text.

I also tried reading it while on a treadmill (a situation that usually gives me a headache when I tried it using the kindle app on my Touchpad) and it was quite pleasant. Best of all is that I can zoom up the text size so I can read it while it is on the treadmill reading stand (it's too far away for me to read hard copy unless it's in HUGE type. Getting old is _not_ fun).

But the strength of the Touch is also it's biggest problem for me - black and white. I read several magazines each month and reading them in B/W is lackluster at best. Magazines are more enjoyable on the Fire, especially publications such as Wired.

The touch interface is great. So far its been very smooth and glitch free. Love the feel of the screen - has a bit of texture to it. I have to say, however, that I am a bit concerned about the screen longevity. The Touch overall feels a bit fragile and less "solid" than the Fire. I'm not deducting any stars for that since it's just an impression, but it will be interesting to see if the durability of the Touch screen is better/worse/same as the Fire (and vice versa). I'll be getting a case for it for sure since it's going to be getting bumped about.

I'll be using the Fire mainly at home and for reading material that works best in color (and, of course, video - need to relax the mind with mindless entertainment as well!). The Touch will be living in my briefcase for reading while commuting (I take the bus and subway, so lots of time to read) and for killing time prior to an appointment. The longer battery life and smaller size makes it a better traveling companion than the Fire. I don't have the Touch 3G version, so I'll have to make sure I keep a few books on my to-be-read stack so I don't run out when I'm out of wi-fi range.

Granted, if I could only have one device, I'd stay with the Fire since that offers more entertainment options, albeit at twice the price. But the cost is not excessive, so I treated myself to both. With a Fire and a Touch I've got all bases covered (until, of course, the next glittery gee-whiz piece of electronics comes out...).

Arlo is not perfect, but it is wicked close.

What's Great: You can put it anywhere within range of the link/router. The alerts are reliable, if a little slow on the uptake. The picture is good. Set up was simple and worked the first time. A reasonable amount of cloud storage is free, and it's easy to download whatever you want to save. The cameras are easy to move around to wherever you need them, and you don't have to set them up again.

What's Okay: A person who walks fast can get through a room almost faster than Arlo can start recording. Now, it's still much faster than an old Belkin Netcam HD, which sends pictures of where the motion WAS. Before the picture. And the D-Link 930L, which is a fine monitor cam, but has never been able to send a snap or a clip, no matter how many times it has been set up to do that. However, both of those cameras have audio and stream reasonably good images via their apps (the Belkin video resolution is way better than the Dlink). That makes them okay monitors next to smart security sensors - if the sensor alerts, you can look to see what tripped it and listen to see what's going on. Arlo will - most of the time - catch whatever set it off and let you know within seconds. And it's free, not an extra $$$ feature.

What Could Be Better: The link thing is enormous. It could be a little less expensive. And it would be WONDERFUL if it integrated with Z-Wave or Smart Things. The plan here is to station the Arlo cams near other devices that send push notifications - Nest Alarms, Smanos smart sensors, etc.

How It Compares: Beats the Canary I couldn't get to activate. Way better than the other netcams in the house. Love it. Just added another camera.
