I really wanted to love this keyboard. In fact, I have purchased three of them over the past 18 months. If it weren't for the fact that two of them simply stopped working altogether with the steady red LED problem along with complete lack of function, I would probably have given this deice a 5 star review, and that is all of the variants that exist of this keyboard. When it works, it is a wonderful device. The problem is, there are clearly some major quality issues.

First off, what is it about this keyboard that is so fantastic that makes it so popular if it has so many problems? Answer, it feels wonderful, and when it works, it's a dream. It is the right shape and size even for practically all typically sized hands. Maybe even for some of the more tiny-handed men out there. Microsoft has perfected the bezel curve of the ergonomic keyboard in the Sculpt, and the amount of travel it gives each key is perfect. The feedback of the keys (as in the feel) is perfect as well. The apparently physical quality of the device seems well made (if though it clearly has some design flaws). Even the amount of "clack" that the keyboard makes is satisfying without being obnoxious.

So what's the problem? Aside form the things people have talked about ad nauseam (broken keys, losing that tiny transceiver means the keyboard is useless, etc.. being the seemingly biggest issues) so along with practically all of Microsoft's consumer-grade products, support is nowhere to be found. While MS offers comprehensive support plans for their corporate products, you are on your own with accessories, even if they are expensive bluetooth accessories. They don't even host proper forums for their accessories (there is no category for this on their official forum) and any information elsewhere on the internet about the Sculpt is strangely scant, so trying to find out what the steady red LED means is definitely a no-go. Anything I find is either for another model or simply doesn't map to this condition. Therefore, I can't even find out what the red LED light even means, let alone attempt to resolve the problem. Their phone and chat support offers no meaningful help as they are unfamiliar with the device. Since I have a Mac they balk and say the device isn't supported on a Mac, even though I have been using it for 9 months beforehand without incident. Also, the red LED turns on immediately after the new batteries go in so it's probably nothing to do with signal and a failure of the device itself. This seems further evident since the bottom of the keyboard that is underneath the light actually gets warm to the touch, so I should assume the keyboard is fried. This would be the second Sculpt keyboard that this has happened to in less than a year so this is not an outlier. I don't do anything to my keyboards that would kill them like this. My old Logitech Wave that I keep having to go back to keeps on ticking.

Also, note that apparently USB 3 interferes with the wireless signal between the USB dongle and the keyboard, a problem I have personally experienced when my keyboard strangely stopped receiving input temporarily for a few seconds and then resume. I thought I solved the problem by using an old USB 2 hub to get the dongle physically closer to the keyboard as I thought it was a reception issue that is so common with Bluetooth devices. (I am not even sure if this even uses Bluetooth and it might just be some proprietary RF signal.) But in fact, I later learned that it was the use of a USB 2 port that was far away from my USB 3 ports!

Sadly, as tantalizing as this device may be, I would steer clear of it. It's nothing but trouble.

I tried 2 other antennas at this location and was less than thrilled by the results. One was an amplified unit that I purchased years ago that had two vertical antennas that could be independently positioned forward or backward up to a ~45 degree angle from a straight, vertical position with a rotating base. I don't recall it's brand, but it worked fairly well most of the time, but I found myself going back to the old method of adding aluminum foil to get the best reception. The second antenna I tried was an RCA amplified bar antenna. It picked up most channels, but I had to change its direction back and forth depending on whether I wanted the CBS or the NBC affiliate; I could receive most all other channels with either direction. I returned that unit to WalMart.

According to AntennaWeb.org, I should receive 27 channels from 13 stations; the government site stated that I should receive 8 stations with a strong signal, 1 station with a weak signal, and that I would not be able to receive 1 station in the area. With this antenna, my TV found 49 channels this morning when I re-ran the scan, including all the channels listed on both sites that I mentioned previously. The first night that I ran the scan, I was able to pick up over 50 channels, including Channel 5 from Nashville! It was very cloudy that night, and I assume that reception was due to a propagation anomaly since I have not been able to receive that channel since then.

I highly recommend this antenna. For the record, I ran this test 11 floors up in a high-rise apartment building in downtown Louisville. As others have noted, very slight changes in the orientation of the antenna significantly affects reception of some stations. My antenna is currently attach to a window on one side and bends around the frame and attaches to the wall on the other side of the antenna. (I recommend getting some of the 3M replacement strips to attach the antenna so that you can re-arrange it as needed.)

Q- see 12 camera security system is a nice way to protect a home or business from threats. Install the cameras in different sections of the home or company and then access from home, online, etc. for top level security.

This security system seems much more complicated than it really is and the reason, I think, is due to the number of cameras. Looking at all of those cameras, out of the box, is a little bit intimidating and it leads one to believe that setup will take days and even weeks to complete. But it is actually much simpler than it looks and there is no need to install all 12. Just use the number of cameras you feel is necessary and store the rest for later use.

With this security system in place, you can access the live feed through the internet and even on your mobile phone via the Q- See applications. This is great for convenience and its one of the security systems best features. Other security systems have this feature as well, so it’s nothing unique. But it is very easy to use and it lets you monitor specific places on a property, for maximum security. Wherever you might be, home or away, you can take a look at what’s going on by pulling the mobile phone from your pocket. It doesn’t get much easier than that.

The one issue I have with this system is the same one others have complained about, and that is the wires. In the modern world in which we live, we expect wireless technology more and more. This system is wired and it could present some problems as you try to tape wires and otherwise conceal them from view. If this was a wireless system and I could place the cameras anyplace I like, then I would be hard pressed to find much wrong with this product. But I know many people who would likely reject this product immediately for this reason alone.

Security is important, especially for those who live in less safe areas or who operate a small business in a vulnerable area. With Q- See watching the home or business, you can feel a little more at ease. The cameras detect motion and can quickly help you catch a person in the act of theft, trespassing, or vandalism, providing proof positive of what happened and where. Like I said, the lack of wireless technology is a problem but if you can get past that issue, you will find that this is a very good security system for home or business needs.

All the controls and ports are located on one end, which makes it easier to deal with the large size. There's an on/off rocker switch. I wish it had a more solid "click" to it - it has a rather soft touch, so it can be inadvertently switched on/off when moving it if you grab it the wrong way. It has a single 3-prong female outlet to power an AC device, and 2 USB outlets. The USB outlets are a nice addition, since it can be used to charge phones, tablets, etc. without having to unplug the inverter and plug in a conventional car USB adapter.

The housing is plastic but appears pretty sturdy. The plug that goes into the cigarette lighter is decent. Works fine, but feels a little on the flimsy side compared with the overall unit. The cord could also be a bit thicker for greater durability or, ideally, coiled so it does not get tangled. But quite workable as-is and MUCH easier to deal with than an inverter that does not have a cord and plugs directly into the car power outlet.

Performance is very good. I had no problems running a 60 watt cooler using the inverter. Power delivery seemed fine and steady. I don't have test equipment to measure the power quality, but the cooler ran at a steady pace.

The inverter does get pretty warm in use, and has an internal fan that kicks on to keep things cool. The fan can be heard, but the sound is not what I'd consider to be noisy.

It's important to know the power demand of whatever you're plugging in, plus keep in mind that some devices, such as coolers, have an initial surge demand. For example, a 60watt cooler may use 60 watts when running, but will pull 100+ watts when it starts up. If you try to run something that attempts to pull more than the inverter can supply, the inverter will shut down for safety (both for itself and the item attached). According to the specs, this can handle a surge of 350 watts, but I'll keep any surge loads I put on it at not more than 300 watts to be safe.

Although 300 watts won't go far, this is a handy item to keep on hand not only for power on the road, but also to serve as a power source (albeit limited) when the household power goes out. While there are some faults with the unit, overall it is a good performer and a decent value for the price. 4.5 stars rounded to 5.

Another thing I like is comfort. I can wear these for a few hours at a time without even noticing them. For sports phones that is a major plus. If you like music super loud these are not going to make you happy. On the other hand, high volume defeats the purpose of sports phones since you need to be aware of ambient noise and your surroundings. The sound is fine. It's what I would expect from quality tweeters and a reasonable size woofer with a decent driver. It does not compare to a decent set of bookshelf type monitors like the JBL LSR series but the price is far lower so I guess they're ok for PC speakers.

But the excellence ends at the sound. The speakers do not have an analog signal input from the computer (there is one at the puck for a MP3 player or whatever). Instead, the signal comes via USB. The problem is the speakers do not come with any drivers. Bose assumes you have the drivers already on your Windows installation. That's a very bad assumption as many people do not have the drivers (just do a google search on Bose Companion 5 drivers to see). There's no help from Bose here. The drivers cannot be downloaded from their web site. I called Bose's tech support and after half and hour they were not able to solve the problem. I eventually solved the problem myself on my Windows 7 Pro 64-bit install but I think it's terribly lame that Bose cannot provide the driver for their product. If I wasn't using the pre-load install of Windows they assume everyone uses, then I would be screwed.

So exactly what do I get for this odd USB input in lieu of a standard audio input? Nothing except incompatibility and the inability to use the speakers apart from a full blown PC. The audio quality and features are not improved by USB audio input. Period.

Room mode correction should be a straightforward feaure on speakers like these. It is not. Although my sound card supports it, the Bose speakers do not have the DSP to do it independently. The lack of sound-card independent RMC doesn't justify the high cost of these speakers. If it were included, the price would look a little better.

I installed the Companion 5 system on an Ergotron cart. The two speakers fit perfectly under the monitor the way I wanted (I removed the stands). The acoustimass is bulkier than I would have liked but I think it's fair to say a smaller module would not perform as well and for most under-desk installs it would be fine. What I do think it's fair to complain about is the poor design of the acoustimass module case. Despite being very heavy, it features a plastic rear end-cap that is fragile. Come-on. For the price, give me painted steel not brittle plastic. The case is also oddly shaped with curves that prevent anything but a bottom-down mount position. The case is not designed to be mounted in a down-firing position, up-firing or on it's side or upside down. The case is also not equipped or rated to be flown or ceiling mounted (it could fall apart and drop parts on people below). Bose should know these are all viable positions. Not everyone can have this thing on the floor with like six wires running out for people to trip over -- seriously, that is totally not acceptable in a public space.

Bose has a habit of not publishing Watts RMS specifications for their amplifiers or speaker handling abilities. I sort of understand not wanting to confuse consumers who don't understand driver efficiencies, but at least give us some max. 1 meter SPL's so we have some clue how loud these things are. As it is, the Companion 5 is loud enough for a PC system in a fairly live medium-sized residential room. It's much louder than my Wave system which proved way more anemic than it was made out to be. The Wave is useless except in the smallest bedroom. I use the Companion 5 primarily in my kitchen (on the Ergotron cart). The kitchen is fairly live but has some acoustic paneling to tame some of the reverberations. If I were putting this system in a small classroom, I would think twice. As a PC system for someone who sits right in front of it, it's obviously perfectly good. I probably wouldn't even use it at half-volume sitting that close.

I bought the printer because it was affordable, and had lots of features. I wanted something with a duplex document feeder scanner, full duplex printing, color, and flatbed scanning. This seemed to have it all. As a scanner, it's pretty good if you manage to stay away from the HP software. As a printer, the quality is decent, but the ink situation is enough to make me never buy from HP again.

I'm sure HP read lots and lots of letters from angry customers complaining about their ink prices. Indeed, with other HP printers, it can be frustrating to be charged $35 when you run out of black ink. HP's solution to this can be seen with the 564 ink cartridge - the colors are $10 and the black is $12. Seems cheap!

Here's the awful truth: the black ink lasts about 30 - 50 pages. This is not an exaggeration. You need to replace the ink ALL THE TIME. The printer also has a bizarre habit of using ALL of the colors even when you're printing things that look black and white. So even if you're not printing very much in color at all, the printer will inexplicably run out of colors. Since the ink cartridges are so small, it seems like the printer CONSTANTLY has a low ink warning, and is CONSTANTLY stopping with out of ink errors. So even though you're only spending $10 - $12 on each cartridge, you're buying tons of them, and you need a huge stock for replenishment. This is HP's marketing department guiding the hand of their engineering department and delivering a crippled product. You will learn to hate this printer. It will constantly need your care and feeding, and you won't save any money on ink.

Here's a tip: in the print settings on your computer, you can tell it to use black ink only. That's a lifesafer.

Side note: the wi-fi on my unit has gone out twice. Out of warranty though, but the range on the Bluetooth is excellent, so not that big a problem for me. Don't know if it's endemic, or isolated.

There are "true wireless" earbuds on Amazon for half of this price, but I have tried several of them and they all suffer from poor-to-mediocre sound quality as well as poor battery life. These Plantronics earbuds cost more, but they have great sound quality as well as great battery life. I hear a good amount of bass as well as good clarity in the higher frequencies. My favorite music sounds muddy on cheaper wireless earbuds, but sounds great on these. 5 hour battery life per charge is almost double what the cheap earbuds give me. The ear hooks look clunky, but they are very comfortable and never fall off when I'm jogging or working out.

As with all "true wireless" earbuds, you have to control them with a series of short and long taps on the sides of the earbuds (to change volume, skip around in your music, answer phone calls, etc). If you have a hard time remembering all those commands (as I do), you can always pull out your phone and do the same thing from there.

If you cannot afford "true wireless" earbuds at this price level, my advice is to forget the "true wireless" design and look at Bluetooth earbuds that have a wire connecting the two sides. That style is slightly uglier than "true wireless" but has much better battery life and sound quality for similar price levels and there are pretty good products for much cheaper prices than the "true wireless" design.

I see some review complaints about connectivity and charging problems. My earbuds have worked perfectly with no dropouts, etc. As with any electronic gadget, there is always the possibility of a manufacturing flaw. I would definitely return a product that did not work flawlessly.

Note that this particular Plantronics model is not noise-cancelling or noise-isolating. You will hear some background noise, which is safer if you use them when walking or working in a busy environment. Plantronics does sell noise cancelling earbuds that you could choose instead if that feature is useful and important to you.

Overall this is a nice device. I do wish it were touch screen operated, but that's not a deal breaker. It has tons of storage and will hold more songs than you could listen to. I'm still trying to figure it all out, but it looks like it will do everything I need it to.

I have an LG TV 47" so I thought another LG product might be the best course of action (of course the money involved had to do with this decision), so I went to my local Best Buy to get a glimpse of what is out there. Besides this LG sound bar they had quite a few choices. I quick referenced them to their reviews and came to the conclusion that most sound bars are just about at the same level in terms of overall performance. I did see a Bowers and Wilkins?, priced around $2200, which is way more expensive than the tv itself (but was taught that audio is supposed to be the greater investment for the true tv viewer), and this sound bar frankly was fantastic, truly a thing to behold. But $2200 Buckaroos are a long way from $300 and I did get the tv at a great bargain price, so cheap instead of expensive became the call of war.
For what I got this soundbar does everything I wanted done. It was very easy to install through the optical option, and even though the first unit I purchased had troubles pairing with the subwoofer and was returned immediately, the second was the charm and now it works very nicely with the added plus that it certainly did not require a Kamikaze investment. Works very well and it adds a great sound capability to the living room in our home which was the intended site. Some shows are better than others but even the subwoofer does its magic and is a lot of fun to crank it up once in a while, specially for the internet type movie sites (like Netflix, Amazon, Vudu, etc.) that come with the smart tv and required some sort of subscription. Their sound, specially amazon and netflix, was way below average and even at maximum volume on the tv it was very sad. I could hear it but one of the members of the tribe is a little more than a little hard of hearing and was always having trouble (probably the main reason why I decided on a sound bar in the first place).
Needless to say this soundbar delivered what was expected of the product and now my living room is one loud area and when the subwoofer is doing its thing you can feel it kind of in the furniture itself, like some of the controllers in PS3 with the added vibration. Minor thing but rather invigorating, for the whole room now sounds like a mini theater without having had to add several speakers coupled with tedious connections, which certainly I am not qualified or inclined to want to do myself. I just put the sound bar in the same table in which the television rest and the subwoofer about 6 feet away and voila! Just waiting for the neighbors to reassure me as to the loudness, kind of like its baptism when they finally complain (makes you feel a little bit proud that you are putting enough noise to draw the attention of nearby houses, silly but what can you do sometimes?), so for now I am very happy with the purchase and glad that when necessary I have the equipment to raise the noise way higher than it was capable before. 4 very solid Stars!

Honestly, I hate surface mounted conduit. But there are times when it is required, and in those cases better than nothing. I own my home, so of course I put all permanent links properly inside the walls, but even then, there are times when the Cat/RG/other jacks are not directly behind the furniture holding the devices that need the cables. In these cases, I prefer to mount these with screws, and then caulk and paint them into the painted baseboards so they blend in better, although they have made these with tape for truly temporary installations.

There is just one connector for an inside corner and an outside corner (on the x/z axis). And in my opinion, these are the only two you should really need, and you probably need more of them. I am never going vertical up walls with cables; I just go from the jack along the baseboard to behind the furniture...if I need more than that, I'm afraid I need to just stop being lazy and tear down a wall or something.

I get that if you are in an apartment or a rental property, you may need more flexibility with this. But in my opinion, if you can't do a proper wall-mount TV install without surface-mount conduit, then you should just use a TV stand as God intended because this is not enough to make cables acceptable in such an install (although honestly, it is better than nothing).

I paired this up with a Onkyo TX-NR809 home theater receiver and i'm extremely pleased. Its a bigger improvement sound wise from my RSW-15 sub from klipsch . I've owned the Klipsch Reference line since around 2002ish and they sound just as good today as they did after a few hours of break in. The reason why this middle brand 12 inch improved the sound quality in my room is purely my hearing style preference. I love front firing subwoofers my old one had a passive 15 inch behind and front firing but air flowed behind so the sound felt strange, In this unit, the bass is very deep for a 12 inch and has 3 options. Movie, music and flat settings . Each one can be customized. My room is large or slightly under a large. It fills everything with tight bass.

I have to run it on +3 volume on the subwoofer with my receiver set to reference (dead center) if I want extra bass.. Even if the sub itself set to 0 (dead center reference) it still produces tons of large bass. Especially with bass tracks and movies. For me to listen to bass music like drumming bass, Deadmau5, DJ baby Anne I have to set the subs volume to -8 so it doesn't disturb neighbors and I STILL GET BASS! One of the reason I went with this 12 inch was to control the deep bass from extending and having cops called on me. It didn't help. I have absolutely no problem with this.If anything it reinforces its a good subwoofer.

TIP: for many of those using receivers that do auto calibration. Its better to do yours subwoofer settings by hand and personal hearing preference. Many auto-calibration systems like Audyssey have a tendency to ask you to lower the subs volume on the unit and mutes the bass sound. This is normally done to adjust the speakers hertz frequency and measure the room but system like Audyssey do not take bass into account. So your speakers will probably get shifted to see itself as "large speakers" even if you have towers. This reduces overall bass tracks your subwoofer plays because it thinks the other speakers can reproduce low bass. To fix any lack of bass, change the hertz settings of each speaker at a starting point of 80hrz. This will feed the subwoofer bass tracks that the others speakers can not reproduce. Satellites speakers crank it up to 120hrz or more.

-LFE (low frequency effects) in your receiver settings to 120hrz. Sub crossover or LFE settings are in the receiver itself.
-all speaker herz settings to 80 or test by going higher. Some have a setting for small and large Set them small even if you have towers unless they have powered subs built into them.(this is normally in the settings of the speakers in the receiver) Not the sub itself.

This allows your receiver to control where bass gets redirected. If you set the receiver to control every speaker, you would disable similar settings on the subwoofer itself, That way you don't get the sub and receiver having a double filter effect. The only thing you raise up and down would be the subs volume control and equalizer settings IN THE SUB. I avoid lowering and increase sub volume from the receiver , instead ,do it by hand on the unit.

From what I’ve read, there are many factors that contribute to the success of an instant photo: the camera, the lighting, the temperature, the subject, how still you are when shopting, the film itself and how careful you are to keep it in the dark during its developing. That said, you will just have to try it out for yourself!

I’m new to the vintage instant camera scene, but I’ve already learned how easy it is to mess up a shot.

My only complaint is the price, but it’s not like there is any other option. Hopefully some day, they will be able to produce it more efficiently and thus cheaper. Until then... I’ll be very choosy about taking a snap.

Oh! And it might be helpful to note that my camera didn’t want to eject the film after the dark slide. To fix this, I found a resource online that suggested the following:

—Open the camera to reveal the film cartridge.

—Locate the thin, long strip of plastic (on the cartridge) right in front of where the film would come out. Just beneath this strip is a thin black Mylar sheet.

—Carefully bend back on that plastic bit to remove it. Might take a little rocking back and forth. It will snap right off.

—If the film is still not ejecting once you close up the camera and go to take another photo, you can open the camera again and fold back the little Mylar sheet to eliminate the resistance of the photo popping out. I used my nail to fold it (bend it back then fold it to keep it down and away from where the film pops out).

^I realize these pieces are there to keep the film dark and being contaminated with light, but this has caused me no problems thus far. I have done this with 3 of my vintage cameras and film. Do so at your own risk, of course!

Hope this helps. (:

These things are a great way to reliably reach farther than an HDMI cable, but you need to still understand the limitations. Video requires a lot of bandwidth, so the quality and length of your cable is directly related to how realistic it is to reach the maximum resolution and frame rate.
I already have an older one of these from a different brand, which I bought a couple of years ago for a projector in the back of the room (switch between TV and projector, but entertainment system is in front of room and projector is in back, hence the need for a long run of cable). That older one claimed to work at 1080/60p, and in my initial tests it did. But once I ran the long cable, I was able to only get 720/60p or 1080 at only 24p. 1080 at 60 was just too much bandwidth and the adapter just couldn't handle it over a longer cable run.
This adapter, however, is rated at a higher spec for 4K. Swapping my old one out with this one, I'm happy to report that now I can get 1080 even at 60p from point to point. Could I get 4k at that length? I don't know, my projector doesn't handle 4k, but I'm guessing as the length of cable increases, it will limit what spec you can reliably expect. But I am very pleased with finally getting 1080p at this length of cable, so 5 stars!

This is my second Sony HX camera. My first was a Sony HX-50 that died after several years of use (lens motor stopped working). This version is improved in a couple of important ways. Most importantly, the popup viewfinder is tremendously useful in daylight conditions. The viewscreen is often hard to see in sunlight, but that is never a problem with the viewfinder. Opening the viewfinder is a little clunky, but you get used to it. The viewfinder does have a focus lever so using it with glasses is no problem. I also like that the GPS locks on much more quickly than older cameras (that often had GPS that were too slow to be useful). Despite the features, this camera is slimmer than my old HX-50.

The main downside to this camera (and probably all compact big-zoom cameras) is that the image sensor is very small, which limits the quality of your images. Even in bright sunlight conditions, my photos are always grainy when viewed on a large screen. They may look fine on a cell phone screen or a low quality viewer (like Facebook or Instagram), but when viewed full-screen on a computer screen, the image quality is noticeably more grainy and less dynamic than photos from a better camera. Photos are still much better than any cell phone camera, of course.

A big zoom camera is great for sports and wildlife and if you want a big zoom in a pocket sized camera, you'll be hard pressed to find anything better than this. For sports and wildlife photos, getting closer to your subject is often not possible. I've taken usable wildlife and sports photos from hundreds of yards away, even miles away for landscape photos. If you don't need the big zoom or can tolerate a bigger camera (like a one-inch or micro-4/3 or APS-sized sensor), however, you can do much better than this (for a bigger price).

In addition, transfer speed, resolution and picture quality is greatly increased - making the entire system more useful. In my experience, I found power is much easier to manage doing it this way as opposed to having to run separate power supplies to each camera.

This POE switch provides ample power for four security cameras, even those with pan / tilt capabilities. It is easy to install, requires little space and is reliable. While I had not used this brand in the past I will not hesitate to in the future.

This is an all around outstanding product that I wouldn’t hesitate to recommend. This unit is sure to hold up well and perform even better.

I've had problems with Pixmas in the past, mostly having to do with wireless networks and having to reinstall the software over and over to try to get them to hang on to network settings. I can't guarantee that this printer is going to be any better in the long run, but the set-up actually works pretty well if you use the standard version, not the WPS... and I'm getting way ahead of myself on this one.

To begin with, the printer requires a lot of time for set-up. You're not going to be doing this on the fly, so set aside an hour or so to: 1) remove all the tape of which there is much, 2) read over the instructions 3) install the ink, 4) run a print alignment 5) set up your wireless connection (about which more in a moment) 6) install the software (which takes a good 15 minutes or more), and 7) put the machine (and yourself) through its paces. Yeah, it's going to take a while.

Now I know you can read about the features on your own, so I'm here to tell you about the things that work for me and those that don't. First off, the wireless set-up is confusing. Choose Standard instead of WPS and save yourself some headaches unless you're a computer whiz kid. After the third error message in the WPS set-up I went to standard, entered my pass code and had the connection up and running in about a minute.

Once that was done and the software was installed I fired up the Canon Image Garden. First I scanned an image and attempted to rotate, crop and fix any deficiencies I found. The scan was over sharp and looked a bit jagged, but a little fiddling with the Canon software fixed that. Canon software also rotated and cropped perfectly. One really nice feature is that they remind you to put the printing side of the paper down in the paper cassette. How many pieces of paper will that save?

The biggest complaint I had was that it didn't give me a choice of which paper cassette to use for printing, so I got a ridiculously truncated image on the first try. I believe it chooses the paper based on the size of the image, which I get, but at the same time that limits flexibility in printing. I opened another photo processing program and it allowed me to print from whatever cassette I liked. Coupled with a better suite of applications for correction and enhancement, I think it's safe to say that I'll be using the Canon software almost never.

Printing on plain paper is clearly not going to be as satisfactory as it is on glossy, but in some cases I found it surprisingly good, good enough to give you an idea of what sort of image you're going to end up with when you switch to photo paper. It's also more than good enough for printing out emails and web pages.

Scanning and printing are both pretty fast, another plus. And the copy function works pretty seamlessly without any sort of computer interface. Just punch a couple of buttons and Bob's your uncle! It does take a bit of time to warm up and is a little noisy but no more so than any Canon printer I've ever used. It's not bothersome, in my opinion. You might feel otherwise.

Inks are easy to install, but you'll find refills pricey, no question. I suspect off-brand ones are available or will be soon enough.

In short, it's a good, inexpensive printer for a home or home office. Use photo paper and settings and get the full quality the MG5420 is capable of producing; I think it's pretty remarkable. The photos I printed out are as good as or in one case, better than the original. That's a powerful recommendation in my book.

Smart watches have gotten more popular with the release of the Apple watch. They tend to have a standard set of functions, such as access to instant messaging, email, time, alarms and a lot more, typically tied to your phone. Not all smart watches are alike, though, and offer different sets of functions, better connectivity and other various differences from one another. This particular smart watch offers the mainline set of functions, setting itself apart through the user interface which is more polished and clean than most others with which I have worked. That said, I have a couple of quibbles with it, leaving room for a little improvement.

This is a standard-sized watch with a rubber wristband that can actually fit a larger wrist like mine. I have trouble finding watches and watch bands that fit me, so the fact that this one fits me is a pleasant surprise.

Powering it on, the user is immediately greeted with a complex and fairly complete visual menu system with tiles for every function available to the user. This is a standard presentation for a smartwatch, but this one looks a bit more polished and clean than the others I have seen. Switching to other menu screens just requires a swipe gesture, as to be expected. I have big hands, and this means that, for me, using a stylus makes working with this watch a lot easier. This is not the fault of the watch but a reality of working with a small device.

My first issue with this watch came when I paired it to my phone. The date and time on the watch were off, so I expected that it would grab the time from my iPhone when I paired it. It did not. Instead, I had to dig for the clock application and manually set the time. I dislike this and think that having it set itself when it is paired is much more accurate and cuts effort on the part of the user. For Android users, there is an application to allow for syncing up the time, date and more, but iOS users are out of luck for now. To the manufacturer's credit this is made clear on the product listing so this is not a surprise. Regardless, I am of the opinion that the watch should fetch the time, not rely on being sent the time. In the grand scheme of things, though, this is an annoyance, not a deal breaker.

There is a fairly comprehensive list of functions provided by this watch in addition to time/date and phone answer. Through the menus the user has access to call logs and function, Bluetooth functions, a remote finder function, a pedometer, a sleep monitor, a reminder function to get up and move on occasion, calendar and clock functions, audio functions, video functions and a few more.

One of the interesting functions that this watch offers is a camera. So, I tried to use it and it complained that there was no memory card available. Reading through the limited documentation included, I was unable to find anything about a memory card. I finally noticed that the back of the watch has a small groove where it can be popped off, and when I removed the back I found the battery which is removable (replaceable - another pleasant surprise). Under the battery is a slot for a micro SD card.

Adding a memory card comes with a big catch. It requires removing the battery to get at the holder which in turn clears the clock and resets it to midnight 01-01-2015. So, adding the memory card requires me to set the time again. And again if I remove the card.

Although I think the time sync functions of this watch are lacking, it is otherwise a good smartwatch. The interface is professional and polished and the whole provides access to a large number of useful functions. It's priced well too. Overall, this is a solid offering worth a look if you are wanting a smartwatch.

This is a dual review, as I own both the Contour + 2 and the Contour Roam2. I don't work for nor do I have any affiliation with Contour. I've had the Roam2 for more than 6 months, but held off writing this review until I had the +2 to compare it to. Although I don't own a GoPro, several friends do and I do their video editing so I'll chime in on the Contour vs. GoPro at the end.

MOUNTS:
Contour uses the same proprietary mounts across their lineup, so interchangeability between the two should be fairly easy (but doesn't always work out that way). I've found some to be flimsy(hat mount), while others are damn near bomb proof(suction cup)! The rotating lens means you can mount it in just about any position, however it is difficult to know that you've framed the shot with the correct orientation! Had an important video recorded upside down - laser level only lets you know it's level, not if it's upside down! One of the best features I've found is the ¼ by 20 thread on the bottom of the Contour, pretty much universal to all modern cameras and there's a TON of mounts out there reasonably priced.

SOFTWARE:
The Storyteller program needs to be installed on your computer and is fairly easy to use, but not intuitive, you need to play around a bit before you can figure everything out. The editing ability is extremely limited. (I use imovie). Software is free, and although you can use the camera(s) without first updating I suggest you do that first! The +2 also has an app that I use on my iPhone 5 - it too is free and pretty easy to use - but not as capable as the Storyteller program. The downside is you HAVE to use the Storyteller program to change settings on the Roam2, AND you have to use it if you want to use any of the GPS data with the +2.

ROAM2:
Got this for Xmas last year and immediately swapped the included 4GB micro SD for a 16GB. SUPER easy to use - charge, point, and slide the slider to the on position. Video quality is good, first few outings I had it set for 1080@30 and was very happy. In editing I found one clip I had to slow down and was slightly disappointed at the quality - since then I've got it set for 720@60 and haven't had any issues - video quality is still good (even in slow mo). Low light does induce more "noise" to the video, but if there's ambient light (streetlights etc.) you can still get decent vids. Sound quality isn't all that, it's usable, but in high winds or at speed - forget it. Battery life is really good at around 2 hours. The camera itself is very well built, one of my first uses it got throw (by an idiot) about 8ft into about 4 inches of water over concrete - few scratches, but still kept recording. This led me to look for something to help protect the aluminum body - Glock Tape, works amazing, adds some protection, but most importantly gives it some GRIP!

CONTOUR +2:
Only had it for a week or so, really wanted it due to the Bluetooth (to help frame shots) and was wanted the waterproof housing (worried about watersports damage on an upcoming trip) the GPS would be a plus. Once again amazing build quality - this things tough as nails. First thing I did was hook up to Storyteller and get the latest firmware update - less than 5 minutes later I was off and running! Pairing the Bluetooth took a couple of attempts, but once connected has excellent range (20 or so feet with obstructions - close to 50ft line of sight!). Using the app you can check status of battery, GPS, and memory as well as change settings and start stop recording - wish you could watch videos but oh well. The app has about a one second delay between what the camera "sees" and what you see on your phone - pretty amazing! Attached to my suction cup mount and went for a drive - took about 30 seconds for the GPS to lock on the first time (since then it only takes maybe 5 seconds). GPS is accurate. The video quality is great! Uploaded vid into storyteller and the GPS data was also great - until I exported it then there was a lag of about 5 seconds between the data being displayed and the video. Waterproof housing is bulky, yet seems a bit flimsy - still not sure it could survive 200 ft of water. Came with HDMI to hook up to TV - works really well. Haven't used the mic adaptor yet. Battery life seems to be around 1.5 hours, but spare batteries are cheap.

COMPARISON:
Even though the video specs are the same between the +2 and the Roam2, the video quality of the +2 is noticeably better - even in low light. Sound quality on both suffers in high winds or speed. They both have the proprietary T-rail mounts on both sides, but the ¼ by 20 thread is about an inch further back on the +2. The Roam2 is waterproof without housing to about 3ft, but the +2 has the waterproof housing. The +2 also allows for filming while charging. The +2 has the HDMI out, as well as a jack for external mic. The +2 has the Bluetooth app, plus GPS - that combined with replaceable batteries and the better video make it worth the extra money.

CONTOUR vs. GOPRO:
I absolutely love the form factor and the mounting options available for the Contours. The Contour line has their own proprietary mounts, but the ability to use the ¼ by 20 thread mounts for other cameras (even the GoPro mounts) plus the rotating lens means there's just more ways to mount the Contour. That being said the GoPro Hero3 flat out destroys the video quality of the Roam2, and slightly edges out the +2. Of course this difference (even over the Roam2) is completely removed once video is uploaded to Youtube or other sharing sites as they compress the video during upload! I've yet to see a GoProH3 recording 1080 go for more than 75 minutes. Sound quality between all three is about the same. The GoProH3 app uses wifi - and has about a 3-4 second delay - still works for framing shots, but not much else. The GoPro also has the advantage in that you can change settings in camera - but it is a complicated affair(the +2 only allows you to choose between two predetermined settings). GoProH3 doesn't have GPS, or rotating lense. Contour recently lowered the price on the +2 it's now $50 cheaper than the GoProH3. Also it seems they changed pricing on their mounts - I went with the Contour line because of the simplicity of their system, more mounts, cheaper price, and the form factor. Now that they're cheaper it's a no brainer.

SanDisk has come out with an extension to their array of MP3 players, beyond the Clip and the View. Their new mp3 player, the Sansa Fuze, is definitely geared towards casual someone who just wants a basic, functional, and well-put together media device for their pocket.

The Sansa Fuze may look like a tiny device at first, but this thing packs some serious features. It has the ability to playback music, video, photos, FM radio, as well as audiobooks. The features for the Sansa Fuze are very impressive to say the least, as it also features a microSD card slot to add extra storage space, content, etc.

The first feature we will focus on is the one which will likely get the most use, the audio aspect. The music menu is organized with artist, album, song, genre, etc. There is also a recently added section which shows the most recent songs added onto the device, as well as a top rated section.

The album menu allows you to see album icons as you are scrolling through the various albums. There is also the ability to form a playlist directly on the player.

The sound quality is very well-done. If you have a great set of headphones you will not be disappointed in the least bit.

The video aspect is definitely not the highlight of the Sansa Fuze. Part of this is due to the low power of the device, and partly due to the screen itself. The supplied Sansa Media Converter does make it easy to convert movies into a format for the device though. A typical movie will take up a little under, or over 1GB. The video looks respectable, but can get a bit choppy at times. One very cool feature about the video is the ability to add a bookmark while watching it.

The photo viewer is very standard as you can view photos from the internal memory of a microSD card. You can set up a slide show with time intervals, and add music as well. The images looked quite sharp.

The FM radio feature is done extremely well on the Sansa Fuze. You get some great reception and the auto program feature picks out crystal clear radio stations. It also has the ability to record radio in WAV format.

This works with voice recording as well thanks to a microphone located right below the microSD slot.

Podcasts and audiobooks are pretty self-explanatory, but one issue with the audiobooks is the lack of a bookmark feature.

The overall user interface for the Sansa Fuze is put together nicely, set up in such a way that a first-time user could pick up this device and feel right at home with it. You have a scroll wheel as well as a home button and a middle click wheel. The scroll wheel can also be clicked up and down, which can make things a bit confusing at times. Overall though, beyond a few hiccups with organizational aspects of the UI, this is one easy device to use.

Getting media onto the Sansa Fuze is extremely simple as you can use any desktop media player to create playlists and such, easily syncing them to the device. It also supports drag and drop without the need for any software. We used Windows Media Player as well as a few other media players to test this all out, and syncing was as simple as can be.

The quality of the device itself is top-notch, as the screen can put out some great contrast and vibrant colors in spots. The screen is extremely clear and does a nice job with photo presentations. Battery life is equally as impressive, as I have been getting around 20 hours on each battery charge thus far. Video playback came in at around 6 hours on a charge.

The package comes with a proprietary USB cable and a pair of earbuds, pretty basic.

Also shipping with the Sansa Fuze is a great bonus, a microSD card which comes with DRM-free music from more than 50 new and emerging artists. This is a great way to immediately test out the music capabilities of the Sansa Fuze, and also adds value to the entire package. Music videos, images, and more are also included on the microSD card.

Overall SanDisk has done a great job with the Sansa Fuze.

--------------------------

He'll be like, "What the... why do you have a picture of my mom?" LOL! But you can select photos to hide. So if you have 5 photos, you can easily hide 4 of it, then it will only show 1 photo all day. If you have 200 photos, you would have to select 199 to hide. The joke is probably not worth that hassle. LOL! To pull it off, you also need to lower the brightness so that it matches the brightness of the regular surrounding pictures. And of course, hide the wires as best you can.

Card Magic Trick:
-------------------

I wasn't expecting much given the price of this item, and I got pretty much what I expected.

The charging port is hard to reach and the LED charging indicator is difficult, if not impossible to see, without having to move the foam earpiece covering.

Setting up/pairing the device is pretty easy. Press the button for 4 seconds or so and you’ll hear a pleasant female voice say, “Hello”. This means the power is on. Continue holding the button and the device will enter pairing mode. You’ll hear the voice say, “Ready to pair.” When pairing is complete, you’ll hear the device say, “You’re connected” and tell you how much charge the battery has. So far, all I’ve heard is, “Battery full.” I have no idea what other battery indications the voice will give – perhaps only at 3/4, 1/2 and 1/4? Or maybe percentages?

The buttons are the biggest drawback with this device. Actually, it's really just one multi-function button on the right earpiece. The button functionality is not like any Bluetooth headset I've used before - very non-intuitive. The button has no label at all and the tactile feedback is nonexistent at times - I press the button sometimes and there's no "click" feeling. If a song is playing, it doesn't seem to matter where I press, the song stops if it is playing. When I press again, anywhere, it starts playing again.

There is no volume control on the headphones at all. You’ll have to adjust the volume from your phone/audio player. There is a bare bones EQ function. You control this by clicking the multi-function button 3 times in rapid succession. Each time you do this, the device advances to the next of 3 EQ setting – balanced, bass boost and JLab signature. The “balanced” setting seems to sound just like what it’s named – balanced or equal high, mid and low tones. The bass boos is decent – not overbearing. Not sure what the last one is, but if the pictograms in the manual are any indication, it boost the high and low ends. The EQ function does provide audible feedback – the voice announces each setting by name.

There's a next track function, but no function for going to the previous track. The next track function requires holding down the multi-function button for 2 seconds. There's no audible feedback for this function (other than a very short moment of silence). When you hear the silence, let go IMMEDIATELY. If you hold the button down for too long the Bluetooth connection will be severed and you'll have to reconnect.

Apparently, there's no ability to fast forward or rewind within a song or audio book. You'll have to do this on your phone/audio player. Pretty poor design if you ask me. BTW – I use this only with my audio player, so I did not test the phone/mic functions, but I’d be surprised if they were robust.

The instructions are minimal at best. The manual is one piece of paper printed on 2 sides. Unfolded, it's about the size of 2 business cards - about 4"x4.5" (10.16cm x 11.43cm). One side has instructions and the other is all promotions/disclaimers, etc. That's it.

Sound quality is acceptable - decent bass and stereo separation is good. I’m no audiophile though. The product description says it has "Noise Isolation", which is marketing speak used by all on-ear headphone manufacturers. It simply means the ambient noise is slightly reduced because the headphones cover your ears. Bottom line - there's no tech/function in this device that does any active noise cancellation.

The headphones are a little snug/tight, but not so much to be uncomfortable - at least that's my opinion after an hour+ of testing. Not sure if this will be true for something like a 3-4 hour flight. I’ll test this out in the near future and will update this review, if possible.

The charging cable that comes with the item is 9” long (22.86cm). Not very useful at all, but better than nothing.

On the plus side, the manufacturer did provide an extra set of foam earpiece covers - the set that comes on the headphones is orange. The extra set is black.

Bottom line, for $15 I wasn't expecting a lot - well maybe better button functionality, but hey, what can you do? As my granddad used to say, “You pays your money and you takes your chances.”

Took delivery of one of these 18" 640 LED ring lights yesterday.

As I shoot through it at test subjects, the overwhelming response is, "Boy is that bright!"

I had my camera down to ISO 200 and working at about f/5.6 or so.

The supplied diffusion sock is not quite enough. LEDs are really annoying to look at.

A lighting manufacturer at NAB 2013 explained to me that LEDs put out most of their energy in the UV spectrum. The way they emit visible light (at least some of them) is to excite tiny amounts of phosphors placed over the LED itself, similar to how a fluorescent lamp excites phosphors deposited on the inner surface of the tube.

It also means that to be safe, manufacturers need to build in a UV filter. I sincerely believe that we instinctively realize such bright LED light is bad for our eyes and react with a squint.

Then again, your poor subject also has 640 very bright point sources searing their eyeballs.

The diffuser helps spread the light a bit, and it works as far as it goes, but my plan is to cut arcs of additional diffusion material and attach them to the light, over the LEDs, under the diffuser sock.

The gooseneck is functional and the 5/8" socket fits a standard lightstand nicely, though I don't know how long the fine threads of the locking knob will last. With care, it'll be fine. Just don't crank the knob down or you may strip the thread out. Won't be an issue unless you are hanging the light from overhead. On a stand, gravity is your friend.

What it really lacks is a way to store and transport. It arrives in a square cardboard box about 1-1/2" thick. After you attach the gooseneck, it can't fit back into the box. I don't want to unscrew the gooseneck every time to put the light away, so I'll have to locate a large, flat case of some sort.

*****
UPDATE:
The http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B002JPKWK2/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o01_s01?ie=UTF8&psc=1 case to carry artwork holds this light, its power supply and even a small light stand very nicely.

*****

You also need to wrangle the power supply, which has a permanently attached 2.5mm x 5.5mm angled coax power plug with its approx. 2-meter cable on the output side and on the input, a two-prong removable AC cable, also about 2 meters long. The light runs on 15 volts. There's a remote control multi-pin socket, for an optional remote.

On the back is an on/off rocker switch and a large dimmer knob that gives smooth control of intensity.

The light is sturdy and, as I said, extremely bright.

Best part: it really flatters the ladies! Every wrinkle disappears. And that circular highlight in the eyeball is really unique.

After a very quick test shot this afternoon of a woman friend, my coworker looked at the results and exclaimed, "It makes her look like a model!"

It's such a different look over "normal" lighting that it's sure to make certain shots really stand out.

And when the ladies ask me to put the "Remove ten years" filter on, I'll actually be able to do it.

The Lexar 32gb 3.0 USB Thumb Drive is likely the first usb 3.0 drive that I have had that has exceeded my expectations. It's not unusual to see speeds that disappoint when a drive claims high performance but this isn't the case with this drive. In addition to that, the sliding mechanism to protect the usb connector when not in use and the aluminum housing makes this feel like a premium product that will last.

When transferring large files from a pc via usb 3.0 from an SSD I saw maximum speeds of 140 mb/s and likely an overall average of 130. I was able to copy 13.6 gb folder of diablo 3 with a mixture of smaller files and larger data files in less than 2 minutes. That is outstanding write performance for a USB thumb drive. And read speeds are just as impressive as I was able to copy that same 13.6 gb's back to the same SSD drive with read speeds averaging 300 mb/s! I'm so used to usb drives letting me down when i was hoping for so much more.

The build quality has a very premium feel to it. It slides into your pocket without catching like some usb drives that have a rubber texture. The slide mechanism also feels consistent and doesn't feel like it will fail anytime, in fact i find myself fidgeting with it because it is so well done. It's not going to come out on accident and it does require you to "mean" to open it for it to slide out. It comes with a lanyard as well but I don't plan on putting this on my keychain anytime soon but was a nice to have feature.

Overall I am completely satisfied with this Lexar Drive and I would highly recommend it over some less expensive options.

I received these phones as a review sample and wanted to test the claim that they are studio quality. In point of fact they are very close. What I mean by studio quality is they are neutral sounding - there is no bias towards any particular frequency band. These are fairly even on the highs, mids and lows.

Of course, if you are listening to modern music that emphasizes low frequency response with a lot of bass you may want to check out other phones that do a better job. I will say that while the frequencies are naturally divided, the separation is excellent so I am certain these phones have a crossover.

Since there are ample specs in the product description (and two video reviews at the time of this one) I will spare you a recitation of that information. I tested these using a few key albums, and also plugged the 1/4 inch connector directly into my Roland RD-300NX keyboard to hear that instrument's natural responses. Both tests confirmed that these are studio quality. However, audiophiles who want unbiased sound will also love them. I played some of my favorite test albums like Miles Davis' Kind of Blue, Ahmad Jamal's Live at the Pershing and some 20-bit mastered CDs. In all cases the frequency response in each band was perfect and the ability to hear nuances (including the natural reverb on Kind of Blue) was a treat. More importantly I heard the albums the way the engineers wanted me to hear them.

To be sure I do have other phones that are at this level of quality, but most are in a much higher price range. I did not expect to be impressed with I accepted a review sample, but not that I've had time to put these through their paces I am impressed. They are now in my practice room/music studio and there they will remain. Definitely recommended.

I am usually not a fan of ear bud-style headphones as I have trouble finding sets that are either comfortable or have good sound. More often than not, buds have been tuned to have the bass either too strong or too weak and they sound very unnatural. Sony did a good job with these and got them sounding very balanced. They’re not perfect when it comes to comfort but there are ways to remedy this.

These are not active noise canceling (ANC) phones. Sony offers another model that is ANC-capable and they’re excellent but an order of magnitude more expensive. If you need ANC, this particular set of buds cannot do that so consider other options but be prepared to spend more.

These are sport-style ear buds in that they come on a neck harness and they are wireless. They connect easily via Bluetooth though they come with an adapter so they can be corded and used with devices that cannot work with Bluetooth. One concern with this type of phone is that often the cord is a little short between the harness and the buds, meaning a turn of the head pulls the cord a bit and can dislodge the buds from your ears. This particular set has some extra play in the cord so I have not had this issue as of yet. The cord on either bud can be “shortened” on either side by pulling the slack through tensors on the harness to reduce play in the wire.

In terms of use for sports and exercise, these feel a bit more fragile than most and I would caution against using them for doing anything much more active than running. They might hold up just fine, but these are a bit more pricey than most and are not ruggedized. This is probably my main complaint with these.

Comfort-wise, these are not bad. I have had better success with these than most, though I still greatly prefer over-the-ear headphones most of the time. The inserts are relatively soft and pliable and they do fit well, and the set comes with multiple sizes so adjustments can be made to get them to fit just right. In researching, I found that there are plenty of replacement tips; so, they can be swapped out if need be to find something that fits better or is more comfortable.

The main consideration about any set of phones, regardless of price, is the sound. In my mind, Sony has always had good quality products that do a fine job of balancing the sound. These ear buds are very much in line with my previous experiences. The sound profile is very balanced and even and the result is natural sounding playback. The tendency with the majority of manufacturers is to heavily push the bass. The bass in these is present and you can definitely hear it but it is not so pronounced as to dampen or overpower the rest of the profile. The midrange sounds good (particularly for ear buds) and had the right depth, meaning music sounds warm and not like it’s coming out of a tunnel or barrel. The highs are bright and clear but not piercing. I would stop short of saying these are audiophile quality, but the sound is much better than most bud-style earphones.

These are not your typical, cheap set of ear buds. These are better than the average and they are designed to be more comfortable and useful in an active lifestyle. They sound great. My only complaint is the construction - the harness in particular feels fragile. If you don’t need ANC and you don’t anticipate using your phones for heavy physical activity, these are a great choice. If you need something a bit more rugged, you might consider other options.

This is a very complete kit and does contain everything you need to setup a Raspberry Pi 3. Yes, the op system installs easily and, with luck, you can be up and running in less than an hour. So, why the 2 stars?

It gets 2 stars because the Raspberry Pi is probably one of the most frustrating devices I've ever tried to put to any real use. For example, I wanted to set it up so I could use a VNC server on the Pi and a VNC client on my Mac (OS X El Capitan). After three days of almost non-stop failures, I'm sick of this thing. Researching how to get this task done leads you down a black hole of internet articles and posts on the Raspberry Pi site, most of that give different instructions, use different commands, tell you which files to edit and what to put in them, and almost none work, period!

The core problem rests squarely on the Raspberry Pi organization. Their own website is full of conflicting posts on how to do just about anything beyond a basic setup. Few, if any posts state which model of Pi is being referenced, and many bear no date. All in all, it's a very frustrating experience and, while I like to tinker with these things, a little success is required once in a while to keep me chugging along. I think I'm done with this thing. I had hoped it would finally be a Linux for the rest of us. Unfortunately, it's just as convoluted and difficult to use as any version of Linux out there (my opinion).

However, if you're looking to explore the Pi, this kit has everything you need to do a basic setup of Linux. And, should you want to use it as a web server, file server, media server, you're really on your own. Drink lots of coffee and plan to pull our lots of hair.

I have worked with a lot of ANC headphones, and I have a different pair of JVC phones that have served me well. I looked to these phones as a possible replacement for a dead pair of Bose QC-15 phones that finally just wore out. These are good phones that balance sound quality and ANC nicely.

The ANC function is what interested me most about these and I set about testing them. These work very well but they are not as aggressive as Bose or Sony when it comes to actively cancelling out low-frequency noise. This is a good thing in most cases as the aggressive ANC on Bose and Sony is actually uncomfortable when turned on. Where the two bigger players go all-out for maximum ANC function, these go for "good enough for most" and in terms of how they compare against other manufacturers such as Sennheiser, Philips, and other well-known brands they compare well. They cancel out the lion's share of low droning noises such as road noise and fans, enough so that turning on music at low volumes is still workable in noisy environments.

The sound profile is another important consideration and I have seen a wide variance in sound quality, particularly among ANC phones. These get the sound profile fairly close to right which is a refreshing change. The bass is present and strong but isn't pushed forward as with so many other headphones. The midrange is warm and gives music a decent depth. The highs are clear and bright without being shrill. These aren't audiophile quality phones by any means, but they are better than many I have used.

These are over-the-ear phones which is my preference. I also like that these fit snugly and don't slip off whern I look down which is also a personal preference but it's important to me. If you like a very light set of phones these probably are not quite the right fit for you; if you like a set that fits a bit more firmly, these are good in that regard.

These are comfortable too. The ear cups are padded nicely and I can wear them for a couple of hours before I need to take them off for a few minutes. Most headphones I have worn get uncomfortable after a while, and these do also but it is not as quick as with many.

My one complaint is the way these are powered on and off. Instead of a simple on/off button or switch, the cans swivel to power them on and off. I can see the potential for taking them off and leaving them powered on, resulting in reduced useful runtime.

I like these phones and have been working with them quite a bit of late. They're not a complete replacement for more aggressive ANC phones but they get the sound profile right and they are comfortable enough to wear for a long flight. These strike a nice balance between comfort, ANC capability and sound quality.

This is my first experience with Ultrabooks. Up to this point I have worked with laptops that are designed to be desktop replacement systems or family entertainment systems, so the journey into the land of Ultrabooks is a new one for me. So far, I have mixed feelings about this system, mostly due to HP's recovery media creation tool, but my overall impression is a good one so far.

In terms of size, this is a very thin and dainty notebook computer, roughly the size of a fat magazine. This gives it a very small footprint and it is relatively lightweight, making it good for stuffing in a briefcase or carry-on bag (though there are better cases for this kind of thing). I set it up on the kitchen table and as soon as my wife saw it she exclaimed "It's so cute!" Indeed, it's an attractive machine.

One of the things that caught my attention when reading the specifications on this machine is that there was no mention at all of a DVD drive. The packing materials even state "no optical drive". Sure enough, there is none so loading up software will require a USB DVD drive or a properly loaded thumb drive. This is not a huge deal but it is something that must be kept in mind - not everyone will appreciate having to get an additional drive just to load up software. I am not sure if HP offers a DVD R/W drive as an accessory kit.

There are exactly two USB ports on this notebook - one USB 2.0 port and one USB 3.0 port. For the traveler working on a plane or a student taking notes in a class, this does not matter. However, when working at a desk and getting synchronized with the office computer having only two USB ports may be problematic. This can be overcome by using a hub, but again this requires extra hardware. It all depends on the usage - two ports may be plenty. In my case and for my purposes, two is usually sufficient.

There is also an HDMI port, an Ethernet jack and an audio output jack. As is typical with most laptops, this one has an SD card reader. What this notebook does not have, though, is a VGA or DVI output. This is not necessarily a problem as this is a notebook made for someone on the go, but it does mean that connecting to a projector requires using another method.
This notebook is Bluetooth capable. This is a good thing for a lot of people. For me, though, it is less important as I have no Bluetooth accessories. I do appreciate the availability though so that I can connect accessories to it in the future.

Screen type is important to many people - glossy, matte, anti-glare... This particular system has a very bright and clear glossy screen which is fine for me but may disagree with others who dislike the reflections that occur and the glare from lights. Keep this in mind.

Pleasantly, there is not a huge amount of "bloatware" on this system. Looking through the list of installed software, HP has not overly cluttered the drive with extra stuff that you won't need (though there is some stuff that I know I will never, ever use). MS Office is preloaded as is Norton Internet Security - these are simple to uninstall if there is no need for them. That said, HP and Symantec have arranged a two-year license on Norton Internet Security which is outstanding for a new system right out of the box - every system I have seen up to this point came with only 60-90 days of updates for the bundled internet security suite.

My first order of business when I brought the system up was to launch the recovery media creation tool. I plugged in my DVD drive, kicked off the process, and burned 9 DVDs on the way to making a set of 5 recovery DVDs. The process errored out repeatedly, complaining of errors though the DVD media I have has been reliable. I am not sure if there is a weakness in the creation tool, the DVD drive or the platters, but the process took a lot longer than it should have taken. Regardless, there is something else about the process that is even more troublesome - HP allows you to make ONE and only one copy of the recovery media. If one of the five DVDs goes bad, then it's all over. This is specific to HP - Sony and Asus both allow you to make multiple copies, and my other HP laptop enforced the same limit of one copy.

I dug into the performance measurement tool and the system reports a Windows Experience number of 5.6, driven by the graphics chipset (and it was the desktop graphics, not the gaming graphics, that was low). The highest number was actually the SS hard drive at 8.1, even outscoring the CPU and memory! This is a snappy little system and while it's not built for heavy gaming it has enough horsepower to handle many games.

Relating to performance - because of the solid-state drive, power-on to operational time is less than 10 seconds. I absolutely love how fast this machine boots up!

I am no fan of touchpads and to be honest I find the touchpad on this notebook worse than average. It is raised which makes it too easy to inadvertently tap it while typing, and because of the way it is raised it's too easy to get stuff in the crevices around it.

As far as traveling with this notebook, it should be said that there are smaller, more portable machines out there. This one has a 13.3" screen but I have seen much smaller systems. Then again, these smaller systems usually have less power and are less capable. It comes down to whether you prefer more compactness at the expense of power or more power at the expense of compactness.

This system comes preloaded with Windows 8. In a nutshell I find it to resemble a cross between Windows 7 and MS Zune. I am not going to go into a full review of Windows 8 but I will very briefly summarize - though it's best suited for tablets, it actually works nicely on this notebook and though there is a learning curve it's not bad.

Finally, I should mention the speaker system. My very first HP laptop came with Altec Lansing speakers built in to the unit. This system comes with Beats audio, and I have found them to be roughly equivalent. Sound quality is very good, especially coming from such a small machine.

HP has put together a very nice system in this Ultrabook. It is small, fast and powerful. I do not like the way it builds recovery media (and restricts you to a single copy), and I am a little bit concerned by not having more than 2 USB ports, but when considering that this machine is built for the traveler or student, this is a very nice system that's worth a look.

One thing we have a lot of use for in this household is Bluetooth headphones. Whether it is for work, keeping privacy in the house, using with phones, exercising, running, walking, or other uses, everyone in the house goes through headphones. I was very interesting in these especially for exercising as it is hard to find a good pair that stay in.

WHAT ARE THESE LIKE?
These earphones are meant to be used for activities that are rather intense- hence exercising, moving around, etc. These earphones come with a short USB cord for recharging and a few sizes of gel type fittings for different sizes of ear canals.

HOW ARE THESE TO USE?
They hold a charge for six to eight hours depending on how intense the listening time is and if it is consecutive or not. The controls are easy to use on the right ear wire. It does not tell you who is calling, but it does ring in the ear. Answering was easy and the call went through well with decent volume. They do stay in the ears quite well for more intense activity. Once in a while I might knock one out if I am intensely exercising, but most of the time they have been good.

SOUND?
The sound is good, but tends a little toward the flat side compared to other earbuds I have used. We have found that breaking them in by using a lot has helped them to sound better than they did at first, so they are really not bad.

COMFORT?
That is where the stars come off. Yes, they stay in the ears, but after wearing about an hour or so, they really begin to hurt. It is not the size of the cushions, but the hard plastic under them that presses against the ears. Two of us have tried them out and it does it for both of us.

WHAT ARE THESE BEST FOR?
These seem to be the best for exercising, running, walking, or an activity that is limited to an hour or so. They are good as far as sweat and water resistance goes. Recharging time is pretty good it can take from one to two hours to fully charge, depending on the day.

THE BOTTOM LINE
For really cool looking earbuds that stay in the ears during more intense activity, these are a good choice. Any time over an hour, however can be uncomfortable. Music playback is good, but not overly dimensional if that is something you are concerned with. We like them for exercising, walking, or running.

MY RATING
Four stars for these, due to lack of dimension in sound and discomfort after wearing a while.

Installation is straightforward, and you should definitely download the THX software to get the full benefit of these headphones. An icon for it was not automatically added to my desktop, but I was able to find the software in the Creative folder (it's not the Alchemy one; I don't know what that is). The software allows you to adjust and save equalizer settings as well as game-enhancing features under the TruStudio Pro tab: crystalizer, surround, bass, dialog plus, and smart volume. Each of these can be adjusted in percentage increments, so you can tweak them to be just perfect for whatever game you are playing. Clicking the play button on this tab loops a sample video with sound to allow for experimentation. A VoiceFX tab allows you to morph the sound of your voice using a bunch of presets so you can freak your friends out! I like using the Deep Voice preset, because I sound like a man when I answer my Skype phone.

The ear-surrounding cups cradle my ears for an immersive sound experience and are not too heavy, so (except for the cord attached to a USB port) I can forget I am wearing them. I've already lost the little foam mic cover, though, because it slips off a little too easily.

As far as attaching to your computer goes, you have a USB plug-in with a small rectangular THX TruSoundPro module attached. Your headphones, with separate (thankfully color-coded) mic and headphone plugs, plug into this module. When I forget I am wired and walk away from my computer (as I too often do), the headphone plugs pull out of the module first, leaving the USB plug in my computer, still sensing the headphones are plugged in. That's a boon. Volume adjustment wheel, mute switch, and a handy shirt clip are built into the cord, which appears to be of a decent length. Bottom line: Overall, this is an excellent laptop/tablet setup. The screen is simply gorgeous, the speed is excellent, and it easily morphs between a laptop and a tablet. Windows 8 can be a bit of a pain, as can some of the hardware design quirks, but overall, I’m finding it to be a solid performer.
