* This is the real deal! Every component is high quality, and the NVR unit is externally and internally immaculate. Why do I have to even say this? Because I've tried other NVR systems. I have encountered NVRs with flimsy dented cases, and messy soldering jobs on the motherboard.
* 4TB is pre-installed.
* You get 8 POE cameras! A mistake I made as a newbie was thinking all I have to do is get POE switches, then I would be able to get rid of power adapters for any camera. That is incorrect! A camera has to be designated as a POE camera in order to use POE switches and POE NVRs.
* You get eight 65 ft ethernet cable. If you can run those cables back to the NVR, which has 8 ports in the back, then you won't need to hook up any intermediary POE switches. I plan to use at most four cameras, so If I need to hook up a POE switch, the four extra cables will come in handy. However, more on this issue later.
* Included are also outdoor plugs to protect your wire connections.
* PLUG & PLAY... As long as you run the ethernet cable back to the Ethernet ports of the NVR, it is plug and play. If for any reason, you need to find the IP in your service provider's router admin, look for HEROSPEED DIGITAL TECHNOLOGY. That's the name it shows up under.
* Unlike most security cameras, the live feed of this NVR system has no delay, it's real time, or pretty close to it.
* If you're using a KVM switch at your computer, so you can switch back and forth between different sources... I said in my video that once I get a USB cable to link up the KVM switch with the NVR, then I should be able to use my PC's mouse and keyboard, which are connected to the KVM switch. Well, since then I've learned that what I said is half true. I'll be able to use the mouse, but not the keyboard. The NVR doesn't respond to any keyboards no matter if it's through the KVM switch, or directly connected to the NVR. It only uses the onscreen pop-up. You will need to use the mouse to select the letters and numbers from the virtual keyboard.

THE BAD:
-----------
* Like I said above, it's plug and play as long as you connect each camera directly back to the NVR ports. It goes without saying, but the NVR also needs to be connected to your router or nearby switch to be online. I'm running into issues testing POE switches. If the camera is not directly connected to the back of the NVR, the system cannot find it. There are 16 channels available in the NVR, and only 8 ports in the back, so obviously, this should be compatible with POE switches. But so far, I can't get it to work. I've asked for help from OSI, so we'll see...
* No guidance or instructions on how to install the actual cameras. For a moment, I was SMH. I was looking for the bases. I thought my package was missing them. But I realized the bases were already threaded onto the cameras. For each camera, you need to unthread the base, drill the base onto the ceiling of your choice location, then thread the main camera body back on it.
* Another nitpick is that installing under a ceiling will not always be ideal, or possible. It would have been great if they had included some adapters so that we can install them onto walls like bullet cameras.

Despite the little nitpicks, I still rate this 4-Stars right now. Might bump it up to 5-Stars if we can get the POE switches sorted out. I'm a newbie, so I know this might be easy for experienced networkers. The manual is a bit lacking. There were no discussions on how to install the cameras, and it assumes you'll be directly connecting all cameras back to the NVR, so it doesn't discuss the use of POE switches at all.

And unlike cheap brands, the UI is responsive and smooth. Not the smoothest out there for sure, but more than acceptably smooth considering how much a flagship smartwatch costs compared to this.
It has support for voice commands, but I honestly found that feature kind of gimmicky more than useful. The higher end version of this includes a speaker which might make the command function more useful as sort of a digital assistant, not to mention the ability to take phone calls from your wrist. But the model I got to try out lacks the speaker, which is a fine compromise for a cheaper price tag all things considered. The battery life at first was just OK, a few days on a charge if using lift-to-wake functions, but just as on my Mi Band tracker of old, I found if I turn off auto-wake and rely on using the button to wake the display, the battery life goes from counting in days to counting in weeks. That's the killer feature of this device- the ability to leave it on to track fitness and sleep habits without having to charge it so often. I'll have to charge it more than my old Mi Band's monthly top up for sure, probably at least 2x a month, but that's still very manageable.
So that's it, after years of loving my Mi Bands and considering it the standard by which all practical fitness trackers should be judged, I'm finally moving on to an Amazfit watch. This is a difficult value to beat.

I spend a great deal of time in a computer lab where there is literally over 1,000 running systems. In this environment, ear protection isn't absolutely necessary but without it there's some discomfort with which to deal because of all the fans in these systems and the requisite air handling units. I already have a pair of Bose QC-15 headphones but I am not a huge fan, so I recently purchased a pair of Sennheiser PXC-450 headphones for use in this environment. After an initial break-in period, I have come to really appreciate them.

This is going to be a comparative review, though primarily about the Sennheiser phones. Bose is generally regarded as the gold standard when it comes to ANC headphones, so matching the Sennheisers to the Bose is a good match-up. I'll break it all down into categories: Noise Canceling, Comfort, Sound Quality and Build Quality.

Noise Canceling:
Active noise canceling is THE primary feature of these phones and each has its strengths. Bose is, without question, the more capable ANC set when it comes to removing noise. This supremacy comes at a price though - because of the aggressiveness of their ANC, the wearer often feels a "pressure" on the ears when using the phones, something not present with the Sennheiser set which is close to Bose's level of canceling. Where Bose went to extremes to eliminate noise, Sennheiser went with the thought of "good enough for most". To be sure, both sets do a nice job of eliminating low frequency noise, enough to make air travel more pleasant if you dislike the rumble of plane engines.

They work in the car too (if you're not driving). I tried both sets in a moving vehicle and all do a fine job of eliminating road and engine noise. In fact, it was quiet to the point of eerie in the car. So, if you're a passenger on a long trip, either of these will work to suit your needs.

For the Sennheisers, you don't have to use ANC to listen to music as they provide the ability to override ANC and work like normal headphones. Bose, on the other hand, is an all-or-nothing deal and requires ANC to be on when listening to anything at all.

And that brings up a nice little feature on the Sennheisers - the "talk-thru" function, which allows a listener to cut off all sound and turn on a small microphone so that one can carry on a conversation without having to remove the headphones. No other headset I have ever used has this feature and it has already proven to be a handy tool.

Both sets require a single AAA battery to provide ANC. The battery life is definitely better with the Bose - mine last about a week between needing new batteries, whereas the Sennheiser set needs a new battery every other day.

Comfort:
The Sennheisers are the most comfortable headphones I have ever worn - period. The padding is buttery soft and they fit over my ears with no issue. Other reviewers have said that it seems like they just melt into your head, and that's a very accurate way to describe them. The Bose are nearly as comfortable, though they are slightly smaller.

Where the Sennheisers have a slight comfort disadvantage is actually in their size. These are big headphones and when they are worn around the neck instead of on the ears, they tend to rub on the neck and sometimes (depending on what you're doing) they can get in the way. If you take them off, or don't wear them around your neck, there's nothing about which to complain.

Sound Quality:
Sennheiser has always had premium sound, and the PXC-450 headphones demonstrate why they are the champs when it comes to quality sound. Though not audiophile phones, the PXC-450 brings awesome sound quality even at low volumes, with very full midrange and decent bass. The Bose sound great, except that the bass is too rich and without an equalizer in the mix the bass is enough to give me a headache over extended periods.

Build Quality:
I have not had the Sennheiser set very long but so far I have had no trouble with them. They feel rugged and sturdy, though they are mostly plastic so they do scratch and twist easily. The cord is heavy gauge wire, a welcome improvement over the cabling on Sennheiser sets I have worn in the past. The Bose set is a little more flimsy, with lesser gauge wire.

In summary, I find that the Sennheiser PXC-450 headphones are a better product than the Bose QC-15 headphones. They sound great, feel comfortable and they do a fine job of canceling noise. Bose does have better ANC and if that is the main thing you need and you don't mind the sensation of pressure they put on the ears then Bose is a better choice, but in almost every other aspect the Sennheisers bring more to the table.

My daughter and I do a lot of photography of jewelry. We have had a variety of tripods and camera aids. This kit seemed like a good one for us. I got it.

WHAT IS THIS KIT LIKE?
CASE
This has a hard case that zips around the edge. It has a pocket in it to hold things in place and a cupped side to allow for the tripod storage.

LENS BAGS
There are bags in here which fit small medium or large lenses. I don't have any lenses yet, but I do have a small light that fits in one.

CLEANING CLOTH
These come in a zip topped plastic bag. This is pretty nice and works well as is expected with microfiber cloth for cleaning glass.

QUICK RELEASE CAMERA STRAP
This comes in a nice package with good instructions in it. The idea is that this helps stabilize the camera when you are taking a lot of photos. You can not have to grip the camera so hard so your hand does not get tired too. If you accidentally slip your grip, it does not crash to the ground.

This had a learning curve to it, but I finally figured out how to use it for me where it was helpful.

LENS PAPER
This paper allows you to clean the lens off gently wet or dry. The wet means that you use the Altura cleaning solution for greasy heavier prints.

PUFFER CLEANER
This is a rubberized ball that when you squeeze it, there will be a blast of air that will blow things off of the lenses. This works quite well when I get a particle on the lens so I don't have to touch it.

BRUSH
This is when the dust won't blow off the lens or other glass you can gently brush it and then blow it away with the puffer cleaner.

EMPTY BOTTLE
This is for alcohol or lens cleaner.

TRIPOD
This is why I wanted this kit the most. It has an ingenious design to it. It folds up flat and quite small, yet when you take it apart and tilt it, you can stand it up for close photos, or use it in your hand. It has rubber on the bottom to keep it put, and it also has a rubberized grip if you want to hold it. The camera platform tilts, but it locks into place which I love. This is working great for us taking close up photos of some of the small jewelry we are photographing. It has come in really handy.

What I love is that we can pick it up and use it by hand if we need another angle than the table top one.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This kit is a nice kit. I got it mostly for the tripod, but the cleaning accessories and the wrist strap make it really nice. The puffer ball is one of those things that you don't realize you need until you have it.- at least for me. The case is protective and easy to travel with.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. I am happy with this kit. It has worked better for us than I expected. We will be using this a lot in the future too.

I had my concerns because I've researched Powerline Adapters before, and there is talk about how your home's electrical wiring may cause your adapters to work or not work depending on where you plug in your adapters. For me, the process was pretty painless. I plugged the main adapter (GPL-2000PT) to a wall outlet next to my Frontier Gateway. Then an ethernet cable connects my Gateway to this adapter. BTW, the GPL-2000PT is the smaller of the two adapters. For some reason, my brain correlates MAIN as being BIGGER. So without looking at the model numbers on the device, I connected the bigger adapter next to my router initially and got it wrong, and had to start over. Anyway, so remember the smaller one is the one that gets tethered to your router. Next you plug the bigger adapter (GPL-2000WAC) to wherever you want to have the new wi-fi network. Press the Security button on the main adapter, then press the Security button on the other adapter.. wait for them to pair, and voila, you have a new wi-fi network. In my case, I was pleasantly surprised that everything worked because I needed better wi-fi in the garage, and there weren't any wall outlets available. Manual specifically recommends using wall outlets. I have these outlet boxes that the previous homeowner had installed along exposed 2x4 beams. I plugged the adapter into one of these and crossed my fingers, and amazingly, everything linked up. Speeds are super fast and snappy too.

The hiccup I run into, which is the same hiccup I run into every time I play around with gadgets of this kind whether it be powerline, meshes, or wi-fi extenders.... is the part where I would like to change the SSID and password. The default they give you is always something that's hard to remember, so you always want to change this. I can never get to their user interface with their provided IP's. The idea is that once you're on the adapter's network, you should be able to go to the provided address to access the user interface. It never works for me, no matter the brand. Either there is something about my network that I'm not understanding, or there are many consumers in the same boat as as I am. In any case, I will tell you what does work for me every time.. I simply go to my own router ADMIN. So if you're Spectrum, go to your Spectrum admin, if you're Frontier, Verizon, etc., go to their router admin. Then look for your new Nexuslink adapter. Your router would have assigned it an IP address. Type that ip address into the browser, and it will take you to the Nexuslink user interface. So whenever you can't get to a user interface provided the manufacturer of a powerline adapter, wifi extender, etc., just go to your own router admin and get the IP address that it was assigned. BTW, when you're browsing your router admin for the IP address of the adapter, you might not know what you're looking for since it may not be labeled by your router properly. So you'll need to find it through a process of elimination. All the IP addresses listed will show whether the device is connected by wi-fi, moca, or ethernet. So you can ignore all the wi-fi and mocas. Look for the ethernet connection that is unfamiliar to you. Mine showed up as "UNKNOWN." I have several devices connected to my network as UNKNOWN. I simply tried them all out, and one of the addresses eventually took me to the Nexuslink user interface.

If any network expert is reading this, I'd love for you to chime in below in the comment section and explain when it comes to this part regarding accessing the user interface of an adapter whether it be powerline, wifi extenders, etc., why the default given address in the manual never works for some of us. This hiccup doesn't deserve a star subtraction since I've experienced this with every other brand I've tried. Anyway, I can now access my garage camera blazingly fast, versus the 50/50 hit or miss connections before. This is 5 stars!

Problem #1: Camera eats up normal AAA Energizer batteries quickly. Maybe get 5 pictures and then it quits. Change to AAA Lithium Entergizer Batteries. Now, you are OK. The sensor on the camera trips just after a few underwater photos.

Size, and functionality seems comfortably nice. Not too technical to get started using this camera. Found this camera a great first step for beginners who want to document their scuba dives, take photos on surface, on the boat, on the shore, etc. But, hold on... when you want to go scuba diving:

Problem #2: Does not have an underwater setting for diffused lighting. Only Flowers and Landscapes. What dah? Is this not for underwater use? Hello! All of my underwater photos could have improved by 100 percent if there was a setting for underwater lighting. The sunny days at the shore, boat photos, trees and countryside photos, ok. These were nice, the detail in the landscape photos were good. You can even use the camera without its plastic shell. The protective casing makes this an excellent choice as a first step scuba camera. But, how are the photos underwater? This is a $100 camera, so please do not expect high quality photos from your squid, lobster, or grouper ... posing for you underwater, even at 25 feet. This makes a great first step camera, getting your feet wet with underwater photography.

Problem #3: strap holder is on right side only (for right hand use.) Better if there was a strap holder on both sides, for those who need on left hand side (underwater.) Why? My first hand experience is that you want to use this point and shoot camera using either your right hand or your left hand. Not both. This camera is a quick shot camera, not "oh, wait a minute, pose, look this way, now smile, ok, cheese ..." This camera sits on your right hand or left hand while diving. Now, if you see that nice fish, and want to take a picture, you try with one hand. If the strap is on the wrong side, it blocks your ability to use the left hand to hold the camera. So, this camera is ONLY FOR RIGHT HANDED folks. But, do not let go of the camera underwater, you may loose it. Right? Not really. Nice thing about this basic camera is that it float to surface (rather than sink into the bottom.) Wow, did that save me a few times. Dropped off my wrist. Then floated for a few feet, and I got it back. If it sunk down 300 Feet, I could have kissed this baby --- good bye.

I have taken about 50 surface images, and 50 underwater images, using this Intova. All 50 surface photos, with reasonable sunlight, were excellent considering this camera. Of the 50 photos underwater images, about 10 were acceptable, the other 40 were blurry and not acceptable. Yeah, I had to spend another 15 minutes per each of the 10 photos to convert the poor colors into something more exciting, adding RED, adding CONTRAST, adding BRIGHTNESS using a photo editor. But, I did get 10 acceptable underwater photos. And that was great. Really Great. These photos were generally above 25 feet.

Scuba divers need to know the difficulty of taking photos underwater while attempting to swim around reefs, wrecks, squid, lobster and other photographers. Buy this camera as a first step. Just correct that battery issue, take lots of pictures, and learn the responsibility of underwater photography is the PERSON BEHIND THE CAMERA. For $100, not bad, eh?

I have had good success with Kingston products (in particular their SSD storage) so I was pleased to have the opportunity to work with this encrypted thumb drive. It has a lot of promise and it works better than other encrypted drives I have used. There is one drawback, at least for me - it does not support Linux (if it does, I haven't figured out how yet).

I have the 16GB version, and the thing is built like a tank. It has a metal casing around the inner workings and it can handle some abuse. That's good news if you keep these things in a briefcase or loose in a bookbag.

Setup is easy. When it is plugged into a Windows machine (I do not have access to a Mac so I cannot speak to that use case), the software is available and can be used to set up the drive with a password. That's pretty straightforward. If you forget your password, you can wipe the drive and start over but you cannot recover your data. So, choose your password wisely.

Copy rates seem to be decent - a little slower than similar-sized drives I have that aren't encrypted but not prohibitively so. It's a trade-off, and a small one at that.

When I popped this drive into my Linux machine, the kernel saw it immediately. However, all it could see was the setup partition which is approximately 100mb, a far cry from 16 GB. The drive is smart enough to hide its data from foreign OS-based systems so your data is safe. Linux is gaining users though, and being able to access the data from a Linux system would be good, even if there was a tedious process to get to the partition but still requiring a password. This is better than other encrypted drives I have used in the past which made the data scrambled but was still accessible. However, not being able to use this drive under Linux is a problem for me.

To be fair, it is not advertised as compatible with Linux.

This is a good drive and from what testing I have done it works well. That said, it does not support Linux and that is a negative for me. Hopefully Kingston will release a Linux-based version (or a software layer) for it in the future; for now it's only usable for me under Windows.

This time I experimented to see if I could get Debian Linux distro running on the NVME on my older workstation.

It took a few tries. Getting the OS to boot directly from the NVME was a no-go. Since the NVME is mounted on an adapter card, I had hoped it would trick the system into thinking it was just an ordinary SATA drive and boot from it. But that didn't happen.

So what I did was installed all the Linux OS EXCEPT for the boot folder on the NVME, and put the boot folder on the SSD HDD. So it boots from the SSD but the entire OS is on the NVME and runs from it.

Step one:

The partition manager in the Debian installer didn't want to partition the NVME at first.

So I bailed out of it and used GParted (Gnome disks utility couldn't do this) to "create partition table" and selected msdos as type. That wiped everything and turned the whole drive into unallocated space. From that point the partition manager worked.

Step two:

From the linux bootable USB installer I partitioned the SSD (not the NVME) with a primary partition labeled (to be mounted) as /boot. (You can make this partition most any size from a few GB on up---the boot files don't require a lot of space.) The remaining space I manually labeled as /msc.

I partitioned the NVME so the installer would put everything else on it, starting with / (root). You can simply make the whole NVME / root and the installer will take care of putting everything else on that drive, or you can do what I did and set up size-defined partitions for /home, /usr, and so on.

It worked. The SSD does the booting to the NVME, which then runs the OS. And it did improve speed.

Great board. Install was simple. Most ports are in decent locations with no real trouble with cable routing. First boot was normal and got me right into the bios screen. Make sure you update the bios before doing anything else. I made the mistake of setting my memory to DOCP1 (to get my DDR5 set to 6000) before updating the bios which resulted in black screen, no post. A quick cmos reset with the back panel button and I was back in business. Updated bios to version 0805 and then enabled DOCP1 and everything else went good with no trouble at all. I did notice that once I had had Win11 installed, my boot times were slow. Did some research and found that there's a bios setting "memory context restore" that needs to be changed to enabled. After that the boot times improved drastically, but still not as quick as my previous AM4 system. I'm sure it will improve with future bios updates. With a 7700X cpu, Cinbench R23 multi-core score is 20k (about the same as my previous 5900X). Timespy score with an RTX4080 is 29k, which I got to 30k with a quick oc. So far so good, it's a fast and stable motherboard.
I do have one con: CMOS battery was DOA! I found this out when I removed power from my sys to setup another pc. I had to go back in and setup all of my bios settings again (then saved my profile until I could get a new battery. I recommend swapping the battery (CR2032) before you set it up and to save your profile in the bios. I guess it costs extra when buying a $500+ motherboard to get a working cmos battery. -1 star.

TLDR: Dropped my GPU temps from 75c to 50c under full load. Reduced fan noise considerably since I went from 5 case fans at 100% to 3 at 30-50% most of the time. LED's are ok. If you want to run cooler temps and less noise, get this!
UPDATE: after a month of use everything was still great. I did make a bad mistake that ended my card. I didn't want to take the cooler off to properly attach the back plate so I was just sitting on top of the card. All was well until I stupidly tried to move a fan from one side on my CPU cooling tower to the other, while my comp was on..... I KNOW, I KNOW, I"m an idiot. I dropped the fan which bounced around my mobo and slammed into the top of my card. Shorting everything out. GPU is toast, rest of system is questionable. Be smarter than me, DONT TAKE SHORT CUTS. TURN OFF YOUR PC WHEN WORKING ON IT AND PROPERLY ATTACH EVERYTHING! Still hyped on the this cooler. Aiming to still use it on my new card IF I can ever get one without taking a second mortgage.

I used this on a XFX RX 580 GTS 8GB Black edition. In a M-atx case, the stock cooler fans would run full RPM just to keep it at 75-80C under load. Add in 5 case fans (@full RPM) to keep the air flow fresh and I had an annoyingly loud heater just a few feet from my chair. Stumbled upon this in a random search and after reading a few other reviews I decided to order it and see how it goes.

Install was straight forward enough. If you can reapply thermal paste, you can install this cooler. Placing the heat sinks on the VRAM and VRM is time consuming but unlike others I found the supplied thermal sticky pads to be fine after applying moderate force for about 10 secs. Only issue I had was clearance on one of the VRAMs as it sat close to the plate and could only be half covered by a heatsink. Getting the placement on that one took slightly longer but by using a few dry test fits I was able to get it placed perfectly.

The MOSs are on the left on this GPU so I was hesitant but after a week of using it I haven't seen any issues with VRM not properly cooling. Board doesn't support junction temp measuring so I have no hard data on if they are hotter or not, but I do feel airflow around them and performance is still great.

The rad and fan were easy enough to install. In a M-atx case it is tight. It was a squeeze and took a few tries to properly get everything where I wanted but once in I have no complaints. I did hear "coil whine" from the pump once, but quickly sorted out that some pressure was being applied to one of the tubes right near the pump, once I shifted it a little, the whine stopped and never returned.

The LEDS are ok. The controller is adequate. The LED along the side of the GPU mount is a nice touch, really adds a higher end feel to the finished product. Obviously this isn't a high end ARGB controller but its got more than enough setting to make it fit into your overall lighting needs. Personally I just wanted some plain old solid white. I do find the white to be slightly bluish in the fans but I chalk that up to ARGB vs the RGB LED case fans I have installed.

-I did have to cut some of the metal shroud for the front of the GPU back plate. I didnt want to run no plate on top of the board and obviously it wasn't designed to have water tubes go through it. The UPRIGHT SMART WEARABLE POSTURE TRAINER is an "anti-slouch" posture trainer that really works! I discarded my [[ASIN:B00N9P8GMW Lumo Lift]] after a week or so, because my sitting posture is pretty good, and I rarely slouched badly enough to trigger the Lumo Lift. In contrast, the Upright buzzes me whenever I start to relax my posture even partway to a full slouch.

The Upright needs to be pasted to your back with gentle adhesive pads (60 included), rather than pinned to your clothing (like the Lumo Lift), but the greater sensitivity makes the extra effort worthwhile. Packets of one-time-use adhesive pads are available from the Upright web site for about $15.

You can wear the Upright between your shoulder blades if you're going to be standing, walking, and sitting; or at the small of your back if you're an Upright novice or generally sitting. As long as it's turned on, the Upright works even without the accompanying app (Android or iOS) that tracks your training progress. The Upright app uses Bluetooth to connect with the wearable Upright.

The app walks you through the simple setup, which mostly involves (1) finding the proper spot for placement on your back, and (2) calibrating the device so that it can detect a slouch. Once it's calibrated, the device will gently buzz you whenever you sink into a slouch--which inevitably happens as your muscles tire from holding a single position--so that you can straighten up. (There is no sound. The product page video that demonstrates the buzz is kind of amusing.)

When you create an account (free), the app collects information about your height, weight, and age, and then generates a daily posture training program that is personalized for you. The training program begins with your wearing the device for a few minutes, and then for longer and longer sessions. At the end of a session, the app gives you a score, based on how long you held your upright posture. (Mine was only 86%, because I intentionally slouched to test the buzz.)

The Upright arrives fully charged. The app tells you how much charge is remaining in your Upright. When you're charging the device in the supplied charging dock, a solid red light tells you that it's properly connected and charging.

As convenient as this product makes hooking up networking cables, the cheap screws that come with this wall plate make installation a nightmare.

Do yourself a favor, if you have an extra light switch plate laying around, use those screws instead. I've installed two of these ethernet wall plates into two different low voltage mounting brackets. There are no threads in these mounting brackets. You're essentially creating the threads as you go. This necessitates a greater amount of torque and the screw heads are shallow. If using hand tools, this will require immense amounts of force to prevent stripping the heads. Normally, only a small, flat blade screwdriver is all that is required. But this installation works best if you have a powered screwdriver that will provide the necessary torque.

If you can run the screws in and out prior to installation, it may prevent some headaches. I did something similar to the first low voltage mounting bracket I purchased too.

You'll also find that if you have some screws from an existing light switch plate, that they have a deeper slot and are half the length. The provided screws were much longer than necessary. I replaced the screws on the second wall plate I installed after backing out the originals with a set of pliers after the heads were damaged.

To put this into context, I have the right tools and do more DIY than most other people I know.

I selected this keyboard/touchpad with the idea of using it with my tablet. Admittedly I mistakenly thought it was a Bluetooth keyboard which would have made it suitable for my tablet but this turned out to be a misunderstanding on my part. That said, it has proven to be a very handy keyboard in more ways than I had originally planned. In particular, in addition to working with Windows and Linux it works with Raspberry Pi which opens a whole world of possibilities for this keyboard.

This keyboard is very small, barely bigger than a Hershey bar, and it has a full set of keys as well a touchpad and mouse buttons on the right side. This is sufficient for doing pretty much everything you’d want to do, including surfing the web, text editing and software development. Granted, the size makes it less than ideal for some of these functions but it does work as a full keyboard/mouse combination if you want to use it that way.

Right out of the box, the switch was on and the keyboard had completely drained its battery so it had to be plugged in and charged overnight. This was a surprise but was not a big deal, just unusual.

When connected to a Windows 8 system the OS recognized it and immediately it was usable. It required no special drivers, no configuration changes or anything else – just plug it in and turn it on. It worked the same under Linux as well.

The real test for this keyboard/mouse was on a Raspberry Pi system. The keyboard connected and worked without a glitch – expected since it worked fine with Ubuntu Linux but not guaranteed as the kernel was known to work but the hardware was not yet tested. With a second external keyboard connected it was possible to type on both at the same time and also to use the other keyboard as a regular keyboard and the other just as a mouse.

There are a number of other SBC types and designs out there, and there is no reason that this device should not work with any of them that have a Linux-based kernel. Embedded Windows system should also support it as well.

Though I have not really tested the full range it is good to at least 10 feet. At that range the system still recognized input from the keyboard and touchpad without any issues.

So far I have found only one issue with this keyboard and that’s the space bar. I habitually press the space bar in the middle, and on this keyboard the press sensors are on the ends. The spacebar is not quite stiff enough and when pressed in the middle it bows instead of pressing down on the sensors, thereby not registering the press. To get it to recognize the press I have to press on the ends specifically. This is a minor irritant and is a very small price to pay for what this device offers.

This is a very small but fully functional keyboard/touchpad combination that works with multiple configurations. It connects easily and so far has given no real operational issues. Keep in mind that this thing is extremely small, though, which is great for portability, mobility and economy of space but less pleasant for systems that aren’t being transported anywhere.

I will be keeping a close eye on this router, which I just purchased yesterday, because it seems too good to be true. So far, in my 24 hours of usage since purchasing it for $29 at Walmart (sorry, Amazon, I was in a hurry) I have found it to be flexible and powerful in my unusual application, which is remote and requires 100% uptime with occasional bursts of heavy usage. Mine is a factory-fresh rather than refurb unit, incidentally.

I'll admit I had some trouble believing a router this cheap could be as good as this one turned out to be (assuming it stays reliable-- but, the one I bought trumpets a lifetime guarantee on the box). I expected something dumbed-down, with seriously constrained functionality and annoying firmware. (This model's v3 hardware, although Broadcom BCM5356-based, is not compatible with alternative firmware such as DD-WRT due to its problematic NVRAM size.) It's a single-stream design, with an internalized antenna, potentially suggesting performance limitations. And it's from Netgear, which I've frankly not had great luck with before... but it's been years since I've tried one of their products, and the reviews here are generally good. Most of the negative reviews here relate to support experiences, but my networking knowledge-level is expert, so ...what the heck, did I mention it was $29? An easy roll of the dice.

Though my application requires custom configuration, I initially started the unit using its web-based wizard, which you access by connecting your computer (via cable or WiFi) and pointing your browser to 192.168.1.1. With the unit connected to my cable modem, it set itself up quickly and voila, Internet. For most people this would be good enough and the job would be done. Kudos to Netgear for delivering the product with WPA-2 encryption enabled! They provide a SSID and password on a printed label. So, you're good to go. And its default configuration is just fine for most folks' usage.

For my application, however, I needed to cable several devices including a VoIP adaptor (a la [...] and a server with several ports exposed to the Internet. The unit needed to be set to a specific IP address scheme, SSID and password. And a dynamic-DNS utility on the server needed to communicate with my DNS provider. ...To accomplish these and other advanced tasks, the browser-based configurator at 192.168.1.1 has an Advanced tab. Proceeding through the settings is straightforward and similar to other reasonably-configurable routers. The default settings established earlier by the wizard remain intact in the Advanced panes so you are starting from a known-operable configuration. All good.

So I proceeded through each of my customizations, taking care to click the Apply button after modifying any pane. Usually there's a ten-second delay during which the unit sets up the new settings; a few necessitate that the router reboot itself. Everything went smoothly.

So, for $29 I'd replicated an unusual configuration and everything was working. But how well?

Okay so my wife had to take an important international FaceTime call as I was finishing up. So, for a while there the server was downloading some massive updates, two ssh clients were talking to the server, VoIP was in use, six WiFi clients were doing whatever they were doing, a 3G microcell tower was initializing and downloading firmware updates to itself ...and FaceTime was running smoothly with a high frame-rate on her third-gen iPad. A nice acid test!

In particular, I did not feel the need to mess with the unit's default QoS settings... and additional props to Netgear for including QoS in a router this inexpensive!

So far, I'm impressed. It's hard to imagine a better value in a router. I'll update this review if there are any reliability issues, but so far, so good. So excellent, in fact.

I was researching the best way to get high speed NETWORK speeds to a downstairs room. The cable modem was installed into an upstairs room (left side of house) and the WIFI speed in the first floor room (right side of house) was sufficient for most internet streaming services (about 60Mbps) However I needed higher network bandwidth for accessing a NAS.

I sought out solutions that could avoid having to run an ethernet cable from the first floor to the second floor. First I tried ethernet over AC PWR. I received the same speeds as WIFI. Then I found these MOCA adapters, once installed they appeared to work great. I got sufficient speeds but not quite as fast I wanted (about 100Mbps) But once they were installed I would experience constant drops in connection across all devices. It would go out for anywhere from 30 seconds to 10 minutes.

Customer service was great and responsive via email. We verified my setup and hardware were all compatible with the MOCA adapters but the only thing that could cause issues was interference in the coax cables. Since those cables are all inside the walls already, there really wasn't anything else I could do unless I wanted to run new coax.

Ultimately I decided to run CAT8 ethernet upstairs.

I purchased this HDMI Capture USB device to record a Windows desktop session. What I noticed is that the passthrough video quality is very bad. What is clear text coming out of the computer becomes blurry by the time it gets to the TV. What this means is that you can't keep this device plugged in permanently to record when necessary. You'd have to settle for plugging it in only when recording. Perhaps for gaming devices that have larger text and buttons, it wouldn't be a big problem.

This device can also be used to live stream by plugging it in to the USB port on your PC. A few problems here:
-- This is only USB 2.0
-- The USB port is also used as the power supply for the device. This means that if your PC doesn't provide enough power through its USB port (especially if you have an external drive plugged in to the device), you won't be able to use this function. They did not include those two-headed dongles to provide additional power.
-- The drivers are bad. I was able to get OBS to preview the device only after a lot of changing inputs around. VLC will not work with it.

What I do like about it is that while the passthrough quality is pretty bad, the resulting recording isn't. You can certainly tell that it is a recording, probably due to the video compression but all of the text from the 1080p desktop is readable.

I also like the fact that you can record directly to a USB drive with scheduled recording capabilities. The UI of the built-in software is straight out of VHS days but it does the basics of what you need. The convenience of being able to press record on the remote to start your capture means you can set up your PC how you need it without having to also manage your desktop recording software.

There's a lot to like about this monitor, but also some clear drawbacks. Let's start with the good news.

In typical HP fashion it comes very well packaged to survive pretty much any measure of rough handling in transit. There's a "quick start" guide that is taped to the front of the monitor that walks you through the setup (which is very straightforward). There's also an excellent user guide in PDF on the included disk.

The overall design is very attractive. It's very slim, lightweight and easy to position. I'm using it with the included table stand since my wall-mount options can't handle a monitor this large (it does come with a metal plate with VESA-compatible holes should you want to use it with a mount).

I used this on both a PC and as a video monitor hooked up through my AV receiver. For both situations I used the HDMI interface.

The sound quality is very good compared with the typical built-in speaker. It lacks bass "punch" but is quite acceptable.

Now for the so-so news: picture quality. It's good, but not "wow" good. Picture quality was somewhat drab looking, lacking crispness and contrast despite spending a lot of time tweaking the video quality with the many options available. It becomes worse when viewed off center (although it does have a decent viewing angle).

It comes with a remote which could be very handy for switching inputs, tweaking the picture, adjusting the sound, etc. I say it "could be" since the remote it comes with is horrible. It's small, which is good, but all the buttons are flush mount and have black on black lettering. It is very, very hard to see which button is which even in bright light. Forget about finding the right button in dim light. Truly horrible design work.

While there are pluses, and it is hitting an attractive price point, I can't see this being worthy of anything more than a little above average (3.5 star) rating. It's a decent, but not exceptional monitor (with a total design failure of a remote). Worth considering if you are looking for a large monitor without breaking the bank, and have moderate expectations as to video quality.

An air mouse is not something you would normally use with a PC-based system unless you are trying to save space or are giving a presentation in which case it is a convenient accessory. Such a mouse is a lot more useful for things like Smart TVs, though it is also useful for embedded systems like a Raspberry Pi. I have used several air mice and I was curious to see how well this one would compare to others I have used. So far it has worked well, under both Linux as well as Windows. I will state up front that I have not used it with a Smart TV.

At a glance, this little device looks like a TV remote and little more, but it is quite a bit more than that. It does work as a remote, of course, but it also works as a mouse with a full-up keyboard. On one side of this device there are all of the controls you would expect to find on a remote for a Smart TV remote – volume control, channel settings, mode buttons, play, search and more. Flip the unit over and there is a keyboard, with 38 keys and most regular keyboard functions accessible through function key settings.

The unit requires two AAA batteries, not included.

I decided to try it with my Linux workstation, running CentOS 7 with a 64-bit 3.10.0-series kernel. I did not have to load special drivers and I did not need to do any special configuration at all, it was just plug and play. I was able to move the mouse just by waving the device in front of the screen and several of the buttons on the remote side worked as I would have hoped – Home took me to the browser home page, volume controls worked, Search worked, the menu button brought up the menu for the current application with focus and more. The keyboard portion worked as it should and I was able to type, though I found it a little awkward after being used to a full-sized keyboard for so long.

I also tried it with my Windows 10 system and I got nearly identical results. It required no drivers, no special configuration, no extra set-up – it just works as expected. The buttons works the same under Windows as they did under Linux for me and I was able to navigate as desired.

This is a good air mouse that works well under Linux and Windows. It should work fine with smaller systems like the Raspberry Pi (which uses a derivative of the Linux kernel). As an added bonus, it is relatively inexpensive. If you need an air mouse, this one is worth some consideration.

I have a strong interest in photography and I always keep an eye open for lights and equipment that will help me take more creative or impactful pictures. I selected this light with the intent of using it for creative photography and so far I am pleased with it. I have other LED lights that have similar functions, but this one is different in a few ways that set it apart.

This is a wand light as opposed to a square LED bank. As such, the light distribution is a bit different. It can directly cover a longer (wider) area which is handy when putting together a mock-up with miniatures. It has a couple of mounting options too, utilizing either a miniature tripod (included) or magnetically attaching to a metal surface. I do wish a clamp was included such that it could attach to the tripod horizontally, but such clamps are available if they're needed.

This light is VERY bright and can easily light a small room when at full brightness. It can be dimmed to cast a soft light too which is good. It's not exactly the most ideal light source but it will work for general lighting in a pinch.

The temperature range goes from 2500k (very warm and orange-y) to 9900k (blistering cold white) and everywhere in between. Getting the color just right is relatively easy though it does take a little patience and experimentation to get it right. Do keep in mind that because this is an LED-based light, the temperature band setting is quite narrow and presents a different light profile, one that the camera can see but the human eye cannot. In addition to "natural lighting" modes it can be set for specific colors too such as purple, red, blue and so on.

Charging is done via a USB-C port, and the charging cable is included. I have not tried using this as a power source to charge my phone though the documentation doesn't say much about that. A full charge on this light lasts a while, though I have not drained it all the way down to find out how long it will last. Obviously the runtime is variable based on mode and brightness, and what is interesting about this light in particular is that it displays the estimated runtime on the screen based on current settings - this is a nice feature that I have not seen on a lot of these lights.

There are some creative modes for use with video or for special effects in a live setting, though the usefulness of these modes is dependent on the user. I personally will never use them. However, in the right hands these might be very useful for a project. There are several effects available, including police flashers, tube TV glow simulation, flickering candle and more.

The light comes with a nice canvas carrying pouch that provides basic storage and protection.

I really like this light and will be working with it more in the coming weeks and months. It has some nice features and it has good color and brightness ranges. It's not terribly expensive either.

I have run extensive tests on this camera over the last several months and I must say I’m very impressed with the performance.

Personally I have been working with security camera products for over 15 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from large systems to single camera nursery monitors. I work with a group of security professionals and we regularly consult on large corporate projects and write about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well - I understand what to look for in quality cameras and the places manufacturers tend to try to save money on which makes an inferior product.

Over the years the security camera technology has vastly improved becoming less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install residential security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings.

This is advice any professional security analyst will provide and what we tell everyone of our clients. If you are new to home security camera systems, we recommend going with wired (non-WiFi), NVR or computer based recorders run with systems such as Blue Iris. This type of system is infinitely more secure and stable. While initial setup costs are a bit more the security it affords is worth every penny. It always pays to research the products, discuss them with those in the field, understand vulnerabilities and PLAN YOUR SYSTEM PRIOR TO PURCHASING ANYTHING. If you are at all tech savvy at all you can do it. While there is a bit of a learning curve it is not awful and in the end you will be thankful for the time you spent in the beginning as it will save you time, money and endless frustration.

I have set up, tested and reviewed more security systems and individual products than I can possibly remember. Without question my go to solution for home security solutions is a computer based, Blue Iris system with PoE cameras run off of quality PoE switches. This type of system is not only easy to operate but is highly secure.

While this camera is not natively a PoE camera I’m happy to share the 5 Pairs Passive PoE Injector and PoE Splitter Kit with 5.5x2.1 mm DC Connector RJ45 Power Over Ethernet by Exgoofit ( https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B07F82YK6P/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_asin_title_o03_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1 ) allow for this camera to operate almost identical to a PoE camera. The power adapter must be plugged in where the Ethernet cable is plugged in with the first pigtail adapter while the second adapter plugs onto the cameras power port and Ethernet jack. By utilizing this you can avoid the security concerns associated with WiFi cameras and still only have minimal wires run to the camera.

As with any component there are a host of factors to consider. In terms of cameras more megapixels is not always better. For instance 2MP cameras often perform better in low light while 5MP will allow for more detail when lighting is good. This camera is 2MP which is ideal for the vast majority of installation situations.

Highlights of this camera include:

Awesome Pan Tilt Zoom - Utilizing a 110° wide-angle varifocal lens and the head rotating 355° horizontally and 90° vertically, a 360° view is easily obtained. This makes this camera an outstanding choice to be placed on a corner of an eave where it can constantly monitor the largest possible area.

3.6mm Board lens - in my tests over the last couple of months I have been fairly impressed with the performance of this Fixed Focus 6mm lens coupled with the 1/2.8" Sony IMX307 CMOS with ICR image sensor. While this will not allow for near as clear zooming as a varifocal lens it is adequate in most circumstances.

Low Light Capability - this lens is decent in low light. Images are ok at low light, far better than the vast majority of similar cameras in this price range. IR lighting is dependable and nighttime / low light images are better than expected. My tests showed accurate images within 75’ of the IR lighting. By using both 4 IR lights and 4 bright LED lights this allows the camera to capture more details than many of the others on the market.

ONVIF Compatibility - critical for using with software such as Blue Iris. I have set it up with advanced features such as Patrol and Watchdog utilizing multiple detection zones.

2 Way Audio - I have had no issues utilizing the 2 way audio through Blue Iris - sound is accurate, clear and minimal lag.

Video Compression - This camera utilizes Smart 265/Smart 264/M-JPEG compression allowing for the smallest file sizes while maintaining the highest quality.

Great build quality - this camera is well built and will hold up outside in all conditions. That being said this is not a small camera in any way.

Over the course of my testing this product for the last several months I’ve been thoroughly impressed. It loads into Blue Iris without any issue and advanced features work without any trouble. By using the PoE splitter kit (referenced above) you can easily make this a secure camera by avoiding the use of WiFi. Build quality is excellent - this is made to last and hold up even in severe conditions.

This is a product I would definitely recommend. While this is the first ENSTER camera I have reviewed I look forward to seeing other cameras they create. All indications point to this being a manufacturer that builds high quality security cameras that are dependable and made to last.

This case was recommended in several build guides, and seemed to be highly rated on Amazon, but I must say I'm quite disappointed.

Pros:
(1) It does the job. It's roomy -- in fact, it's really big. There's room for a really big graphics card without taking out any drive cages.
(2) Comes with four quiet fans (2 intakes in front, one large intake on the side, one exhaust on the back), and room to add more on the top.
(3) Having a couple of usb3 ports and audio/mike ports in the front is very convenient. Having the power supply at the bottom (in the back) also worked well for me.
(4) All the bits come apart and back together without too much trouble.

Cons:
(1) I had a lot of trouble getting my EVGA power supply to install, because the screw holes didn't line up nicely. Finally managed it by using a combination of power and adapting to what the case gave me.
(2) The 5.25 drive bays go in the conventional way, with the backs near the mobo for easy connections. But the 2.5/3.5 drive bays go in sideways, which might seem convenient at first, but now you have their connectors on the other side of the box -- so you're threading your power and sata cables around, and creating a bulge of cables etc. And that extra wiring room that the case promises? It doesn't extend all the way to the front, apparently the artists overcame the engineers (or they fought and the users lost). This arrangement also means that it's harder to share your sata power cables, depending on what you're trying to do with your setup.
(3) As others have pointed out, those nice intake fans aren't standard, they would be hard to replace individually. I'd have to replace all of them with standard case fans, I think.
(4) I wasn't as impressed with the cable management as many others were -- while it was useful to be able to run some wires on the back, that also made some of the shorter ones trickier to connect. Also, I find it easiest to place the box down on the side to work on the inside. Having to flip it over or keep it standing vertical wasn't my idea of convenience during assembly, and it made things really tricky when I wanted to add another hdd.

Neutral:
(1) An inexpensive mini-speaker (for POST beeps) would have been a good idea to include with the box.

All in all, I'm not unhappy enough to curse it, but I'm also far from recommending it. I'd look around more the next time, so 3* seems about right.

This is my review of the Opiheyoo Portable RGB Video Lights 3100mAh Rechargeable LED Camera Lights Mini. For a photo light the size of a thick cell phone, this little light is brighter than I expected and has useful features. First, you can use it while plugged in or if your battery is charged (and mine came fully charged), you can use it unplugged. And it's so portable!

If you use a lot of electronic gear, you'll probably find adjusting the various features very intuitive - I did. The dial for adjusting to colors is also the power button. Just push it in without turning it. You can adjust the color temperature with one of the dials, and you can adjust brightness with the third dial. All your settings show on a small screen that also shows your battery life. Since I'm tired of using a large, wired ring light for smaller items, this smaller light is great. And it's so portable!

The light has a tripod hole on a wide side and another on a narrow side. It fit my ball head and monopod without a problem. The light comes with a silicone soft box, a tripod adapter (I think that's what it is) and a charging cable/adapter.

A quick word about expectations. This light isn't going to replace my 4 500-watt photo floods on heavy duty stands. It's the size of a cell phone. But for close ups, fills for smaller subjects, macro photography and like that, I found it more than bright enough. I expect it would also be a good selfie light. For its size, it can be dialed up to be very bright.

One more thought. If you're one of those people who can see flicking in LEDs that other people can't see, you'll see the flickering here - I do. But it doesn't affect the pics at all.

I'm very happy with this light. It delivers everything I wanted - adjustable brightness, adjustable color temp, nice and bright, and it can be used plugged in if you forget to charge it. Add in the two tripod holes, and I'm very happy I chose the Opiheyoo Portable RGB Video Lights Mini . If anything changes, I'll update this review.

The response and feel. I'm going to continue gaming on it for a while to see if I become more adapted to it. It just feels different than what I'm used to. It most likely has to do with the key spacing more so than anything else.

This is definitely a nice keyboard and I recommend it. I will most likely continue to use it as my daily keyboard for a while longer to see how it holds up over time.

MY HISTORY WITH THIS PRODUCT:
I've owned this headset for almost a full year. Technically, I've had two of them, since the boom mic snapped off the first one and had it replaced. I use these every day, for multiple hours and a variety of uses (VoIP calls, gaming, music, and movies).

PROS:
The audio quality, when it is working, is good. The bass in 7.1 mode is great, and the overall surround sound is pretty convincing. They are comfortable and rechargeable via USB.

CONS:
The biggest problem here is the wireless connection. Both headsets I owned suffered from this same problem - they would frequently just restart or lose the signal and reconnect. The process takes about 3-5 seconds each time, and sometimes you get multiple restarts in a row. It doesn't sound too bad until it happens when you're watching a movie and you have to quickly pause or rewind a bit because you suddenly couldn't hear anything they were saying (which also completely pulls you out of the movie), or when it drops out in the middle of a phone conversation, or drops out at the worst possible moment in a game... It happens probably two dozen times a day, if not more. At first, I didn't care too much about it, but the first time you have it drop out 3 times in a matter of a single minute, it's simply maddening. Imagine going randomly deaf for several seconds throughout every day of your life, and you'll get a sense of what it's like.

If I could simply plug the cable in and it would use the USB cable to transmit the audio instead of wireless, that would be perfect, but when it's plugged in, it simply charges the internal battery - you still get audio interruptions all the time. The interruptions will also reset the "mute" status on the mic, which can be troublesome if you're intentionally muted on a conference call and suddenly your mic is on and people hear you eating lunch.

Second problem is that the power button is a bit flaky. If the headset is plugged in via USB and powered off, sometimes it will not power on unless you unplug the headset and THEN power it on (and then you can plug it back in to continue charging). I thought it was a defect in my first headset until the same thing happened with the second one.

A minor third problem is that the boom mic is a little flimsy on the construction. I am careful with my toys, but it still cracked and finally snapped off one day when I was lowering the mic to use it, and that was only a few months into owning it.

OVERALL:
If they would fix the wireless, I would rate this 4 stars in a heartbeat. If they fixed the power button, it would go up to 5. That said, the G35 seems to be the G930 but wired, and cheaper. The number of times that I've wanted to really make good use of the wireless (go to another room and keep the audio going) is far less frequent than the dozens upon dozens of times that the audio cuts out, so it's just an unacceptable point for me, since that is what this headset is about.

I waited almost six months to write this review because I wanted to "cool off" from my installation experience that would have caused me to rate this 3 stars. I am also now able to fairly assess this tablet after a few months' use.

I wanted a highly-rated unrestricted (open) tablet that provided great graphics and sufficient screen space. I purchased this to use on a Wi-Fi network only for when I didn't want to boot up my laptop to check mail or see a movie, etc. I also did not want an Apple tablet because my boyfriend has an iPad 3 and the Apple products have restrictions. I also was not impressed with the graphics on his iPad. I was considering a Kindle Fire HD 7" but that tablet was too restrictive as well and was geared to Amazon junkies. I am an Amazon junkie but I also do not like restrictions on products I purchase. During my July 2014 research, I discovered that the Nexus 7 tablet was the highest rated Android next to those more restrictive tablets.

After I received the Nexus, I wondered if I had made the right decision. First, I was surprised that this came with no documentation (other than the business card sized diagram of where all the ports were and a warranty and safety agreement in both English and French). The documentation didn't even say how long I needed to charge the unit. I charged it overnight and then had immense trouble getting this connected.

The router I was connecting to has MAC filtering enabled so I needed the MAC address. However, I couldn't get the MAC address without setting up the device. Also, I couldn't set it up because I couldn't get the MAC address. I could have fussed with the router and turned off MAC filtering/security temporarily but I had to get to work in the morning right after the unit completed charging. I then tried connecting via three other networks (my library for one, my work another, and another Wi-Fi connection). It still would not connect. Because I didn't want to wait until I got home 12 hours later to fuss with my router I wound up asking a tech support person where I work. He connected me via his personal MiFi mobile hotspot.

Apparently, Google Nexus only connects to certain networks if the first time setup has not been done. I tried several open networks. My co-worker's MiFi mobile network connection, although I suspect mine would have connected had I temporarily removed the security on my router, was the only one that would allow me to run the automatic setup so that I could connect. After setup was performed, I was able to get the MAC address from the settings "about" tab. I was also able to connect to the three other networks I tried previously and after inputting the MAC address, I could also connect to my router. It was apparently the initial setup process that prevented the connection.

This Google Nexus would have gotten five stars if they enhanced the user experience by:
1 - Providing a MAC address either on the unit or on a piece of paper for those that have MAC filtering enabled.
2 - Providing a documentation pamphlet with the unit that:
* Tells the user how long they need to charge the unit the first time.
* Explains to the user that setup cannot be run on all networks and sometimes they will get an error message. Therefore, they might say something like "using your own network is advisable" or provide an explanation of why certain networks (including totally open ones that allow all connections) would not work. Perhaps there is some sort of technical protocol that is not available on all networks; I have no idea.

Other than the above, I absolutely love my Google Nexus. I've been using this for almost 6 months and it has met my every expectation. It charges in less than four hours; lasts about 3 hours if I'm constantly using it; lasts about 3-4 days when I'm using it for about 10 minutes daily. I've used this for email, movies, web surfing, pictures, etc. App availability is unending (Kindle, LinkedIn, Battery Doctor, etc., etc.) I tested the screen image next to my co-workers Kindle Fire HD 7" and there is no discernible difference in quality or resolution. Images and movies on this device are superb. If I attach my [[ASIN:B00N4SIIFY APLWL USB 2.0 A to Micro B Cable 6FT-TPE jacket-Blue]] to my laptop, I can both charge the unit and also access files on it from my laptop such as the photos located under Nexus 7\Internal storage\DCIM\Camera directory (that's Computer\Nexus 7\Internal storage\DCIM\Camera in Explorer).

Overall this is a quality tablet that did not disappoint me once I got past the initial installation and lack of documentation headache. In the comments section of my review, I put links to Google documentation I found helpful as well as to the 2014 review I used for my research.

UPDATE Jan 6, 2015 - Right after I wrote this review I had a problem where my Nexus was shutting down automatically and every time I went to use it I had to power it back up. After doing an Internet search I was able to fix this by going to the Play Store app on the Nexus, then selecting "My Apps" and accepting all install updates. There were a few updates that had not installed and this was playing havoc with my system. After I did this, the Nexus remained powered up and has been working fine the last several days.

Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse is one of the better computer accessories I have used and it offers a noticeable improvement compared to traditional computer mice. Its unique shape makes it much more comfortable and a no- sliding- necessary design eliminates the need to drag your mouse across a flat surface to move the computer pointer on your screen. To move the pointer, all you do is move the large, red marble trackball. There is less strain on the fingers and wrist, making for a more comfortable experience.

Besides the added comfort, another advantage of the Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse is that it requires less space than a traditional mouse. Because this mouse is stationary and doesn't need to be dragged across a desk or other surface, it can fit into many small spaces. You don't need to make room to drag it, so it can be placed in tight quarters. This is great for those who work in offices with limited desk space.

The Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse offers four buttons to use for clicking. The large tabs on each side of the mouse are used for the usual right and left click functions and then there are two smaller tabs right above each of the larger tabs that are used for various functions. These two small tabs can be programmed to perform several things, and many will likely program them to scroll since this Logitech mouse doesn't have a scroll wheel. But the tabs can be programmed for other things, too. Since I don't necessarily need to scroll, my small tabs have been programmed as browser back and forward buttons. This makes life a little easier because I no longer need to move my mouse to the top of my screen and click the forward and backward arrows in the upper left corner. I just click my small left tab to go back and my small right tab to go forward.

The Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse is a marked improvement compared to the standard mouse, but I admit that it does take some getting used to. Having used a traditional mouse for most of my computer- using years, I had grown accustomed to sliding my mouse across the desk surface. Thus, when I started to use the Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse, I kept sliding it around on my desk also, even though I knew this mouse didn't need to be dragged. It took some time to break this habit. It also took time to get used to the sensitivity of the trackball. The slightest movement sends your pointer flying and when I first started to use this mouse, I would continually underestimate the precision of the Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse. A couple weeks ago I put a protector on a phone and they had a really great trick for positioning - which I used on this big thing, too. I don't think I could have gotten it exactly right had I not used this method: Before peeling any film, lay it where it needs to be and use scotch or masking tape (easily removable kind) to tape the long edge nearest the 'tab' to be pulled. (2 pieces positioned a couple inches from the ends should do it.) Then lift the film and start pulling the tab to remove the plastic a little bit at a time - with it up in the air a bit, adjust so it's straight (the tape keeps it aligned) and let the uncovered tabbed corner adhere to the screen. Slowly work your way diagonally pulling, adhering, and (I used a credit card) smoothing out. It just takes a bit of patience. I have zero air bubbles and just one tiny speck of dust I'd missed.

The [[ASIN:B00093GGMY Calumet Quickring Speedring]] folds in half and locks. I believe the Calumet ring will do the trick. Undo the lock and all the tension will relax. It's been forty years (!) since I first saw a video camera in high school, a big b/w camera with a backpack that contained the batteries and internals. It was impressive! Then we used a kind of mini-VHS video recorder to share kid videos with our parents maybe 15-20 years ago. Then I got an iPhone which had kind-of video capabilities. So I guess I was ripe to be blown away by this Sony FRAX53/B.

It's small and compact, like a small football. The swing-out screen is breathtakingly crisp and the internal operating system and menus are not only in color, but accompanied by clear, bright sound! I charged the battery and took a video of one of my cats. I could not believe the clarity of the image when I viewed it on the screen! The video is of such high quality that it's easy to overlook the still camera, which is remarkable. High-resolution, bright images. The "Photo" button is kind of oddly placed, it's not easy to operate it while you're holding the device with its right-side hand strap. You can also use a "Manual" mode and twist the lens to achieve custom focus. There's a 20X optical magnification which ought to satisfy anyone.

The Sony software is thorough and functional. The camcorder will transfer photos and video wirelessly if you have a fairly modern computer. I had to use a PC laptop rather than my elderly Mac. That meant using Windows 10, which led to some baffling moments trying to figure out if anything was working.

Between the Sony software and the camcorder and our WiFi setup and Windows 10 I found that the best thing to do sometimes was just WAIT. Windows would give me bad information and I would misinterpret that as an error. Ignore what Windows is telling you and be patient while the FDRAX53/B does its work.

The printed manual is basic and you'll want to spend time reviewing the online documentation. I'm still trying to figure out how to use the Sony FDRAX53/B and a "U-Stream" service to get a live stream going. There is a LOT of technology packed into this camcorder! Expect to spend some time reviewing it all. As I mentioned, Sony packed a TON of features in this device, and there's a learning curve to really understand and appreciate them all.

If you're planning a vacation or expecting a newborn child, BUY THIS CAMCORDER! You cannot take enough videos and photos of your kids when they're young, and the same goes for vacations -- this camcorder is small enough to tote with you (it does not like fog or water, though!) and the QUALITY of the images are incredible! It's not so heavy that it's going to be a burden.

The sound is very good, and there's a "gun" style microphone if you want to A) avoid wind noise B) capture audio of what you're shooting (like at a kid's soccer game) rather than local chitchat.

One thing that occurred to me while I was fiddling with the camcorder in my right hand, that being that if you were holding one of your kids in your left hand and the camcorder in your right hand and they both began to slip... which would you grab? This camcorder is THAT nice. Between the quality of the camcorder and its fantastic lens and the Sony software for image management and manipulation, this could be a major hobby in and of itself. You can easily edit, trim and combine videos with sound and add captions and text. For a consumer level product, the video and image editing suite is quite impressive. You will want a fairly modern computer, as I mentioned.

Something I come back to again and again as I figure the FDRAX53/B out is the absolute wonder of it. The small size, the quality of images, the ease of operation -- I just can't get over it. Beyond sensational and well into the realm of magical. I've never seen anything like the FDRAX53/B before.

If you've been using a "free" router provided by your ISP, this Linksys router will give you some interesting additional features not found in the freebies. A guest mode lets you create a separate network with a separate password and access to the internet, but not to other devices on your network. A USB port lets you connect a hard driver or printer that can be accessed by any device on your network. Parental controls let you limit access based on time of day or web address.

There are supposedly performance optimizations based on media prioritization and beam forming, but I have no way to test whether those actually work or not. I had no problems with connectivity and performance, though my home is not really large. Media prioritization supposedly allows you to give higher priority to selected devices on your network, which could be useful if for example you want to allocate a lot of bandwidth to streaming video and less to other uses.

Setup and configuration is always an issue with network devices. Make sure you access is using a generic DNS setup or you will confuse the setup process. Once I figured that out, the setup went smoothly. The setup makes you create a Linksys account to manage your router remotely. Network control is nice since you can login from anywhere to manipulate your router settings; but if someone hacks into the Linksys server, you could be in trouble. There is an option to disable network access in the settings.

The main issue I have with this device is that the configuration software is too simple. Simplicity is good for people with only basic computer skills, but it also leaves out a lot of things that more advanced uses will want to do. For example, the guest SSID is your main SSID with "-guest" appended; there is no way to create a custom SSID for guests. Also, the USB port sometimes work for me and sometimes not. Rebooting usually got it to work, but that is a big hassle. This is a cheap way to store music and videos on a central hard drive, then play them on any computer on your network.
