The build quality as well as the fit and finish of this amplifier board is better than most of the cheap TPA3116 bluetooth boards on eBay and AliExpress. When connected to decent speakers and a 24V switching power supply with sufficient current drive capability, the performance of this amplifier is quite impressive for its size.

Four potentiometers in the front, from left to right are: bass level, treble level, treble volume (volume for the two stereo channels) and overall volume. These pots, as well as the speaker outputs in the back are clearly labeled on the PCB. Tone and volume control circuit appears to use a couple of 072 opamps and an SGM358 opamp. These are not high-grade audio components, simply a low cost solution for a product in this price range. Except for the electrolytic capacitors, most components are SMD.

I tested this amp by connecting it to a pair of Sound Appeal 6.5" 2-way bookshelf speakers for the stereo channels. I did not have access to a passive subwoofer at the time, so I connected the subwoofer output to a 15" bass guitar amplifier speaker cabinet. I used a 24V 5A switching power supply. A 24V 5A power supply may not be sufficient if you are driving 4-ohm speakers and a 4-ohm or lower impedance subwoofer, but all three of the speakers I used were 8 ohms, so 120W of power input was sufficient. With the right speaker setup, the volume output of this set-up can get quite high, even in a big room. Partly due to the efficiency of the 15" bass speaker I was using, it was possible to achieve a quite impressive "thump". Distortion levels are not low at high volume levels, but having the subwoofer output on a separate TPA3116 chip makes it possible to keep somewhat reasonable distortion on stereo channels even when playing bass-heavy music.

Connecting to the bluetooth interface was easy and straight-forward. The amp remembers the previous bluetooth pairing after being powered down.

A few observations about the shortcomings of this amplifier:
- The heat sinks are quite small, and they don't have any mechanical support. Even when driving 8-ohm loads, the heat sinks get really warm at high volume levels. If you are driving 4-ohm speakers at high volume levels, thermal shut-down is possible. If you are using a 18V or lower power supply, you probably won't have any thermal issues.
- There is only a 1000uF 25V filter capacitor at the power input. 25V max rating is a bit too close for my comfort, I would have preferred a 35V capacitor. You really need a well regulated DC power supply to drive this board.
- Bluetooth has a built in antenna on the PCB, but no external antenna interface, making it impossible to mount this board inside a metal case without doing some surgery to the board.
- There are no line level inputs. Bluetooth is the only input option unless you are willing to do modifications on the PCB

Overall, for the current price of $26.99, this is a very nice bluetooth 2.1 amplifier. If you have a couple of decent bookshelf speakers and an old subwoofer lying around, the volume and quality of the sound you can achieve with this amp will be better than any integrated bluetooth system that sells for less than $100.

Update: I recently tested this amp with [[ASIN:B00NOA58RS Dayton Audio B652-AIR 6-1/2" Bookshelf Speaker Pair with AMT Tweeter]]. These speakers are 6-ohms, so it's possible to get a little power out of the amplifier, and especially the high frequencies sound noticeably better.

I am specifically using these to step up 3v to either 5v (for USB devices) or 12v (for a strip of LEDs). I've set up two so far, and they work pretty well. The pot is very sensitive, so that you can bump it up by tenths of a volt or less. The pads are pretty easy to solder to. The power delivery is relatively clean, I have some flicker on the LED strip, but that seems to resolve itself fairly rapidly - for sensitive applications you might want to run through a capacitor to clean things up a bit.

The unit is moderately efficient, but becomes quite warm - when converting from 2xAAA Lithium batteries (3v) to 12v, with an approximate draw of 200mA the converter (both the top of the transformer and bottom of the board) temps at about 116F within three minutes or so of operation. Pretty warm, warmer than I would typically like. I might try hooking up a 9v instead to see if this knocks the temps down a bit, or if that fails, adding a thermistor to mitigate the risk of a thermal event.

Would recommend for general experimentation though.

- you get two USB ports and one parallel port, making this both flexible and an added value if you plan to locate all of your printers in the same space. The added value stems from the fact that most single-port print servers are in the same price range, and almost all of them only support printers with parallel ports.
- it works in network environments based on Microsoft Windows, Netware, Macintosh, UNIX, or any combination, making it standards-compliant and open. I especially like the step-by-step instructions on the manufacturer's web site for integrating this device into Linux-based LANs. It can also be queried and managed via SNMP in an enterprise network.
I am less pleased with the supporting web site. Although it is rich in useful content and has up-to-date driver downloads, well written FAQs and a wealth of technical information for Linux and UNIX users, the pages do not display properly in Netscape 4x. Considering the excellent UNIX and Linux support for the product and in the FAQs this was a surprise since most of those users will be using Netscape 4x as their browser. This is more of an inconvenience than a problem however.
Overall, this is one of those rare products that does exactly what the manufacturer claims it will do, and it works flawlessly.

I bought this cover and the Zing Pro Zoom cover. I like the Op Tech D Pro Zoom better.
Pros:
It was easier to get on and off my camera then the Zing.
It fits my camera and accessories nicely.

Cons:
To securely close the cover, there is a flap that has 2 snaps. You wrap the cover around the back of the camera, and snap the flap closed with the 2 snaps. I'm not a fan of snaps. These were easy to snap closed, but Velcro would have been much easier.
There is a strap attached to the inside of the cover. It came with 2 ways of attaching the cover to your camera so you don't lose the cover:
1. a piece of leather that attaches to the camera by screwing it into the tripod mount. This piece attaches to the strap with a snap. I could see either end of the leather coming apart - the side with screw could detach or the snap could release.
2. A ring that can go around the lens. This ring attaches to the strap with a snap. I don't like having things attached to my lens and the snap could release.
I came up with my own method of securing the cover to my camera. The bottom of my battery grip has a connection point for a strap. I had an extra set of Op Tech Uni Loop connectors (https://www.amazon.com/OP-TECH-USA-1301062-Uni-Loop/dp/B0010HA6A6/ref=sr_1_1?ie=UTF8&qid=1485137755&sr=8-1&keywords=optech+uni+loop).
I attached one end to the bottom of the battery grip. I attached the other connector to the strap by looping the strap thru the connector loop and snapping the two snaps on the strap together. Using the uni loop connectors, I clicked the two pieces together. I think the weakest point is where the snaps are attached. I'm going to sew a few stitches next to the strap as a precaution in case the snaps come undone. You can use any type of strap to secure the cover to the camera. I also attached a photo using an extra camera strap from one of my point and shoot cameras. If I used this method, I would still sew a few stitches next to the snap. I like the uni loop method. If the cover gets in the way, I can just disconnect the uni loop clips.
I'm happy with this cover even though I'm using a different method of attaching the cover to my camera. I dropped the rating to a 4 because of the use of the snaps.

Even though I have always had an interest in astronomy I was never able to work a course in this subject in my college schedule or afterwards. When I saw this telescope offered I realized that now I had both the time and the means to explore my interest a bit further. I had very little difficulty setting the scope up, and spent some time familiarizing myself with the various components. I practiced using this by checking out objects in my neighborhood, and managed to get an 'up close and personal' view of some birds in a neighbor's yard and quickly realized that this scope was powerful.

That evening I took the scope to an upstairs window to see what I could see, and despite the pesky street light was able to get a great view of the full moon (btw did you know that it sparkles a bit?). I saw details that I had only seen in photos before which was fascinating. Then I decided to take a look at Mars, which was near the Moon that evening. That is when things got complicated. The finder scope and the main scope need to be synced, and I don't know how to do this (yet). With some fiddling, and aided by Mars' close proximity to the Moon I was able to find Mars, which was exciting but for some reason it was distorted (it had a starburst appearance). My husband and I fiddled with various lenses and combinations to try to eliminate this but were unsuccessful. The experimentation was further complicated by the touchiness of the stand....it was difficult to make small, smooth adjustments and to keep the scope locked in position. Some of this is no doubt due to our in expertise, some I think is due to the equipment.

My enjoyment of this scope would have been much greater if more instructions had been provided. We discovered, more or less by accident how to lock, at least partially, the scope into place. We managed to make some focusing adjustments by trial and error. Even some rudimentary instructions in a small booklet or even a sheet or two describing how to adjust, focus and lock the scope as well as an illustration of the scope with all the components clearly labeled with a brief description of their function would have been greatly appreciated. This is a basic instrument, one that will primarily be used by beginners or novices who will not necessarily be familiar with this equipment. Basic instructions should have been included. As it is my unfamiliarity with the various aspects of the telescope make following many of the instructions I do find on-line difficult to follow.

Despite this problems I am enjoying my new toy. I found the stand to be steady, and the tray located on the stand to be a handy place to put lenses and covers. As I mentioned earlier this is a surprisingly (at least to this beginning user) powerful scope. I'm going to play around with this some more, and will probably upgrade some of the lenses and add some accessories based on my experiences. Besides star gazing I think this will be a great item to watch birds or wild life, and it is certainly portable and forgiving enough to take on a camping trip.

  9.) The SSD is nothing too special. While yes, any SSD is faster than not-an-SSD, this is on the lower end of the spectrum in terms of NVMe performance.

Overall, I really enjoy the Surface Laptop 4, but it’s not hard to see where Microsoft could make some massive improvements and solidify the Surface line as THE Windows 10 systems to buy.

Slept two nights with these headphones in their stock configuration and decided I could create something far superior.
For several years I’ve owned and extensively used a pair of the original wired SleepPhones. They are extremely comfortable. The drivers are only 2-3mm thick and sandwiched between two layers of felt. The fleece headband stayed in place without feeling constrictive. It was also easy to wash - open the hook and loop closure on the back, pulled out the speakers and wires, wash, dry, re-install.
By contrast, MusiCozy uses thicker drivers (granted, the frequency response is better than the SleepPhone drivers) then adds a rubber cover, then covers that with a thin jersey fabric. The headband was painfully tight, and I don’t have a big head (22.5”). After the first night, I stretched the headband over a small throw pillow for a day and that helped a bit. But the second night, the thick drivers hurt my ears so bad I took the whole thing off. I mostly sleep on my side and stomach. It’s also tricky to charge because the port is only accessible if you line up the slit in the jersey fabric just right. Some simple product testing would have identified these issues. But for $20, I couldn’t be happier….. why?
SleepPhoness wants $100 for their bluetooth units. I’m sure they are top-notch but I didn’t want to spend that much. Here’s my solutions: The entire MuziCozy headband was disassembled….all two components. The bluetooth receiver / battery compartment and speakers come out easily enough. The fake ‘control panel’ on the front isn’t needed. The speakers have a rubber cover that is not needed. Once that is removed, the speakers are only 3-4mm thick, which is good. I disassembled the wired SleepPhones as well. The felt driver covers were re-used with the MuziCozy drivers, then the whole thing was re-installed into the SleepPhone headband.
This is the best setup - the headband is comfortable, I can still use it to cover my eyes, the sound quality is improved, and the MuziCozy charge port is easier to access thanks to the large velcro opening on the back of the headband.
My girlfriend, by contrast, likes absolute silence while sleeping so she uses the MuziCozy headband to make sure her earplugs don’t fall out and to cover her eyes.
So the entire unit has gone to good use, just not in the way it was delivered. I’m happy with the results but the original product need some redesign.

I do a LOT of work in front of a computer, and was getting these for when I work at home. At work, I use a Logitech 930 headset that I really like. I got these so I wouldn't yank my laptop off the desk when I get up. I got bluetooth, thinking they'd be easy to sync to my various devices. So, here's my breakdown:

Range
I can go upstairs and grab a few things or go two rooms away and I still get a signal. The range is pretty good on these.

Playback Sound
The playback sound quality is okay. Not blowing me away, but alright. I listen to music, no vocals, to block out the office noise and keep my head focused. The playback audio goes into tin-can mode when the mic is enabled. That's something I didn't realize as a limitation of how bluetooth handles the two signals. That took me a while to figure out.

Microphone
The mic is okay. It just flips me out that the playback goes into "phone mode" when the mic is enabled.

Battery
Well, I've only had these a couple of months. But, the battery seems to go at least as long as I can stand to keep them on my head. Max has been about 2 hours at a stretch before giving my head/ears a break.

Fit
I'm an adult and my head is average-sized, not large. After maybe three months these cans are still a bit tight. The cups don't quite fit entirely over my ears and get uncomfortable after maybe two hours --like, *ouch* uncomfortable.

Heat
These cans get pretty hot after maybe 45 minutes. Hot like I just got out of the shower and I need a towel in my ears hot. I don't think I've ever had sweaty ears like this before from a set of headphones.

Sync
I've easily sync'd these to Ubuntu 14.04 & 10, Windows 7, and OS X Mavericks.

Would I recommend these to a friend?
No. I like not having to carry a dongle around since bluetooth is in all of my computers (one has an $8 dongle that works just fine.) But, they get so hot, and are still not comfortable on my head and ears after maybe 100 hours of use. So, for the $50 price tag, I'd probably have to say no. If they were $25 and just to make the occasional phone call I might recommend them to a friend, but not to wear for any period of time. If they were just a bit more comfortable, and breathed a bit better, I'd change my mind. Maybe in the next revision, Photive?

PROS

1. Its microphone works well.
2. It has a camera cover for privacy, and the camera produces a good picture.
3. Its noise canceling feature works well.
4. Its firmware worked well to connect the microphone to my desktop.
5. I was able to make it work for Zoom calls with my grandchildren.

CONS

1. It took quite a bit of practice for me to get this equipment to work properly.

I have also bought the RF-62 II (floor standing speakers) that match this one, the first thing I noticed was everything sounded natural. I have owned Klipsch for over 10-11 years and felt it was time to upgrade. The other thing I noticed was extreme clarity with natural sound. I was surprised since I had some doubts they could improve on my Reference Center 3. Beyond clarity, the highs seem more balanced with everything blending in perfectly with the rest of the sound.

Now, keep in mind my old Klipsch set everyone praised it till no end. When I upgraded everyone (father, friends and neighbors) noticed the sound was natural and not overly expressive. What I mean by overly expressive is "bright sound", this is not a negative since Klipsch speakers are designed to be efficient. But the Reference 62 II lines seem to have been fine tuned and the sound outputs its tone more natural and pleasing to the ears while being dynamic. It truly is an upgrade.

For those of you unfamiliar with klipsch, don't be afraid, they have been around for 65 years and dominate the Mars amphitheater market and movie cinemas. I am 29 years old, and ran into the reference line when they first came out in 1999 (15 years old) and was blown away. I did not make the purchase till 2002 and have been a fan of Klipsch since than. My side hobby is audio and have worked the audio video field threw college and I have Klipsch to thank for catching my interest. it surprises me many are hooked on Sony speakers or speakers they sell in regular stores like Bestbuy, Walmart etc etc (excluding Magnolia high fi). The Reference line is NOT the one in your local Bestbuy. Those are the Synergy line.

Every other speaker sounds like pillows are blocking the sound. lol. I have had friends say that same line to me a few times. The sound is very different from other speakers. The best way to describe it is concert or open field type of sound. I even thought about switching speaker manufacturer. After spending a month listing to other brands. -None- came close. The clarity of the Klipsch speaker design is enough to make you stay.

The upgrades like the magnetic grills are a plus. You no longer have to worry about the plastic stubs breaking off or them sticking. Everything looks more uniformed as in constant; unvarying; undeviating. I also like the speaker design. The copper color on the speaker and design make them stand out instantly with a modern look that is not overly visual. Just enough to catch everyones attention. They look beautiful with grills on or off. Even minor touches like Klipsch logo on top of the grill and etched Reference line at the bottom of the grill are well done.

Note: I am running a high end amplifier with all matching Reference 62 II lines (soon getting my matching back speakers). I have manually calibrated my system, but have everything set to reference level and occasionally pump up the level of my front and center to +3. (reference level is 0. the starting point). You can tell a good speaker when you don't have to alter anything like equalizer or increase speaker levels. Those of you using Audyssey or any type of microphone for calibration you may want to experiment manual calibration since the mics sometimes are inaccurate, or may calibrate your speakers to low or to high. This may be why some reviewers get low volume sound or to loud.

You have to take into consideration that your amplifier, setup, speaker position etc all play a key role in everything.

I wanted to find a cheaper alternative to my wife's wireless Bose headset, something with decent noise cancelling for flights and work. So far I've used Bose, the MPOW H5, Treblab, and Woltix with ANC.

Nothing will compare to Bose noise cancellation - but these Woltix are actually really nice for the money. The MPOW H5 don't have as good audio clarity as the Treblab, but at the end of the day I got noise cancelling headphones for the noise canceling. I ended up returning the Treblab and the MPOW H5 and I kept the Woltix because they are more comfortable than the MPOW and had the best low-price ANC. The MPOW also had some sound interference issues randomly when the ANC was on, and the Treblab had a slight hiss to them when ANC was on.

I ended up keeping the Woltix brand. They just work, they're very light, and they are not too tight on the ears. The Active Noise Cancellation isn't as good as Bose, but they actually work pretty well for a $65 set of wireless ANC headphones. For the price, I'm very happy.

The ONLY thing I don't like about these is that there is no battery meter display on my iPhone when these are connected via bluetooth. With the other brands there is a small battery meter. I have no idea when these are low, so I just charge them like once a week.

So, quick breakdown of my experience with these wireless ANC headsets:

Bose: Best noise cancellation, good audio, comfortable, but definitely expensive!
Treblab: Best audio, worst noise cancellation (you can hear a slight hiss when turned on), comfortable, but large and they don't fold down too small.
MPOW: Good audio, good noise cancellation, but was getting some weird sound interference with the ANC on sometimes. Tight on ears.
Woltix: Good audio, good noise cancellation, most comfortable (way lighter and less tight on the ears than the MPOW), and fold down the smallest. No battery meter displayed on phone.

So, let me start off by saying, this isn't the best quality webcam on the market. But for the price, no one is expecting it to be. And it is FAR from the worst! During the Covid Pandemic, all the regular brand name webcams were sold out so I found myself trying out a bunch of these no-name brands from Amazon. The last one I tried actually had a much harsher fisheye effect in the corners, as well as over-saturated color. This one seems far less cartoony and more realistic in color reproduction, as well as being somewhat more rectilinear (photo speak for straight lines being straight, not as much curved distortion). There is a bit of fisheye curve on the edges, but it is very usable and didn't make my ceiling look concave like my last one I tried. See attached images for examples of the room's wall distortion. It's there if you are looking for it, but not terrible when you're looking at a subject. The microphone is just meh. I have a desktop mic and the sound out of that was MUCH better, especially because you can get it closer to your face than the camera. But the fact that this HAS a mic is a good option in a pinch. I would just strongly recommend an external mic if you want people to hear you clearly. Also something I didn't know before trying this:
It is MANUAL focus! That means it won't follow and focus on you automatically, you have to twist the lens until you're sharp in the view. It actually isn't that hard to nail focus, the depth of focus is pretty deep so once you've set it for your standard sitting distance, you likely won't have to change it ever again unless you walk away from the camera. A fun side effect, however is that the focus lens gear lets you push it to EXTREME MACRO distances! So you can do insane closeups of things if you want to, for example, put a webcam on an ant farm maybe? I tried it out on my desktop speaker, and in one picture you can see the relative size of it compared to my desk and then the closeup you can see the detail of the scratched plastic where it says Harmon / Kardon. Ha, if nothing else this shows me I should probably get new desktop speakers too! These are beat up when up close! A fun and versatile camera for a good price. If you need autofocus tracking, this might not be for you though.

[[VIDEOID:1be91bfc02339bd396543d05da1fee38]] There are SO many things about the Angel's Horn turntable that impress me. But, first, you need to be a true audiophile to appreciate the way this turntable was designed and built.

Gone are the days of the automatic turntable, where you just drop on a stack of records and walk away. Those things were the WORST! Sure, you were free to do other things for longer periods of time. But, they were very harmful to your records. A true collector would NOT even consider having one of those things.

First, the body of the turntable is ONE SOLID PIECE OF OAK! No particle board, no hollow box, no cheap crap!

Then, there is the direct one-belt drive, no multiple gears or belts. And the motor has ONE job, the turntable. Changing the records and setting the tonearm are YOUR job, as is true with any turntable worth it's status as 'top of the line' with this one.

Now, the tonearm is another factor. As we all know, too much pressure on the record (or too little) can affect the quality of the sound, not to mention the wear on the vinyl. And, vinyl is a fragile medium, revered as one of the best sources of true stereophonic sound. We vinyl fans collect the best recordings and do everything we can to preserve that quality. When we play our records, we do so with love and care. The tonearm on this turntable is built just for us. It's counterweight is perfect, allowing us to adjust the balance to a microgram. I've not found a tonearm with a more accurate adjustment as this one.

The ability to switch between input types is a nice feature. Some of us prefer to provide our own preamps, allowing us further tweaking of the sound quality. I do. Thank you.

The dust cover is great for those that have their turntable out on top. I have mine contained within my entertainment center and opted to leave it off.

I am VERY happy with my Angel's Horn turntable and very happy to give it five stars.

I have had the opportunity to review many headsets and headphones over the years and without question the recent technological advancements have aided this area by leaps and bounds.

I can not recommend buying Bluetooth 5.2 enough over previous technologies if your devices support it. Nearly all devices that are Bluetooth 5.2 capable, including this one, will be backwards compatible with earlier technologies as well.

Battery life is outstanding with these headsets lasting a solid 5 hours each in all of my tests. It is easily charged using the included charging case which will allow the earbuds to be recharged several times from its one full charge. Since the earbuds can be used together for stereo sound or individually you can potentially double play time by using one at a time.

This unique charging case is powered via an included super fast standard USB to USB Type C cable. This case will allow the headsets to be recharged even when you don’t have access to electricity.

After receiving, I made sure the case was fully charged then confirmed each earbud had a full charge. After verifying full power within each earbud I followed the simple pairing instructions and had no problems whatsoever. Once the earbuds are removed from the case they first pair with each other then you simply pair with your Bluetooth device.

The design of these headset makes it so it fits securely in your ear and is relatively comfortable. As someone who has used many of these units, this design is not the most comfortable as the weight is all on the ear canal. I’ve found headsets that are worn only supported by the ear canal can end up being painful when used for extended periods.

The sound from these headphones is decent - from the rich bass notes to the vibrant midtones to the bright treble. I tested these headphones with a wide range of audio - from audiobooks to jazz, heavy metal, country, classical and blues - everything sounded reasonable.

I have listened to both music and audiobooks through these as I moved throughout my home and it will easily pick up the signal through walls up to 25’ away, and even more without obstacles. This is a decent set Bluetooth headphones.

While these are great for listening to music, how are they for calling? The sound through these headphones is absolutely outstanding - on both ends. That is not always the case. Many of the other headphones I have tested, while they sound good to the person using it - those who they are speaking to can’t hear them clearly. It is no fun having a conversation where the other person keeps saying, “huh, what did you say?” You won’t have to worry about that with this set.

If you are looking for a decent headphone set, especially one at a reasonable price, with decent sound and reception and has the power to last this is a great choice.

The main feature we wanted from this was to pull the photos from our iPhone without having to sync all the time. Sometimes our phone gets filled so quickly with photos and videos that we can't take any more and we're not near our syncing computer. That's where this comes in handy.

In order to use it fully, you have to download the compatible app (which is free), connect the device, and let the app and device access your photos, contacts, and calendar. We have a few microSD cards lying around, and so far our brands (Kensington and SanDisk) worked fine, even though the packaging is adamant in having you buy their brand of cards. ;)

The app itself is pretty easy to use, but I'd rather have the main syncing buttons appear on the first page. When you open it up the app is split into three "pages" that you can swipe through to select. At the top are icons to select the app and card memory (though I'm not sure why you'd back up the phone to the app over the card), and then at the bottom you get features to sync to other apps. Those aren't why we got this product, so when you swipe right you get the buttons to sync the photos, contacts, and calendar. You can sync selected ones or sync them all to the card. We usually just select all, even if we know only pictures and videos have been added since the last sync; we just like to be cautious.
Syncing takes only a few minutes. To confirm that all the photos and videos have been synced, I removed the memory card and plugged it in to both my computer and an Android device. I was able to navigate the folders in the card without issue (that is, no restrictions as I thought there might've been since it was an Apple's synced history going into Windows and Google machines) and see all the photos, etc. You can also navigate the folders via the device in the iPhone, but the thumbnails sometimes take a while to load.
Initially I didn't think the videos were backed up, but that's because they didn't have that little play icon on them as other videos usually do. When I scoured carefully through the dates, however, I found them all, and no noticeable resolution loss. Perfect!

So far this is exactly what we wanted and it works just fine.

If you're like me, you've done some research (extensively in my case) on comparing these two speakers, and have probably come out with a vague case for each of them. Some prefer the Miccas, some prefer the Pioneers. I decided to order both and find out what the deal is for myself. And although I haven't ordered many speakers, I've been a headphone enthusiast for many years.

FYI, I'm using these with a sub (Dayton 1200), so I can't comment on their performance by themselves.

The Miccas sound pretty good, with clear highs - solid performers for movies. But they never made me very impressed by their sound. They seem serviceable, good for the price but not particularly great. They are by no means a bad speaker, but they are a bit thin sounding, kind of one-note.

With the Miccas, if felt like I was listening to music, but with the Pioneers, I felt like I was feeling it. They have a lush tone that is very musical, and I noticed I was bobbing my head to some songs I wasn't before. Better dynamics, soundstage - they really allow you to get lost in the music. Even though the driver size is the same, everything sounds bigger, with more depth.

And even though they have less treble energy than the MB42X, they seem to retrieve a bit more detail. Certainly not "veiled", just darker in tone. I'd prefer there to be slightly less treble than too much - just make sure to remove the grill, as it can make them slightly too dark.

For $20 extra bucks currently I think it's a no-brainer to get the Pioneers, unless you can't particularly stand speakers on the warmer side. I have the center channel coming in today - I've heard mixed reports on it, but if it's anything like the bookshelves I'm sure I'll be satisfied.

I got my Kindle Fire HD for Christmas and ordered this case because I wanted a keyboard and the price seemed right. There are some annoyances that I listed under Cons, but to me they're not dealbreakers. I am happy with this case and really like having a keyboard with the Kindle.

Pros:
The case securely holds the Kindle. I definitely feel better about letting my kids play games on the Kindle while it's in this case than when it's not protected.

I like the look of the case overall. The stitching is sturdy and the leather is nice. It's like a little dayplanner when it's folded up. (I kinda wish it came in a solid color though. All black or all white or all red would look better to me than highlighting the closure in a second color, but that's just my personal opinion.)

I love how light the keyboard is and how it can "clip" on and off magnetically.

It was super easy to set up even though the directions were written like they were translated into English from a foreign language.

I thought the little red flap at the base would get in the way of typing but it really doesn't. It can fold underneath or just be held down with my wrists without any discomfort.

Cons:
I am not sure how to tell when the keyboard needs to be charged other than to plug it in whenever I remember. A red light appears while it's charging then goes away, so I assume it's ready at that point. I haven't used it enough for it to wear out completely, but I wish there was a way to tell how much charge it has left since I use the keyboard here and there and don't want to charge it all the time, especially if it doesn't need it. (But I also don't want it running out on me.)

The keyboard is small and I haven't gotten used to it yet. One example is that the apostraphe is made by hitting Fn+L, and I keep forgetting that then hitting all kinds of wrong buttons trying to backspace and fix it. This is frustrating because I can type 108 wpm on a standard sized QWERTY keyboard without many mistakes. I think this will just take some getting used to due to its small buttons/size. The keyboard is in great shape though, and I haven't had any sticking or falling off keys like some other reviewers have mentioned.

The Kindle seems to take a while to recognize the keyboard each time. It gets a little annoying when I just wanted to type something quickly and be done. (I am still unclear if I am supposed to go into my Wireless/Bluetooth settings each time I turn on the keyboard or if it will in fact recognize the keyboard eventually if I just wait. I usually lose patience and open up the settings.)

In order to charge the Kindle, I have to either take it out all the way or lay the case flat and open the bottom velcro flap. So it can't really be used with the keyboard while it's charging.

The case doesn't really work vertically. If you fold it in half, the keyboard gets in the way and needs to be removed. And it doesn't stand up vertically on its own.

[[VIDEOID:f53c751d61201ca1c677033815f33f9d]] 1. Appearance:

Yay: Sleek, smooth, shiny glossy black finish; trim and slim
Nay: Fingerprints!!!

2. Weight:

Yay: Only 3.3 ounces

3. Responsiveness:

Yay: The buttons are touch sensitive, and they light up. It's a lot easier to start and stop filming, view and delete videos than the earlier model.

4. Specs:

Yay: 60 minutes recording time; HD-Quality video; 4GB memory

Yay: Charges using a USB port. On-screen battery indicator tells you when it needs charging. Charges while you're uploading the day's footage to the computer. Does not use regular batteries or require a separate charger.
Nay: You'll have to make sure it's charged before you leave home if you're not toting your laptop. No chargee, no filmee.

6. Charging:

Yay: Easy if you're using a laptop. The USB arm flips up by sliding a button. The arm is at the top of the camera, so it's lying in a horizontal position when connected to the laptop.
Nay: Not easy if you're using a desktop, particularly when you already have the receiver for your [[ASIN:B001DJ9GOS Logitech Cordless Desktop Wave Pro (920-000919)]] plugged in. I tried using a USB extension cable, but got a message on the display that said it was too hot and had stopped charging.

7. Uploading:

Yay: Just connect to your computer

8. Making movies:

Yay: All your clips are displayed on the computer screen, and you can edit them to select just the parts you need for your movie. Dragging and dropping puts the chosen clips together for final editing. There's a choice of 7 tunes you can use for your videos, or you can select your own. You can upload straight to the internet.
Big Yay: You can fiddle with the background sound, making your added music softer or louder, or taking out the background sound altogether. This is very useful in situations where a perfectly good shot is ruined by the sound of Aunt Bertha's burp, Uncle Fester's fart or Clint's curse word. You can also use this tool to make yourself sound like P!nk, Pharrell or Pavarotti on your next karaoke video.
Nay: You can't use the same video clip twice in one movie. You can't change the fonts for the title or add subtitles. The software doesn't offer a choice of movie styles like the older version. (The attached video is a combination of a Flip movie and a Windows Movie Maker project)

9. Misc yays and nays

Comes with lightweight soft cloth case that's pretty good at rubbing off fingerprints and stuff

Doesn't work well in low light situations

Zoom is limited

Not good with close-ups, especially graphics. Don't bother trying to film the fine print or even the logo of that new widget that you're thinking of buying - you won't be able to read it when you get home.

If you have shaky hands you'll need a tripod.

Conclusion:

This is an excellent camcorder for recording memories and capturing embarrassing moments. Totally idiot-proof, amazingly lean and light, and completely portable, you can easily film, save and store your directorial triumphs, or share them on the web.

It does have a few limitations, but most of them can be worked around.

I am so very pleased with these headphones. I was expecting them to sound pretty good given the Sennheiser lineage, but they really set me back on my heels with the sound quality, comfort, and overall design.

Let's start with the easy one - how they look. To my eye, they are very nicely styled. Classic-looking rather than flashy. I especially like how the headband is not excessively padded -- it does not stick out when you wear them. Very elegant overall. Everything looks and feels high quality.

They also hit the mark regarding comfort. I usually have a 1 hour limit when it comes to over-the-ear headphones, in that after an hour of wearing them I've reached my limit of tolerance. These, however, felt wonderful. They are light enough that I hardly noticed the weight. More importantly, the ear cups fit me just right. Cushy enough to seal out ambient noise but not at the expense of having my ears feel like they were trapped in a vice. They felt just as good well into hour 2 as they did in the first 15 minutes. I found the headband also very comfortable for long stretches without getting "sweaty head" as I get with other headphones.

But it's the sound that counts. To my ear, these `phones deliver in spades. I started off with some Stanley Clarke. Wonderful -- ample bass but not at the expense of hearing every string being plucked. I listened to School Days a couple of times in a row, just amazed at how good it sounded. The same for Florence and the Machine -- solid, deep bass but not overwhelming.

Next up was Metric to see how vocals come through. Again, superb. I was finally able to figure out some of the lyrics on Synthetica that never came through clear enough on my ear buds. Regina Spektor was also an absolute pleasure to listen to and have all facets of her unique vocal styling come through so clearly.

I also tried them for movie watching on my Fire, and again was very pleased. Dialog was clean and pronounced; explosions were, well, explosive.

The noise isolation is quite good. These are not noise cancelling headphones, so some ambient noise will leak in, but it keeps out everything other than the most significant ambient sounds.

I really can't fault these on any criterion. They look great, feel great, and sound great. Granted, the price is not so great, but good quality costs. If you're a demanding headphone user, these are worth the money charged. Highly recommend.

I got excited to see one of these small portable LED style ones that actually had a decent native resolution (most of them can accept 1080p, but are in reality only 800x600 resolution, or sometimes worse... 640x480!). This one is actually capable of displaying 720p of real dot resolution, which should make it at least as sharp as my Viewsonic and other traditional HD projectors. Ok, perhaps I'm spoiled, but I'm comparing this to our Viewsonic 720p projector that, to be fair cost me 3-4x as much.
And for the most part, it DOES work, however there are some caveats to its use. First of all, it doesn't seem as sharp as my 720p projector, even though it should have the requisite amount of dots. It's OK, its definitely better than the cheap 600p projectors, but something just isn't quite there when comparing side by side. It also doesn't get all that bright, but I suppose that's expected from the LED tech being used. You'll need black out shades or use it only during the night. Then there's the color- it isn't great. It works, but it has a cheap color reproduction that looks kind of flat and lifeless. Dark scenes sort of all blend together and become nearly impossible to see. It lacks the vibrancy of even an inexpensive television from decades ago. It gets the job done, but hardly the "theater experience" if you've been waiting to see that latest action/vfx film the way it was intended. It will look better on your TV at home, the only thing this has going for it is the large projection experience. For example, if you just want to give your kids a backyard movie night and don't care that the color and detail won't be as great as your indoor system, it will do the job on the cheap. I personally would not give up my mid-range projector for this one.
One thing that I found particularly annoying is that rather than the optical zoom and focus dials found on usual projectors, there is only a focus and tilt dial. No zoom. That means you have to physically move the projector closer or further to get it to reach the correct size you are shooting for. That actually got in the way of using it in a couple of specific places my other projectors can be used at optimal sizes.
That's not to say it gets everything wrong- I DO like that it is small and light and can even be turned on it's back to aim at the ceiling. That's something my big projector can't do, due to the airflow and cable management sticking out the rear. It also has a standard 1/4" 20 threaded tripod mounting point, so you can place this onto a tripod and get maximum mounting freedom. That will come in handy as I've always wanted to watch a movie in bed on the ceiling. But otherwise, don't think this projector will be as good as the other mid-rangers out there. This is still very much a low end projector. You'll have to spend at least 2-3x as much to get a decent home theater style experience, and much more if you want a high end one that will handle FHD/4k to get the real deal. This is more of a specialty use item.

Long story short, my review sample was immediately recognized by my Samsung Galaxy Note 3 phone when I plugged the dongle into one of the ports on my [[ASIN:B00KMKKJWW Unitek USB 3.0 hub 4 port Bus-Powered OTG hub]]. It was also immediately recognized and functional on my ThinkPad T61 running XP.

Other reviewers will probably cover the wi-fi setup, but I got this for another reason. I hate wi-fi because it can be slow, too many things can interfere with the signal (such as microwaves) and there is always a security concern. In addition to being a wi-fi extender, this works great for extending the range of your router's wired connections, which is how I am using it. There are two parts to this; one is the sending end, which you plug into your router via included ethernet cable and then into an electrical outlet. The receiving end of this has 3 ethernet ports and you can connect up to 3 devices by ethernet cable. If you use it this way, there is no setup at all. It truly is plug and play and worked immediately for me. The setup sheet doesn't make it clear that it can function this way, but there is a picture on the box showing it. Also, I was very pleased with the fact that both pieces included a pass-through outlet, which is a great feature. It would seem that this would keep you from losing an outlet. Maybe and maybe not. Here's why. Both pieces are quite long. If you plug them into the top outlet of a typical 2 part outlet, the devices will cover the second outlet. So just plug them into the bottom outlet, right?; then the top outlet is free. Maybe. The problem is that the devices are just a little too tall and you cannot fit a 3-prong gounded plug above them. You can use a 2-pronged plug and it will mostly likely fit. You would think someone would have tested this when they designed the product. It's that slight design flaw that caused me to knock one star off my rating. Other extenders of this type that I have seen are small enough to fit with another 3-prong cord above them when plugged in to the bottom of a 2-part outlet.

If you have a large house, it is possible you might have more than one main electrical circuit running through your house. This only works if you plug both devices into the same master circuit. Of course that is not the fault of the device; that will be true of any range extender of this type.

These power plug range extenders have been on the market for a while, but nice someone finally decided to include a pass-through outlet, but too bad that the device isn't just a little smaller so that it doesn't partially block the second plug in a 2-plug outlet when plugged in at the bottom. Note these do need to be plugged directly into a wall outlet; can't be used off a power strip. That could be an issue if you are short of outlets, as I am.

The connection speed wasn't quite as good as I expected, but it is adequate. The units heated up a little, which I didn't like, but not uncomfortable to the touch. I also have experience with standalone extenders that don't use the powerlines in your home; they work just about as well and some of them also have ethernet ports; the only difference being that you are going Wi-Fi to the extender and then going back to ethernet if you want to use a cable, whereas with a powerline extender, you are going through wires all the way. Those standalone extenders only require one outlet too.

I have used other TP-Link products and generally they seem to be of good quality, so I don't hesitate in any way to use their brand. Made in China, which is common for electronics products.

I'm on my second One and it is a vast improvement over the former models. The design is wonderful; it looks like a gem. The two older models were designed in a hairpin shape & served as the clip. The flaw in the design was that the repeated stress on the curve from attaching & detaching it to clothing caused the curved end to crack. The One's design is slim, polished, and elegant. It slips easily into a silicone, non allergenic holder which has a built in clip for attaching to clothing. The sleep band is also improved. The unit slips into a pocket & the band itself is far more comfortable & easier to don.

The prior models required a charging base. The One charges on a simple design USB charger. This let's me charge just about anywhere; my laptop, PC, a USB wall adaptor, even my car stereo. However, the battery life is unbelievable & charging isn't a real issue & when it does need it, it is completed pretty quickly. The Bluetooth sync is wonderful. With former models, the sync took place while on the charging base. The One comes with a small USB dongle so that whenever my One is within range, it syncs automatically to the FitBit Dashboard (free, BTW); no need to remove the unit from my clothing. ALSO, with a BT smartphone (I have the Galaxy S3), I can sync via bluetooth through my phone app.

The feature set has improved. Not only does it track my steps (and distance), it also tracks my sleep (time I went to bed, time it took to fall asleep, how many times I woke up during the night, time I got out of bed, total time in bed, total time actually asleep), flights of stairs, VAM (very active minutes). I can set goals and it will send me messages to encourage me or award me "badges" for my accomplishments & milestones. I can even set vibrating alarms.

Using the dashboard, I can manually log & monitor my weight, BP, water intake, food intake. FitBit has an extensive database. When you track your activity, it will also track your calories burned. The dashboard also allows for custom goals & provides detailed graphs of progress. There is a huge community of FitBit users that one might choose to join for encouragement and challenges. Additionally, the FitBit is compatible with many, many fitness apps. Finally, the FitBit One is sweat, splash & rain proof.

The FitBit ships complete with the unit, the sleeve/clip, the wireless dongle & the USB charging cable. The customer service provided by the manufacturer is nothing less than STELLAR. And this particular price with free shipping is unbeatable.

Anyone who doesn't own an iPod or iPad probably won't see the utility of this device. However, for those who know the limitations of a 16GB iDevice, this can come in very handy to extend your storage.

One caveat is that given the cost of the Airstash at the time of writing, if you haven't yet taken the iPlunge, it might be better to go with the 64GB iPad 3 or 2 in the first place. However, if you already own the 16GB, then getting this device becomes an economical option.

The tech specs are covered in the product description, so below are some of my observations based on my experiences using the Airstash with an iPad 2.

Once the Airstash is powered up (by holding down the power button until the green indicator light turns on, then releasing it to see the light flash rapidly three times), you can connect your device to it wirelessly. However, in order to take full advantage of the Airstash, you will need to install the Airstash+ app which you can download from the Apple AppStore for free. This app allows you to access the files that you have copied to the Airstash. Alternatively, you can use a browser and browse to airstash.net for the same functionality.

While it may look like a flash drive on steroids, and works in a similar fashion when you plug it into your computer's USB port, I found it was not as straight-forward a matter when being used to save files. Accessing the files you have placed there is simple enough, but in order to save stuff to it using your iPad/iPod, your app needs to be WebDAV compatible. The Quick Start Guide supplied with the device briefly mentions that once connected you `launch the WebDAV compatible app of your choice'.

Now, if you're like me, then you probably have no idea what this means. What I've discovered is that WebDAV is some kind of `format/protocol' that allows you to save your files to the Airstash. The problem is, not all apps are WebDAV compatible. Apple's Pages, Numbers and Keynote are, but QuickOffice isn't. So if you're a Microsoft Office user like I am, accustomed to QuickOffice, then this device might not be for you. You can read your Office files from the Airstash, but you wouldn't be able to edit them and save them back to the device.

Other observations...

Without installing additional software/apps, mp4 (movie) files on the Airstash played easily on my iPad, but not avi files. (I didn't try digital movies but the product description says that you can play movies loaded on it on your device.)

I couldn't figure out how to save stuff directly onto it that I had downloaded to my iPad, like apps, attachments, books, etc. Maybe there is an easier way, but I had to sync my iPad with my computer first, then copy the files over to the Airstash from the computer.

The iPad could open epub books (in iBooks) and pdf files saved on the Airstash. Presumably there shouldn't be any problems with music and photo files, but I didn't test these either.

It took about 8 minutes to transfer 366MB from my (old) laptop to the Airstash using USB 1.0. With newer computers this should be faster.

Some pros, some cons - consider this is you have an iDevice that needs more storage space.

I was going to wait until I actually had truly tested and used this before I wrote a review.  I got this free as a review unit.  The problem is that I can't use it without spending some money for cables, as it does not come with cables.  StarTech says that's on purpose since people have different cable needs, especially different lengths. The cables that StarTech has available for it are over $21 each, which comes up to well over $60 for my 3 computers, almost the price of the switch.  With 4 computers connected, the price would be even more.  Okay, so they don't provide cables, but for the price of the switch, maybe they should at least give you a coupon or a voucher for one or two cables or a discount on the cables.  Interestingly the 2-port version does include cables; the 4-port does not.  StarTech's cables are nice, as they combine the needed USB with the VGA cable; otherwise you have to run two completely separate cables (one VGA cable for monitor and a USB cable for keyboard and mouse).  If you have USB cables as most people do, you can easily purchase the needed VGA cables inexpensively.  This brings me to the first real issue I have with this switch.  The master monitor connection is a female connector, which is standard.  Unfortunately the 4 computer monitor connectors are all male connections, so you can't use a standard male to male VGA cable that you would normally use from a computer to a monitor.  You have to get male to female VGA cables (which are typically called extension cables).  Why they would use this non-standard method of connecting monitors is puzzling.  A couple of reviewers were also concerned that this switch does not come with a power supply.  That's usually not a big deal as I found out that a power supply is not necessary, as the switch gets it's power from the USB connections.  There is no explanation as to why it has a place to plug in a power supply, although in some cases if you have a lot of USB devices connected to your PC, you might need additional power that a power supply would provide, so I assume it is for supplemental power.  It's good that they provide a way to add additional power, if you need it, even if not the actual power supply.  The next issue I encountered was trying to determine whether or not you could switch between computers with a hotkey sequence on your keyboard or whether you actually had to reach over to the switch and press the button for the computer you wanted.  Apparently there is no keyboard switching or if there is, no one seems to know what keys are used.  I read the manual for the setup and was concerned that it states that for PC to get the switch to work properly, a couple of BIOS settings for PC need to be changed.  I am not even sure that my computers have those particular settings, especially my older computers that sometimes have more limited BIOS settings available.  I have had 3 other KVM switches and none of them needed a change to BIOS settings.  Given the problems that others have had with this switch in that it doesn't always work flawlessly, I am not sure that I want to take time to test it right, since I already have a nicely working KVM switch.  I still have to buy cables.  On the plus side, this switch appears to be well built with a metal case; not cheap plastic.  It appears to be nice and solid and just heavy enough.  If the issues I mentioned are not a deal-breaker for you, I think this is worth trying.  I will update my review and add or subtract stars once I have a chance to test this in actual operation.

I've been using a clip-on light for my Kindle Touch when reading at night. It works, but I don't like that there's a separate piece of equipment I need to keep track of. This all-in-one solution has proven to be an effective way to light up the Kindle without having a separate light.

The case itself is nicely made. The cover is soft and cushy; the interior is a nice "suede" type material that wont harm the screen. All the stitching is even and tight. The Kindle fits in easily and is held securely. The cover has what I assume is a magnetic closure. It works well, and keeps the case closed in transit, but opens without having to undo any snaps or zippers.

The light is attached on the back of the case. When needed, you undo a protective flap (has a snap button), flip the light over the top and secure it in place with a "hook" that's built into the top of the case. The on/off switch is on the side of the light housing. Takes only a couple of seconds to get it into position.

The light is more than adequate for reading is a dark room. It uses 2 button batteries (CR 2032).

IMPORTANT: my case came with a plastic protector on the batteries to ensure the batteries remained fresh in transit. This must be removed before use or it will appear that the light is non-functional. Unfortunately, there are no instructions about this (I guessed it was the issue when the light would not turn on).

While it's great to always have the light as part of the case, the downside is that the light housing creates a bulge on the back side of the case. That makes this more cumbersome to toss into a briefcase since it increases the width. But, for me, it's a fair trade-off since I don't have to remember to bring the light with me.

I'll give this 5 stars, but 4.5 is a more accurate rating since it should come with instructions with regard to the battery. I also think the battery cover should be thicker (no problems so far, but it's a thin plastic) as well as the lens cover (very thin plastic that bends easily). Those quirks aside, I'm finding this to be an excellent case for my Touch.

As a child one of my favorite things to do was to look at things under a microscope. I vividly remember gathering a water sample from a swamp near the house and looking at a sample and finding my first paramecium. It has been years since I have owned a microscope, but with this microscope I can see how things have advanced and changed. This one does not have the same magnification as that microscope I had as a child but it is a lot easier to use and I can still see things with it that I cannot see even with a good magnifying glass.

This unit looks more like a drill press than a microscope, in terms of the design. The scope itself fits on a metal shaft and two turning knobs make it easy to raise and lower the scope in relation to the base. The base has two clips for holding down your slides or paper or whatever else you want to look at through the scope. There is no eye-piece on the scope – the image is viewed on a computer screen instead and the connection is made via USB.

Included with the scope is a software CD and this must be installed to use the scope. Installation is quick and painless. I installed under Windows 10 64-bit and had no issues. After installation I launched the software immediately.

The software consists of a view/capture application and a supplemental application for saving your work. The main part of the view & capture app is a live window that shows what is visible through the scope. As the object or slide on the scope base is moved, the image updates in real time. I found it a little awkward to line things up just right at first but I finally did manage to get things in the viewer just as I wanted them.

I started with a gray piece of paper that I thought was solid gray, but I found that the gray is actually a micro dot pattern like magazine print. More interesting was the corner of a $5 bill showing not just the print pattern detail but the fine fibers in the paper. A penny, cat hair and a very close-up view of a microfiber cleaning cloth all proved to be interesting subjects. Attached to this review are some of those detailed images, my favorite being the penny. I have not yet gone to the culvert near the house to gather water samples.

The software allows for two different capture types – photo or video. I have only played with the photo capture so far but it it very straightforward – click the photo button, either on the application interface or on the USB cable where the light level can be adjusted and the image appears in a list on the right side of the application window. If you double click the image you can save the image to the hard drive, zoom in on it and do a few other operations.

Linked to a tablet instead of a computer, this is a great travel scope to take with you. It is well-suited for classroom use as well as for use in the office.

I like this microscope. It is very easy to use, it does a good job of magnification and images are nice and clear. It is very different than the microscope I used growing up, in ways that I like. It's so much easier viewing on a screen than looking through a viewer, making this more fun to use too.

I'm a huge Lensbaby fan. I've been using them with my Canon SLRs almost since they first came out, and have assembled a pretty extensive collection of them over the past few years. Yes, I am a lover of blur. It's one of those creative effects that you either love or don't (although I certainly will admit it can be overused with some horrible results). I've recently been playing around with Micro Four Thirds cameras and was thrilled to see that Lensbaby came out with a model specifically designed for the MFT format.

Quick primer for those not familiar with a Lensbaby: it's a very simple device that allows you to tilt the focal plane of the lens to shift focus to any area of the frame and produce a smooth blur effect. It can be in a small or large part of your photo depending on which of the several aperture rings you choose from (all supplied with this Lensbaby) and how much tilt you apply.

This particular version of the lens, called the "Composer" is part of Lensbaby's new Optic Swap System, which allows you to use any one of several optics (plastic, glass, double glass, pinhole/zoneplate) that you can easily swap out of the main body. This comes with the double glass optic - the other optics have to be purchased separately.

The new Composer design allows you to lock the tilt into place for some level of repeatability in your shots. A lot more convenient than earlier versions of Lensbabies, which required you hold the tilt with your fingers. Now it's just pick your aperture and your optic, tilt, and snap away!

This lens comes with an extra you can't get with other Lensbabies for other camera formats - the "tilt transformer." This is an attachment that will allow you to use any Nikon-mount lens as a close approximation of a tilt/shift lens (only close, since you really only get the benefit of tilt and not shift). With this attachment and a "regular" lens, you get a movable sliver, a line of focus, as opposed to the movable point of focus you get with a Lensbaby Optic. Same basic principle, but it produces a slightly different look.

Build quality is good. There's a lot of plastic in it, but my other Lensbabies have performed very well over the years with zero problems. The product comes nicely packaged, but only has minimal instructions. That's not really a problem since the company website has a lot of resources on how to use Lensbabies, plus has photo galleries, forums, instructional videos, and a lot more. Very nice resource if you own one. If you're not sure if a Lensbaby is for you, that should be your first stop to see what type of effects their products can produce. I've spent a lot of time there, and it has been time well spent. The company itself is excellent when it comes to customer service. I've contacted them a couple of times with questions, and they answer emails promptly.

This lens is versatile, and is more convenient to carry (both the Lensbaby as well as a MFT camera itself). I've found with all my gear that convenience of toting it means I'll carry it more often, and thus have more opportunity for taking great shots. The tilt transformer is a wonderful addition - you can play around with a tilt lens at a fraction it would cost you to buy a real tilt/shift lens.

While pricy for a Lensbaby, when you add up all the features it brings to the table, I find it to be a real winner. Highly recommend if you have a MFT camera.

A keyboard used to be a rather boring, under-appreciated, rectangular attachment to your computer, useful for typing stuff, and for catching stray staples, bits of paper from your paper punch, dust and assorted DNA particles.

Now here comes the Wave Pro, with a sensuous curvy design, and a whole lot of kewl features that you never knew you needed until now. This model comes with an MX1100 Cordless laser mouse, both sharing a common USB micro-receiver.

Features:

Cordless Keyboard

1. Windows Vista Flip 3D button, that helps you to switch between application windows easily. With XP you get a pop up list of your open windows, but with Vista you see your windows in 3D view, and then use your arrow keys or mouse to choose your next destination page.

2. Zoom keys to get that paragraph to a size you can read, even without your progressive lenses.

3. Special Vista keys that bring up all the Vista features, and all your picture files, each with the click of one button.

4. Navigation keys for multimedia - volume, mute, play, pause, stop, fast forward, skip back. This is a very handy feature - kind of like a monster sized remote control

5. One button to bring up your Media Player

6. One button to bring up your Media Center, where you can listen to music, or watch a movie, tune in to the television, view your picture files in a slideshow, check out MSNBC.com and more.

7. Call up a handy calculator in a jiffy

8. Sleep button

9. Fn key to give each of the function keys a second job to do, such as launch Word or Excel, your favorite website, your IM page or e-mail or favorite search engine.

10. Battery status indicator.

11. Contoured keyboard with palm rest for comfortable typing. This design works very well for people who can type with the proper fingers, but also does the job for the two-fingered corn-pickers among us.

12. Displays actions on your monitor for a few seconds so you're less likely to accidentally hit your Caps button without noticing it.

Cordless Mouse

See: [[ASIN:B001DJ64C0 Logitech MX 1100 Cordless Laser Mouse]]
(NB) On its own this mouse uses 2 AA batteries, but when packaged with the keyboard it uses a rechargeable battery.

Cons:
1. The keyboard is pretty big (albeit understandably so) and takes up quite a bit of space on the desk. I'd get around this by typing with the keyboard on my lap and my feet up on the desk, but they tell me it's not good office practice.

2. The mouse uses rechargeable NiMH batteries - good for saving on dead batteries, but a real pain to keep track of the charger, which you'll need once every six weeks.

Conclusion:

The "Ayes" have it - regardless if you're a whizz at data entry or a two-finger wonder, this keyboard makes a lot of functions easier, and the Media Center and handy navigation keys put it way ahead of other keyboards.

Add it to your own Christmas list this year.

Amanda Richards, November 3, 2008

I received this as a free review sample. The reason why I docked it a star is the active tablet window needs improvement (and that could have been one of the stand-out features if properly designed.) Here is the problem: it's the perfect size for an iPad Air 2, but could not accommodate my Tab 2 10.1 inch tablet. It did hold my Samsung Tab Pro 8.4 (even in an Otterbox Defender case). The vinyl window wrinkles and also reduces sensitivity when you interact with your tablet.

If the active tablet window is unimportant to you, then the rest of this backpack is a winner. Pairing my phone to the bluetooth speakers was as simple as flipping a switch and scanning for it on my phone's settings. And the speakers are loud with better than expected sound quality. I was pleased with that - some thought went into the speakers.

The padding is more than ample for protecting electronics, and there are sufficient pockets for the geekiest geek. What I like, though, is the storage areas are not overly complex. I own a Booq bag that is a storage dream come true, but almost requires a photographic memory to remember were all of the pockets are. This one is designed much simpler, but still efficient and effective.

Construction (except for the active tablet window) is first rate. The tablet window is marred by a difficult zipper, whereas all of the other zippers on this bag are sturdier and smooth. The outer fabric seems tough (I have not had it long enough to make any claims beyond that), and all of the seams are reinforced, straight and tight.

It's very comfortable and can be adjusted to evenly distribute the weight of a fully loaded pack. Considering that the bag itself is somewhat heavy this is a major plus for me.

I do want to note one thing about the backup battery: it is rated at (and stores) the full 4000mAh. However, like all batteries using this one's technology it's only 70% efficient, so expect about 2800mAh of usable capacity. That is not a flaw in this bag, but a reality that I wanted to point out so your expectations are properly set.

Overall, this is a well made bag with some innovative features (battery back-up and bluetooth speakers). If the active tablet window is not an important feature it's definitely worth considering. This one will be replacing my Booq because the storage is there without the complexity.

This is a fairly standard surge protector with 12 outlets with only two of those set apart for the larger adapters. The selling point that it attempts to sell consumers on is the usb ports, including one type-c so this review will concentrate mostly on those ports.

As far as the surge protector portion of this product, the face outward, which means that the longer style chargers that comes with some electronics will not plug in without taking up an extra socket. With only two set farther apart for power adapters, this power strip will not work well for a location with routers, modem, and NAS.

Now on to the USB ports. Five USB ports share a total of Five amps. It means that is the power strip is completely filled, it will only deliver one amp to each port. The type-c port is only useful if that is the only cable you can find because it does not support any fancy features such as quick charging or type-c pd, although it does support up to 3A so some phones may actually consider this "fast charging". Do not expect to replace a true 5-port usb charger with this power strip.

I bought the Manfrotto 808RC4 along with their 190XPROB Pro Tripod and the Manfrotto MB MSTRAP-1 Tripod Carrying Strap. All at Amazon. Here's why:

This head gives you unlimited control in all directions. The large knurled handles allow you to grip and adjust the tension on the pivot points to any degree you want. I use it to pan video, I use it to do off center composure and metering. I love how rock steady this thing is when I am shooting my 60and 120 second exposures with my 300MM lens. Rock steady. And the rotation is greased smooth, nary a glitch.

With a bubble level and two straight levels you always know where you are. And gradients to indicate -30 to +90 tilt for replication. Great for panning video or shooting stills for a panorama. There are two "softening springs" to slow the movement of the tilts as you reach either end. You can disengage them if you wish.

I have friends that went with the ball heads. And regret it. They are fast, but not accurate, especially with a long lens. With this head you can adjust the tension and just ease the camera around without having to adjust it again.

Now hear me on this. I see other reviewers not so happy with the way the shoe is a little tricky. Let me say that by practicing with the shoe mounted to your camera and paying close attention snap it onto the head three times and you know all you need to know. You may have to practice a few more times to get it in the dark but I tell you that you are going to love it. When you snap the camera onto the head it automatically engages and you have no worries. The double safety has stopped me from dropping my camera twice. Lesson learned at no cost.

As to the tripod - sturdy is the word that comes to mind. And NOT overly weighty. Together the head and tripod are 7 lbs. With the strap - which I did not buy at first - this rig is rock solid and you won't even know you are carrying it. I don't even notice the combo. I hike several hours at a time and have been know to stop in a panic on the way out and feel on my back to see if the whole thing is still there! I think a big part of the "weight" issue is how it is carried. In your hands it feels hefty. On your hips, 7 lbs feels weighty. Across your shoulder diagonally, head down? It ain't even there!

The tripod has a wonderfully steady center column assembly that comes up and tilts over to the horizontal - great for macro shots or simply needing to place the camera where you aren't. The legs are sturdy and the snap retainers have just the right tension - not too hard to snap open or closed, not so loose that you worry whether one might slide. I also like that the center column is not attached to the legs with the typical arms of lesser well made tripods. Makes for very easy folding and stowing. I love the leg angle presets - easy to use and not worried about them slipping. The rubber grips on two of the legs are a hand saver in chilly weather. Nice touch.

So, in case you haven't figured it out, I love this rig. If I were going trekking across country for days I might want a little less weight, but for day long trips, portraiture or car trips this is the ticket.
