Let me begin by saying that I am not gifted in the arena of art. I am more technically oriented and as such I use tablets in different ways than most people. For that reason, this is likely going to be a very different review than that of most others on here.

I use pen tablets for handwriting and as general pointing devices as I find them to be more comfortable than mice and trackballs. I started experimenting with tablets a couple of years ago with a Bamboo small, which worked well but was just too small for me. I then compared a Bamboo Fun Pen & Touch to an Intuos4 and it took no time at all to determine that for me, the Intuos4 was a much better choice. With the release of the Intuos5 I jumped at the chance to compare it to the Intuos4, and so far I like it but I have found a couple of things about it that are, in my opinion, less than ideal.

I am using an Intuos5 on a Core i7-based laptop with 8 GB RAM and Windows 7 64-bit.

The very first thing - installation. Installation was about as painless as could be. I plugged in the tablet, installed the drivers and I was able to start using my tablet immediately without any issue. That's a big plus right off the bat. I have had trouble with installs in the past, in particular with the Bamboo Fun Pen & Touch, so having a smooth install is a great relief.

There is one thing about the install that troubles me, though. This tablet is capable of left- or right-handed use, so by simply rotating the tablet it is easy for anyone to use it. However, unlike the Intuos4 the Intuos5 only has a USB plug on one side, and it's the edge that always faces away from the computer. This means that the cord will always run above or below the tablet when plugged in unless it's plugged in to a USB hub of some sort. Perhaps that is not a big deal to some, but to me it is a minor irritant. The included USB cable is long enough, though, that I can hang most of it off the far edge of my desk. I suppose it's a good thing that my desk faces the wall.

I immediately grabbed the pen and started writing, and what I have found is that the Intuos5 seems to be a little more sensitive than the Intuos4, which means I can write a little more softly and still get what I want from it. Wacom did a good job of adjusting the sensitivity to the pen and subsequently turning off the touch feature. With my Bamboo Fun Pen & Touch the pen had to be very, very close to the surface of the tablet before touch was disabled, and even then the tablet kept trying to zoom on me as I wrote. Not so with the Intuos5 - the sensitivity to the pen seems to be good up to about an inch from the surface, which is fine for my purposes.

The surface of the Intuos5 does seem to be a little rougher than that of the Intuos4, so expect the nibs to wear more quickly. Though it has more texture it still feels very natural to me and I have no issue with writing on the surface. That said, why make it rougher so that it eats the nibs faster?

While the buttons along the side are configurable, I don't mess with them. I do use the scroll ring though and it works well. It is sensitive to light touch and so far has given me no trouble at all.

For a good graphics test I brought up Corel Painter and did a little doodling. The tablet and Painter work together quite well. Painter was able to determine at what angle I held the pen and it allowed me to make nice strokes and then reverse the pen to erase without any hassle. I really have not tried to push the tablet through all of Painter's features (which would do a great job of showcasing what the tablet can do) but I did enough to convince myself that the Intuos5 is a strong tool for the really artistic individual.

The Intuos4 has a small, no-frills 3-button mouse where the Intuos5 has touch features that make it work like a giant laptop touchpad. This comes down to personal preference. I never use the mouse on my Intuos4 but the touch features on the Intuos5 are very handy and convenient. Others may find the removal of the mouse to be a deal-breaker.

So far, the handwriting recognition seems to be about equivalent to that with the Intuos4. I have had to adjust my writing habits because of my using tablets for this, so a lot of the retraining took place long before the Intuos5 came. The recognition software does a reasonable job of reading my handwriting but it still makes mistakes and requires more patience.

The Intuos5 is a really nice pen tablet. It is comfortable, it is sensitive and it has two modes for accepting input. I question why Wacom placed the USB port on the outside edge of the tablet, and I also wonder why the surface is more rough than the Intuos4, but of all the current tablet offerings on the market right now this one is the best. It's not perfect, but it does try hard. I'm satisfied.

Wow! Talk about an effortless, totally-bubble-free installation of a screen protector on a large tablet! This crystal-clear MOSHI IVISOR XT NO-BUBBLE SCREEN PROTECTOR installed in less than a minute on my Kindle Fire HDX 8.9" tablet--or in about two minutes, if you include the time it took to wipe the screen with a microfiber cloth (included). The "secret" behind the easy Moshi iVisor installation is that only the black band around the edges of the protector sheet has adhesive. When there's no adhesive in the middle of the protector sheet, you can't catch dust motes or air bubbles between the sheet and the tablet's backlit viewing area.

Also, the protector sheet is made of stiff plastic that makes it easy to handle. You just place the sheet gently on the tablet, using the camera and light sensor cutouts as a guide, and then apply light pressure to the black edges to secure the adhesive. If you get the placement wrong, you can try again, because the screen protector is removable. It can even be removed, stored away, and reapplied at a later time.

Once the screen protector is installed, it's virtually invisible. There is no loss of touchscreen sensitivity, and the protector itself is crystal clear. I've installed a lot of screen protector film--on cameras, cellphones, and 7" and 9" tablets--and until now I thought it would be impossible for anyone to make a screen protector for a large tablet that would go on bubble-free and also be invisible after the installation. This Moshi iVisor XT screen protector has proved me wrong.

The non-audiophile (i.e. reasonably priced) receivers used to have a "contour", or "bass boost" function (even the previous Sony model had it), which greatly enhanced the audibility of lower frequencies when played at low decibels. This one lacks it (and it sounds like most of nowadays sold receivers are like this), hence the sound coming out is quite flat (also for treble band), unless you go really loud. I will not regurgitate the product specs since they are not only complete, but have been validated by more than a few previous reviews. I'll stick to some key observations about the review sample that I received and why I think this light deserves five stars.

The main reason why I love this light is price and performance. I own a few other music stand lights and they either perform on par with this one, but are priced twenty-five percent (or more higher), or they are not as well made.

Features are also more than I expected for a twenty buck light. For one thing you can easily get seven hours of continuous use on a single charge. I did a rundown test on mine and it remained illuminated for a little over seven hours before it started dimming, That was with both LEDS in each head switched on. I ended the test when it started appreciably dimming, but even at seven hours this is more than adequate since I actually do use this as a music stand light and the longest performances are less than three hours.

Another feature that I love is the LED indicator in the USB A end of the charging cable. It will be red until the light fully charges, then it will turn green.

Note: there are two things that I do not care for: (1) the charging end is a barrel connector instead of a micro USB connector, so if you lose of damage the included cable you are going to have difficulty replacing it, and (2) the barrel connector does not completely seat into the charging port. It charges, but I would be hesitant of using this light in a studio where you wanted to suppress all electrical interference. I am not sure there is any from this light, but the fact that a conducting connector is partially exposed gives me pause.

Bottom line: for stage performances this light is better and brighter than most other two-LED models and illuminates sufficiently to read music or lyrics. It holds firm when clamped to my music stand, and the flexible arms allow me to position the lamp heads for optimum reading while staying put.

I found myself needing to teach from home, like most US teachers, because of covid-19. Using zoom and whiteboard software locally, I would attempt to maintain some of the same methods I use in class, but also knew I'd need to do a lot more "showing" for that low ratio of students showing up for conferences sessions. Another teacher loaned hers to me to test for a few minutes. It did the job, so I decided to get one myself.
I really only use Windows for games that won't install/run in linux. My distance teaching wasn't going to be from Windows if I could help it.
This worked right out of the box. It didn't have all the functions, but it worked as a mouse would. It meant I could write (doing math work) in the whiteboard software without trying to do it with a mouse or fumble equations in real time with an equation editor or giving too much away using Geogebra.
I'm also a lefty, so that proved annoying quickly. It defaults to right handed mode, and the body that holds the electronics gets in the way. So I HAD to find drivers. Thankfully at Github (search Linux driver for Veikk-brand digitizers ) there is a driver. Installing was not too bad (had to compile myself - and had to find a fix for something getting in the compile way, search ""FATAL: Module veikk not found in directory" and a potential fix" at github).
Viola! The touch sensitivity works just fine and I can rotate the orientation, by manually editing parameters in /sys/module/veikk/parameters
Great, but then I had to find the GUI, because it kept resetting my orientation setting any time I rebooted. Search "Configuration tool for the VEIKK Linux driver" at github for the gui installer. It gave me hassles to install, but somehow I got it installed. Idon't use it much, but somehow it also keeps my orientation setting correct on reboots, and that's what I cared most about. I could change button configs and the sensitivity curve, but I'm not there yet.
Openboard (foss whiteboard) actually works with the touch sensitivity, but Activinspire doesn't. No big deal. Gimp doesn't until you set it to in device settings. Krita didn't need to be told what to do and works wonderfully.

My complaints:
The PITA driver installation isn't one really. They don't officially support linux - THAT is worthy of a complaint though. For those using linux, I'm going to guess, still, many are used to dealing with this.
The placement of the USB cord is annoying when in lefty (108 deg orientation), as the cord comes in your direction.
The drawing surface isn't huge, but that's a given. The challenge is that the sensitive area goes very close to the edge, making it hard to draw on the edges if you are not using this on a regular flat surface. I'm using it on my lap, most of the time.
The pen is also thick! 7/16" or 11mm diameter. Not super comfy. My hands aren't small. It makes using the buttons a little less than optimal, but I don't use them much yet anyway. I'm sure as I do more art with it than math, I'll want to customize that. I have an older wacom stylus I'll try to locate and see if it magically works. It was a far better fit.
All said and done, I do recommend this. I might even buy one of the larger ones.

I've said it a thousand times: "I think I could really get into (real) photography, but I just can't take another hobby that requires me carrying a whole bag of equipment across the world. If I get a DSLR, I won't take it to the places that I'd like to use it the most." Well...I think they made this camera just for me. I believe this camera to be capable of "real" pro photos, just the same as if I bought a DSLR and a single lens, which many people start by doing. It also makes a startup punk like me look like a pro, much to the chagrin of the real pros.

My other cameras include a DSC-H20, which is an older Sony model with a 10x zoom lens, multiple point-and-shoots, and a waterproof/shockproof Panasonic that I really like for my basic, worry-free shots.

My main question about this camera was, why does it appear to be Sony's flagship compact camera in every way, but yet it doesn't have the 30x optical zoom lens that some of the other Sony's have (or even the 10x of my DSC-H20)? I knew there would be an answer, but to find it, I had to start digging into camera specs, something I've been meaning to do for a while.

First, pro photographers tend to think that if you're using much zoom under most circumstances, then you're just being lazy. You need to get closer. In a landscape shot, zoom tends to flatten things out. I may have never noticed this, or WHY this is. You know, you go on vacation, take a lot of pictures, come back and some look great and others look bad. Maybe it's true that every time I zoom in on a landscape, I'm really just ruining my shot.

The other thing is aperture. Aperture basically tells you how clear the background of your picture will be versus your foreground (I'm just learning this myself, so camera pros, feel free to comment with better verbiage), a lower number being better if you want a totally clear picture, and the lowness of that number being what you use to compare the quality of lenses. It's also good to have a high end on the range because that allows you to take those artsy photos with something super clean up front and a blurry background. I've also seen some neat head shots taken that way, where even some hair starts becoming blurry.

Anyway, the low aperture on this camera is 1.8 all the way zoomed out, and 2.8 all the way zoomed in (you can set it as high as 11 in either case). This is a tight range with great numbers (notice that even here, you lose a little bit by using zoom). My camera with the 10x zoom has an aperture equal to 3.5 all the way out, similar to the 30x zoom cameras Sony has now. It makes a big difference, even to my amateur eye.

This camera, and my subsequent research, has allowed me to let go of the 10/30x zoom. Yes, those cameras are great, but this is the flagship mini for a reason. Now I understand. Just taking random pictures in my neighborhood, although so boring compared to my favorite International backgrounds, I can clearly see a quality difference.

The other main spec for cameras is shutter speed. This can be set for 1/32000 of a second all the way up to 30 seconds. The quickest shutter speeds will capture an instant in time without blur, while the slower ones will capture more action with some blur. They are also good for low light scenarios to expose the shot to more light. Very slow speeds should be used with a tripod or the camera set down someplace. This camera makes a noise (not an obnoxious one) when on auto and using a slower shutter speed, to keep you still. It's very intuitive and works well.

While you will get better shots than you ever had before using this camera on auto, the dial wheel allows you to set either aperture or shutter speed as a priority and leave the rest on auto, perfect for people that want to understand what a real camera can do, and who want to set up pro shots without yet knowing everything.

The controls on this thing are awesome. I love that there is no touchscreen to fight with and that everything is so intuitive. Great praise to Sony for knowing what fads aren't worth it. (One fad they did latch onto is that 180 degree rotating screen, which really is fantastically convenient and feels quite strong and well done). While we're talking about it, they also put in the fantastic viewfinder and the pop-up flash, which all completely recess into the body of this thing (an amazing work of engineering art).

Speaking of the flash, you won't use it often. Even on a cheap camera, I try to keep the flash off, but this thing does an amazing job of using ambient light for exposure (I believe this is the third pillar of photography). I swear, I have never seen such clear pictures in very low light. Instead of being grainy, I can pick up minute details (even zoom-able), and they appear brighter than the actual place they were taken. This, I believe, is because of the 1" image sensor they are touting. I'm impressed.

The 960fps thing. With only two seconds, this may be hard to set up the shot you want, but 2 seconds seems a lot longer in 960fps. Even just shaking your leg on camera, you'll see the odd aftereffects of your socks moving like you never did before. Stupid example, but that's the point: the details you get from 960fps slow-mo are amazing.

4k video. I really didn't care about all this until some guy at a conference pointed out how 4k has been used for pro video for years. Instead of multiple cameras to cover a hockey game, for example, you could just use one and zoom in on anything you want and still have high-def video. I realized we probably will move over to actually using it at some point. Well, here's your chance to actually use that 4k TV. It's awesome. It really is.

A note on SD cards. While most devices can read SDHC cards, which went up to 32GB, the reason they want you to have a SDXC card (which can be from 64GB to 2TB in theory) is because the speed ratings are higher. You need the speed rating of 3 (>100 Mbps) to really use these big data transfer functions. I suspect the 960fps is all that can be held in RAM, and that those speeds are way too fast for even the newest and best card (hence the 2 second limit on 960fps).

Suffice to say that I love this camera. I appreciate each of its mechanical and electrical features and how they're perfectly integrated to make this small, marvelous camera. Even in the leather case (not included), it's about the same size as my H20, certainly portable enough to have it when you want it, but with enough features and technology that you're not sacrificing anything in your photography.

This little monocular/camera has an unique design. Canon made lots of compromises to build it for this size and price. As with any gadget that is full of compromises, it is not for everyone.

As the product description states, this camera has 2 optical lenses (nominally 100mm and 400mm equivalents) and one digital crop to 800mm. These are paired with a very small image sensor (1/3 inch) to get the camera down to this size. Because of the small sensor, the camera is really only usable in bright sunlight; image quality is mediocre to poor indoors or at night or even early or late in the day or on cloudy days when the sun is not strong. The 100mm and 400mm are fixed lenses, you cannot zoom to levels in between those 2 values.

The viewfinder has pretty good brightness and resolution, but is somewhat small, so looking at it for long periods of time was uncomfortable to me, especially in lower-light situations when the image quality was not so great.

The minimum focusing distance is 3 feet with the 100mm lens and a huge 15 feet with the 400mm lens. That makes this camera impractical for most closeup photography.

Battery life is a mediocre 1 hour of screen-on time or about 150 photos. You have to beware of the time limit if you are using this device as a monocular. While you can recharge the device in the field via the USB-C port, that is awkward at best since you have to hold the fragile battery door open while recharging it.

Those are the main limitations to this camera, so who is it really for? The 100mm and 400mm lenses are equivalent to about 4x and 16x zoom levels on a smartphone or point-and-shoot camera. The Canon camera has no wide angle lens, but if you are carrying a smartphone with you, you can use that for your wide angle camera. I believe today's top-of-the-line iPhone has a 2.5X optical telephoto lens, so the 4X and 16X lenses on this Canon are huge improvements if you like telephoto photography. Samsung and Pixel Android cameras are little better, but the Canon still beats them at 16X.

I think this Canon camera is useful for casual photographers who want to take telephoto snapshots of wildlife, daytime sports, architecture, etc. This camera is small and lightweight enough to easily fit in a purse or coat pocket or even a big pants pocket and it takes better bright sunlight telephoto photos than most smartphones. The camera lets you wirelessly copy photos to your smartphone for editing and posting to social media.

What are your other options? Companies like Sony and Panasonic sell good compact point-and-shoot cameras with 720mm telephoto lenses and better sensors than this Canon camera. These cameras are a little more expensive and a little heavier, but about the same semi-pocketable size as this Canon. Of course, interchangeable lens cameras like SLRs or APS mirrorless camera will let you mount huge expensive lenses that can take fantastic telephoto photos, but are usually too big and heavy to carry around if your primary purpose is not photography.

I'm giving this camera 3.5 stars because of list of limitations is maybe too long for most people, but I think it does have its place for some people. I do wish they had used a bigger image sensor to improve the image quality and low-light ability, even if that meant making the camera a little bigger and heavier. Even many smartphones have bigger image sensors than this Canon camera.

I have worked with a lot of different headphones, mostly active noise canceling (ANC) phones but also more traditional phones. Over the years I have had several Sennheiser phones and they typically have balanced sound and good build quality. This set is a step down from many of the others with which I have worked, though they’re still decent.

My preference on headphones is over-the-ear phones which for me are more comfortable. These particular phones are on-ear, and these pinch a little after extended wear. They’re better than some of the other on-ear phones with which I have worked, but I still prefer over-the-ear phones. One preference I have is a headphone that clamps down fairly tightly when worn so they’re less likely to slip off when I tilt my head down; these are a lighter fit.

These are Bluetooth-only phones and as such cannot be used with non-BT devices. This is unfortunate but isn’t a deal-breaker. These connect easily and quickly.

These are not ANC phones, but they have excellent passive noise canceling which is quite surprising for on-ear phones. They reduce ambient noise in my office considerably, which us especially noticeable when running a large fan that I use to generate white noise. I am pleased with that aspect of these phones. These are still not as effective as a set of ANC phones.

The sound profile is fairly typical of Sennheiser phones, though the bass is mildly beefed up.. The trend with phones these days is overdriven bass, and these do increase the bass response a little bit but not to a headache-inducing level. The midrange is full and warm, and that’s a good thing as many times the increased bass comes at the expense of the midrange. The highs are bright and clear without being piercing. Overall, the sound is reasonably balanced, but certainly not audiophile quality.

Build-wise, these actually feel a bit on the cheaper side which is surprising. These aren’t exactly fragile, but they are definitely not of the same build quality as other Sennheisers I have used in the past.

These are probably best described as entry-level headphones. They’re not the highest quality, and they are not the most sturdy, but the sound quality is fine and the cost is right. The main thing I would change is the addition of an audio port so they could be used as wired phones.

This BOSE SOUNDLINK COLOR BLUETOOTH SPEAKER may not be the ideal portable speaker for serious audiophiles--because it has no treble/base buttons, only volume buttons--but I love mine. The sound is rich and full, whether it's paired with my old Sony Bravia TV, iPad2, or Kindle Fire, or connected by AV stereo cable (3.5mm M/M) to my MP3 player's headphone jack. The volume is controlled by the device the speaker is connected to, or by the plus/minus volume buttons on the speaker itself. The speaker also has an Aux button for the direct cable connection, and a Skip button that lets you go forward or backward in your music selections.

This Bose portable speaker can support two Bluetooth-connected devices at once, so you can switch between two devices (e.g., an iPad and a Kindle Fire) without repeating the pairing process every time. A great feature! The speaker automatically connects with the last-connected Bluetooth device, and switches devices when you press the Bluetooth button. The speaker's voice prompts help you with pairing, and tell you which two devices are currently paired. The voice prompts can be disabled, if you wish.

This Bose speaker is definitely an improvement over the speakers built into my old Sony Bravia TV. Voices are much clearer--including the dialogue from British TV shows--and the sound is far richer. Of course, using this speaker instead of a TV sound bar is only a temporary solution, because the speaker needs regular recharging. I use messenger bags as book bags to take books and tools to and from work every day. I favor canvas bags because they are tougher than nylon and they are a bit more masculine-looking. This particular messenger bag is a little more stylish than some of the others I have seen and so far I am happy with it.

A messenger bag is characterized by the fold-over flap that snaps closed over the main compartment. This particular bag has a very colorful and decorative weave that makes up the entire flap and the result is a softer and more supple flap than if it had been made of the same canvas material as the rest of the bag. That is not a fault or imperfection by any means but needs to be mentioned as a difference. Compared to the flap, the rest of the bag is more coarse and rigid.

Everything about this bag suggests quality. The stitching is very tight and the materials are even and there are no imperfections (nicks and cuts) that I can find on this bag. The stitching used to attach the shoulder strap to the metal loops on the bag, as well as to attach the leather trim to the canvas, is visibly thicker and stronger than what was used to hold the canvas portions of material together. I like the fact that there is some manner of reinforcement on the bottom of the bag (stitched inside so it is hard to know exactly what kind of reinforcement was used).

Instead of actual snaps, the flap is attached to the front of the bag using magnets. These make it a lot easier to open and close the bag.

In the main compartment of this bag are three pockets, one zippered and two smaller pockets that are open on the top. The smaller pockets are ideal for cell phones, small note pads, a calculator and the like while the larger pocket is big enough to accommodate a checkbook or a small book; it is not quite wide enough to handle a DVD case. There is a front pocket that is just barely wide enough to handle a 10” tablet (though I would put a tablet in the main compartment instead). Finally, there is a zippered pocket on the back that is slightly more narrow than the front pocket because of the zipper and is good for papers and maps.

This is a nice messenger bag and I like it. It is made very well, it is spacious enough to handle a couple of technical books and it looks nice.

If what you're looking for is a complete backup utility, that's reasonably easy to use, this one might suit your purpose.

Installation, update, and activation are easy, similar to other Symantec programs. (This one also uses Live Update.) I do have an objection to the fact that Symantec never does a full uninstall -- they leave around stuff in the registry, as well as LiveUpdate, and it requires extra work (and some technical skill) to remove everything. I take off one star for that.

The setup is quite simple, especially if you follow their procedures. A full system backup is recommended, and the program will nag you about your system being "at risk" if you don't set up the full backup. You can in addition set up backup jobs for selectively backing up some of your files and folders. So for instance you might want to do nightly backup of your key folders, and weekly or monthly backup of the full system.

I would recommend that you use a network disk (NAS) for your backup -- there are many not-too-expensive products available, and I've been quite happy with the Buffalo products.

You can also use this program to do remote management of other computers on your network, but be aware that each computer needs its own license for the program.

One thing I don't like is that the backup files are not copies, they are in a compressed format. For daily backups I prefer to be able to make normal copies of files, so that I can go quickly to the backup folder and find a backup copy I might want. This optimizes my time and convenience over computer time and disk space, and this is how it should be. Or at least, this should at least be an option.

I take off another star for the nagging about full system backup, and the unavailability of a simple file backup or file sync (backup by copying selected files/folders directly from one disk to another).

But overall a solid program that does what it says, and does it competently. Just make sure what you want is what it wants to do. :-)

My main TV - and thus my comparison point - is a Sony Bravia Z series from 2009. Here are some things I think are outstanding about the Samsung. I'll try to only talk about things that aren't mentioned constantly:

1) I dislike the overly contemporary look of most high-end Samsung TVs, and therefore don't usually consider them for purchase. This, however, is a classic looking TV that won't look old next year and doesn't draw attention to itself at the expense of everything else.

2) Sony - and most other companies - no longer make a high end 32" model, which is stupid. My main TV is most likely to have a local computer nearby. It's the kitchen and the bedroom where I need the SMART features most. For that reason, this TV actually has very little competition.

3) USB ports. These are outstanding, especially if your network is too slow for streaming (or if you don't have a port nearby and your wireless is slow). Where my older Sony only plays some pictures off USB - and way too slow to actually want to use that feature, this newer Samsung can play almost all my media files locally or use a wireless mouse/keyboard. I have one USB port filled with a Logitech receiver, which allows me to use a mouse and keyboard I have stashed under the bed. Haven't actually bothered to use those yet (except for testing), but it's nice to know I could turn them up and use them without having to mess with any options. In the other USB port, I have a micro-SD card reader about the same size that always has 32GB of TV series that I can watch in a pinch, say if they put on some reality crap instead of a decent show that I was expecting over the air. Neither USB device can be seen except from the side. It reads the files on the micro-SD card directly from the source menu and as quickly as Windows Explorer.

4) DLNA. As much as I love that micro-SD card USB reader, you really don't even need it because the DLNA features are pretty mature. The fact that it reads .mkv files so easily, and you can control integrated subtitles and audio tracks so easily is amazing. My other TV requires transcoding for anything but MPEG, which really bogs down the processor on my laptop. I really recommend Wild Media Server because it works so well with both this and my Sony, and can easily spit 720p to both TVs (different shows) simultaneously. I couldn't get Serviio or Mezzmo to work as well. Samsung apparently has some freeware available that you might want to try as well.

All that said, despite the high contrast ratio, I don't feel like the picture is quite as good as my older Sony (which I believe only has a CR of 100,000:1), even after a lot of playing around. As you'd expect from its small size, it does play SD (and lower) very nicely on its screen without pixelization (Comment for 32" ONLY!). Even so, I love this TV for the bedroom, and felt the price was reasonable. It may get moved to replace the TV in the kitchen one day, and it will be great there, as well.

Also, I would prefer a browser with adjustable transparency over the TV, as the PIP version has the sound and picture cutting out sometimes. Even so, I would absolutely recommend this TV if you're looking for a 32"er.

Oh, but one more thing: I just had some apps "pushed" on me, like the cell phone companies do to your smart phone. If this continues, I'll be lowering my rating. I did not buy a TV to have a bunch of useless crap sold to me. A warning to you, Samsung.

Sony's Handycam line of video recorders has been a solid choice for years, and with the introduction of the HDR-PJ430V Handycam Sony has brought another excellent recorder to the market. It produces excellent quality video, it takes good still shots and it has some features I have never seen in other camcorders.

This is a very small, compact and lightweight camcorder, roughly the size of a box of butter sticks. Out of curiosity I put the camcorder with the battery installed on the kitchen scale and it weighed in at under 14 oz. The small size and very light weight make this camcorder very easy to hold in one hand without fatigue. This is very good news for people who either do not have a tripod or would rather hold the camera for all of their work.

At first power on, the user gets to select all of the necessary first-time settings - date and time, language and other preferences. This is all done on the touch-screen LCD. My last camcorder did not have a touch screen so I was minorly surprised by this feature. It also revealed the one and only issue I have had with this camera so far - the touch screen is slightly unresponsive compared to other devices I have used that offer the technology, and I find myself having to be very deliberate about accessing the screen's features.

Once the first-time defaults are set, this camcorder is ready to start recording. Without too much thought about what I was doing I pointed the camera at a target and started recording. As I panned the room, the camera made the necessary adjustments for light and dark, making a huge adjustment as I passed the screen of my computer and adjusting back to normal lighting as I passed it. This is a normal camcorder feature and it seems to handle the light differences very easily.

The zoom is above average. From about 40' away the camera can be zoomed in enough to read small lettering on a box. This is great for recording when the subject is at an appreciable distance.

The camcorder also seems to do a very good job of auto-focusing, which it does as light conditions change. Setting the camera close to a wall and shining a light around it, you can actually see it making focal adjustments on the screen and settling on a good balance of light and focus.

Video quality is, in a word, outstanding. Videos I have taken have come out exceedingly clear and bright without a lot of graininess that I have gotten with lesser camcorders. Even zoomed in all the way, image quality remains very good. Sound is also very clear and crisp.

Where this camcorder excels over any other camera I have used, though, is in the image stability (anti-shake or anti-jitter, if you prefer). Sony makes a big deal about their stability component and it works as well as advertised. Turning the camera around so that the lens is facing the user, one can jiggle the camera and actually see the lens being adjusted as the camera moves. It moves very much like an eyeball which honestly is a little creepy but it works very well. If holding the camera instead of using a tripod, video will definitely come out better as a result of this feature.

This is not just a camcorder, though. It also takes still shots. I like that this camera can be used as a still-shot camera, and though the user can make a few adjustments to make the image come out better, most of the settings are automatic. I have had better success with dedicated still-shot cameras, personally, though I have managed to render some good photos with the Handycam as well. The camcorder definitely does a better job than the typical smartphone when it comes to taking photos... It is very convenient to have a single device doing the work of two.

Probably the most interesting feature of this camcorder is the built-in projector. I had low expectations of this feature until I actually tried it. Projecting roughly 30' down a dark hallway, the projector built into the camcorder lit up the wall with bright, clear images that looked great. As I moved farther from the wall image quality diminished as expected and it got better as I got closer, but this feature really does work nicely. It does not work well enough to give a professional presentation, of course, but it is fine for entertaining small groups and for quick playback right after shooting. Be aware, however, that the projector runs through all available images and movies in one sweep without taking a pause between.

The software that installs when the camcorder is plugged into a computer is called PlayMemories Home, and it is actually a decent application for managing the content on the camera. It has more features than one would expect from the software that comes with a device. It allows for importing/exporting media, making basic edits on media (such as quick color adjustments and trimming/cropping), putting together slide shows, creating CD/DVD media, share online with several social media sites and a lot more. Most included software packages (at least, the ones I have seen) provide for much more basic handling of media.

The camcorder is supposedly wifi-capable, but this requires an accessory that I do not have so I cannot really comment on this other than to say the capability is available.

One of the things that Sony's HandyCam series is known for is the infrared/night vision modes that allow for better filming in extremely low light conditions. This particular camcorder does not seem to have that mode. It does recognize low-light conditions, but there is no option to turn on night vision recording. Though not a feature I really need, it is important to realize it's not available on this model. Curiously absent from this camcorder (considering that infrared is not available) is a light. So far this has not been an issue but I am curious to see how it does outside on a moonless night. Now, all of this said, Sony does have an accessory that is available that adds both a light and infrared capability. If you need a light or infrared with this camera, you will need that add-on, but be aware that it's a little pricey ($150 as I write this, which would bring the overall cost of this camcorder with the light to roughly $1000 at this time).

Sony's new HDR-PJ430V HandyCam is a very nice camcorder with some interesting and useful features. It produces very good quality imagery, it is very easy to use and it is very compact and light which makes it a camera that can be used for a long period of time without fatigue. This camcorder is very much worth consideration if you're in the market for a good-quality device - especially if the projection feature is of interest.

I've been watching a bunch of electronics repair videos lately and thinking back at my past purchases and the electronics I threw away, I wondered how many devices I could have rescued. Determined not to let electronics repair scare me off from tacking them, I decided to start collecting the tools that I need to do my own repairs.

I started with an affordable, but well-reviewed soldering iron: the Pinecil. A good silicone mat (same one as StezStix Fix), and now a microscope.

The LLIMINK Digital Microscope 7'' LCD, Coin Microscope is a great product. In the box, you'll find all of the accessories you'll need to get started, including any cables that you might need. What I wasn't expecting of this device is that it is actually battery powered and that the battery is removeable (see my pictures) -- very much in line with the Right-To-Repair philosophy. The remote control was a nice addition as well (taking a picture seems to be only controllable from the remote so make sure you don't lose track of it).

The base of the microscope is aluminum with two built-in LED lamps that are separately powered from the microscope itself. They provide additional lighting from other directions if you need it. The microscope itself has bright leds that shine directly downward on the board.

If the microscope mounted LEDs are causing too much glare, there is a collar that can be fitted to the scope. It will block the LEDs and instead, reflect them so that the light is indirect. Kinda like the lamps the dentists use. You're not blinded by the bulb when you're looking up at those lights.

Moving on to the screen, it is a 7" screen with passable quality. The viewable angle isn't great but it gets the job done. Any issues with the screen quality is solved by connecting the included micro-hdmi cable to your monitor. I've included pictures of both the 7" screen and the ouptut from my monitor.

I've already done a couple of simple projects with the help of this device. I built a garage door opener and gate opener using microcontrollers that are connected to my home automation system. I'm building my confidence with electronics and soldering. Hopefully, I can keep more devices out of landfills by repairing them myself.

Many cars on the market come with a rear-view camera that allows for seeing where the vehicle is moving when in reverse. Often the view appears on a dashboard screen. This is handy when parking and maneuvering while the vehicle is backing up. For vehicles that do not have a rear-view camera the alternative is to add on a kit that provides the same functionality. This is my first experience with such a kit and so far I am pleased with it. It does require doing a little work on the vehicle to set it up but the effort is worth it.

The package contains everything needed to set up this camera system. In addition to the camera and the screen, the kit includes the mounting screws for the actual camera as well as all of the wiring to connect everything together and to the power (reverse lights). There is also a mini-remote for interacting with the video screen though this is slightly inconvenient.

I spent a good deal of time reading and rereading the directions and concluded that the instructions could have been better. There are three pieces of documentation in the box; one shows a generalized set of four different configurations for connecting everything together (the fourth diagram on this sheet matches the configuration you want), one is a photocopied image of a wired system and the third is a “User’s Manual” which is one half-sheet of paper with a brief summarization of the product. There really needs to be a better documentation set than this.

If you are not skilled in working with electrical systems, either plan on this taking a good while or have someone you trust install the system. It’s not especially hard to set one of these up, but it does take some patience and a little bit of knowledge of the layout of the car’s wiring. I have worked on car electrical systems in the distant past so I had a vague familiarity, but it still took me a while to have everything set up and working.

Once wired the system is fairly straightforward to use. If it is wired up properly (meaning everything is connected to power on both ends and the two main components can see one another) it works nicely. The image when the camera is feeding to the monitor is bright and reasonably clear; the brightness can be adjusted as needed which helps when using this system at night. Another reviewer commented that he used a different camera connected to this system - while I am personally satisfied with the image quality, it’s reassuring to know that you can use another video camera if desired or necessary.

The addition of the remote will appeal to some, but for me it’s a component that can easily be lost. The menu system on the monitor provides the same functionality as the remote and this is good enough for me.

This is my first experience with rear-view video systems and though it gave me a little trouble setting up it was from lack of good documentation and inexperience, not from being a bad product. Once installed this is a nice and easy-to-use video system. Time will tell how long it works.

Let me start off by saying I've owned Kindles and other e-readers so I can say I'm already somewhat familiar with the concept. I really like what I'm seeing here for the price of this product! This is a small / affordable e-ink device that makes it ideal for all kinds of things.
Personally, I'm a big fan of Overdrive to take books out of our local libraries for free on readers. My biggest complaint on Kindle readers is that this was always a hassle - I needed to do it ON A DIFFERENT DEVICE. A laptop or phone with a browser was necessary because you could not access Overdrive to explore content directly. On the Kobo, like other non-Amazon devices, you are free to browse directly on the reader, find a title you like and click borrow, all for FREE and 100% legal! This is a huge selling point to me. My kids can browse the YA and children's' section and find all kinds of content right on the device using an account they made with their local library card.
The screen is great for little hands as well as big hands, it even looks great displaying some graphic novel pages (albeit in greyscale obviously). I found that I had zero problems connecting to my Wifi, and downloading books is fast and easy. Battery life is excellent as well! The only caveat is that when you DO need to charge it, it's the slightly-older micro-USB charging plug. I wish it would have been a USB-C as most of our micro USB cables are being replaced with the new standard, and in 2021 its a little weird to still have a new product use an old standard... but this is a minor issue at best.

Some really cool mentions:
1) There IS an experimental web browser function. It's very limited, mostly due to the limitations of using E-ink instead of a display that can be updated faster like LCD/OLED, but super cool for browsing websites for text articles!
2) You can manually load a document to use as a screensaver!! This was a very cool find for me. There's a folder on the device when you plug it into your computer called .screensaver , and if you place a document in there (jpg, pdf, whatever) it will display it when the device is powered off / sleep. I actually put our weekend calendar information on there so we can refer to times / reminders, and stuck some magnetic strips to the back of the reader. Now it sits on our fridge when no one is reading, displaying our calendar and saving us at least one sheet of paper to print per month! Then whenever someone wants to read, my kids (or me!) can take it off the fridge, read a few pages, then put it back there for the next person. Because the Nia is a small and light tablet, it stays on really easily! My old Kindle was too large and fragile for that.

Way to go, Kobo!

I love the look and feel of this VERSO "DARWIN" CROCCO standing cover for the Kindle Fire HD 8.9" tablet. Red is my favorite color, and the faux crocodile texture is really fun.

This cover holds the tablet firmly with silicone-enhanced elastic corner bands (patent pending). The bands have a rubbery material on the underside of the elastic that grips the surface beneath it, so the tablet does not slide around inside the cover or want to fall out. (I have screen protector film on my tablet, which seems like a good idea when a tablet is held in place by elastic bands rather than a hard plastic shell. This [[ASIN:B009NHU556 3-Pack Ultra-Clear Screen Protector)]] is easy to apply, and you get three chances to get it on right.)

The cover's built-in stands are quite intriguing. There are two of them attached to the inside of the front cover. One stand supports the tablet at a low angle for typing; the other supports it more or less upright for watching movies. Both provide comfortable viewing angles. The stands themselves are flat, microfiber-covered pieces that match the rest of the cover's interior. You pick the stand angle you want, and open out the appropriate stand. The stand is connected to the cover on top and also with a ribbon underneath, so that the stand converts into a triangular support for your tablet. This design is very clever, and I would consider it perfect if I hadn't already tried the [[ASIN:B009X0167Y Marware Vibe Standing Case]], which is a little easier to set up and offers more viewing angles.

This Verso "Darwin" Crocco cover has an elastic band that holds it tightly closed inside a book or tote bag, as well as an automatic magnetic wake/sleep feature. For the wake/sleep feature to work, you must insert your tablet with the camera at the left and the charging port at the right. This I don't like, because the charging port ends up at the tablet's bottom edge when you use the stands. This means you are limited to using the low-angle stand whenever your tablet is plugged in, because the plug contacts the table top. (With the Marware Vibe cover, the charging port ends up at the tablet's top edge, so you can use the tablet at any angle when it's plugged in.)

According to the accompanying retail literature, this Verso "Darwin" Crocco cover is "compatible" with the Kindle Fire HD 8.9", the Nook HD+, "and more". Because the cover holds the tablet with elastic bands, it should fit any tablet near in size to the large Fire or the large Nook. However, it is definitely too small for an iPad 2.

For me, it's difficult to choose between the Marware Vibe cover and the Verso "Darwin" cover. But in the end, as usually happens, good looks win out. My 8.9" Kindle Fire HD tablet is going to stay in the red faux-crocodile-skin cover, which is eye-catching, looks and feels luxurious, and is extremely well made.

I'm having a serious problem with the Denon DHT-T110 TV Speaker Base that apparently the other reviewers are not having. I called Denon Technical Support and after spending a lot of time behind the TV set making sure all the wires were hooked up correctly and then pressing different buttons on the Denon Speaker base, they can't figure out what is causing this problem. And the problem is this: No sound signal is going to the Denon speaker base through the TV from the Roku player. The Roku works just fine through the regular TV speakers and is connected directly to the TV via HDMI. When the input on the TV is set to stream via the Roku no sound comes through the Denon and it turns off. If I increase the volume on the TV speakers you hear sound. If the input is changed to TV with the TV sound off, sound will come through the Denon. Also, if a DVD is played on the DVD player which is connected to the TV, the sound comes through the Denon. It just won't put out sound when the Roku input is being used. And that's a real bummer for me because we watch a lot of Netflix and Amazon streaming through our Roku. I am using the digital optical cord included with the Denon Speaker Base. I have it connected to the Digital Optical "Out" on the back of my Sharp 37" flat screen TV to the digital optical "In" on the back of the Denon Speaker Base.

I will keep working on this problem, and if anyone reading this has any idea that might fix it please say so in the comments section. I would love very much to have it work and to raise the star level to 5. When sound does come through the Denon it's great! Loud, clear and no buzzes or rattles whatsoever like when the volume is turned all the way up when using the TV speakers. I love that it can get loud and there's no rattles or weird vibrations. and the night mode is very useful since the TV room is located underneath the main bedroom and my husband has to go to bed early since he has to go to work early. I like to stay up late and watch Netflix/Amazon or other streaming channels through the Roku (oops! That doesn't work through the Denon) and I keep the volume down lest it wake him up. I was really looking forward to using the Denon night sound function.

The Denon tech suggested hooking everything up to another TV to see if the problem is the Roku player or my TV. Unfortunately, I don't have another TV to test out the units to try and isolate the lack of sound from the Roku player to the Denon. I was really wanting to use this for night listening, but since I can't I will take the Denon to my mom's nursing home and hook it up to her small, flat-screen TV. Since she's half deaf, it might can help her hear the sound better. I will update this review afterwards.

Original review:

Surprise! I actually love this computer.

I mean, I am a bit of a power user, so I have a big gaming laptop and a couple of servers throughout my house, not to mention a few purpose-built niche laptops. So while I was a bit skeptical of this machine before it came since I saw the low price tag, I think it's awesome for the right purpose.

I mean, I totally get what "Chrome Books" are trying to do - be low price, low weight computers that run basically "from the cloud". But who really wants a computer running Android? I mean, there are phones for that. So running Windows 10 is a great idea. (Not that I love Windows 10, but if you install Windows Classic Shell and tweak, tweak, tweak away...turn off all permissions, get rid of all the stupid crap they're trying to sell you, use an offline account, then it is almost as good as Windows 7).

Anyway, you don't get a lot of fancy new stuff, but what you do get is important: 1080p screen, mini-HDMI out (odd choice, would have gone for micro or even full, but whatever), 2 USB 3.0 (No C), a micro-SD card reader, headphone jack, and a M.2 expansion port.

64GB of ROM is pretty small, but they installed so little bloatware (just one program to make the touchpad better - I uninstalled it because I didn't recognize it, am paranoid, and figure I can adjust it with whatever is built into Windows) that you have ~45GB free. Should be enough for stuff like MS office and other junk you may want. But you know what, I have a 36TB NAS, and Windows works flawlessly with it, so if I'm using this as a home machine, it's not a problem. I don't much care for public cloud, so if I want to take this on the road, I can always stream (usually still reach my NAS) or just throw in an SSD (by the way, it only takes the small form factor) or a giant micro-SD card (although admittedly either of these factors takes away the fact that this item is inexpensive to begin with.

6GB of RAM is sufficient for a computer that is not meant to be a workhorse.

It's really thin and light and with a real keyboard is just delightful as opposed to dealing with a tablet; a tablet always disappoints me when I'm trying to get something done quickly. It also boots up fast due to NAND memory. It doesn't even look cheap or anything. It actually looks pretty good.

It has a regular "wall wart" type AC adapter instead of the usual laptop power brick. I like this, but the cord is a little short (on the other hand, it is likely easily replaced with something in my electronics closet) The barrel adapter goes into the right side of the device (which is not abnormal, but less normal than the back or the other side in my experience) and the unfortunate part is that it will partially fit into the stereo mini-plug port for headphones on the same spot on the other side, which is likely to cause some confusion.

The only apparent downside is that the keyboard seems...like it vibrates slightly. Like it's not held in tight enough or something. I mean, it does have nice keys and overall I like it, but it just feels slightly weird, although still much better than a tablet roll-out keyboard.

I actually really like this little machine. Not for my main computer or my only computer, but definitely for easy browsing, or a multimedia machine for a teen, or a school computer, a travel computer, whatever. I'd use it for plenty of things, happily.

If you're cool with the memory - and living off a NAS, an SD card, or the cloud - and you're looking for something small and usable, definitely give this some consideration.

Having this clear-sounding radio, blasting my favorite music, is a nice pick-me-up as I shower. But does the design offer me anything more than what I would expect from a typical shower radio?

PROS: It's cleverly designed to mimic the shape of a shampoo. It melds easily into the background. My initial fear was that I would accidentally grab it instead of the real thing, but so far that hasn't happened.

Purchased the Amplify HD from Ubiquiti Labs. Very first Mesh router.

I did however buy the main rougher first and next month adding the mesh points. I wanted to see how good was the coverage on the solo unit before dropping the full amount on 2 mesh points. I'm running ATT Fiber, and wasn't use to using a forced gateway modem. (had to look up connecting a unit to my gateway) My speeds are 300 down and 300 up. Directly connected to the unit I get full speed up and down sometimes lowest down at 280/290 but always full amount or more up stream. Its blazing fast, the app is smooth and the unit has a soft touch that's hard to describe, almost like felt/metal/plastic. Feels premium. As others pointed out, by tapping the screen, you can cycle threw connections (direct connections), time, up and down speeds to see how much data its pulling or reveal the units ID.

PROS: Easy to connect, open and set up. REALLY GOOD RANGE. Much better than the default hardware provided by ATT. I will update the review next month when I get my mesh point. By the looks of other reviews, it shouldn't be an issue.

WARNING: if you're running 1000 down and up. You have to set the router to hardware NAT to ON. Keep in mind this is for direct connections, not Wifi speeds. If you're using 1000 down and up, its common sense to be directly connected. From what I read in thier main forum not using it caps at 500 down and up. You also may NOT need to turn it on. ONLY if your not getting the full speeds in test. So it may work like normal. It also has a built in BRIDGE MODE. If your gateway doesnt have bridge mode. (MOST DO).

#MY SET UP ATT 300 FIBER

At the time of writing this is the new gateway from ATT. Doesnt use bridge mode, but has IP PASS THREW in the firewall settings online. You select the Amplify unit, save and restart everything. This is after connecting the Amplify unit to the provided Gateway and have it running. OR you can set the Amplify unit to BRIDGE MODE and it restarts and avoid doing it from the gateway side. You do lose features doing this. change the settings on gateway side so you dont lose features. After that, the Amplify HD takes over router duty, working side by side. In my case, the Gateway passes the information to my Amplify unit and it takes over. I than just shut off the WIFI from my ATT Gateway and only use the Amplify HD wireless connection.

Update 3/14/2019

Purchased the mesh point and very satisfied with the add on. But wanted to give people a heads up. You can use the single mesh point with a 3rd party router, extending the connection. But does not become a TRUE MESH system that way. You need their router (the cube) and mesh points to become a full mesh system. Also, in the review I stated that it maxes out on 500 wifi speed, that is due to it unit being a duel ban system, instead of tri-ban. (3 bans). 500 max wifi speed is more than enough and using it with the Mesh points improves speed and coverage.

I’ve tested a few similar sets of ear buds with mixed results but I was really impressed with this set.

I read the instruction manual - removed the tiny stickers on each ear bud and plugged in the case. It achieved a full charge in just over an hour.

I removed the ear buds from the case, the right one first and then the left and they paired with each other immediately. I went to my Bluetooth settings in my iPhone and found Haylou-GT1_R and my phone paired with the set with no issue.

I was surprised at the sound quality these tiny ear buds deliver. They can definitely be turned up as loud as you’d want to listen. The bass, midtones and treble is on par for ear buds - even those that are much larger.

I did figure out that the initial way I had them in my ears was upside down when I went to test the calling features. The microphone needs to be pointed towards your mouth for best audio reception and sound quality improves a bit in this position.

Call quality was excellent for both hearing the other person and them hearing you.

In my testing the earbuds had no problem receiving within the 33’ stated range (actually making it to around 40’) and even received clearly through multiple walls - 2 rooms away with the doors closed and many obstacles in between.

The only issue I struggled with was tapping the ear bud to stop / start the music and answer / end calls / activate voice assistant and skip tracks. There is no button, you just tap an area of the exterior of the ear bud but you have to tap a very exact area which isn’t necessary easy to locate as it is not differentiated from the rest. It would have been helpful if the manufacturer put a different texture in that area so you could feel it with your finger to locate it.

While the manufacturers claims these last for 12 hours I found it was closer to 8 under normal use - still excellent. And the case will charge them without it having to be plugged back in which is always a nice feature.

These earbuds excelled in all of my tests showing that they are a high quality, dependable product.

This is a set I wouldn’t hesitate to recommend.

I got this hard shell case in the Clear style mainly to see if the grippers on the bottom of the case would keep my MacBook Pro Retina 15" from sliding off my [[ASIN:B00IV3AEZY lap desk]] when I'm climbing in and out of my recliner, which is where I work. The package comes with two pieces constituting the hard shell case, a screen protector that I may or may not use, and a protective keyboard skin that I know I won't use.

The case is GREAT. It is a perfect fit for my Mac, and I don't even realize it's on it except for the fact that it works MUCH better than the rubberized grips on the bottom of my Mac to hold it firmly on my lap desk—it stays put even when the board is slanted at a 45-degree angle! I wish I had gotten this when I first got my Mac, because I do have a few scratches on it now that this case would have prevented. The fit is so tight, the only thing I don't like about it is that I do have a [[ASIN:B00D6A2Z2C palm rest protector]] on my Mac, and on one side it won't quite fit underneath the case's tab. I'll probably wind up taking a hair off the protector so I don't notice it so much, but I wouldn't have to because it looks like it will stay stuck.

I don't really know how the keyboard skin compares to others on the market, because I hate the things and won't use one. I can say that it does fit the keyboard well and provides cover from spills. I think you can see from my photos how it fits; also how the case fits. The one with my chiweenie Bingo in the picture was taken when I had my lap desk at a precipitous incline, and there was no sliding!

The screen protector has a top and bottom. I thought at first it was not going to fit right, but it's because I had it upside down. It has a protective film over it that you remove once you place it on the screen. I don't know yet if I'm going to use it, because we've got a lot of dog hair floating around and I'm not confident I could get it on without dog hair under it. That happened when I first put the hard shell case on, and I had to remove it and put it back on again.

One thing to note about this case: there are no installation instructions, and there is a definite right way and wrong way to put on both pieces. The lip on the bottom part goes in the front, and the open part is in the back where all your ports are. The top of the case has three tabs on one of the long sides and two tabs on the other. The three-tab side goes at the top of the screen. I don't think you can see these details in my photos. You really can't see that there is a case on it at all unless you look closely.

I'm still just knocked out at how well the grippers on the case grip my lap desk. I broke my last Mac by dumping it off into the floor—actually, Bingo did it. This case is great insurance, and the price is definitely right, even if you wind up only using the case. But with all three protective items, this set is a real bargain. I got this item free in exchange for my honest review, but had I known how great it was, I definitely would have bought it a long time ago.

I've used Skullcandy products before and always found them to be on the mediocre side of a brand name, so I had what I'd think are pretty realistic expectations for this set. At first I just assumed this was their attempt to break into the now flooded market of inexpensive completely wireless earbud market. And you know what- it turns out that's not a bad thing at all.
These offer some impressive fidelity in sound, and unlike some other earbuds which crank up the bass to compensate for being tiny drivers, this actually delivers what I'd consider more realistic sound reproduction. It isn't too bass heavy, but the bass is still there. To be honest, that's something I'm used to hearing only on higher end speakers which don't have anything to prove other than just be good. I was actually surprised to find the microphone was half decent as well, as I've never had a good experience with calls on earbuds before (the mic is just too far from your mouth to work well). These aren't going to be as clear separating your voice from the background as, say, a mic that is closer to your mouth (wired or protruding mic arm), or whatever magic Apple has in their airpods to pull off that directional sound, but honestly I was expecting worse and this surprised me. So, 5 stars for being an above average offering at an excellent price. I'd say that makes this a good value product!

The scroll wheel is similarly well-made, with a smooth feel and slight indents when used for fine-tuned movements. The DPI selection switch is right behind the scroll wheel for easy access. Our AV department bought a BDP-300 so we could release our HD video content on Blu-ray. We bought the expensive Blu-ray burner for the computer, we bought the expensive authoring software, we bought a bunch of expensive BD-R and BD-RW recordable disks and we bought the expensive Sony BDP-300 player, with an eye toward buying a bunch more for our conference rooms if the system worked. It didn't.

We found that the BDP-300 will not play back BD-R or BD-RW discs. Though it might have been possible to be upgraded via a firmware update (like its REALLY expensive big brother can be firmware upgraded) it most likely never will. Thanks a lot, Sony. Way to make an integrated system. No wonder Blu-ray has been so slow to catch on. Thus we as a very large company cannot commit to Blu-ray because we can't play the recorded Blu-ray disks back on even a $400 player. Sigh.

Secondly, if you connect to a digital display that only has DVI-in via an HDMI/DVI adapter or an HDMI/DVI cable adapter, the player doesn't work. I suspect the problem is connected to copy protection schemes built into the multiple HDMI standards.

So, if you have an older HD display that only has DVI-in, forget this "reasonably priced" Blu-ray player. You'll most likely need to use the analog YRB (component) outputs, which is an inferior signal to the digital HDMI output. I did a component/HDMI comparison for my wife and she definitely picked the HDMI as the superior output picture.

There is a workaround that allows the HDMI/DVI to work, but it's a pain: First, connect both the HDMI and component cables to their respective inputs on the display. Now, before powering the player on, manually disconnect the HDMI cable from the back of the player while leaving the component cables connected to the display. Then power up the player and switch the display to the analog "component" input. You can now see the menus and the Blu-ray disk will be able to be played. After you get the movie running, manually plug the HDMI/DVI cable into the back of the player and switch the display to the digital DVI input. The Blu-ray disk now works and allows the menus and other overlaid controls to function normally. As different HDMI copy protection schemes get adopted this trick might fail.

If you have HDMI-in on your display, the player might work, but no guarantees. Bear in mind that the HDMI standard is constantly changing. I think they're up to at least HDMI 1.3 so far, and counting. And a totally new plug protocol is on its way for computer monitors, too, called DisplayPort, which might make it to TV sets, but who knows?

After this little problem was overcome, I finally got to see the picture. It was very nice, especially after I got to see it via my HDMI-DVI workaround. Definitely better than the analog component feed.

The overlaid menus allow you to access the menu anytime, without leaving the movie. Pretty cool. The menus are also more animated and better integrated.

Audio quality is fabulous. Both Dolby and DTS sound great because with all the storage capacity on the disk, the signals don't have to be compressed as much as they are for a standard DVD.

If you want the very, very best audio, though, you can select "uncompressed" and route the RCA audio outputs directly into your amp's dedicated preamp inputs. This takes the Dolby and DTS compression systems out of the picture altogether. So you are hearing multiple uncompressed audio tracks sent directly to your amp.

The worst part of the Blu-ray player is the time it takes to "boot" up. It's really a dedicated computer running an operating system. Java, at least, and maybe more. Thus it takes a full two minutes to fire up. You press the power button and nothing happens. After about ten seconds, you get a display that says "power on." After about 90 seconds, the machine is finally ready to play your disk. Give it a lot of time to fire up, especially the very first time you plug it in. After the initial plug-in/power-on sequence, the manual says it will be subsequently faster. But not by much. And the system can "crash," requiring you to turn it off and reboot. It happened several times to me as I moved too quickly between menu selections.

Overall, this player can put out a great picture, eventually, and after learning a bunch of quirks. I don't think it's ready for prime time, though. For the price it should be much better: faster boot up and with the ability to play back recorded Blu-ray disks.

Buy the BDP-300 knowing you will be replacing it for some reason in a year or two.

UPDATE:

I rented Universal's Hellboy II on Blu-ray tonight.

It crashed the player. Think "Blue Screen of Death" but without the blue screen and a longer boot sequence. I repeated the process six times.

I was about to flame this inop player when here on Amazon it was suggested to update to Firmware 4.20.

I went to Sony's site and found even newer 4.30 firmware. You download the exe and click on it to uncompress it. This creates an ISO disk image. You burn this to a new CD as an image (very important--an IMAGE, not a data disk.) Turn on the player and stick the CD in. It took 13 minutes for the update to install. When it's done it says "DL OK" on the player.

Player works like it's supposed to. It will play BD-R, too. In fact, it can even play a weird hybrid I can make with Sony Vegas editing software where I can burn a Blu-ray disk image to a standard DVD and play it as a
Blu-ray.

First of all, the signal quality is great over my 300' of CAT5e cable going from my entertainment system in front of my room to my projector around the back (cable goes behind walls and snakes around furnishings to get where it needs to go). It is fast and responsive, and the lag seems minimal if any. I love that it can also be used as a pass through, and that it only requires power on ONE side! My old HDMI extender required a power adapter on both the tx and rx side, but this can actually send power over the network cable (PoE) so that the other side does not need its own adapter. Now THAT's awesome!
This is one of the primary reasons I was interested in this, as there are two times I use such an adapter: When I use my projector instead of my TV for movies, and when moving a camera around at an event that I want to send a live feed back to a screen or streaming box for. Currently I have to supply power at both ends of the network cable, but I imagined ONLY needing power on the receiver, and having THAT power the transmitter. For example, in the case of the camera, I could have the screen receiving the signal send power to the transmitter by the camera using PoE and be somewhat more free of tethered power on that side. Also, when using the projector, I could turn on the outlet controlling the projector via remote and have it power on the transmitter behind the TV as well. Less wires and outlet spaces where already difficult / congested is good! THE PROBLEM, however, is that this thing misses its potential by only sending power from the TRANSMITTER! In other words, I can send power from the tx with PoE to the rx side, but the RECEIVER can't power the transmitter! It only goes the same direction as the HDMI signal. This, to me, was disappointing as that's the side I wanted to save from having more wires to plug in. Not the receiving side. That side is never an issue to supply power.
So I was a little upset about that. But otherwise, it is a solid product that seems to do what it claims to, and so far seems more reliable than my previous setup. If it could send power using EITHER side, it would be perfect! So close this time!

I own ALL of the kensington line of trackballs (clearly a trackball nut). From the original Expert Mouse (using a serial connection) all the way to this one. I can see how some purists are very touchy about their trackball performing and as it becomes an extension of interfacing with the computer, it's critical that it performs well.

PROS:
* Nice compact footprint; Not too demanding for space.
* Comes with the little ergonomic squishy thingy for a wrist-rest.
* The ball 'stays in' the unit even if you turn it over! This is a new concept for their trackballs! (you can pop it out if you need to condense for travel)
* Scroll wheel is nice; A feature present only in the higher-end trackballs.

CONS:
* BUTTONS! YUK! The button has some kind of contact issue where if you press it gently enough, you hear and feel a little 'click' but you didn't actuate the button! You must press it harder, and get a louder firmer CLICK! (really kinda mushy) to click it! I have tried different spots on the button and it's all the same! This is ALMOST a deal killer for me, but I'm going to give it some time, see if the button wears in and that false-click goes away over time.
* Scroll wheel is not free-flowing like on the modern expert mouse. With that sucker, you can fling the wheel and it will roll atleast for a half-second or so! This one really resists movement so it's more like a mouse-wheel than a scroll-wheel. It does not have a 'ribbed' feel, it rolls smoothly but it's not a 'on rails' as other models.

My personal favorite is still the modern expert mouse. It's massive (like a little tank on your desktop!) but you can navigate quickly with it, and use it in the manner a trackball was designed to be used.

Hope my review helps you!

Over the last year, I've tried various hdmi capture devices and this one is the lowest priced and best of them. The most common problem with capture cards are their drivers. Custom drivers either introduce too much lag or are simply unsupported by various software.

OBS, of course, fully supports this product and VLC can open capture device successfully . Turn off buffering in OBS or VLC and you get near real-time performance.

I've tested this capture device with FireTV and Nintendo Switch and both worked well.

I've even connected this to my phone through a USB-A to USB-C connector. On Android, it is necessary to download a "usb camera" app, but I can say that with the right software, this device will work.

In the last week, I've been using this for my Zoom calls. It had no problems working with my Alienware M17xR4 with AGA, The AGA has an ASUS Rog Strix 1080 Ti in it with 2 27" Monitors and a 55" TV attached to it. I was able to add a fourth monitor using the DP on the USB hub, but the 4th monitor also worked through the video card as well. It took a little load off the graphics card but seemed to slow down the system a bit. It's kind of like using the internal monitor on the laptop when docked. Usually both are not detected only one, but for some reason I am able to connect both and that's how it should be considering that was the goal of USB in the first place.

Overall this is one of the best hubs I have owned to date. It adds a lot of functionality for a good price. The Micro-SD and SD card readers are easy to access and use. It's very user friendly and required no real setup even in my advanced environment. That kind of shocked me to be honest. It even works with virtual machines when configured. I like tech. I've had a computer since the commodore Vic-20 came out. That being said I'm not into competing with or against other computers and computer users. I don't run testing or speed diagnostics on my hardware. If it works and feels or seems to be working as advertised and expected I'm completely happy. I just don't care to sit here are see how many micro-seconds faster my new drive is than my older ones.
All that being said I use external drives exclusively for maintaining backups of my personal files, photos, documents, music, eBooks, Etc. Everything else I can simply reinstall in a couple hours. I don't have that many things installed. My computing needs are simple. But I have lost files due to a drive crash so I meticulously make weekly backups of my important files.
