I selected the Meade 20225 TerrStar telescope as my youngest son is often asking me where to find certain constellations in the sky and has always been interested in celestial events. I thought this telescope might be a good entry level scope with which to foster his interest. While it does work, I would hesitate to recommend it, mainly on the basis of its build quality but also for its usability.

My son decided to assemble it himself and it was done by the time I got home from work. He had no issues putting it together and he managed to get it assembled correctly without any assistance. In short, it's easy to put together. However, his very first comment to me was that it was very cheaply made, and it did not take long to determine what he meant. The whole assembled unit is slightly wobbly and a little unstable though it does not feel like it will tip over without a little help - I would be more concerned about it breaking outright. There is much more lightweight plastic than metal and there are numerous opportunities to break components which all feel cheaply made.

One of the packing decisions made was to put the lenses in the carry bag which is folded up in the box. So, until we realized this we thought the lenses were not included in the package. While this is not a major problem - all the parts are there - it does show a lack of understanding of the consumer who is likely to call the support line first before searching the carry bag.

We took the telescope outside and started looking for objects in the sky, and we discovered a serious issue. Once we find something to view, the scope's positional setting is so loose that even the very slightest bump either knocks the object from view or causes the scope to shake which makes viewing impossible. At a minimum the scope itself should be mounted tightly and should move only with deliberate effort. I have found no way to tighten this up which is very unfortunate.

I have trouble recommending this telescope. It's very cheaply made and this shows all through the product from assembly to use. Research other options before selecting this telescope.

[[VIDEOID:ce9372435451bc2c3bda4d2794c79f4f]] I am really impressed with this camera. The Flip MinoHd package pretty much does everything the average user needs it to do. The Flip comes partly charged right out of the box, but they do suggest that you let it charge for 5 hours before you use it. I plugged it into a USB port on my laptop for about an hour before using it and the battery was fully charged. Operation is a cinch. Turn it on, point and press the red button. The zoom in button is + the zoom out is -. Delete is a trashcan. How much more obvious can this be? The only problem I have with the recording is that pressing the zoom controls doesn't always produce the desired effect immediately and I tend to get a bit of a jitter in the frames where I'm trying to get it to recognize the command. Of course I'm still getting used to holding the camera, so I expect that I'll get steadier as I learn the feel of it in my hand.

Uploading your vids to your computer is also simple. Again, plug it into a spare USB port and there they are. There's software included on the camera's hard drive, and it's a nice little program called FlipShare that helps you label, sort and share your vids pretty easily. Though again, I do have a quibble with the saving part. It will only let you save to your C drive in the video library. Meh, I figure it's simple enough to copy the vids to another drive when I'm done. The software also helps you cobble together shorter vids into a movie, complete with music -- you can use the tunes they've provided or any MP3 on your computer -- which can be softer than the sound on the video, louder or which can replace the sound completely. Their selection of music is fairly uninspiring, but what can you really expect? We have an old DVD player in our basement that tries to up convert but it is not always that great. It has some nice features that were great when we got it, but we wanted another one to replace it that did not take up so much room.

WHAT THIS WAS USED TO REPLACE
The DVD machine this replaced was a really old Philips. It played all regions. No fancy settings, except a sleep timer setting that shut it off after so long. The menu was ancient and very clumsy to navigate.

DID THIS PLAY AS WELL AS THE OLDER ONE?
This DVD player played DVDs as well as the older one. So far we have not had any issues with it. It was only hooked up to the HDMI and the used a mini USB to USB cord the plugged into the outlet. We made sure that it was powerful enough to run the player.

PICTURE
The picture was comparable to the old DVD player- perhaps a bit nicer in some cases. I am actually surprised that it has performed as well as it has.

TRAVEL
I have to say that traveling to a cabin we go to occasionally was nice. We are able to bring this DVD player with us to plug into any TV and watch some DVDs if we want to. It is without TV service so DVD is the only way to really have entertainment if we want it.

DOES IT PLAY BLURAY?
This is not designed to play BluRay.

ANY ISSUES?
This is not a top of the line DVD player with super high definition. If you are looking for that, this isn't it. Is it good DVD quality? Yes. I think so. If you have the right set up, it is a great way to take up little room and still be able to play DVDs. I am not sure I would have this as my permanent player in my bedroom or anything. But it is great to use once in a while at home or travel.

THE BOTTOM LINE
Although this is not fancy or super high quality, it plays DVDs as well or better than our old player so we are happy with it. The footprint is small and it is portable.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. This is a decent player and so far has been good in a pinch to use for playing DVDs. I like the small footprint and portability especially when we have to go somewhere for a while. It is nice to be able to tuck it into our luggage/bags to take with us. The remote is a bonus.

A seller replaced a different defective FM transmitter unit with this one for me (mine has the Kollea brand name on it, but this is the identical unit, private-labeled). This is a better product than what it replaced, but is not without it's flaws. I have three (*UPDATE: now four, and the fourth one is a deal-breaker--see below) complaints with this unit:

1) It will not automatically reconnect to my phone about 75% of the time. I have to manually shut Bluetooth off and turn it back on on the phone, sometimes a few times before it pairs successfully. This is a hassle--a PITA. Every time I get in the car, I have to go through this process--every time power is cut from the transmitter, actually, so if your passenger knocks it and it pops out of the 12V socket, it will have to be re-paired, which is supposed to happen automatically, but does not, and you then have to go through the process. Frustrating.

2) Charge output is only 1.0A. this is why I returned the first one--phone gives a "slow charging" warning when charging from this unit, regardless of what USB cable I use (I tried four different cables, all of which I know for certain can carry 2.1A).

3) Callers have occasionally complained they cannot hear me well when using this unit, and I occasionally (but not often) encounter FM interference. I believe Bluetooth itself is part of the problem, and anyone who has used a few Bluetooth headsets or units like this knows audio quality is terrible. Period. We just deal with it. Add to that the burden of having to transmit your signal via FM to a car stereo and the user-side audio (what you will hear in your car) is always going to be craptastic.

4) (*UPDATE) When paired, voice recognition on my phone, which is usually quite good, becomes severely impaired. This is also likely the culprit for complaint #3, above. I suspect this is because when paired, it tries to use the built-in microphone for voice recognition instead of the microphones on my phone (of which there are 4). It is disabling the extremely good microphones in my phone (Nokia lumia Icon which is well known for having incredible audio input) and using the unit's crappy microphone instead. This microphone is located in the unit, which is attached to the center console of my car near the shifter, and thus picks up all the vibrations and related road and engine noise transmitted through the structure of the car as I drive. This approach is terrible. I have stopped using the unit for anything requiring voice input, including telephone calls. In other words, this is just a big awkward charger now, and one that charges painfully slowly (see complaint #2). If it were possible to disable the onboard mic, and use the mics in my phone instead for calls and voice recognition, this would be a much more serviceable unit As it is now, it is just a piece of junk.

Cannot recommend this item. There are definitely worse products out there. I have not tried them all, but of those I have used, this is the best one so far. I will likely keep using it until the lack of automatic pairing pushes me over the edge with it one day and I get something else. (*UPDATE: this thing just does not work well, and I am now looking for something else.)

I have worked with a number of trackballs, my most successful being a Logitech M570 which served me well for years. I finally wore it out and after some research I purchased the Logitech MX Ergo to replace it. I have had it about three days, and it has already proven to be exactly what I had hoped and more. I was attracted to the fact that it works both as a wireless mouse with a USB receiver as well as a Bluetooth mouse. I have two computers on my desk, one being a Windows 10 system and the other being a Linux (Arch-based) system. My old trackball worked with both though I had to move the receiver between the systems, so I went with the assumption that this one would also work with both.

I connected the trackball to my Windows system via Bluetooth and it has been flawless in operation. It connects without intervention and it works exactly as expected - all buttons work as they should and the operation is very smooth and predictable.

I plugged the USB receiver into the Linux machine, pushed the channel button on the trackball and it immediately started working on the Linux machine, even though it was still paired to the Windows system via Bluetooth. It works exactly as it should and I have had absolutely no issues with the trackball on my Linux installation. So now, I can switch back and forth between the two systems with the push of the channel button and without having to connect or disconnect anything. It simply works, and the switch-over is fast. The take-away for me is that I no longer need two mice on the desk.

I friend came over with his MacBook and there was no issue at all with connecting the trackball via USB. We did not try connecting via Bluetooth.

The trackball has a metal plate on the bottom that is held in place with magnets, and depending on how the plate is attached the trackball can be tilted to ease wrist strain. The plate serves another purpose too - it adds a lot of weight to the trackball. Even without the plate, the trackball is hefty and has some mass to it, but the plate just makes it even more so. The Lensbaby Edge 80 Optic is one of Lensbaby's "swappable" optics for its line of lenses. It has a focal length of 80mm and features a 12-blade aperture with a range from f/2.8 through f/22. It can function as a regular 80mm f/2.8 lens when facing forward on your camera, but this optic's special feature is that it allows you to employ the usual Lensbaby bend and tilt to reposition your plane of focus along any point not parallel with your camera's sensor plane.

The usual Lensbaby lens tilt allows you to place the point of focus (with varying diffusion all around that point) but did not allow you to change the plane of focus itself. With this optic you can put a "slice of focus" through your image in creative ways. For example, you can highlight a certain aspect of the photo (such as producing a portrait where the eyes are in sharpest focus and everything else is softly blurred), or you can create the "false miniature" effect where the objects photographed take on the appearance of miniature scale models. The optic also has a close focus mode that will allow a close focus distance of 17".

There is a bit of learning curve for this optic. Expect to play around for bit before you get the hang of it. There are some good video tutorials on the Lensbaby site. I included a couple of example photos with this review.

You don't need to swap lenses to get back to "normal." As I mentioned earlier, the Edge 80 behaves like a normal 80mm lens when you aren't employing any of its tilt features. The aperture ring on the optic adjusts smoothly, and focusing and tilt occurs on the lens body itself. The shift from regular focus mode to close focus mode is a little tight -- you have to firmly pull the front edge of the optic outward. But, I imagine that's as it should be to avoid it shifting by itself.

My one source of frustration so far is in detaching the optic from the lens itself. Suffice to say you will need to review Lensbaby's instructions for this, and practice several times before you can successfully detach the optic. My first try took almost half an hour, which is not a delay you would want to experience in the field. I did get better with practice, but it's still a bit of tricky. Older hands might suffer more than younger hands. I've found in practice you can get by with swapping out other Lensbaby optics from the lens without detaching the lens from your camera, but with the Edge 80 optic, you really need to detach the whole lens first in order to get the optic out of the lens. That will allow you to get the best grip on the components when performing the detach maneuver.

Note that the optic in this product listing is not sold with a lens. The Edge 80 only works with the latest line of Lensbaby Lenses (NOT the 1.0, 2.0 or 3G). You need at least one of the current Lensbaby Lenses to use this optic. The optic works with the Muse, Composer, Control Freak and Scout lenses; it can also work with the Composer with Tilt Transformer, but you need to buy the Macro Converters in order to use the Edge 80 optic with that lens. Note too that if you want true macro capability, you will need to buy the Macro Converters anyway, regardless of which Lensbaby lens you have (their earlier Macro accessories will not work with this optic).

Normal in-lens tilt-shift lens are expensive ($1200-$2500). While the Edge 80 does not give you all the features of such a dedicated lens, it is a highly affordable alternative that provides enough capability for many tilt/shift needs. It's a great way to get into this type of photography without breaking the bank. Highly recommend.

I was trying to setup a studio for a multi-cam live Q&A web-broadcast, and this unit came highly recommended. Turns out this might not be the best choice, and the whole experience sort of leaves a bad taste in my mouth.
First the good:
The functionality of this device really impressed me! All I wanted was a live HDMI switch that would let me keep the audio separate (so it would be live regardless of camera active) and wouldn't blank the display when swapping inputs (which consumer hdmi switches do, as the connection re-negotiates). This unit goes far beyond that, using industry standard production controls for cuts and cross fades, title / graphic overlays, and even some basic Chroma Keying for doing live green screen (that was a surprise!). The little LCD is pretty neat too.
And now, THE BAD:
THERE IS NO HDMI OUTPUT. It only supports SDI, which no one mentioned to me when I said I wanted to toggle between HDMI sources. There is an HDMI preview which shows you multi-view (all the cameras in a grid), but no regular HDMI output. Only SDI, which is ridiculous to me. You have the HDMI port there, at least give us the option to choose whether it is multi-view or program out! Black Magic claims they didn't offer the HDMI out because the connection isn't reliable, so they want to push SDI as the output. But that isn't acceptable, the hardware is there, give us a choice! The result of this stream is going to an internet broadcaster which supports an HDMI input only! Now I'd need to purchase yet another accessory to convert the final product back into an HDMI signal so it can get where it needs to go.
Oh, and speaking of additional accessories that need to be purchased, THE BOX LACKS A POWER CORD. You have to source your own. I received these as a free review sample. I want to point out that these are hard-wired only. They use a 3.5mm connector and ARE NOT bluetooth. If you want phones for critical listening and transcribing music (or listening to a raw feed before mixdown) these are perfect. Bluetooth always entails some loss of sound quality, but these, and other direct connect phones, do not.

They are neutral enough to pass for high end in-ear monitors (IEMs), but there is a little bias on the low end. As long as you take that into account you can mentally compensate when listening to raw feeds.

One of the things that I found impressive is I could not detect any bias towards the mid range frequencies, nor do the high end frequencies sound compressed. For me this means that I can listen to acoustic jazz and hear the music as originally recorded. This is especially important for a lot of mid 1950s recordings before engineers started playing games with the mix. For these phones I sampled tracks from [[ASIN:B00CJYWUM6 At the Showboat / See What I Mean? / Settlin' In]] and [[ASIN:B000QQV5FM Dorothy Donegan Live]], and listened to the entire two hours and forty-eight minutes of Erroll Garner's [[ASIN:B00ZJ5QXDO The Complete Concert By The Sea]]. That test proved that these phones are absolutely superb for folks for love music.

While this is claimed to be for Android, I tested it on an iPad Air 2 and a ThinkPad T61 - it worked beautifully on both. In fact, on the ThinkPad I was playing from CD instead of an MP3 file and the sound quality was better than a direct connect from my Note 4 phone.

A few notes about the physical characteristics and features: I tested out the control block using my Note 4 phone and found it to be less than intuitive. I prefer controlling functions using those integrated in my Note 4 (including EQ.) I love the tangle free cord, and the comfort of the phones though. Everything about the construction and sound are of the highest quality.

Even worse, after I emailed VisionTek, it took days before I got a response. They wanted to know how I was doing the benchmarking. This was stupid: my original email gave them enough details to know that the USB 2.0 speeds I was seeing could not be due to benchmarking flaws. Nevertheless, I gave them another detailed answer. ORIGINAL REVIEW:

I ordered this drive a couple of months ago, and have been using it steady ever since.

I wanted a thumb drive that is really an SSD. In particular, that uses a proper controller, as opposed to the crap el cheapo controllers in almost all thumb drives. This VisionTek drive is one of the very few that fits the bill. I bought it instead of Corsair's because it is slightly physically smaller. The review that best informed my judgement was this one:
[...]

Overall, I am pleased with this drive.

It has been, and remains, reasonably fast for an SSD drive in this form factor. For example, using the freeware benchmarking program AS SSD just now, I measured:

sequential read speed = 156.91 MB/s
sequential writes as 101.43 MB/s
4k random read = 16.74 MB/s
4k random write= 63.26 MB/s
4k-64 thread random read = 16.76 MB/s
4k-64 thread random write= 72.84 MB/s
read access time = 0.155 ms
write access time = 0.347 ms

(The above was measured in the drive's first partition, which is a 8 GB FAT32 partition that I have strictly for backwards compatibility with certain software or operating systems that require it, such as GParted or Clonezilla live images. I do most of my storage in the second partition, which is all the remaining space formatted in NTFS with 4K block size.)

My device gets warm, but NOT HOT (where I define the start of hot as when it becomes uncomfortable to touch).

I love the fact that it has a cap, and that the cap can be put on the back when plugged in. My previous thumb drive was a Sandisk Extreme Pro slider which eventually broke; never want a slider again.

I have 3 moderate complaints that prevent me from rating it at 5 stars. First, it is bigger than I would like. Sure, it is still small enough that you can still carry it around in your pocket, and I do, all day long, but I would like it to be smaller if possible. Second, the case, while made of high quality metal, has some edges and corners that are sharper than they out to be. Third, the paint has started to chip in places (like those sharp points).

Overall, this is the best thumb drive currently shipping that I am aware of, but it could be improved. VisionTek: I hope that you are reading this review.

When I first purchased my 3 TB MBL some time ago I was quite pleased. Network access, remote access, even an android app. In short, everything my DLink had plus the app and a nicer look on the shelf. I used it extensively for pulling up photos on my cell phone when I was bored as well as to store my most important files. I didn't back them up, a back-up drive is something I kept saying I would add later...

14 months later (note the 12 month warranty had just expired) the drive stopped being accessible over the network. I spent a week and at least 40 hours of my time going back and forth with tech support by e-mail and trying every option they could offer, and the result was that they deemed the unit broken. They said that the unit can not be opened because that would break the drive inside, and they said that they can't fix it. They "kindly" offered me a referral to one of several companies that give them a kick back for data recovery services. Incidentally, I asked two for pricing by e-mail and they didn't respond.

So I took the unit apart and bought a new unit and took that one apart and swapped the drives. Neither one worked. After talking to support again it turns out that WD didn't want these to be upgradable because if they were upgradable you could buy a cheap drive instead of a new unit so they code each board to the drive that will be in it. TO make matters worse, they encoded the drive in a Linux format that no known version of Linux can translate. Attaching it to my Linux system I couldn't mount it using any utility. Several Linux recovery programs couldn't do anything either.

Okay, having told you why I will never buy a WD NAS again, I should now tell you how to fix this if you have the same problem that I do: DiskInternals makes a program called Linux Reader. That's right, Linux can't read the drive but a program designed to read Linux drives from within Windows can! Recovering the data to a drive is time consuming though. I tried it all at once but that froze after a few days. Then I tried one major directory at a time and that worked better. But recovering nearly 3 TB of data has taken a very long time! I'm about 3 MONTHS into the recovery effort and I have about 400 GB remaining. After starting on my wife's computer because mine is a laptop and causing a few crashes and a lot of delays I finally had to pull out an older computer and set it up just to run this program.

If anyone has the same problem and can't get this solution to work, I'll do my best to help if you simply reply to this review and give me all the details. If anyone is considering buying a WD NAS, I want to encourage you to buy a DLink model 323 (I think the 325 is the current version but it is missing some features so I'd get an older one) instead. I've had that thing running for 5 years without a glitch!

I happen to use a D-Link DIR 1360 as my internet router at home, and while it does a decent job broadcasting signal around me, it is located at one corner of our home which means the opposite corner of the house has too many barriers for a fast signal. And if I want to take my laptop out to the porch? No reliability at all!
But with this placed a few rooms over from the router, it has greatly extended my network and the speed of things nearby it. It was super simple to set up, too! I'm not sure if that's just because I happen to have a D-Link router, but all I had to do was press the setup button on the router and extender while plugged in next to it, then once setup I could unplug and move it wherever I wanted to extend to. No app or IT knowledge required! Literally press the button, wait a few minutes for the lights to turn green, and good to go! The access point matches the original name of my router, so it is all completely invisible to the user. The device picks whichever device is closer / stronger and automatically connects to it without any user intervention, much like a cell phone. Now, this is only possible because my router supports this mesh-style setup. Otherwise you'll have to do one of those alternative SSID things where the device sees two networks and has to decide which one to connect to. The first was is preferable obviously, and just works better in addition to being cleaner.

With my laptop in my living room (on the other side of the house from my router), I used to get somewhere between 20-40mbps in my speed tests downloading. That's not terrible, but I'm paying for 300mbps service! But with this plugged in the middle of my home, that jumped to 80-90mbps reliably! Still not the 200+ speeds I get if only a room or two away from the router, but definitely an improvement by almost 2x... and spots outside on the porch that rarely had coverage before now do.

HOWEVER, like any extender, this WILL introduce some lag to your network. This is the part I was warning about in the headline, as most people think extenders will improve your performance across the board, which isn't true. While my download and upload speed improved, my Ping time degraded from 8ms to 14 (lower is better). That extra hop from the extender back to the router has a cost. Now, that difference shouldn't make a huge difference in most things, 14ms is still pretty respectable, however a larger ping lag can effect real-time performance like lag in multiplayer games and video call performance. Arguably, in those cases, a lower ping is more important than higher speeds. So if I'm having trouble with gaming lag or video call echo, I'd probably unplug this and go with the original weaker signal to the router directly. But if I'm going outside, or just streaming Netflix etc, than the download performance is more important than the ping. So, make your decisions wisely... I've seen too many people running multiple zoom devices over lockdown and think a wireless extender is going to solve their problems, but in fact just made everyone's zoom calls worse! But this isn't the fault of the device, that's inherent of how all extenders work. So, I'm still giving this 5 stars for being an excellent instance of what it should be: a way to boost transfer speeds and extend range that's dead simple to set up.

Have now completed the installation and hookup of this antenna. The first test was to listen to Mixed Bag, 90.7 FM which was always full of static. Now this station comes in crystal clear, loud, and strong. Note that I decided to mount this antenna on the side of my house, just beneath the peak of my low roof facing the back yard. I had a quantity of twin 300 ohm cable which I wanted to use. Using a 300ohm/75ohm converter, I simply attached the end of the cable to the two 300ohm screws, protecting the connection with electrical tape. I measured and fabricated a wood mounting plate (see photo) and then screwed the mast bracket to it from the back. The wooden support board was then lag screwed, in turn, to the outside of my house just below the peak using 5" long screws. I then installed the antenna and mast, after reversing it. It now extends upwards vertically yet does not interfere with the roof line. The versatility of the mast permitted me to accomplish that.

(This review is preliminary. I assembled the antenna but am not yet ready to install it.
Assembly tips:

- Both curved antenna segments are secured to the antenna cross bar with the supplied hardware.
- The ends of one (bottom) segment are held in place with two phillips head screws. First, remove the curved metal clamp. line up the holes in the segment and, maintaining hand pressure on each segment end to ensure that it is seated firmly into it's curved metal seat, insert each screw and secure. Do not over tighten these fasteners. This is the "bottom" of the antenna, opposite the 75 ohm connector side. Attach one leg of the segment at a time.
- The ends of the second (top) segment are held in place with two hex head nuts. You will note that each nut is topped with a rubber 'O' ring. This is used to keep the nuts from threading off until assembly. Do not attempt to re-use these as they are not spacers or washers.
- Again, seat the ends of the antenna segment firmly in place, aligning the holes over the studs. Holding down the segment, install each nut. Do not over tighten these nuts.
- The closed loop ends of each antenna segment may now be gently guided in front of the black plastic locking clips. Once the looped ends are in position, firmly, yet carefully snap them into place. The circular antenna shape has now been completed. If assembled patiently and slowly, damage should not occur to the antenna.)

I've been working in video production for over 2 decades now, and bought my first teleprompter for infomercial style videos back in the early 2000s. Let's just say, much like camera tech has gotten smaller and more efficient, so has teleprompting!
The concept is pretty simple and hasn't changed- angle a piece of glass in front of the lens with a black drop material behind it to create a sort of 2-way-mirror, then reflect text in reverse (you know, because mirror?) and your subject appears to read their script off your lens while the camera doesn't see the text at all.
Things that are still true from back then:
- Your text has to be reversed. My old one came with PC software to do this, and since iPads weren't really a thing yet, we used laptops that could fold all the way backwards (Thinkpads mostly). This, surprisingly does not come with software. But no matter, there are some free ones out there, and my personal favorite is just using powerpoint. We reverse the images and make a slide show that the subject can advance with a standard presenter remote. None of those things are included with this set, but if you've been doing corporate and commercial video, you probably have access to this already.

- You will have some loss of exposure due to the mirror. This isn't a big deal, if you're lighting a scene properly you should be able to easily compensate for this, you just might need to hit that ISO or aperture to brighten it up a bit more. Just something to know.

- Your subject needs to be comfortable reading without his eyes darting around the camera. This is just standard teleprompter stuff.

Things that HAVE improved with this model:
- It now attaches to the tripod! In the old days, unless you had the budget for a proper display one that was embedded in front of the camera, you needed to do this with a stand for a laptop or monitor lying horizontal while the camera tripod was behind it. Not very portable, so it stayed in my studio. This one can be brought along to a location shoot and set up rather easily!

To be honest, that one improvement makes all the difference in the world. I barely used my old teleprompter because I couldn't take it out of my studio easily, and most of my gigs are on location shoots. This is going to make testimonial / narrated production videos SO much easier to shoot out in the field!

Just keep in mind you'll need to figure out the display mechanics (software, presentation, speed, remote, etc) on your own. This just gives you the physical hardware to get it done, the mechanics of it will need your own creativity. Would definitely recommend!

I needed a simple dock station to copy some hard disks. The All in 1 HDD Docking System fitted my needs nicely. I was able to insert an old Maxtor IDE drive in the first slot and a brand new SATA SSD in the second slot.

I had hoped to test the one-button copy feature so I powered it up and tried to follow the directions. Both drives were recognized, however I could not get the docking system to perform a drive copy. This could be due to either a brand new, unformatted SSD or due to the use of the Linux EXT2 file system (not FAT or NTFS). If I have a chance I will test copying between two FAT file systems.

With both the Maxtor and SSD plugged in, I added an SD card. I could mount the card and read the files from it, or copy files from it to either of the hard disks or to my system disk!

I tried using both a CF card and an SD card at the same time. However, I was not able to successfully access both at the same time. When I removed the SD card, I could read the CF card.

The device came with a short manual which was written in broken English. It was marginally useful and largely discussed how to use the PC Clone EX program that came with the docking device.

The docking system includes a USB hub. To test it, I plugged a Seagate USB hard disk into the USB port on the front. I was able to copy files from my camera's CF card to the Seagate USB drive. As a final test, I plugged a Maple Mini embedded ARM processor into the other port on the USB hub and uploaded an Arduino-compatible sketch. The USB hub works great!

I ordered the iHome Alexa Built-in Bluetooth Speaker Portable Wireless Waterproof Rechargeable Lights Up to Music, with Speakerphone, Passive Subwoofer, Carry Strap, Durable Shockproof Floatable Design (IBT158) to replace an old sub par portable speaker that I’ve had for years. The iHome is quite the upgrade with the built in Alexa, better sound and being waterproof. I’ve had this product now for several weeks and would like to share my thoughts.

I must say that the sound is pretty good and packs a punch in such a small size. It’s much better than the much smaller and several years old portable wireless speaker that I have been using. In fact there really is no comparison at all. Let’s just say that it is the best sounding portable wireless speaker that I personally have ever owned. My daughter who “borrowed” the older speaker some time ago (and she never gave it back) keeps asking to "borrow" the new iHome as she says, “it’s louder and sounds WAY better”. I absolutely agree with her. Plus the lights on this thing are a nice touch, and there are options (via a button on top) to cycle through and change the color options or turn them off.

Setting up the iHome for Bluetooth and Alexa was easy and very straight forward, and there has been no issues whatsoever. We are mainly an Android household however my oldest daughter uses an iPhone and everyone has had the same great experience. So far my only complaint is that the Bluetooth connectivity distance isn’t the greatest but with that said, none of my Bluetooth devices really have much range in our home so I am not going to knock points off for that. The sound out of this little guy makes up for the Bluetooth short comings and the bonus of Alexa being packed into this as well as the waterproof features make this a great value for the selling price.

One thing worth mentioning is that to use Alexa, you can’t just say “Alexa” to activate her. You do have to physically press a button on the iHome speaker to access her, which isn’t a huge deal breaker, but because of this, you can’t use other Alexa devices to make an announcement and have it broadcast to the iHome speaker. Being fairly new to the Alexa and smart home world, I am not going to hold this shortcoming against the iHome device. It actually makes sense that with this being portable, you wouldn’t want to have Alexa always listening and drain the battery while on the go. Speaking of Battery life, it's decent but not spectacular by any means. This is pretty subjective however as usually when I use the iHome, I'm listening to it at a pretty high volume ;)

Another observation is that this uses micro USB to charge, and I really would like to see more devices using the newer and better USB C charging capabilities.

As far as the “waterproof” capabilities go, I must report that I have yet to float the device in a pool or let the kids play with it outside while running through the sprinklers. I know that it says it’s waterproof and it absolutely looks like it would hold up to getting wet as it is very well built, rugged and quite solid, but I don't want to risk ruining this new toy that the whole family has been enjoying so much.

Most of the places I have lived have been reasonably safe, so I have never felt any pressing need to add a camera security system to my home. I already have an alarm system, which is useful, but no camera system. I decided that it would be good to be able to see people at the main entrances to my home/property and this convinced me to add the Arlo Ultra - 4K UHD Wire-Free Security 2 Camera System to my house.

Setting this security system up is simple enough. You have to mount the included 2 cameras and it doesn’t take much time to complete this step. I placed one of them by my front door and the other one just outside my garage, facing the driveway. The gated entrance to my backyard is right there, and I usually leave my car in the driveway and not the garage, so this seemed like a good place.

There are many things to like about this security camera system, like the wide angle of view that is good for seeing from my backyard gate to the end of my driveway. You can even speak back and forth with someone at your front door and this can prove useful when you want to avoid talking directly, face to face, with solicitors.

With the image quality, although it isn’t as sharp as I expected, it seems sufficient to me. I haven’t experienced any intruders thus far- knock on wood- so I haven’t necessarily needed to get crystal clear details. One limitation I have is that I haven’t owned a camera security system before. This is a first for me, so I don’t have any point of comparison. Still, the picture quality seems good. And I like the notification system. Any motion detection is set up to record, so you can see what is going on and you know quickly.

The app itself is user- friendly enough but one thing to keep in mind is that the Arlo Smart Servive and cloud recording are free for only the first year. After that, you have to pay for a subscription. I will wait to see if the system is worth my while, then decide whether to subscribe. A year of free usage time should be sufficient to make the call.

Security is important and the Arlo Ultra - 4K UHD Wire-Free Security 2 Camera System is a good way to keep safe. Two cameras are definitely better than one because I am able to secure the two areas of my property where an unwanted individual is most likely to show up. The Sonys are still some of the best and the standard by which I judge other headphones in this style. BUT... at the time of this review, the price of this Philips product is less than half of what I paid for my Sony. Are the Sonys better? A little. Are they twice the price better? NO WAY. This is far better quality in sound and build than the cheapo bluetooth headphones, and if I didn't try them side by side with my Sony, it'd be hard to tell them apart. The feature set are similar, including the app control which actually made the phone really easy to pair as well.
One thing I actually really like about these is that there are more buttons than the Sony alternative. A dedicated button for mute, a dedicated button for noise cancellation, and of course power/pairing. But there are also touch sensitive controls on the ear cups, which I did not realize at first. I have mixed feelings about touch controls, I feel like they are easy to accidentally trigger, but so far it's actually been pretty good.
I think for the current asking price of around 150, the pros are solid enough to be worth recommending.

I'll admit, I've bought into the Amazon/Kindle crack. I own three now, the old e-ink, the old Fire and now the Fire HD. All in all, the Fire HD is a great tablet/multi-media/entertainment device. It's something I use pretty much every day and can take anywhere, and it's easy to figure out and set up. It also comes with fantastic customer service.

I wanted a set of speakers to use mainly for my Kindle Fire and MP3 player, but also as my computer speakers. Due to space constraints, a 2.0 system was my only option, since a subwoofer (regardless of the size) would be problematic.

So the search began. There were several speakers that sounded great, including the Creative Gigaworks, M Audio and Audioengine. However, they lacked the convenience features I wanted such as ease of connecting/disconnecting a tablet and volume control without having to reach out and touch the speaker.

The Bose Companion 20 initially caught my eye because of the control pod. That was a great solution to my problems since I could control the volume right on my desk plus have the ability to plug in/unplug a tablet very easily. The sound quality sealed the deal - everyone who hears these speakers think they are a 2.1 set due to the ample bass. But, the bass is not at the expense of clear mid and upper ranges.

I use these 60% for music and 40% for video, and for both applications, the sound quality has been just wonderful. I'm also impressed that they sound just as good with the volume dialed way down as they do at moderate or blast-out-the-walls loud.

The control pod is very well made. It has a nice weight to it and a non-skid backing so it stays put. The volume control works very smoothly with a solid feel. I'm especially fond of being able to turn the speakers on and off by just touching the control pod.

You can connect it to the PC and to an aux device (such as a tablet) and use both at the same time. That's important since I want to listen to music or a video from my Fire, but still want to hear a chime when an email arrives.

My complaints are that the control pod cable is a bit too short for my needs. It's about 5 foot long, which is ample if you have the speakers next to your PC, but I have my speakers on a shelf above my desk. I was able to arrange things to make it work, but another foot or two of cable (or the ability to purchase an extension) would have been nice. It's a custom cable, so an off-the-shelf extension is not possible.

My other complaint is the price. I was able to get a used pair for half of the regular price. I think these are a bit overpriced at the regular price. But, Bose hit a really unique niche - the ability to have great sound without any compromise in convenience. If you want both, there's a high cost for admission.

If the price is not an issue, these very much deserve a hard look if you're in the market for a great sounding pair of 2.0 speakers. Highly recommend.

This AMFILM PREMIUM SCREEN PROTECTOR FILM CLEAR is an excellent choice for protecting your Google Nexus 7's touch screen. It's easy to install, absolutely invisible once installed, and doesn't interfere with the sensitivity of the touch screen. I was able to achieve a bubble-free installation on the very first try.

The installation instructions (printed on the retail packaging envelope) are easy to understand. The film itself--the middle layer, which is sandwiched between two masking sheets that are removed at the beginning and end of the installation--is stiff enough to lay down easily. Unlike some protective film, the adhesive doesn't aggressively grab dust motes from the air while you're installing the film. You get two sheets of film (giving you two chances at a perfect installation), a microfiber cleaning cloth, and a stiff cardboard square for smoothing out bubbles.

Because Google Nexus 7 protective film needs only one cutout (for the camera), it's especially easy to install. Just be careful that you center the film with the hole over the camera, and align it parallel to the tablet's top edge so that it lays down perfectly straight. When I got a tiny overlap at a top corner, there was a bubble at the edge that wouldn't smooth out. Rather than remove the otherwise bubble-free film, I raised the corner and trimmed the film with scissors--which fixed the problem.

THE GOOD:
--------------
* Very easy to set-up, app is intuitive to use and follow.
* This is a very complete kit with a hub, 6 entry sensors, 2 motion sensors, and a keypad. You don't need to use everything, or install everything in one day. I started off just my garage door and the front door. Same thing with the extra keypad. There is already a control panel on top of the hub. The idea of they keypad is for quicker access to the control panel. So ideally, the keypad will be next to your bed on a nightstand or something.
* Hub is not obtrusive at all. I have it next to a soda can for size reference.
* Sensors work really well. I was concerned about the garage door sensor because usually I get bad wi-fi in the garage. I put the hub near my living room. The garage sensor worked flawlessly. Anytime you open the door where you've installed a sensor, there is a chime that goes off on the hub. You can disable this chime if you wish.
* No need to subscribe to a service, which is perfect for us. We live in a fairly safe neighborhood, knock on wood. But there are times when everyone is gone, and no cars are parked in the driveway. So these are the times, I'll arm the system.

THE BAD:
------------
* The sensor and the magnet has to be half an inch or less apart. Installation will be tricky for some of you. My front entry door has a raised decorative trim that makes this impossible. I made it work by having the sensor at a weird angle, and half the 3M backing isn't even attached to the trim. I will need to think of a solution for this. Or better yet, ADT should have thought about this ahead of time and given us adapters, spacers, etc.
* If you choose not to subscribe, like in our case, you should understand the system is nothing more than a deterrent. You hope the loud sound will be enough to deter would be criminals. If it's not, then no authorities are coming unless you called them yourselves.
* The instructions assumes we all know the industry lingo For example, "Entry or exit delays." It would have been nice if the manual explained what this means. I had to search online for more info. It's basically the time the system allows for you to properly turn off the alarm before it goes off. That's my understand from YT videos of other brands. I couldn't find an exact "Blue by ADT" video on this matter.
* Whenever you arm the system, it takes forever, like 60 to 90 seconds, and during this time, there is a CHIME that's counting down with the seconds. Once the system is armed, then it shuts up. There doesn't seem to be a way to mute this. You see, I'm a night owl, so I don't need to arm the system until very late like 1 or 2 am. People are asleep at this time, the chimes will wake them up. I have contacted customer service, we'll see what they say.
* The 2 yard signs and stakes are great, but the 4 stickers they give for your windows are tiny. My Brinks windows stickers were bigger.

Overall, I'll rate this 4-Stars. And base on the customer service response, this might go up to 5-Stars, or get bumped down to 3-Stars. There has got to be a way to mute the chimes when arming the system. If there isn't a way, then I will bump the rating down because that would be ridiculous. So, 4-Stars for now.

I feel like it was just designed to look like a gee whiz thing and get your money, not really concerned about whether or not it really worked. Save your money. Instead, buy polishing rags and buffing compound from outfits that do this sort of thing for a living. You will very likely be happy and for a much longer period of time.
Polishing plastic is not that hard, but it is NOT EASY either, because it takes a lot of patience and some properly applied buffing compound and elbow grease. IT TAKES A LITTLE TIME no matter how you do it. This device is trying to make you think it is physically and temporally easy. No magic machine exists that can polish without some work. I think that maybe the product COULD have worked, but I doubt if the company leader-persons who oversaw the packaging and function decisions that dragged it's quality and capability down are accountable for their poor decisions. The contacts on both the USB and Lightning connector ends are precision made and mate perfectly to the ports to which they were designed to connect. The outer jacket is thick, but not too stiff to make handling it a problem. There are strain reliefs on both ends to ensure a long service life.

Bottom line: when size (in the form of cable length) matters this is one of the very few on the market that is a full three meters long. Add in the fact that this one is made to perform like an Apple OEM cable and the value should be apparent.

This is among the companies that has been discovered spying on the US using their cameras - the firmware this camera comes with is long outdated and, in fact, can not be updated to anywhere close to what is current. This is far too risky for me to install on my system.

Any camera you install on your system should have the latest firmware installed and you need to have a good understanding of network security protocols. Cameras such as this one, that are older versions of cameras made by manufacturers that are blacklisted - while still being sold, people who understand the industry avoid them - are an invitation for hackers to invade your system.

While the specs on and price of this camera seem decent - this is not a camera I recommend. This poses far more risks than it is worth.

USB 3.0 uses a different connector on the drive, so you need to use the USB 3.0 cable that comes with the drive. A standard USB 2.0 cable won't work because it has a different connector on the drive side. On the computer side, it's a standard USB plug, so it fits both USB 2.0 and USB 3.0 jacks on the computer.

I use this to move many GB's of data from my PC to my Mac laptop. The PC has USB 3.0, so it's blazing fast to move data from the PC to the external drive. My Mac laptop has USB 2.0, so it takes longer to move the data from the drive to the Mac. But it works. Drive capacities are now so large that USB 3.0 is a huge advantage. It takes quite a bit of time to move 1 TB of data at USB 2.0 speed.

I have worked with a lot of different sets of headphones and ear buds and have gotten a good feel for what sounds right and what doesn’t. Specifically with ear buds I pay attention to the fit as well as the sound, which are two areas where many manufacturers get it wrong. Anker did a good job with these though there is a soft spot in the sound profile.

I used these with an iPhone 7, and initial pairing was very quick and painless. The buds found each other (another issue I have seen with other sets on occasion), and these paired without much fanfare or issue at all. That’s really all you could ask.

These fit like a dream. The package contains several silicone plugs of different sizes so you can get just the right fit for yourself, but I found that the ones already on the buds were actually a perfect fit. I popped these in, gave them a turn to lock them in place and they sealed perfectly. I am especially happy with how well these fit in my ears and actually stay there.

The sound isolation is on par with what you’d expect. When not powered on and streaming music they are the equivalent to a cheap set of ear plugs – enough to block out some sound but not completely silence the world.

The sound quality is very good but the sound profile could use a tweak. The bass is strong but not overdriven to the point of causing headaches. There is a tendency to overdrive the bass, so having good bass that’s not overpowering is nice. The highs are bright and clear too. The midrange is another matter and feels weak (though not non-existent). This is the first switch that I have owned that can be configured.  That's a big plus.  Once you determine the IP address of the switch, you simply enter it in your browser, enter the default password (which you can change) and you are into the setup program that is internal to the switch. There are two reasons why I didn't give this a 5 star rating.  1) The indicator lights showing active ports are on the same side as the cables. In all honesty, I can't say that the lights ever provided much benefit and could be distracting, so this might be an advantage to some people to have both lights and cables on the back. Strange that you need to use a device other than a computer to do this and it is rather a nuisance.  Apparently there is no Windows version of Netgear Insight.  You have to use your IOS or Android device.  Another problem I had is that you supposedly can change your password on your device, which I tried, but apparently the password did not meet the requirements, but was never informed of that by the program.  I was able to change the password on the device after getting into it via the IP address.  Netgear makes good products and I have purchased other Netgear products in the past with good results. This item is one version of the OSSC, and turns out it is not case-compatible with the official one, having several different components populated on the board, so it will not fit in the normal OSSC cases.

It is not at all confidence-inspiring that the manufacturer here deviated from the official board layout and component selection. The PSU is extremely cheap, and some things are just incorrect.

Some of the components I noticed were different are:

- the screen: The height of the screen is quite a bit lower than what's shown in pictures of the official OSSC, and on closer examination, it appears the screen was soldered to the wrong side of the board because of layout issues.
- the buttons: the buttons here have yellow nubs on top, but the official one has low profile tactile buttons. This is another point where 3D printed cases made for this (such as those sold by Laser Bear) will interfere with this OSSC, preventing the case from closing.
- The audio select switch: the switch is mounted to the bottom of the PCB instead of the top. There appear to be traces for the switch on the top of the PCB, but it's not clear why they were mounted to the bottom of the board. Again, this is an issue because cases will have allowance for this switch, and expect the switch to be located on the top of the PCB.

Given that these components were swapped or moved, I can't be certain about the rest of the component choices, and given how cheap the power supply is, I'm not confident at all that the manufacturers here prioritized quality over price in any way whatsoever.

This is a combination product with a 5 foot extension cord, 2 AC power outlets, and 3 full-sized USB power ports. Compact size is great for travel, since older hotels don't have enough power outlets for modern travelers and the outlets are often hidden behind desks or under beds.

Unfortunately, the USB power ports are pretty weak. You get 2.4A divided among 3 ports, so if you're trying to charge 3 devices, each one gets less than 1A. Modern smartphones and tablets will often fast-charge at 3A, so charging with these ports will be very slow. USB powered laptops can use even more power and will complain about being charged at less than 3A.

I don't like that there is no USB-C charging port and no USB Power Delivery fast charging, which are becoming the standard for smartphones and laptops.

This device is not UL listed for electrical safety. As phone and tablet and laptop batteries get more and more powerful, electrical safety becomes more and more important. Most power strips from US brands are UL listed, so I cannot recommend a product that is not UL listed.

With its huge 64GB file storage capacity, this flash drive can theoretically store the entire contents of a PC's hard drive and its operating system. Since I don't have that many files to store on an everyday basis, I am reserving this flash drive to store high-resolution videos and other RAM-eating monster files.

For $80, this is rather overpriced. There are USB drives that are cheaper and will do the job just as well. To make the USB look like it's worth the extra price, Toshiba made the casing unnecessarily oversized - there's no practical reason why the USB case had to be so wide (you will have trouble sticking another USB drive next to it, which is annoying). It's a gimmick to impress the user, nothing more. However, when you hold it in your hand, it's not as heavy as the metallic finish would lead you to believe - it's actually very lightweight, and to be honest, feels cheap. I have questions of its durability, despite the fancy advertising.

To test, I copied all the videos I had stored in my PC to see how fast it would be to store all of them on this monster drive. I was disappointed that the saving time was not noticeably faster, which may not be the fault of the USB drive but rather my computer. However, I have to say it was a relief that I never got the "you don't have enough memory" message, so you can count on this USB to store tons of videos you can't find room for elsewhere.

The only drawback to this single-USB method of storage is that I don't feel entirely comfortable saving so much stuff on just ONE drive, despite its capacity. It's equivalent to putting all your eggs in one basket - what if you lose that single USB - you're screwed. Though convenient, I'd rather spread out my back-up files, so if you use this USB to save a huge file, I'd buy more than one just to be safe.

The other thing I thought was unnecessary was the included encryption software that's included on the drive. You only see it when you open up the Files folder, and there are two lengthy PDFs with instructions on how to activate the password and security options. Fortunately you do not require to activate them in order to use the drive - I've never found I needed such security measures, but if you plan to store financial data on this USB, it's a good feature.

Lastly, I hate the fact that, unlike my other drives, it has a cap. I am forever losing the caps to my flash drives and have since opted to buy only the retractable ones, where you can slide the connector in or out. Too bad this one doesn't have it, otherwise I would have added a star.

So, in short, a mixed review. Give me a drive that's cheaper, that's big on the inside but small on the outside, capless, and I'd buy more of them.

In order to try the over burn feature, I would need the appropriate disks that can normally hold 8.5 GB (DVD+R).  These disks are not too difficult to find online, but the office supply stores only seem to stock 4.7 GB disks.  I guess you either have to special order or buy online.  Most everything that I need to burn can either fit on a 4.7 GB DVD or can be compressed (without much loss of quality) to fit.  It may be false economy to buy the higher capacity disks, as they are nearly double the price of lower capacity.  With burnable media prices being so low anyway, you don't gain much by squeezing as much as you can on a particular disk.  So why did I get this drive?  I like to have a drive on the shelf if one goes bad (and they do sometimes), and then I don't have to wait for one to arrive.  I assumed it was probably good to have one that can burn to maximum capacity as this isn't much more expensive than a regular DVD burner.  Since I haven't actually installed or used the drive yet (waiting for disks), one should not pay as much attention to my review as some other reviewers.  I just wanted people to be aware that you can't insert a 4.7 GB disk and expect to over burn to 8.7 GB.  You need to understand the differences in available media and get the appropriate blank media. Update:  I finally received the appropriate media to test the drive.  It seemed to work good for the first 6 or 8 disks, but then 3 disks in a row had burn errors.  Bad media?  I don't think so; it appears the drive is failing already.  I'll test on another computer and see if it is the media or the drive and update the review again, but right now I can't recommend this drive at all.  UPDATE 2:  I tried this again after rebooting my computer and it now seems to work fine and does indeed overburn, so you can squeeze a lot on one disk.  When I had 3 bad burns in a row, I thought it was the burner, but it may have been bad media.  On the other hand, I suspect something flaky on my PC, as I have had bad burns before occasionally (not recently) and then after a reboot everything was fine again.  I may have too many programs loaded when I try to burn.  That's not the fault of the DVD drive.  Most likely the fault of the burning program (and I am using a major well-know program.)

I have been wanting a new MP3 player for a while now. I refuse to waste my phone with cluttered songs and use. I have watched everyone else I know blow through phones from constant use. I wanted to have a dedicated MP3 player. Let's see how this worked out.

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?
This comes in a nice box- great for gift giving. It has a cord with it for charging and attaching to computer if you want to download songs to it. This does NOT have any internal memory, however. All songs have to be stored on a microSD card. There is port for headphones, mini USB, and line out port.

HOW TO OPERATE
ON/OFF
The power button is on the top of the unit. It has to be held in for a moment before it kicks in. There is an issue with the power button being on the top pressed down easily. The design of this has a raised edge of the case so that it is harder to press on the power button accidentally.

MENU
The menu button is easy to operate. It takes you around the menus using the forward and backward arrow buttons.

VOLUME
The volume buttons are on the outside edge on the right as you look at the case. The + and - buttons are separate.

BACK BUTTON
This takes you back through the menu and you can replay songs too.

PLAY PAUSE
Is on the front of the case and it is easy to access and see.

SCREEN
This is not a full color screen. It is simple and easy to read, however, without graphic clutter.

BLUETOOTH?
I had a heck of a time with this at first. I was not having it work well with my bluetooth headphones and it frustrated me to no end. I was about ready to give this an awful review when I suddenly realized- it was not the player, it was both sets of headphones that were not working correctly! Once I got the headphones working, the sound is BEAUTIFUL on this.

I have also used this with a few bluetooth speakers with great results. I like the solid feeling of the body- it stays put but does not take up too much room.

SOUND
You can change the sound quite a bit with this to be what you want. There are presets and fine tuning settings you can use. Once I finally got this figured out, the sound is amazing.

READ OUT
Again, this is NOT TOUCHSCREEN nor does it have fancy full color graphics. It is simple and easy to read and use.

STORAGE
Remember, this stores all of the songs on the microSD card. There is not any internal storage in this otherwise.

AM I GLAD TO HAVE THIS?
Once I got the problems worked out, I have to say I really like this. It is not as intuitive as some items, but it is really nice to have and I love to play it. I like shuffler or single CD artist choices, etc.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is a really nice MP3 player. It is a bit more rustic than some might be used to with smart phones, but it really works nicely and the sound is great.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. It does what it says, although I would prefer it to have some internal storage as well as microSD, but that is just me. For what this is- it is very nice. I like it and am pleased with the performance.

It says it fits a Nikon D800, but when mounted, the D800 is too tall, barely fitting under the overhead grip arm.

The overhead arm does not extend forward enough to allow the camera to balance, even with the camera mounted all the way to the rear of the baseplate. Thus, even when I'm holding just the front two inches under the hot shoe mount, the camera when mounted with a heavy zoom lens like the 24-70 f/2.8, tilts down. A lighter, shorter lens works better, but you still cannot hold the unit by the foam grip handle without your knuckles scraping the camera's hot shoe mount.

The entire device is of molded ABS plastic and is somewhat flexible in a "springy" way. It appears strong, but remember, your multi-thousand dollar investment is hanging by that little joint in the back of the base plate. If it breaks, it's curtains. You might want to have a safety lanyard attached to a neck strap lug that attaches to your wrist, just in case.

The sleds on the bottom are nice. When you put it down, it's stable, although I had to re-superglue one of the padded inserts on one of the sled rails.

The camera mounting screw is well designed and easy to use, but for some reason, is too long. The threads bottomed out in my camera and would not hold the camera tight. I had to remove the thumb screw and add a washer on the underside of the base effectively shortening the threads. I could have ground off 1/16" or so, too. Not a big deal, but out of the box it didn't work.

One thing's for sure: you need a strong arm to hold this for any amount of time if you have a heavy lens attached. If you are working with a lightweight SLR and a lightweight lens, it's much easier. And seeing the viewfinder is a real problem. And forget about focusing. If you mount a remote electronic viewfinder on the upper hot shoe, it's much easier to see what you're shooting, but now you've added even more weight and your arm will die. (True steadicams went with vests and spring-assisted arms for this reason years ago.)

Overall, the sled is a simple, inexpensive method to hold a camera from above and does smooth out motion well. It's a worthy gizmo to have in your bag.

UPDATE: I attached my Canon HFS-100 HD camcorder to this sled and have never taken it off. It is absolutely the best accessory ever! Perfectly balanced. The overhead handle allows excellent control and fabulous low angle positioning when capturing kids or animals on the floor. The camera's flip-out viewfinder is the key, something the D800 sorely lacks.

This GE Universal Remote Control with Roku or Fire TV Streaming Remote Compartment was quite a confusing listing until after I had read it and studied the images a few times. By then, I had already ordered it, thinking it was going to control both my TLC TV and Firestick. Instead, I learned it controls my TV, and just holds my Firestick control on the other side of the remote. But, after thinking about it, I thought, this could actually help keep me from always losing my remotes.
I have to say that setting it up with my TV was a breeze. I don't have cable, only a TLC Roku TV and a Firestick, so no need for all the numbers and other things on the remote. That's a lot of unused buttons...
Well, it would've been ok, if I didn't keep hitting the buttons on the TV side every time I am trying to use my Firestick remote on the other side. It is almost inevitable. Somehow, I always hit a button that takes me to my TLC TV's home screen and exits the Firestick app and, of course, the show I'm watching.
It is also very bulky to just control two devices, or even its purported four. It is actually huge compared to just having both remotes, which I really still have, but in a more complicated form. There are so many more buttons that I'll never use and so much real estate for such a device. Now, if it really did have the ability to control my Firestick built into the other side, that would probably make it more stable, I would think.

-Very cramped, awkward space for the binding posts. I use banana plugs because I need a quick, easy way to hook them up (standing on a ladder, fumbling around behind the speaker) and there's not enough room back there for normal banana plugs. I wound up buying some right-angle plugs (I got the Monoprice), and those resolved this for me.
-Sound quality is good for an outdoor speaker in this price range but if you don't need a rugged speaker, you can get much better sound for the price. As I'm writing this review, the ELAC Debut 2.0 B6.2 is on sale for about the same price as these Atriums, and the ELAC has much better sound. Bottom line: If you need an outdoor speaker in this price range, this speaker would be my recommendation.

I love the white PVC shielding on this cable - not only is it durable and will help the cable withstand damage but it can be run along a wall and then painted to match the wall color.

I used this 25 foot cable to run between my router to a unmanaged switch that branches to several IoT hubs - a primary connection where speed and a reliable relay is critical - and I’ve been nothing but impressed by this product.

You will not find a better Ethernet Cable - this is really a top of the line cable that you’ll love. This is a purchase that you’ll never regret.

This is without a doubt the best looking soundbar I’ve come across so far. The shape is more than just aesthetics – if you have a TV on a table stand the low profile of the soundbar doesn’t get in the way of the screen. Granted, I’m sure there’s a TV out there that sits low enough that the soundbar will get in the way, but if it does it will be minimal. A few years ago I ran wiring for my main TV for a 7.1 speaker setup. It took many hours, and gave me a new appreciation as to why electricians charge so much for fishing wire through walls. So, the fact that I was able to get this set up and running in about an hour (including the unpacking and calibration time) was a real treat. I would rate the setup ease, and the included instructions, as excellent.

There are a number of great features, the main one for me being the detachable side speakers. It gives more flexibility than the usual sound bar in that you can position them for rear sound if you want that immersive feel, but also use them as standalone speakers for other devices. I had no problems pairing one to a tablet. One potential negative is the internal battery. While the run time is fine – I ran it for a good four hours continuously without a problem – I’ve had enough devices with internal batteries go bad (e.g., the battery will no longer take much of a charge) that I always am wary of internal batteries.

The sound quality was both good and bad, and in an unexpected way. I was expecting that this soundbar would be left in the dust by my wired system at high volume. While it was bested (especially with bass given the slim subwoofer) it was a far closer horse race than I thought it would be. This soundbar can put out a healthy amount of volume and still remain in control of sound quality.

Where it fell short is when it was not pushed hard. Soft passages were weak; dialog was unclear at times. Running this at a soft volume (such as at night when others are sleeping in the house) was not enjoyable – I ended up having to turn on subtitles since I could not make out the dialog clearly. Now, this issue could be exacerbated by my aging ears, but others in the house, who are younger, also found it weak and unimpressive at low volume.

I think most people who get this will be looking to have “big” sound in a simple to set up, simple to use system. On that end, the Philips soundbar delivers. It misses somewhat on the soft end of the spectrum, but the build quality, looks, and flexibility warrant a five-star rating even at this rather lofty price point.

IMPORTANT ADVICE... do not thread the mini ball head onto anything too tightly. This stand is actually fine, it's the cheap ball head that has given me headaches. The ball head has a... I'm not sure what the technical term is for this kind of bolt, but lets call it a "dual bolt." 1/4 bolt is threaded inside a bigger bolt, I presume 1/2. I threaded a mini projector onto this thing, I guess a little too tight. When I unthreaded the projector, the 1/4 bolt was stuck, meaning it was unthreading WITH the projector. So the 1/4 bolt came off the 1/2 bolt. You would think that all it takes are some pliers, but surprisingly, pliers even with teeth, have a hard time gripping this bolt. I had to use my drill press vise to get it off.

To properly use that ball head, you want to thread it onto whatever device you're using, but don't thread it on too tight like me. Then tighten with the lower knob. You might think, this reviewer isn't using common sense. I don't think so at all. Anybody would like his/her electronics threaded securely. The amount of strength I used was reasonable. The issue lies in that inner 1/4 bolt not being secured enough inside that bigger bolt. But I fixed that. Once I was able to unthread the projector from the vise... with the 1/4 bolt now free, but secured by the vise, I then took the ball head body to the vise and threaded the bigger bolt onto the 1/4 bolt a "wee bit" tighter than the manufacturer did.

If you don't have drill press vise like I do, then you better be extra careful using this. 3-Stars.

I have purchased this for a small office, I run mail and a file server so I need to have the network up at all times.
The device is nice and easy to setup, concept is good and the price is not bad. This is where the good ends. I received the unit pulled it out of the box and started playing with it everything works well, then I turn off the stereo and I hear a very faint buzz coming from the unit. Since I work with electronics almost daily (component level repairs) I knew that the power supply will die soon, (it was a sign of a cheap ps).
I decided at only $130 im not going to send it back I will fix it myself (i don't really care about warranty).
Under the cover there are 3 boards. 1 relay outlet board, 2 power supply, 3 controller. The controller board (the one with the display) was ok, it didn't look bad at all. The relay outlet board I have found 2 cold solder spots, that would cause malfunctions with an outlet down the line. After fixing it I pull out the power supply and OMG, that this looks like someone was first learning how to solder, the board had a ton of faults, remaining flux and cotton from swabs. I decided to throw the power supply out instead I installed 12v to 5v converter for the controlls and connected 12v for relays. Installed external plug for a 12v ps and it works great with no problems.

This unit is ok.
It should have a good power supply (a $5 ps from china is 100 times better than what it came with)
It should be using solid state relays (it would be silent, and it would last much longer, also you would only need 5v to supply it)

Good Luck

When it comes to radios, so many of them just don't have the reception that they used to. I came across this one and decided it was worth the try. Unfortunately, the battery choice is annoying, but let's take a look at the radio..

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?
This is a pretty straightforward radio. It has AM and FM. Each band has a horizontal dial on it. The volume button is large and turns the radio on and off as well. You can adjust the tone from high to low which will either focus on voice or on base tones for what you are listening to.

HANDLE
The handle on this is sturdy and easy to carry.

ANTENNA
The antenna on this is sturdy and easy to pull out and push in.

JACK
There is a standard headphone jack.

HOW DOES THIS PERFORM?
This performs beautifully. The reception is exceptional and I can pull in stations that most other newer radios do not pull in any more. The sound is fabulous with a lot of depth to it.

BATTERIES
I really dislike that this takes 4 D batteries. Those batteries are expensive and tend to run out quickly. I don't normally carry them in the house for emergencies, but it would be worth having some since this radio is great and easy to hear.

WHO MIGHT LIKE THIS RADIO?
Anyone who loves to listen to AM still would love this radio. Many of them don't have it anymore which is frustrating. I also found that it is great for older people to have one of these. I know an older gentleman who has been bed ridden and home bound and he loves this radio. It is easy to operate, see, and great sound.

THE BOTTOM LINE
I like this radio. It is good to have on hand for emergencies or for good listening when internet is down or I just am tired of the internet radio channels and prefer to be local. The sound is great and operation easy. Fabulous reception.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. This is a perfect gift for older people or those who really enjoy local radio and prefer an easy to use radio that has great reception. Just be sure to have D batteries for emergencies. If it had rechargeable features, it would be perfect!
