I bought this because other reviewers said it would work. It doesn't. The one that comes with the tripod has thinner sides on the part that slides in. Since it was fairly cheap I will try to file it down a bit. Because it isn't "tight". It is so much bigger.

I've had several Amazon Basics' items since the line was introduced. Most have been quite good. Unfortunately this tripod wasn't one of them.

The feel is cheap and plastic-y. I wasn't expecting bearings in the pan-head but the plastic on plastic mechanisms are terrible.

I tested this item with my Kodak Z990 digital camera. It weighs approx. 21 oz. with batteries.

The camera mount has a good rubber pad for your camera to sit on and the tightening screw has a butterfly head so no screwdriver or coins are needed to attach/detach the mount from the camera. The mount attaches to the tripod with a spring-loaded release arm. There is actually very little contact area on the tripod itself (only two corners) holding the mount in place, also the release arm does NOT have a safety catch.

Pan Functionality - Fully tightened down I can still, with not much effort, swing the head from left to right. Fully loosened the motion is heavy and awkward easily upsetting the tripod's position. Tightening this knob fully actually interferes with the...

Tilt Functionality - The action is not much better here. You can lock the tilt angle into place and it does stay there. There's just as much plastic on plastic drag when in motion. The arm is generously long and comfortable to grip. The side-tilt mechanism goes reasonably easily from flat to 90°. It does not lock in place well.

Leg Functionality - The legs extend and retract with mild effort. They lock into place firmly. With just the larger leg section extended the tripod is fairly sturdy. Extending the smaller leg sections dramatically increases wobble. There is a weight/gear hook for added stabilization but it is plastic and feels easily broken. The swiveling rubber feet are innovative but only held on by friction and can easily become detached. The center stabilizer locks and unlocks easily with only a quarter turn and holds in place well. There is a serviceable carry handle attached to the leg mount section.

The tripod has two bubble levels. The first, a small button level is at the top of one of the leg mounts. The second, a tube level, is just under and inch long and is under and partially obscured by the camera mount. With a camera attached it becomes useless.

The center section extends and lowers via a crank mechanisms and locks in place with a plastic collar. There is no positive safety lock. Loosen the collar and your camera comes down rapidly on its own. Extending your camera this way will only increase the instability of this tripod.

The included carry bag reflects the quality of it's tripod. Its material is unpadded and thin. It has no extra pockets and the half-inch nylon shoulder strap is also unpadded making it rather uncomfortable to carry.

In conclusion... I wouldn't recommend this tripod even as a starter for someone just getting into photography it will only add frustration to the experience. Spend a little more and get a far better tripod or spend a little less and get something of equal quality.

More than anyone, I really wanted alkaline charging to work like other rechargeable batteries but the sad reality is that they're just not made for it.

The reality of alkaline charging:
- Duracells seem to leak more than cheapo "Kirkland" brand from Costco.
- Energizers do not hold charge very well.
- All brands leak eventually.
- Takes a long time to charge.
- Unreliable even if successfully recharged -- usually, batteries are connected in series, which means that if one fails, the device will not work.
- Battery leak can happen while charging or while being used in the device, resulting in a very messy charger and messy device.

So after some dumpster diving (or at least, I raided the battery recycling bins at work), I came home with batteries of various brands. For a while, I really did use recharged alkaline batteries exclusively and kept my Ni-MH batteries in the drawer. What I found was that I needed to change the batteries a lot more often and I couldn't be sure that the battery would have a charge when I took it out of the drawer.

Leaking is a big problem. My charger now has one charging port that is stuck because the liquid got in to the spring mechanism and dried. I also have a couple of remotes and devices that had to be cleaned out because the batteries leaked.

In the end, I had to give up on the idea of recharging cheap alkaline batteries because of how long it takes to recharge and that it can leak at any time, potentially ruining your device (mostly, it's just oily and you need to clean it out with a tissue). I just couldn't trust those batteries.

So why did I still give this charger 5 stars? Although alkaline charging was a failed experiment for me, the charger is still a better-than-average Ni-MH battery charger. It has separate intelligent charging and LCD display for each battery and will trickle charge a battery even after the lights turn green. Other chargers that have the same features cost more -- and without the Alkaline charging capability. You really can't go wrong with this charger.

This past weekend I got to use both the SN600N and the Yongnuo YN568EX with the YN622 triggers. Basically both function completely with the YN622 triggers in both manual and iTTL modes. The only thing that I noticed with the SN600N was that manual power 1/1, 1/2, 1/4 all seem to be about the same output using the YN622 triggers - you have to lower it to 1/8 or less to start seeing lower outputs. Not a huge deal, but I'd like more output options. More on this below:

Here are a few details that a pretty important about these two alternatives to the Nikon SB series:

a) The 568 light is much higher quality - and I really mean the LIGHT quality. It is even, consistent, and clear. On the other hand, the SN600N is very scattered - what I mean by this is there are lines of brightness and darkness from the flash burst. This must be an internal flash "lens" issue - whatever the light is bouncing around and through within the flash is creating texture and light inconsistencies. This is not the case with the 568.

b) Yes, the SN600N is a more powerful flash, but in my opinion, it needs to have more levels of output on the lower end (1/256) because it's TOO bright for some situations. I use grids and modifiers during wedding receptions, and I like balancing the natural light with the flash output. 1/128 with the SN600N is equal to about 1/64 on the 568. I use the 568 at 1/128 quite a bit for details - so this was kinda a bummer to me.

c) The AF beam on the SN600N is better and more centered than the 568 - but they both need to improve designs. The ONLY reason I'm holding onto my Nikon SB900 at this point is the AF beam - which makes accurate AF possible in pitch black - no joke. The AF beam on the Yongnuo is a joke - they need to fix it on the 622 triggers too - it's basically worthless and too bright/annoying to the subject.

d) In my experience using the 568EX, the batteries get warm and stay warm, whether you're using the flash or not. If the flash is on, the batteries will get warm. It also EATS through batteries. I used to be able to photograph 2 weddings without recharging my Nikon SB setup (using SB600 previously) - now I have to recharge between weddings. I've upgraded to 2800mah EBL AA rechargeable (previously using Amazon 2000mah) and it has helped quite a bit.

So this is my current setup: SB900 on camera, 2x 568EX off camera group A+B for reception lighting, and then SN600N as group C for periodic fill. Rather than commit to a single brand, I'm using them all as tools for different situations, because they all work differently. I also am really enjoying the SN600N as on-camera if I don't need the AF beam - the quality of light is bright, crisp and rich - and the SN600N "brain" (basically how it works using iTTL mode) just works really well with Nikon - it's a very consistent flash, sometimes even better than my SB900. I like that it can zoom all the way to 200mm, too. If the SN600N had a better AF beam and better quality of light, I would ditch my SB900 and use it all the time. But I switch between the SB900 and the SN600N for different effects. I actually like the previously mentioned internal lens flash inconsistencies at times - it creates a grittiness that I like.
Works well, takes up a little more space than I would like, but overall does what it is intended.

This LEATHER LAPTOP MESSENGER BAG FOR MEN (by Leather Centric) is made of real leather--animal hide, NOT the man-made “pleather” stuff that’s often marketed on Amazon as “real leather” or “genuine leather”. That’s a big plus, but the bag itself has a lot of minuses.

First, the bag’s styling is so old-fashioned, it makes the bag look cheap. You have to really love the 1950s “retro” look, to like the overall appearance. The bag definitely looks handmade, but it also looks crudely rustic.

Second, although the bag has lots of zippered compartments (inside and outside), it is only 3” deep. It has no expansion gussets, so the total capacity is one laptop or one very thick sheaf of documents. Internal zipper compartments are relatively useless if a bag can’t expand to hold the things added to the compartments.

Third, the bag is difficult to open. It opens with two metal clasps--these are hidden beneath the purely decorative buckled front straps. You have to pull up on both clasps at once to lift the flap, and you can’t do this easily without laying the bag flat on one side, or holding it on your lap. The leather flap itself is very stiff (at least when the bag is new), and this adds to the opening difficulty.

Fourth, the bag has no locking mechanism. Not that it is easy to open (see previous paragraph).

Fifth, the brass fittings must tarnish very easily, because the bag arrives with every single exposed brass piece wrapped tightly in thin plastic wrap. It takes something very sharp to cut the plastic, and you must be careful not to scratch the fittings. (I succeeded in removing the wrappings without damaging the bag, but I punctured my left wrist with an Olfa knife in the process.)

The bag is reasonably priced (about $90 on Amazon). It comes with a snap-on shoulder carrying strap, and has a sturdy, permanently attached satchel handle. The handle is very comfortable. The bag leather is already distressed, so you needn’t worry about scratches. This is a truly rugged laptop bag.

Having the capability to provide super fast internet speed and power at the same time makes this switch perfect for both business environments and as a hub for security systems.

I’ve tested my unit extensively using different security cameras and the results are nothing short of incredible. While most security cameras can be run via WiFi, nearly all of them still require a power adapter be plugged in. By utilizing this hub, security breaches are all but eliminated - by utilizing Ethernet instead of Wifi transmission your local storage unit makes it so there is no easy out of network access. In addition, transfer speed, resolution and picture quality is greatly increased - making the entire system more useful. In my experience, I found power is much easier to manage doing it this way as opposed to having to run separate power supplies to each camera.

I always wanted a Yamaha Aventage Receiver, but until now they all had features I didn't need, let alone wanted to pay for; Enter the RX-A550.

This receiver is designed for people like me who appreciated great sound quality, but could care less about features such as dual HDMI out, dual subs, 7 channel speaker capability, multi-room listening, or Sirius adaptability. In the past I have always been duped into paying for those features, because that was the only way I could get a nice quality WiFi AV Receiver with the functions I wanted.

Couldn't agree more with another reviewer that getting this receiver is really not worth it unless you have high end speakers. Movies and music sound rich and detailed when this unit is paired with my KEF Eggs. Really an enjoyable listening experience, which I would take over a mediocre 9.2 set-up any day of the week.

My favorite feature of these newer Yamaha receivers is the Virtual CINEMA FRONT option. Personally, I prefer all sound to be coming from the front of the room. I know the thought of this makes some die-hard type-A AV people cringe, but hey it's all about personal preference.

This unit is made in Malaysia, unlike my previous lower end Yamaha receiver, which was made in China. Malaysia has been churning out high quality electronics for some time now. One example of that is the "Boston Acoustics Recepter" (not the inferior HD version). I purchased my Malaysian Recepter new in the '90s and it still works as new. Recepters are still selling used for at least 1/3 of original sticker price, unlike just about any other piece of electronics from the '90's.

The Yamaha iOS App has decent look and feel, but the UI that you see on your TV screen has an archaic aura matched only by that of a Commodore 64. This however does not bother me in the least. I bought this receiver to listen too, not look at. Much of the time I am controlling the receiver with my iPhone listening to music, and the TV isn't even on. There other receivers that have prettier user interfaces, but few are as long lasting or rich sounding as the Yamaha Aventage line...

This is not a true coconut water, but a drink that contains coconut water, nata de coco (a gel made from fermented coconut water), and flavoring among the ingredients. I love it because it's refreshing, especially on humid days, and uses real sugar instead of substitutes that I try to avoid.

Each eight ounce serving contains 70 calories with 18 grams of carbs (16 of which are from sugars). Contrast that with the same serving of Classic Coke, which comes in at 95 calories and 26.4 grams of carbs (all of which are from sugars) and this wins from a nutritional perspective. This drink is much lighter than most sodas and I have personally found it to be good for suppressing my appetite as well.

While it does quench thirst, it does not have the sodium content to be ideal for rehydration. Gatorade, for example, contains roughly 100mg of sodium for the same serving size, which is significantly more than the 15mg this drink contains. Moreover, this drink is missing potassium, which is also recommended for rehydration. I am mentioning this because there are coconut waters that are formulated for rehydration, but this one is more of a beverage.

The main ingredient is mineral water, followed by nata de coco, organic cane sugar, coconut water, calcium lactate, citric acid, sodium citrate, gellan gum and grapefruid seed extract.

Bottom line for me: I consume about sixteen ounces of this per day, and during exceptionally hot and humid days about twice that. Although this is no substitute for a rehydration drink, it does quench my thirst and the sugar gives me a boost without causing cramps in my fingers and toes like a soda does.

I have worked with a lot of active noise canceling (ANC) headphones by a lot of manufacturers, including an older pair of Philips headphones. I’ve seen a wide variance in ANC implementation and sound profiles, and to be honest few manufacturers get theirs right. With this set of headphones, Philips comes close.

These are over-ear phones which I prefer over on-ear phones. They fit snugly but not tight, and they actually do a good job of sound isolation. Even if you don’t like the ANC function (which would defeat the purpose of having these phones), these do a surprisingly good job of sound isolation. The pads are soft enough and comfortable enough that I can wear these for quite a while without discomfort. After a bit of time they do start to get a little warm but not to the point that I need to take them off.

These connect via Bluetooth and they connect very quickly. The connectivity of these phones is absolutely amazing: this is the very first pair of Bluetooth headphones I have used that maintains a steady connection up two flights of stairs with closed doors in between the phones and the source. The connectivity alone makes these very much worth checking out.

The ANC function is very good though it is not quite as aggressive as that of Bose or Sony. It is strong enough to mostly drown out a droning high-volume fan (my baseline for testing), such that music at a low volume while the ANC is turned on completely drowns out the fan. While Bose and Sony go to the extreme for noise cancellation, and other manufacturers often have ANC that’s barely there, Philips has implemented a system that is good enough for most. I am pleased with the ANC and will use these phones when I travel next.

The ANC function on these phones can be turned off if desired. There is also a special “awareness mode” that is an in-between mode that doesn’t completely turn off ANC but allows more environmental noise in, and this mode is really designed for permitting conversation without having to turn everything off completely. It works fairly well though the noise this mode produces via the external microphone is slightly harsh and shrill.

The default sound profile is not exactly perfect but it is better than many I have used and heard. These do boost the bass by default though not to an uncomfortable level. Bass boost is very common in headphones and it’s often too aggressive, but these actually give a modest boost. The midrange is a little soft though present. The highs sound bright and clear but not piercing. As a result, the sound profile is not quite perfectly balanced but it still good.

The sound profile can be tweaked via an app. I found the Philips Headphones app, installed it and started messing with it. The app works better than the reviews have suggested and it does a decent job of adjusting the headphones on the fly. The mode can be changed as well as the sound profile to adjust for different could quality based on music type, and there is a custom setting so that the equalizer can be adjusted to taste. The only complaint I have with the app is that there is about a 1s pause when changing modes between ANC. Awareness mode and Off, though this gap does not occur when changing the mode via the button on the headphones.

I like these ANC phones. They’re not perfect but they’re better than average with a good ANC function and decent sound. The have absolutely incredible connectivity, and they can be adjusted to taste via an app. This is a pair to keep on the short list if you need Bluethooth headphones that maintain a connection a long way from the source and provide ANC in the deal.

Though I have a laptop, I decided to use this solid-state drive as a boot drive on my desktop computer. If you are unfamiliar with the difference between a solid-state and a regular hard drive, the solid-state has no moving parts, which makes it silent, fast, reliable, and shock resistant. It has twice the capacity and twice the speed of the solid-state drive I got a couple of years ago for the same price, and blows away a standard drive for speed.

Given the silence and speed, it makes a great boot drive for running Windows, Photoshop, and other programs where speed is a huge advantage. Just to give you an idea, when upgrading from a regular two-year-old hard drive to this solid-state drive, my Windows boot time went from two minutes to about 10 seconds. Seriously, my computer now starts up and is ready to use in like 10 seconds.

What I do is use a solid-state drive as my boot drive and a regular hard drive as a storage drive. Solid-state drives like this are really expensive to purchase if you need any kind of capacity, but a 200 GB drive will certainly hold all of your programs and often used files.

As for this drive specifically, I hooked it up to my desktop and it was immediately recognized by Windows. The drivers installed automatically. In order to make the drive show up as a drive and work in Windows 7, I had to right-click on computer, click manage, double-click storage, double-click disk management, partition it, give it a drive letter, and format it.

As I said, it's a lot faster than the solid-state drive I had from a couple years ago, and there's no problem using it on my desktop machine rather than my laptop.

Having recently dug my music collection (odd how we go back into hobbies after years of stagnation), I took time to curate my setup (and by setup I mean my Note8 with a USB DAC) for optimal listening. Until recently, but "best" headphones were my Shure Aonic 4, which are excellent for the price range. The cable it comes with is okay, but preferably replaceable. It comes with an inline mic and makes a lot of feedback-noise when moved. I know cables are a mixed bag when it comes to audio equipment, so I shied away for years. But rather than place the emphasis on audio-quality improvement when looking at cables, I realized I'd rather get a cable if it looks and feels good. This one fit the ticket.

This is the only cable I have that's meant to be swapped with MMCX in-ear headphones. They pair well with the Aonic 4. First, I'll get the problems I have out of the way.

Since this cable is meant to connect with around-the-ear IEMs, there's a plastic wrap near each MMCX adapter. It makes wearing around the ears easier, but putting them on initially takes a few tries. They are easy to tangle, even if I use the "roadie wrap." Putting them on while on the go proved to be suboptimal; I have to be sitting or standing to put them on.

Sometimes I get some feedback noise, but rarely. Definitely not the same as the stock cable that comes with the Aonic 4.

The biggest problem I have is that the end connection disconnects nearly every time I use the cable. Having a modular cable is awesome, but the connection from the cable to the audio jack doesn't lock. I expected there to be a click, indicating it's on and snug, but no such thing. Since I use this cable while on the go, it's connected to my phone, which rests in my pocket. At least once the cable end will come loose. It's easy to press back in (just a little nudge will do), but it is rather annoying.

Now for the good.

The cable feels awesome. I get now why people prefer to upgrade certain cables. I care very little for how much the audio quality is "improved" (there's too much immeasurable subjectivity in that area), but having a cable that doesn't tangle easily and is very light makes enough of a difference to justify the upgrade. The cable is soft to the touch, though I don't doubt its ruggedness in the long term. The MMCX connectors snap satisfactorily into the Shure IEMs; at least those haven't come loose. The metal ends and Y-splitter are very nice and definitely attribute the cable with a premium look.

This cable has sold me on the reasons to upgrade headphone cables.

The rooCASE Oragami Case seems to be currently at or near the top of the cases, the big advantage of this case being the number and variations of orientations, including both portrait and landscape, and at the price point, is hard to beat.  The oragami cover is ingenious, you can fold it up all sorts of ways, the iPad Air has a lot of applications that fairly beg for portrait orientation (reading a book, newspaper, etc.).  The conventional Apple case supports only landscape, as do a number of competitors (the CaseCrown Omni is one of the better conventional ones).  The Moshi and O!Case are also oragami cases, although the designs differ some.  The rooCASE has a more rubberized or grippy exterior, key because it's less likely to slip and get dropped.  Protection is generally pretty good, but the CaseCrown does a little better on edge protection, the openings on the rooCase tend to be U-shaped, the CaseCrown is more O-Shaped, but otherwise they are very similar.  The Moshi has one advantage, in that it has a back magnet, that lets it stay open better in book mode.  The rooCASE actually has magnets that keep it closed pretty well, but it lacks a back magnet.  The rooCase front cover of course folds up to support quite a number of variations or angles, which is a big advantage over conventional cases, and on a desk or table, is plenty stable.  The microfiber front interior is nice, it tends to help keep the screen clean, but it is worth noting that the orgami pattern tends to show up in the fingerprints and grease, so you do need to clean the screen from time to time.  rooCASE also shuts off the iPad Air screen when you close it, a very useful feature.  The end result is still pretty light and easy to carry, in keeping with the iPad Air design point.  Why not 5 stars?  rooCase is very close, but they could improve the edge coverage/protection, and add a back magnet (ala Moshi), and NuGuard KX probably has the better back protection (at the cost of some bulk), but at its price-point, front and back protection, oragami design that lets you pick multiple orientations and angles, the rooCASE is pretty much unbeatable, and worthy of consideration at any price.

The only indications of how to start appeared in the radio's display window, instructing me to go online to do the setup. After some perseverance, I finally figured out how to use the Reciva Internet Radio site to connect the radio with the services I've been using with my computers for years.

Once I finally got the thing to start streaming (about 4 frustrating hours after I began the set up) I realized that, even less than three feet from my router, the unit stayed in buffering mode more than it actually played music, no matter what bps settings I tried. I don't really know much about the technical end of audio streaming, but my MediaLink router works fine with my two portable computers, and streams video and music from services like Pandora and Rhapsody with no glitches whatever. I didn't see much point in listening to 10 seconds of a song, then waiting through 15 or 20 while the unit's memory silently buffered so it could continue.

Even if you're not a digital audio newbie, if you're looking for straightforward setup and easy operation, this AIN'T IT. I may look further into wireless digital radio --but I doubt it, at least not in the near future.

The visuals of the screen are great, which make for impressive video viewing. Picture is great and graphics are very crisp whether it is a Powerpoint still picture on display or a movie. The audio is great, too. While not a gaming pc, this is a nice one for video/audio usage.

It is a very thin and elegant design. The DVD multi recorder fits nicely along the side panels along with three USB ports, a microphone jack, SD slot, network slot and HDMI port.

The grooved out design around the touch pad is a small detail that has a nice impact on the overall look of the keyboard and touchpad (the touchpad is a bit of a different design with the 'clicks', but honestly, at this point with various keyboards for various devices, I'm used to things being different and just roll with it. But FYI to buyer). Keyboard is nicely laid out with light/'chiclet' touch keys and touchpad is sensitive without being too touchy. Considering that I also have a Asus Ultrabook S500-CA with a twitchy as heck touchpad OOB, this is a welcome relief.

Battery life appears to be great as well. I had the machine in hibernate for approx. 6 hours after machine was fully charged and the battery was not even down past ½ charge after all that time. And while in use, it does last about 6 hours. Considering the size and weight, that's pretty good.

Now for some negatives (or at least not so greats).
Fan vent is on the bottom which can be seen as a negative to anyone that works with the laptop sitting on their lap. I would imagine that the fan would be blocked in this instance and would not function properly and possibly allow machine to overheat? Gonna need a cooler for this one while using it for any length of time.

No SSD at all?

It barely comes in under 5lbs. As stated, I also have a ASUS Ultrabook S500CA, which is a 15" screen and weighs less. It also doesn't have a DVD drive, so.... You're definitely adding weight here for that and a few other options (and losing USB and other ports).

No full Microsoft Office Suite/software (you'll have to pay to get more than a trial version or use something else). Just making that clear. - edited as before I had stated 'Windows'. Sorry for any confusion.

All in all, this is a responsive laptop with impressive visual and audio that can be useful to an everyday user. It probably has some drawbacks to someone needing serious processing (no SSD), but for a lot of users, this one is good. I like ASUS, I find them to be reliable laptops, their designs tend to be good, and this ultrabook is no exception.

For everyday use, I'd give this 4.5 -5 stars. Anything else, take off a star or two.

I've had no real problems with this router. Since I did my homework before buying it cheap, I had read about all of the problems other people have had. In particular, I noted several observations that this device runs hot. That shouldn't be a surprise, since the case ventilation is poor compared to other routers on the market. I put mine in an open space on a wooden desktop and had no problems for a long while. One hot summer day, the router had to be reset, and the case was unusually hot to the touch. I put the router up on a couple of small blocks, to get more air circulation and the problem went away.

My advice, either put it up on spacers like mine, or mount it vertically on a wall or the side of a desk. Make sure you don't block off any air ventilation.

I travel quite a bit and many of the trips I take are short in duration- often only two or three nights. I don’t need a lot of luggage space for these short trips and I like taking backpacks because I can often avoid carry- on and baggage fees if my backpack can fit under my seat. This desire for economical travel led me to get the Case Logic BRYBPR116 Bryker Backpack Roller.

With this Case Logic Backpack, you get a two-in-one backpack and piece of luggage well suited for travel or business. The wheels make it perfect for traversing an airport and with the added straps, you can carry it on your back, like a traditional backpack. There is an outside pocket where you can tuck the straps so they are not hanging out, flopping around when you don’t need them. And the handle can be completely pushed inside the backpack and sealed off with a zipper so that no one sees it. I like these qualities because it means I can make this look like a backpack when I want it to and I can make it look more like a piece of luggage when I want it to.

Inside the backpack, there is a separate compartment for a laptop and I like that you can unsnap this if you like, making for a larger interior space that is just right for stuffing your two- day supply of clothing and personal items. Like I said, my primary usage with this backpack is for travel and I usually don’t take my laptop with me when I’m on a two- day trip, so I would rather have the open space, to make it more like a piece of luggage.

There is one thing to keep in mind if you take this backpack on a plane, and that is the size of pack makes it only barely able to fit under your seat. It will stick out some, so be prepared to have a snug space where your feet normally go. And unlike other backpacks, it’s too rigid- thanks to the handle- to make it collapsible and flexible. To save having to pay carry- on fees on certain airlines, I am willing to place it under the airline seat in front of me regardless, even if it does stick out some. If your flying on an airline that doesn’t charge extra for carry-ons, then this won’t be an issue since you can easily place the backpack in the overhead, which is what I recommend doing. For everyone else, just bear in mind that the length of the backpack makes it a challenge to fit under a seat.

I have a wide assortment of backpacks and luggage in my home to accommodate different needs. This Case Logic rolling backpack is a nice addition to my collection and I like that it performs a dual role. It has suited me well so far and it makes a good choice of luggage/backpack for business people and others who are constantly on the go for short spans of time.

The Aurora R10 is the first AMD computer I've had in about 15 years since the days of the Athlon64. Its also been about 10 years since I had an ATI/AMD Radeon card and I'm similarly impressed with the improvements they've made in streamlining and improving their drivers (that was previously a major pain point and reason I've stuck with nvidia cards over the years)

Overall I think this is a great gaming CPU, it has a solid build and great performance for the price. It can run pretty much all current games smoothly as long as you aren't using 4k. If you are planning to run games in 4k then you probably need a more powerful video card setup. My only real complaint about this system is how loud the fans are when gaming.. its fine when doing most activities but the noise becomes quite loud and annoying when the GPU is taxed. This case does have enough room inside for a 120 radiator if you want to add watercooling, thats not enough to cool both the CPU and GPU but it would definitely be an improvement for not much money.

I have been using a 3-in to 1-out HDMI switch for a couple years and recently the media box for one of my TVs died, so put on connected to the single HDMI input. It works just fine, but I have more than 3 devices I'd like to connect and reaching to change the input is annoying.

I'll give it some time to see how it lasts. If it does well over time, I'll possibly buy another for another TV with only one HDMI input.

After three price increases in two years from Suddenlink, we said Enough and cut the cord to streaming only. We had two Fire Sticks already, but needed something for the living room television. We use sound bars for the 55 and 65" TV's and the Roku remote isn't set up for volume. Not a deal breaker by any means, just make sure you have another way to control volume. We're using the DirectTV Now cheapest option and the HULU LIVE beta for the first two months and then we'll keep the one that has been used most and drop the other. One thing I noticed immediately is with Roku (and the Fire Sticks) the 1080p picture on our big Samsung is much cleaner and prettier than when we had the cable service - we've used only the HDMI connection for years. I'm extremely pleased that we finally made the leap to streaming.

So I decided to go for MSI after doing much research on Nvidia Pascal-Powered laptops. I do a lot of 3DS Max work, and I'm a gamer since the 80's, so I figured, this may be the best route. I didn't want to get a laptop which, in a few months, would already be obsolete, so I skipped some of the other current gen models from the likes of Alienware with 970/980 m cards. I didn't give Asus a shot because I've had a not-so-good experience with my current and previous desktops. My current desktop (which is quite powerful so no qualms there)... had a keyboard issue, and I was only 3 months into ownership. Asus refused to replace it as their one year warranty only covers the PC itself, not the keyboard which I'm sorry, but is part of the system.They said if I paid for shipping they would give me a new one at cost. How generous - after the price I paid for that system.The keyboard is backlit red which matches the red-lit system and impossible to find. My previous Asus had a cheap motherboard / power supply, which overheated only a few months after my one year warranty was up.

This is my first MSI computer, and I have to say, the laptop is stunner. The Steel Series keyboard is a pleasure to type on with its generously- spaced keys, and backlit configurable color spectrum while the non-reflective IPS screen is gorgeous, sporting good viewing angles with colors that truly pop. I love 17" screens for gaming when I'm sitting on a recliner, as I don't feel like being hunched over a desk all night. I haven't used it for VR yet, but I did run the Steam VR Speed Test to see where it stands. On my Asus G11CD Desktop (16GB i7-6700 3.40Ghz and Nvidia 970), the results showed my system just making it into the VR ready green band. The same test on my MSI Laptop had the VR Ready indicator near the very end of the green band, almost off the chart. As for Windows 10 itself -- it's up within seconds thanks to the 128 SSD. There's not much to comment on the touchpad. I never use them - they're the spawn of Satan. I always hook up a wireless mouse.

I haven't had a chance to test all of my games yet, as my laptop less than a week old as of this review, but the few I've tried ran smooth as glass. I downloaded the demo of the updated System Shock which has a 2017 release. Using FRAPS FPS counter, I was clocking in 92-120 FPS. Same download on my Asus was roughly 75-83. I've been heavily involved with the Planet Coaster (Alpha) which is more taxing than most high end first person shooters. I am running large simulated theme parks, with very advanced lighting effects and all graphic options maxed out. With Nvidia GSync (this monitor supports it) enabled, I'm getting a solid 60 FPS .98% of the time. In comparison, my Asus using the same dense parks using V-Sync gave me an average of 45-50 FPS

Thankfully, there is not too much on the bloatware end. Most of the included extras are MSI tune-up/tweaking programs and surprisingly, quite useful. Norton Security however, is bloatware in my opinion. It came with my Asus, it came with this MSI, and on both systems, it was the first thing I deleted. I don't need it. I never will. Stop it.

As far as the audio, the Nahimic 2 Virtual Surround is super impressive. I've had other laptops in the past, and they've always sounded like tin can alley. The sound that comes out of this unit is rich, and at times, the surround effect is quite effective. The max volume could use another notch or two, but it's still quite competent. Definitely game and epic movie-worthy sound.

The system remains fairly cool and quite capable of dispersing heat properly. Running the power hungry Planet Coaster Alpha no doubt generates a ton of heat, but it all seems to flow out of the back vents, so no keyboard hot-spots. One issue: I use a very thin, rigid laptop mat so the back vent heat winds up flowing to my knees which can be uncomfortable. The one way around this is pulling the laptop toward you, allowing for about an inch of the mat to stick out of the back as a kind of shield. A welcome addition is the turbo fan which you can easily access from a button on the left side of the laptop. I usually turn it on for about a minute and it diminishes the heat fairly well. One of the included MSI utilities gives you more access to the fan's options. Besides the fan, the MSI Dominator Pro has additional buttons that handle quick access functions like sleep mode, sample keyboard color layouts, and other options. But what surprised me, shocked me really, was the marked difference in the pulse oximeter reading between this watch, measuring at the wrist, and a fingertip oximeter. I'm currently suffering from dyspnea and while the fingertip measurement is sometimes harrowing, the wrist measurement is always a comforting 96% approximately. I've asked several medical professionals why this is, and I've googled a bit on my own and the only thing I can tell you is that I simply can't tell you why the measurement can be so different at different parts of the body. Nevertheless, I'll take the higher measurement with gratitude because it doesn't add more stress to the mix.

My best advice, across the boards, is to make baseline measurements on all the functions, and compare them to recent or baseline measurements from other devices. I have a sleeve for my tablet that works out very well for me. It provides some protection for the screen and provides some limited protection against drops and bumps. The sleeve I have is the 15.6” version and it fits my laptop almost perfectly. There is a small amount of wiggle room in the sleeve so that the laptop can slide a little from side to side and it’s just enough to make slipping the laptop in and taking it back out much easier. The outer material is a tight woolen weave and it does a good job of repelling water (though it is not completely waterproof). The end result is a very slightly damp surface, nowhere near enough to get the laptop inside even slightly wet. So, when toting the sleeve outside it will effectively protect the laptop inside from rain.

There are two pockets inside this sleeve. One is lined in a fleece-like soft material that gently cushions the laptop and allows it to slide in and out more easily. The other pocket is zippered and it is lined in vinyl; it is a good place to put papers, smaller accessories like a travel mouse and other small items. This pocket is not big enough to handle a lot of extras like a full laptop bag.

I inspected the sleeve closely and I have not been able to find any problems in the way it is made. There are no loose threads, stitching is tight and straight and there are not crooked material patches. The zipper works smoothly and so far does not catch on the material of the sleeve. Overall I am pleased with the materials and assembly.

Overall I'm very pleased with these ear buds. They are my first pair of bluetooth buds and it has been wonderful to not have to deal with cords, especially when working out. I can't tell you how many times I've hit an earbud cord while exercising and ripped the ear bud from my ear. A real pain in the neck (and ear!).

>>>Pros:

Comfort - These fit very well in my ear. There are different tip sizes to create a good fit and, after trying them all out, I went with the medium size. Very comfortable to wear even for long periods of time.

Stay put - I've yet to have them fall out even when doing aerobic exercises or while on the treadmill.

Sound - they sound pretty good. The sound is not as good as my favorite (and inexpensive) corded buds ([[ASIN:B0053R0WWG RHA MA-350 Aluminium Noise Isolating In-Ear Earphones]]) but they are a solid B+ performer with regard to bass response and overall clarity. Keep in mind that good bass response is affected by how the buds fit in your ear, so it's important to try out different tip sizes to see how they affect sound quality. They do get harsh at loud volumes, but for normal listening they are more than fine for my non-audiophile ears. They do reasonably well at blocking out ambient noise.

Setup - I found it straightforward even though I've never had any experience with setting up bluetooth earbuds.

Size - nice and compact so you don't get the "radar dish" look that larger units can have.

Durability - they have a "sweat proof" guarantee which is nice (although I imagine, like most guarantees, there are some loopholes). Overall build quality is good, with a very solid feel to all components.

>>>Cons:

Battery life - The manufacturer claims a battery life of 4.5 hours but I've yet to get more than 3 hours off a single charge. Plus there's no warning about battery life (until you're almost fully discharged) or a visual indicator of how much charge there is left.

Usability - the buttons on the buds are too small, making it difficult for me to push the right one. A lot of fumbling and mis-presses, making it often easier to deal with volume changes on the device, which kills some of the value of having wireless buds. I guess I lack the nimble fingers of the primary target market.

But overall, I'm pleased. The pros outweigh the cons, and I think this is a solid 4-star device.

Dirt, bugs, moisture can easily get inside your backpack. 2) the zippers are attached to each other with a loop of nylon. This is going to catch on things (branches, chairs, doors, etc.) and open. My camera gear is expensive and dear to me, I want to protect it the best I can. Having an opening that doesn't seal completely and can easily be opened wider by accident is a poor design.

Why is the cable size and breaker on this thing so undersized when it is presumably (due to the fact that it is Stanley Max) for running power tools? 16AWG and 13A is actually a bottleneck compared to a standard 15A 14AWG household circuit. Worse is that it is a huge bottleneck compared to the 12AWG 20A circuits I put in work and kitchen areas to accommodate the many tools (e.g., miter saws, medium sized air compressors, etc.) and appliances (e.g., microwaves) that push the envelope on the 15A circuits.

Point is, right off the bat, I can't run large tools on this thing (and that includes some plug-in-lawn equipment), and I can't run most medium sized tools two at a time on this thing (good drills, planers, grinders, etc. often draw around 9A), so what's the point of the multiple outlets except, granted, that you don't have to unplug one to plug the other in over and over again if working with two tools alternately.

On the flip side, this lighter gauge cable does allow this power hub to be lighter and easier to deal with. It does roll up nicely and I like that the cord can be attached on the side so it doesn't unravel itself.

But I think the outlets should be spaced a little further a part, given that the size could accommodate that. That would allow larger plugs, and maybe even some AC adapters to fit. I also think 20 ft. is way too short, especially for the reel setup (it's not that hard to untangle 20ft.) and the fact that this thing is probably large enough to hold more.

You could use it for Christmas lights or something like that - except it is not a true weatherproof cord - or some low power hobby in the house. This has no quality issues, and there are plenty of uses for it, but the name has me thinking it is trying to be in the tool market. To be really effective in that market, it should be 12AWG, accept 20A plugs, be minimum 50' long, and have the outlets spaced slightly further apart.

One of my favorite Nikon lenses is an old 16mm fisheye from about 1977, I think. It has two problems: it is a fisheye and curves straight lines at the edges and it's a non-CPU lens, like many of my aged old Nikon lenses. Non-CPU means I have to remember to select it from my list of non-CPU lenses using that menu feature of the D800, and that there is no focus assist. It's full frame, however, and now that we're back to shooting full FX 24x36 sensor, the old lenses are making a comeback.

That 16mm fisheye costs a pretty penny today and the 14-24mm Nikon f/2.8 zoom is even more. And I'm sure they are both fine lenses.

So I bought a Samyang/Rokinon 800mm f/8 mirror lens for two bills and said, "that ought to be fun, even if it's not that great a lens for such little money." Funny thing: it's a pretty good lens.

That good purchase experience allowed me to select this 14mm Rokinon f/2.8. It is surprisingly good considering it's one third the cost of its Nikon equivalent. Even wide open at 1.5 feet, it is tack sharp.

The main difference between this and the Nikon is that this Rokinon is a fully manual focus lens while the 14mm Nikon is auto focus, although I'm not sure how accurately a 14mm lens can focus automatically. I've often simply estimated the distance and set the lens to that distance using the barrel markings. The focus ring is a pleasant long throw, with the ring rotating about 270 degrees around the lens from infinity to .28 meters (less than 1 foot). Focus drag feels silky smooth. Focus happens internally -- the front element does not rotate.

This Rokinon has a clickstop f/stop diaphragm. It also has a chip in it, giving it enough smarts to qualify as an AI-S lens. To use it on a D800, you have to set it to minimum aperture (f/22) or you get the flashing "fee" in the viewfinder. Ah, takes me back....

Setting it to f/22 (marked in orange) tells the camera what f/stop the lens is working at and allows control of the f/stop from the front selector wheel on the D800. The focus indicator in the eyepiece also works -- you see the left/right arrows and the little ball that verifies it's in focus. It also automatically records f/stop and focal length data in the metadata with the shot. In other words, it's a real lens, just without auto focus, for one third the cost. Old Nikon AI-S lenses have a little lock that holds the f/stop ring at minimum aperture that's not present on this lens, but the click stops are secure and the f/stop ring stays where you set it.

The front element is radically curved and is protected somewhat by the flower petal shaped built-in lens shade. Be careful: that front element is really exposed to the weather.

The front lens cap is terrific and very well designed. It's a durable hard plastic unit that slips over the flower petal lens shade and snaps securely in place against detents in the the lens shade. You have to squeeze both plastic flush-mount buttons on the front edge of the cap to release it. It won't fall off by accident under any circumstances. Only drawback it that it's about 1-3/8" deep and 3-5/8" diameter, so it doesn't exactly slip into a back pocket when it's off the lens.

The cosmetics of the lens are appealing. Even has a brass/gold colored band around the front that mimics real Nikon lenses. The focus ring rubber grip is good and the the body of the lens, minus the front element, is about the size of a 50mm f/1.4 lens. Focus distances in feet and meters are clearly engraved. One nice thing it has that I wish all lenses had is the focal length clearly and largely printed on the side of the lens so you can tell at a glance what it is. Nice. The mount is precision machined and fits the camera like it should. There are five little electrical contacts that interface with the camera body to communicate exposure info. For transport, it comes with an unpadded velour drawstring pouch. May want something a bit more padded if it's bouncing around inside a camera bag against other gear. But the bag's adequate, folds flat when not in use and is compact.

As for performance, I'm not going to go into lines/per millimeter sharpness. What I can say is that it's great for architectural interiors and wide, WIDE rectilinear shots. And in analyzing a snap of my dog I pushed in on his eye as far as I could looking at the D800's rear screen and could see the finest of eyelashes, showing off both the resolution of the lens and the remarkable resolution of the D800's 36 megapixel sensor. The lens distinguishes itself from all the wide/medium wide 24mm/35mm lenses out there. Do I really need to have a heavy, giant, hyper-expensive zoom lens that zooms 10 whole millimeters from 14mm all the way to 24mm? Not hardly. If I need serious wide angle this 14mm will fill the bill nicely, even wide open.

No filters for it, of course, because the front element is so deeply curved.

I'm particularly interested in using the 14mm for video shoots, which I use the D800 for more than for still photography. I'll be able to see the whole world with this lens, even in the most cramped of situations.

This will be a fun lens. Highly recommended.

So I upgraded my home desk (which was an old kitchen table) and decided I needed to free up some desktop space. Also, the desk was smaller and I didn't want the monitor to be closer to me. What I was most concerned about was the actual distance between me and the monitor. Most spec sheets will list the maximum extension distance- how far the arm can bring the monitor to you, but not how far behind the desk it can carry it. I posted questions on Amazon, but really never got a clear answer for the products I was interested in. (So it's actually approximately 2") I decided to pull the trigger on this one and I'm glad I did. (So it's actually about

AESTHETICS 4.5/5 The center pole is stainless steel and the body is a metallic silver/grey color. I like the look of the pole mount like this, instead of the style where it just swivels at the base. My desk and components happen to be all black and I should have put more thought into the color when I bought this. There is a lot of contrast and I think a darker grey or black would have looked better. This style with the gas spring mount has a very chunky arm, however the arm is completely concealed by the monitor.

STURDINESS 4.5/5 I don't really have anything else to compare it to seeing as this is my first stand. However there is little wobble/bounce with the arm fully extended. I am not worried about this going anywhere. If you have the monitor clamped lower down on the pole you will get even less bounce. I do think that the bottom plate of the C clamp should be larger. My desk is particle board and I did put cardboard and foam in between the clamp and the desk to put less stress at the clamp site. They do make professional kits for this, but it wasn't necessary for this.

VALUE 5/5 I paid approximately $40 dollars and I think it was a fair price for the features and performance. Looking at what is available I think $40- 70 dollar range is ideal for most people's needs at home. Below this and the quality/features may suffer. I don't think it is necessary to spend more than this unless you very frequently need to reposition the monitor. I do not need to move it often.

INSTALLATION 4/5 The directions were not written in very clear English (probably poorly translated from Chinese). However, this was super easy to install and I could have done it without directions. The only issue I had was mounting the VESA mount to the back of the monitor. The supplied screws were too long, so I used my original screws, but they were still too long. The plate that screws into the monitor is thinner than the plate on the OEM stand, so the screws in my case were about 2-3mm too long and there is a gap/play/movement. It's not an issue for the moment, but I will have to get some washers or spacers.
The only spring I had to adjust for my 10lb/27" monitor was the tilt spring. It required about 1/4 turn to get the right tension.

TO SUMMARIZE MY COMPLAINTS/CONS

-Color: I knew this when I bought it so it's not really a con
-Mounting: The thinner VESA plate may require additional modifications
-Clamp: The part of the clamp under the table is a little small. I'd be careful if mounting on very thin surfaces. It may require reinforcement.

The WD_Black 1TB D50 Game Dock has quality written all over it. Metal construction for heat dissipation, thunderbolt support, nice RGB lighting, and a fast NVMe drive. It is quite obviously geared toward the PC Gaming crowd, but which segment?

The build of this product screams high-quality gaming accessory. Its outer design is reminiscent of a cargo container and its collection of ports are impressive. Each USB port is well labeled with its speed (4x 10Gb/s Type-A and 2x 10Gb/s Type-C), two thunderbolt ports, one of which outputs 87 watts of power, one displayport, one network port (gigabit), and one 3.5mm headphone jack. Add to this, the 1TB high-performance NVMe drive. All in one sleek-looking, compact container (pun intended).

It is obvious that this dock is geared toward the Gaming Laptop crowd, whether its for gaming or for video/graphics production work, but I find that it really doesn't make sense for me. In my tests, this product does not work without the power adapter (it really should be able to power itself through the thunderbolt port). This means an additional outlet that's drawing power at all times. This would make sense if gaming laptops can actually be powered and charged from the 87w thunderbolt port but I have not seen a gaming pc with discreet graphics that actually accepts anything in that range.

So what other advantage would this product provide? External storage through a fast Thunderbolt connection. At $450, this product provides 1TB of additional storage. Which 2TB NVMe drives available for much less, I would opt to upgrade my internal storage to 2TB instead.

Then that leave the docking station. The ports are all of the high quality and your monitor, network, keyboard, mouse, headset, and speakers can be connected via a single thunderbolt connection. This is convenient, but I don't think this justifies the price as there are many docks out there that work just as well, albeit through a USB 3.1 connection instead.

WD has really done well to package a lot into this dock but is charging a premium for it. Personally, I think that there are just better ways of achieving equal or better results when it comes to upgrading a gaming laptop.

**update**
Coming back to think about it some more, I realized exactly what niche WD was going for: Macbooks. Some Macbooks have only two thunderbolt ports and all of them are not easily upgradeable so this product does indeed provide a value to those consumers. But then does it make sense to spend an additional 35% of the price of the laptop (Macbook Pro 13" is $1299) to address problems that Apple introduced into their laptops? I guess if you're already in their ecosystem, it's par for the course. That's not to say Apple is the only one. Microsoft has made their products impossible to upgrade as well, but none of these are actually gaming laptops.

I received a review sample from the manufacturer and was pleasantly surprised when I opened the box. I was expecting an 'erector set' of many pieces that I would need to put together. Instead I received a complete solution that literally unfolded and snapped into place in minutes.

Set up entails the unfolding and snapping step, plus connecting the antenna to a powered booster box with coaxial cable in from the antenna and out to your TV. Once connected you need to go into your TV's settings, select antenna as the input, then do a scan for available channels.

Since I live close to a major metropolitan area - Orlando, Florida - I decided to test this at a friend's home in Ormond Beach, which is about sixty miles from Orlando and roughly the same distance from Jacksonville. This location tested the claimed forty mile radius for the device.

The true power was when I did a quick test by temporarily setting it up, plugging it in and seeing what channels were available. With the device sitting on the floor the first scan found seven digital channels. Bear in mind that this was laying on the floor for the initial test, which is hardly optimum.

Test number two entailed raising the antenna towards the ceiling (but not permanently mounting it) and moving it around to various spots in a 15x10 foot room. That increased the total channels received to twenty-two, including Orlando and Jacksonville channels that were twenty miles beyond the claimed range, as well as a few channels in Cocoa Beach (right at the edge of the range).

Note that in both tests the Central Florida terrain is relatively flat. In other geographic locations the results may have been vastly different.

Installation does require access to 110/120 AC power for the signal booster module. The mounting hardware that ships with this antenna is heavy-duty and complete. You can use one of the clamps to mount it to practically any pole of beam, but there is a pipe assembly that provides you with even more mounting options. The kit also includes fifty feel of high quality coaxial cable, with a removable double male connector in one end in case you need to run it even farther. You will need to purchase a second coaxial cable to connect the booster box's out port to your TV.

For outdoor mounting (or in a ceiling that is not close to a 110/120 AC outlet) I recommend running the longer cable from the antenna to the powered booster, which can be placed close to the TV. If you decide to place the booster closer to the antenna's coaxial connection make sure you can do with without using an extension cord, which could be a safety issue.

The bottom line is this antenna works beautifully. Since it picked up signals fifty percent farther than the claimed range it greatly exceeded my expectations. For the record, although I received the antenna as a review sample I donated it to a worthy cause after I completed my testing and had enough information to write this review. I do recommend it as a wonderful solution and an alternative to cable if local programming meets your news and entertainment needs.

This is one of the modems that's on Comcast's recommended list for my cable system here in California. When the cable guy showed up to install my Internet service, he checked it out and said "It will work fine." After about an hour of pulling wires around my house, he hooked things up to the modem and I had very high speed Internet service. Pretty sweet.

I chose this model because its upload and download specs are well above what my cable Internet service needs, and because it has advanced features like IPv6. So I'm assuming they got the basic stuff right as well. Other reviewers have said this model runs hot, but I haven't observed that. I have it in my utility room which is in the basement where it's pretty cool to start with.

The lights on the front of the unit show what's going on, which is mostly useful as it boots up. They work well, and are also attractive to look at -- they had a good designer for that. The unit has only 3 connection ports on the back, one for power, one for the incoming cable, and one Ethernet RJ-45 out. If you want to hook up more than a single computer, you'll need to connect this single Ethernet port to a router, or wireless router. I have the cable modem connected into a 5-port NetGear switch downstairs, which is connected to an 8-port NetGear switch upstairs, which is then connected to my Linksys wireless router. My computers then use the IP addresses that the wireless router provides. (It won't work to plug additional computers into the switch that I connected directly to the cable modem because the cable company provides only one IP address. It's the wireless router that hands out additional IP addresses. Each computer that you're using requires its own IP address.) The wireless connection works well for my 2 computers and my Roku box for Netflix. (And the bandwidth available to Netflix is amazing. It spends virtually no time at all buffering before it starts streaming HD video.)

Oh, and of course I had to reboot everything (including the modem and the wireless router) for the new modem to be recognized. For now, I'm keeping my old DSL service as a backup Internet service. Not sure when I might decide to give that up.

I'm a big fan of Kindle e-Readers. We own two of the older generation ones (the last Kindles with keyboard) and for x-mas I bought my mother a Kindle Fire HD 8.9 for x-mas. But, alas, she doesn't seem to have fine enough motor control to hit the small buttons on that device (see my review for that device). So the Fire has been sitting unused on the coffee table for a few months now.

But this is not a review of the Fire HD 8.9. I want to describe my very short experience with the basic Kindle and the Kindle Paperwhite - as they relate to the intended user: my mom. She recently suffered a stroke and one of the side effects is that she now has a constant tremble in her left hand. As she had trouble with the Fire HD 8.9 we went to Staples to see if the more purpose-built Kindles were easier to operate. We were not surprised when she often made mistakes selecting books on the Paperwhite's touch screen. But we were surprised to find that she couldn't even handle the physical buttons on the basic Kindle! From what I could tell, the problems were: the side-buttons (page forward/backward) are much smaller and narrower than they were on our old Kindles (which my mom had no trouble with), so basic navigation among pages became iffy. Similarly, the D-pad is smaller too - and that made selection of books difficult for her. Finally, while I could easily hold my old Kindle with one hand AND operate the page forward button, this is a bit more difficult with the new basic Kindle. My mom could not manage it at all. And since she can't hold the Kindle with her trembling left hand, neither e-Reader was for her. [She is now making do with the Kindle Fire HD 8.9 by laying it on a flat surface and only operating it with her right hand].

I'm still giving the Kindle 4 stars because none of these shortcomings are of interest to the majority of people, but I wanted folks to be aware of the newer devices' potential limitations with those suffering from limited motor skills.

I acquired my Fitbit Sense in June 2021, it has not yet been a month, but so far so good with 24/7 use. I am slow to check out and use all the features, but what I have interacted with so far has been stellar.

I have been using Fitbit products since April 2015- kinda have a love/hate relationship with this brand. I use the activity tracker constantly, and I greatly enjoy the app. So I have stuck with it as I upgraded over the years (Charge x2, Blaze x2, Versa 2, and now Sense). As with many Fitbit users, there is a known frustration with the products. Despite some of my own qualms, and having the ability to spend whatever I want on any fitness tracker I want, I still end up (so far) with this brand. Mostly because I haven't found a tracker and app that I totally like better. I even have a Garmin, but I find that so far off base of accuracy (save for HR), that it is a glorified watch. Garmin seems to do best for actual intended activities (going for a run, going for a long walk, going cycling) where it seems to not be accurate in steps for any other part of the day (only counts about 1/3 of actual steps unless engaged in a longer duration activity, and even then it takes a few minutes for it to start). Also, the app seems to have a lot of info, but doent really tell me anything. That being said, when it was time for me to buy another fitness tracker--I went from Versa 2 to Garmin.. back to Fitbit. I went with the Sense because the price was right, and it was an upgrade over the Versa 2. After my underwhelming experience with the Garmin, I would have happily taken over a 2nd hand Charge from 2015. At least my steps would be accurate.

Ok, so back to the Sense. WOW, the visual on the screen is really clear and precise. Even way more so over the Versa 2, and I had no issues with that. Set up was EASY, and QUICK. Basically, just like in adding any other fitbit, just let it pair and it will very quickly be all set and ready to go. I didnt have any weird upselling offerings, or at least nothing that wasn't fantastically easy to opt out from. Nothing shady that I saw.

ONE POINT that I DO think is important to know is that if you happen to have a Versa 2 (Not sure if this also happens with regular Versa, Versa Lite, or Versa 3), but this could not be added alongside my Versa 2. I had to take the Versa 2 offline in order to add this Sense. I know this is the case with trying to add more than one of the same products, yet I have always been able to have several Fitbits paired no problem, as long as they were different models. SO, I guess the Fitbit app sees Sense and Versa 2 as the same. Not a big deal as my Versa 2 had essentially died after I wore it on a hot humid day and my sweat killed it (then I brought it back to life after putting it in a bag of rice for about a week, Then afterward the battery was never the same. It drained to nothing daily.. and I needed to not have to worry about daily charging.. hence my picking up a Garmin in the interim to see if I liked them enough to spring for a more fancy model--nope-- and ended up buying the Sense.)

Hope it lasts. I love the look. The band is way better than the old pin style. Swapping out bands is so much quicker, easier, less need for super fine motor skills. LOVE the charger. It just sort of magnetizes to the fitbit. No need to clip in.

SP02 wasn't the main feature I was drawn to, but in order to have accurate use it seems a special clock face is needed, and that clock face will drain battery quicker (from what I have read). That being said,

Battery life has been excellent for me.

Love being able to add other apps, and features. Scrolling is easy, turning face on/off is not complicated.

HEART RATE is accurate. I have tested it against my garmin, two blood pressure devices, and a doctors appointment. All saying the same.

Also, I the voice assistant is great. You can choose GOOGLE Assistant, OR Alexa. This is why selecting most recent reviews on this sort of stuff is important, as the early release of Sense did not have Google Assistant, but would soon with an update. True, and they followed through as I have it.

AT THIS TIME, I have ZERO issues, concerns with this Fitbit Sense. I will be back to update as I learn more, or if I have anything worth sharing that is bad. I keep up with my reviews as needed.

I’m a big fan of the Roar since it provides me with two key benefits: great sound and is easy to use. The Roar 2 retains those two benefits and adds one more: a smaller footprint. I’m going to try my best to not overuse the words “outstanding” and "impressive" in this review, but it’s going to be a challenge. This is an impressive speaker.

The out-of-the-box experience is nicely done. As expected at this price point, it comes in upscale packaging. More important, it comes with a pretty decent user guide. That’s significant since the Roar 2 has a lot of features – to call it just “a speaker” really shortchanges it. It’s also a recorder, a power bank, an MP3 player, an SD card reader, a speakerphone – it will even lull you to sleep with Bedtime Mode where it gradually decreases the volume and then powers off. My only complaint about the manual is that it’s physically small, which means the type size is also small. I do wish manufacturers would realize that those of us with aging eyes still like loud music!

And loud music is this product’s forte. I’m able to get room-filling sound while maintaining crisp highs, clear midrange and solid but not muddy bass. I can even go past room-filling to the “let’s annoy the neighbors” levels and still maintain impressive fidelity. Using the Tera Bass option boosts the bass response to the point where you would swear there was a separate subwoofer on the floor. You can see the end plates resonate to help drive the bass (plus it just looks really cool as well).

Day to day usage of the Roar 2 is straightforward even though there are so many features. All the buttons are labeled fairly clearly, albeit at times with small type. I would also have preferred a greater contrast to the labels since sometimes they are hard to see unless the Roar 2 is under a bright light. There are voice prompts for many key features which I found helpful. Normally I don’t care for voice prompts, but these were done in a natural sounding voice at a low volume making them not at all irritating. But, if you don’t like them at all, you can turn them off. There are small, but clear indicator lights to keep you apprised of battery charge level, settings, and other criteria.

The build quality is excellent. This feels as good as it looks, with a solid heft to it, an excellent quality metal grill, and quality plastic case components. All the buttons have a good tactile feel to them. I have it in white, which looks very nice with the gray contrast control pad. My only quibble is that some of the buttons/levers are on the small side. However, those tend to be the lesser used function. The main function buttons (on/off, volume, pairing, Tera Bass, etc.) are larger and easy to use.

The Roar 2 is not inexpensive, but the performance, build quality and features make it an excellent value. If you enjoy great sound and need to keep to a small footprint speaker, these should absolutely be on your short list (and at the top of it by a wide margin). Highly, highly recommend.

I have been learning more about photography and as time has permitted I have been improving my skill as an amateur photographer. I have worked with other types of filters, in particular CPL and FL-D filters, but before now I have never worked with ND filters. I have been able to achieve good results with it and so far I am pleased with this filter though I know I have more to learn about it.

A neutral-density filter is used to reduce light reaching the aperture without fiddling too much with the colors. This allows one to get creative with shutter speeds. This particular filter is adjustable and turns on the lens body face, allowing the photographer to increase or decrease the amount of filtering done. At the lowest setting the filter does very little filtering; when turned up to the maximum filtering level very little light gets through and a moire pattern appears so I do not recommend turning up the filter to this level.

To get a feel for how well this filter works I took my camera outside as a big thunderstorm approached and took some pictures of one of the cloud formations. I selected two pictures from that set, one where I did not use the filter and one where I did use it on about 1/4 strength. Although the filter evenly reduced light levels, the color contrast in the filtered image is much more pronounced and obvious.

The most common use for this kind of filter is to reduce the light levels, then take an extended exposure for a scene with motion, such as a waterfall.

This is a very nice filter and I could not be happier with it. It is very easy to use and it really works well.

These are around the same price as all the junky Chinese wireless earbud brands on Amazon but sound much better, are much more reliable, and are made by a company with good customer service that stands behind their products.

Ankers has several wireless earbuds with the cords that go behind the neck but only these, the spirit, the spirit pro, and the spirit x are worth considering for purchase. Their other earbuds are older models that cost just as much but have less features and weaker specs.

The bass on these is weak but I use these mostly for working out and for that it is fine.

I already have a pair of Apple EarPods but I wanted another wireless pair of headphones as well so I could switch back and forth while the other pair was charging.

These do not work with Apples w1 chip Bluetooth protocol, only apple and beats headphones work with that standard right now so those wireless headphones brands will sound better than anything other wireless headphones will with Apple products.

They also do not have aptx, which is the best sounding Bluetooth standard for anything other than Apple.

Ankers spirit pro headphones do support the aptx standard and supposedly have better bass than these so those are that models advantages.

However the spirit pro cost twice as much as these and only supports Bluetooth protocol 4.1 while these headphones support Bluetooth protocol 5.0.

Why is that important? Because the 5.0 protocol is the new “low energy” Bluetooth standard. Meaning that if you have both a device and headphones that support it you will get much more play time out of the same size battery.

Ankers other most recent model of earbuds, the spirit x headphones, have the same specs as these headphones in terms of the protocols they support but have a different form factor, obviously, and have 10mm drivers while these have 6mm. They also have a little more battery life.

I think I might buy the spirit x headphones as well in order to have a backup and to compare their sound.

As an Apple user the spirit pro headphones are just not worth the extra cost for me since I will never use the aptx protocol and they do not even support the Bluetooth 5.0 protocol.
If they were Bluetooth 5.0 compatible I might consider spending the extra 25 bucks in order to get that extra bass.

While these don’t sound spectacular they will get great battery life when I use them with devices that support 5.0 Bluetooth and they are very affordable.

I live in a family compound which is an old house divided up into several apartments. What makes these walkie talkies useful on a daily basis is the water situation in the compound. All the apartments are connected to the cold water line and a couple of the apartments share a hot water line. That means if you are taking a shower and anyone anywhere in the house turns on a cold water tap, not only will your shower lose water pressure but the cold water flow will abruptly decrease, leaving the hot water hotter than ever. For the apartments that share a hot water line, the same kind of thing happens. Suddenly you are taking a cold shower in a a trickle of water. These walkie talkies have solved that problem. With the group call button you can let the whole house know you are going to take a shower so no one will use any water till you call in that you are done.

Nor is that their only use. Several times a year our town will get a tornado alert. Should a tornado actually appear in our area, the whole family will head down to the storm shelter behind the basement apartment. With the walkie talkies we can make sure everyone got the emergency alert and knows that they need to be ready to move fast if the sirens go off.

One our family members has been sick the last couple of days and these units were in an easy way to check in on her throughout the day to see if there was anything she needed. By assigning each apartment its own channel and having everyone on the same group channel, it is easy to call one apartment or to reach them all, whichever is appropriate for a given message.

The units are easy to use and even our least techie family member quickly got the hang of it. The sound is clear even when calling from apartment to apartment. There is a flashlight function that is fairly bright, one that will come in handy in case of emergency. All in all, our whole family is well satisfied with this product and it deserves a 5 star rating.
