When I first set up a home network, I selected a Cisco "Linkys" G router (EA1300) because I recognized the brand name. Later I upgraded to a Cisco dual-band N router ([[ASIN:B007IL7AKM Linksys EA4500]]), which was--and still is--a superb router. My latest upgrade, to this LINKSYS AC1900 (EA6900) DUAL BAND SMART WI-FI ROUTER, represents another leap forward in the performance of my home network.

The wireless signal is stronger in every corner of my two-story condo. All of my devices (some 25 computers, tablets, music players, Kindles, cellphones, Roku, etc.) connect very quickly. Best of all, I'm getting Comcast's promised high-speed Internet speeds of more than 50 Mbps with the Comcast-supplied new telephony modem. (An online speed test site just now clocked the download speed at 57 Mbps). In fact, my present home network is capable of even faster speeds--the home network is limited by the speed of the slower external Comcast network.

This router is extremely easy to set up. You just connect it, and follow the prompts from the built-in software. Whenever you access the router to adjust the settings, and click on some part of the Menu, you find excellent "contextual" help screens that fully explain the meaning of each of the settings. The Menu is set up differently from the menus for the EA4500 and EA1300, but the basic methodology for the settings is the same--the settings are just presented in a way that's easier for a non-techie user to understand.

I read a newspaper review that recommended NOT buying this excellent EA6900 router, because of testers' problems with the second band and with nonfunctioning USB ports. I think that the testers probably received a defective router--and should have requested a replacement. Even a reliable brand like Cisco may sometimes ship an occasional bad electronics device.

Because I only need a single-band router, I haven't tested the second band on my EA6900 router. (The second band did work fine on my EA4500 router, but using the second band didn't improve the signal strength, so I didn't continue using it.) However, I did test the USB ports on the EA6900, and both work really well. In fact, the router recognized and easily accessed a couple of external wireless storage drives--connected with a 100-foot (!) USB cable--when my PC was flakey about recognizing those same drives when they were connected directly to the PC with the long cable.

I absolutely love this EA6900 router, which I've been using for more than a month now. Because of my home wiring, the router is located a long way from any of my wireless devices, and I have a lot of nearby neighbors with competing wireless Internet connections. But with the EA6900, there have been virtually no dropped connections, and the strong signal is something that I've long been wishing for!

I am director of a small publishing house. I've been using a $1,000 MacBook Pro 11.6 (Lion) laptop for over a year, with the Chrome browser, Gmail, and GoogleDrive as my online backup for laptop-based files of importance. I got accustomed to the trackpad (I switched the scrolling direction) and haven't used a mouse since I got my Mac. I do book production and cover design on it, sitting in the living room recliner (too far from an electrical outlet to use the adapter) but the battery runs down pretty quickly.

I wanted this Chromebook as a second machine for starting and ending my day: browsing and doing the cloud-based work I have to do, like accounting in Wave, managing social network-based marketing, ordering books, searching for cover art, reading manuscripts in Submittable, handling email, etc. My Mac with Adobe CS5 is essential for the actual book design and production, so I basically reserve its battery now for that.

What is amazing to me is how similar this Chromebook keyboard is to my MacBook Pro. The only time I realize I'm not on my Mac is when I hit what, on the Mac, is the caps lock key but on the Chromebook pops up apps. (There is no caps lock key on the Chromebook; supposedly you can press both shift keys at the same time to effect caps lock, but I guess I don't have the right touch because I can't get it to work.) Another slight difference is in how click and drag works; on the Chromebook, you hit the trackpad with your thumb, then drag.

Those who have already gotten accustomed to using Google-related commands for email, clearing the cache, and the like will be good to go without any learning curve. Chrome extensions and apps, of course, work as expected. (I am SO glad I had the prescience to realize a year ago that I definitely wanted to shift to a cloud-based approach!)

Now, a word about the quality of the monitor. I find the type on the screen to be MORE readable than on my Mac. It is much crisper and high-definition. The colors don't match between the two computers, but I'm not sure it's the Chromebook's fault. The Chromebook does seem to be able to sense how to adjust brightness based on the conditions of the room, which is helpful. Sometimes, however, my eyes start smarting, something that happens when I'm working on the Chromebook, but not on the MacBook Pro. I don't know what accounts for this. The sound is better on the Chromebook than on my Mac, especially if I use good headphones. When watching a movie, the color is a bit washed out compared to the really garishly brightly colored sets, but I prefer that.

I'm probably more of a power user when it comes to the user end of a computer, but I don't try to get in and hack things like some people do. Developer mode, need for static IP address, etc., I'm clueless about. But this is a well-built, fast, mostly no-fuss, low-cost and very light-weight piece of work with a long-lasting battery, which is exactly what I wanted. That I also got a seamless experience shifting from one machine to the other for a quarter of what my MacBook Pro cost? That's priceless!

PROS

2. It has a +90/-90 degree tilt, which I am very happy about. I had a hard time finding a monitor with this very desirable attribute.
3. It is attractive looking.
4. It has VESA compatibility.
5. It has a tall, 39-inch pole, which allows great flexibility in placement of the monitor.
6. It has an articulating arm, which adds additional flexibility in placement of the monitor.

9. It is simple to assemble.
10. The price is reasonable.

CONS

I bought a Garmin 60CSx GPS receiver as a replacement for a Garmin eTrex Legend for the purpose of geocaching. My eTrex Legend has served me well (and continues to do so) but I wanted a GPSr with more functionality, better operation under heavy cover and expanded map coverage for hiking and road navigation. Researching GPSrs led me to this unit, and I have been very pleased with it. There are a couple of minor negatives that I have found, but these can probably be overlooked.

I am very pleased with the appearance of the screen when the unit is powered on. The display is bright and colorful, and easy to read in the light. This is true of the daytime display. The night display is not as pleasant, with a hard-to-see color scheme. Backlighting the night scheme makes it a lot easier to read but it is still less than ideal.

The unit's software is very intuitive, a menu- and icon-driven interface giving access to all of the features. I have found little need for the user manual since I fist started working with this device, as everything is clear and easy to find. Buttons on the unit make it easy to find the menus and to navigate without too much hassle.

The base map is nothing special but it is adequate for basic navigation. We have used it to follow our path down the interstate. It shows the major roads and also any waypoints that are close by.

The best feature of this unit, in my opinion, is its ability to navigate under heavy canopy. With my eTrex Legend there were times when my unit would simply not be able to get a lock. The 60CSx has yet to lose signal, even inside my living room. The accuracy does drop when there is sufficient cover but the important thing is that it doesn't drop completely.

One thing troubles me a bit about the 60CSx. The accuracy rarely gets any better than 10-12 feet, whereas my eTrex Legend - a unit costing a third as much - routinely can get down to 6 feet. I do not understand why this is the case. I would choose ability to hold a signal over pinpoint accuracy every time, but why can't I have both?

The 60CSx has a Micro-SD card inside and the unit will take a card up to 2GB inside. That's enough room for a whole US street map. This is a nice thing to have available, as it means not having to decide what section of map to load. Load the whole map and be on your way.

The waypoint management functions are acceptable for my needs, which up to this point has meant managing geocaching waypoints. I like being able to mark a point as "found" and then being asked if I want to go to the next closest point. I have noticed, though, that if I am navigating to a point and leave the navigation menus, the point is marked as found anyway. It would be nice to have the ability to specify "not found" without having to go through the menus to locate the point again, just to change the status.

The Garmin 60CSx is a very nice handheld GPS that will serve you well. It is not perfect, but for general use it is plenty close enough.

I first heard about Cobo Vault on twitter from a few of the various people I follow on there. The thought of a new hardware wallet that was open source (something I really like about Trezor) but also air gapped (no Internet connectivity or USB, bluetooth, etc.) was also super appealing to my ultra paranoid side. I figure as Bitcoin and perhaps other cryptos go up in value, security will become even more paramount so the ultra-paranoia is justified.

Anyway, I started with the Essentials version of the product and I was first impressed with the way the product was packaged nicely; nothing loose in the box, everything protected well. Upon removing it from the packaging, the build quality of the device itself was impressive, setup was straightforward as well.

I really like the fact that the Cobo Vault hardware has a sync to the mobile app. Setting this up is part of the initial setup wizard. Doing this allows you to view the balance in BTC, ETH, etc. or fiat equivalent on the mobile app without actually having the hardware wallet. You can also receive via the mobile app through a QR code. It's likely better to use the QR code off the hardware wallet display itself if you're ultra paranoid but, again, it's an option to use the mobile app only. Keep in mind, you can't view the fiat balance on the hardware wallet since it's air gapped.

For sending, you initiate it through the mobile app but you will need the hardware wallet to complete the actual transaction. This is accomplished through a back and forth process of scanning of QR codes between the hardware wallet and your smartphone.

Because I liked the Essential one so much, I bought another Cobo Vault but this time the Pro version. The reason I bought the Pro version is because it has a fingerprint scanner and I found it to be easier to unlock and perform other operations using that method. Without that feature, you have to either type alphanumeric passwords on the tiny keyboard on the touch screen display or draw a pattern on a display (similar to smart phones). Both seem to be difficult for me as it is a little difficult to type the password correctly on the small touch screen display or draw the pattern correctly without going slowly; especially if you have bigger fingers.

To address this, perhaps having an random ordered numeric dial pad for a password might also be a good alternative.

Battery life: Another reason why the Pro version is superior to the Essentials version is that it includes a rechargeable battery as well as the AAA option. The AAA option seems to have inconsistent battery life and seems to drain really fast for me. I brought this up to the Cobo team and they were really responsive to me and explained why the AAA battery life was hard to calculate and inconsistent at times. Still, it'd be nice if there was some way to bring consistency to AAA battery percentage displayed. That being said, the rechargeable battery is the way to go for consistent use but the AAA battery option is great for long term assurance of the device should it outlive the rechargeable battery.
Suggestion would be to allow the device to be powered and/or charged while in use. Right now the rechargeable battery requires the battery to be detached from the device itself in order to be charged.

firmware updates: I'm really impressed with the frequency of the firmware updates as well as the new features being introduced. A+ on that. Performing the updates has been a mixed bag for me. I've found that for some updates, using the rechargeable battery (charging it to full) and then performing the update works best. Other times, most noticeably the update to 1.40 multicoin, I had to use the AAA battery pack with fresh batteries to update both my Pro and Essential; a fully charged rechargeable pack did not work. I'm confident they will work through this as the product continues to mature.

Which brings me to my last point, the thing that impresses me the most about this product is the response from the Cobo team. They are open to feedback and suggestions and both acknowledge it, respond with great detailed answers and work hastily to incorporate new features. I'm really impressed with the support.

I use a mix of different hardware wallets to store my crypto offline and Cobo Vault is probably my favorite to use right now. I'm super excited to see and be a part of this product line as it matures.

NOTE: I am writing this review for the 1TB platter-based Passport drive.

I have a 250GB Passport I bought several years ago and it has served me well, though it has gotten close to full over time (I never imagined at the time that I would fill that thing up). I have had good fortune with it so I expected the same from this 1TB version, and so far I have been right. In addition to the larger capacity, it is very definitely a speed upgrade from my old Passport.

This is a small drive in terms of physical footprint, approximately 4”x3”x0.5” in dimension. That’s a double-edged sword. On one hand, it is small enough to stuff in a shirt pocket which makes it an excellent on-the-go storage solution that’s almost as convenient as a thumb drive. But, that also means it is easy to misplace or lose (or have stolen if left unattended).

It comes with software that allows you to password-protect the drive which is a nice deterrent in the event that the drive is taken. It’s certainly not foolproof, but it’s sufficient to keep the large majority of unauthorized access out. To be honest, since the drive does not leave my home I have not used the software at all.

When you plug in the drive to a Windows or Linux system, the OS immediately recognizes the drive and it is available immediately for use. In the case of Windows, you can immediately explore the drive and read from it and write to it. For Linux, it depends on how you have configured automount and which desktop management software you use, but the kernel does register the presence of the drive and you can display the partition table.

This is a USB 3.0 drive, making it a huge speed upgrade from my older 2.0-based Passport. This is a great solution for storing all of your pictures, movies, important documents, and as in my case large downloads and purchased software packages. With 1TB of space, I don’t think I am going to run out of space anytime soon.

As a bonus, this is a very quiet drive.

I put this drive on a USB power meter to see how much it draws from the USB port. At rest it pulls 0.17A. When actively reading, it peaks just under 0.6A which is surprisingly low. My concern was that this would add some strain on the USB port over a longer period of time but this seems to be an unjustified concern. That said, I am more likely to connect it to a USB hub instead of directly to a USB port.

So far I have no complaints with this drive. It’s a big step up for me from my older Passport, being larger, faster and more quiet. It’s not cost prohibitive either which is just a bonus. If you need a decent backup drive with large capacity and a small footprint, this one is worth consideration.

I've been using desktop PCs since the 1980s. In the old days we always bought the biggest PC cases so we could add more components like multiple disc drives, CD drives, extra I/O and networking ports, a bigger power supply, etc. These days, computers come packed with features and interfaces, internal storage is smaller and cheaper, USB3 is fast enough for external peripherals if we need them, and more and more computing is done in the cloud instead of on the desktop.

This little 5 inch x 5 inch x 2 inch box is all I really need for my desktop computing needs. The Intel i5 CPU is the same as what most mid-range laptops use. The built-in SSD and 16gb of RAM are faster than the hard drive and 8gb in our old PC that we replaced with this one. There is space to add a 2.5" SSD to increase the local storage space (I'm planning to add a 2TB SSD). The computer has plenty of ports; even a microSD flash card slot. The PC comes with Windows 11 pre-installed and it launched flawlessly when I turned the PC on.

There are 2 limitations for me. First is that there is only one memory card slot which currently contains a 16GB memory card. This is enough for most people (especially considering the mid-range i5 CPU) but if you want to add more memory, you must discard the 16GB card and replace it with a bigger card. Most PCs have 2 memory card slots so you can simply add a second memory card that adds to the first one. The second limitation is that the built-in graphics processor is not suitable for high-end gaming and there is no room to add a high-performance graphics card. If you are a hard core gamer, you should probably look elsewhere.

Considering the size and price of this mini-PC, I think it is fine as an everyday desktop computer for home or for the office. Students will probably want a laptop that they can carry to school, but a lot of adults prefer having a full-sized keyboard and screen and this mini-PC is cheaper than a comparable laptop if you have to buy a separate monitor in either case. If I want more power than my phone when I'm traveling, I bring a tablet instead of a more bulky and more fragile laptop.

My only real complaint about this mini-PC is that the fan is not super quiet and it runs a lot when I am multi-tasking with more than one program running.

This weird little tripod is a useful addition to the gear of any amateur or hobby photographer with a DSLR and the inspiration to take breath-taking and/or unusual photographs. (I'm using it with a Nikon D7000)

Pros:

1. Light and portable. If you don't have a side pocket on your camera bag, just wrap it around a strap or loop.
2. Flexible. As advertised, the legs can be bent into loops and angles for getting shots from weird angles. It can also be wrapped around posts, tree branches, bench rails etc.
3. Convenient. An easy way to get shots requiring a stable camera almost level with ledges or sideways attached to a tree. However, you can only shoot in landscape format unless you get the accessory BH1 ball head. Naturally, with its little legs, you'll be pretty close to the ground if there's nothing available for wrapping around, but you'll be sure to get great camera angles from a worm's eye view.

Cons:

1. Attaching your camera to the tripod is a bit of a pain, requiring a coin (any currency) or a strong fingernail. A better bet is to get the accessory Joby BH1 Ball Head with Bubble Level and attach the quick release clip to your camera beforehand.
2. You need to practice with it a bit to get the stability right, and if you have the legs in an unbalanced position, or on a smooth surface, you can get sagging and camera movement.
3. Trying to get the camera level without the ball head can be quite challenging, and you may well miss the shot. (Of course you can always do the straightening with software, but it's better to get it right the first time.)
4. Can't shoot in portrait format unless you get the ball head.
5. Hard to get the legs back straight with all the segments in line.

Note: It comes with a 1/4-to-3/8-inch adapter attached to the mounting screw, so you have to remove this to attach the camera or accessory ball head.

Recommended (with the [[ASIN:B002CVU4G0 Joby BH1 Ball Head with Bubble Level for Joby GP3 SLR-Zoom Gorillapods]]) for photo walks, theme parks or general walk-abouts where that prize-winning shot may be just a Gorillapod away.

I received this mat as a review sample and own a number of brands to which I compared it. First, there are only nominal differences between and among most of the silicone baking mats on the market, so the main factors are price and construction. For former is highly variable, but if you comparison shop what you are looking for are size and overall construction.

These are about 3/10ths of an inch thick so are well constructed in my opinion. They are designed to fit an 18 x 13 baking sheet, and have a slight textured surface that makes them ideal for not only baking, but for rolling out dough.

Another factor is this one will withstand heat up to 450F, whereas some brands will only go as high as 425F (and others will go higher at 480F). Consider those factors too when selecting a baking mat. If you have never used one of these from any brand they are infinitely better than parchment paper, and you do not have to use any kind of grease or shortening because they are naturally non-stick. Do note that you cannot use them in direct contact with flame or heat source. I mention that because I gave a similar mat to a friend who tried using it on a stove eye. Don't!

If you opt to use these without a baking sheet know that your times will need to be slightly adjusted. That is because the heat transfer is a little too efficient, but also these will cool a lot quicker as well, so when you first use them keep a close eye on baking times by visually checking on what you are baking a little earlier than usual and making sure that this mat is not causing the process to over bake.

Cleaning is a snap and these can actually be cleaned in a dishwasher. More importantly, they are perfect for rolling out dough (I sometimes use a pair of silicone mats - regardless of brand - with one on top and one on the bottom of the dough. When I roll out the dough by rolling over the top mat I can get a more ever, thinner dough.

Bottom line: this mat is well made, has a fairly wide operating range and a slightly textured surface for true non-stick.

You should know up front that this extender only works wirelessly with dual-band WiFi routers (routers with both 2.4GHz and 5GHz).

But it will work as a hard-wired range extender for single-band routers (2.4GHz) using an ethernet cable.

If you have a single band router like we do, it will not detect the wireless network or connect wirelessly. If our neighborhood is any indication, this extender won't work with most home routers. Out of the ten or so visible wireless networks in our area, the extender only detected one or two. The two it detected were two of the weaker signals, but I assume were dual band signals the extender would work with.

After several frustrating attempts to get it connected wirelessly, I spent about an hour with customer support before being informed of this limitation on the extender. The product listing says "compatible with all Wi-Fi routers," and it may be compatible with all routers if set up as a wired extender, but apparently it isn't compatible with all as a wirelessly connected extender. If you want wireless connection to your router, check your router's capability and make sure it is a dual-band router before ordering.

As I mentioned, I did get it set up as a wire-connected extender using an ethernet cable. And it works well for that. It puts a good strong WiFi signal all over our house and much of the yard. I'm giving it four stars for that.

I had the device charged up 100% last night and it still seemed to be charged 100% this morning, but in trying to use it today, it has already dropped to 90% and that's probably from only a few minutes of use.  If I ever get this working, I'll update the review.  At the moment I really don't feel that this is ready for prime time. Controls are easy and intuitive. A clickable button instead of gesture control, so you can tell what you're doing, and don't trigger it every time you brush the hair away from your ear. They're my favorite way to talk on a cellphone too. Nice to have both hands free.

I've used several compact speakers over the years and they all were decent performers. Nothing to compare, however, with my favorite desktop speakers, the Bose Companion 20. While this speaker doesn't hit that mark either, it is absolutely, hands-down the best compact mono speaker I've used.

It's tiny. And I mean TINY - just a bit over 2 inches in height, width and depth. As per the name, it's a cube. About as unobtrusive as you can get.

The build quality is excellent. It feels solid and well-made. It also comes very attractively packaged in a clear, thick plastic box. While I would normally scold a company for what could appear to be wasteful packaging, in this case the packaging is useful: one of my primary uses for this speaker is as a take-along for my laptop, and the plastic case makes for excellent protection against the bangs and dings suffered by my laptop bag. So, in addition to making it look upscale, the packaging has an actual use down the road.

Setup is simple - plug and go. It has three outputs - 3.5mm cord for something such as a tablet, a USB port for a computer, and a 3.5mm cord for headphones. Covers all the bases as to potential uses.

I did most of my testing and playing with this attached to my laptop. Outstanding sound quality that is crisp, clear but still has decent bass. I used it mainly for listening to podcasts and webinars (some of them actually work related!) and the sound quality was miles beyond what I was getting from my laptop speaker, and significantly better than the lower-end portable speakers I was using.

Now, the Cube doesn't sound as good as the Bose Companion 20. That didn't come as a surprise since the entire speaker is about the same size as just the power converter for the Bose. The size of the Bose make them non-transportable; the Cube is a very easy device to take along with a laptop.

It does not have a volume control. I don't miss it when using it with my PC since it's easier to fiddle with the sound level from the PC rather than have to use the speaker. I can see that as a negative, however, for other uses. On the other hand, a volume control device, be it a knob, wheel or button, would detract from the clean, simple design lines of the Cube. So, an equitable trade-off in my opinion.

This is one of those products that I really can't come up with a single negative other than the fact that it is pricy. But, if you value good quality sound but have to keep the speaker as small as possible, it is worth the cost. This is about the same size as the small take-along speakers that run in the $20 range, but provides sound quality that is miles beyond what they offer. Highly recommend.

******* Original review before the drama*******

We've had an older Bose Solo 15 Series II TV Sound System in our living room for a couple of years and we've been pretty happy overall. I recently put the Bose 500 version of this sound bar in our master bedroom and was amazed at the difference, so getting this 700 for the living room was a no brainer. I mostly just expected them to connect as a group and have the same sound, but this 700 is better than the 500.

It's a long, narrow, sleek looking unit with glass finishes that makes it almost invisible in front of the Tv. Our Roku fits alongside without drama. The connections are via digital optical cable or the HDMI. Just turn off your TV speakers - not mute, off from the tv settings. You need to use the included wired headset to fully set the speakers for your room's accoustics. I'm using this bar with a 55", 3 years old, Sceptre dumb tv and a Room streaming stick - the connection was immediate and drama free.

You must use the Bose app to get full functionality out of the sound bar. The app let's you connect two or more Bose speakers with the tech and use them all simultaneously as a group to play music or audiobooks etc. The app also starts the set up for the Alexa link and the streaming services like Prime, Tune In, Bluetooth streaming and others. You can also set 6 favorites as one touch launch options.

Alexa works fine through the sound bar, but the response speed is noticably slower than through a regular Echo. I get a glitchy message saying "This unit is unable to perform routines" every time I say "Good morning". Good morning triggers a specific set of actions from Alexa to turn on our bedside lamps, the bathroom lights, turn off our porch lights, give me the weather and then our daily news brief. Despite that glitchy message, every morning, the Bose performs our routine flawlessly. It's weird, but not a big deal really.

The sound quality is excellent and immersive in multiple settings from music to a movie. The app let's you adjust the sound quality and balance with bass, treble and center. You can also set it for dialogue mode to enhance/clarify voices and reduce background noise - this is very handy for the news or a talk show. Take some time to adjust the settings for what your ear really likes and you'll be amazed at the fullness of sound and all the background details.

After two weeks, I'm incredibly pleased with the build quality, looks, sound and full functionality of both the 500 and 700 units. The 700 wins out by a nose over the 500 for us because the sound is bigger, but mostly because the remote control is better. The remote lights up when you lift it and you can find the buttons instantly. I programmed our TV to the Bose remote and it controls the sound bar, channels up and down and power for both the tv and the sound bar. Bottom line is that I am now looking at buying another 700 for the master bedroom and moving the 500 to our guest suite so we'll have the full set.

It's not black
